text:
Obsession is a menacing example of selling one's soul for our deepest desires.

Much of the film utilizes gruesome body horror sparingly, but when Barker wants to drive the nail home hard, he pulls it off wondrously. There's several particularly brutal scenes that shock with how quickly they arrive in the film. It's as harsh as can be, as Barker pulls no punches for any of his characters. Best of all, he caps Obsession off with an absolutely devious finale.

summary: We need to talk about Inde.
text:
Kudos to all the new talent involved. Curry Baker is bound to have a lot more great films in his future. I am told his shorts on Youtube are great and I plan to watch them this week. But this film hinges on the performance or Inde Navarette. I had never heard her name before tonight, but her performance is award worthy. If Amy Madigan can get the well deserved awards she got for Weapons, Inde Navareete's name should be popping up a lot during awards season. I doubt that will happen, but her role was insanely diffcult to pull off. If she had messed up in the very least the film would have been mediocre.

I don't want to give too much away. I will say the weakest link was Michael Johnson as her love interest Bear. It is more the writing than the acting, but I really did not believe him throughout. Early on he describes himself as a "closed book" and is he ever. The entire movie you'll be thinking to yourself , why doesn't he do this , or that...... But I guess if he reacted more logically we would not have had such a great film to enjoy. It is bloody and gross, but just so well done overall. One last thing. I don't think I have ever reacted to a jump scare scene as much as I did with one of such scenes in this film. Catch it in a full theater. It will be much better than at home.

Horror isn't a genre where acting is going to get celebrated or noticed with awards etc, but Inde who played the lead here Nikki and oh my lord it's an acting masterclass. With the subject matter this film could've been tragic and a bit of a flop but the way she portrayed poor Nikki under the spell of a wish was outstanding!

Humour 10
Acting 10
Gore 10
Everything else... 10.

This is the horror movie audiences have been asking for for years. Unrelenting, brutal, so original, so genuinely unsettling and creepy that at times you start laughing because your body doesn't even know how to regulate. Inde Navarrette is a revelation. Michael Johnston is incredible too. The strength of the acting elevates the premise so much. At no point did I know what was going to happen next, and with each escalation I was terrified to find out. My already high expectations were surpassed by 10 miles. Just brilliant stuff.

summary: I wish for more horror films like this
text:
Obsession has a pretty simple premise, but it's executed really well. The movie knows what kind of creepy, slightly ridiculous horror story it is, and it leans into that instead of trying to hide it.

The best part is easily the lead actress. A lot of the scares come from her performance alone. You feel bad for her, but you also know something is off, and she creates so much creepiness just through her acting.

I also liked that the movie doesn't shy away from how silly or outrageous some of the events get. It's aware of its own vibe and commits to it, which makes it more fun and unsettling.

The weakest part is that the side characters aren't super developed. They mostly feel like plot points, and giving them more personality could've helped flesh out the main character too. But the movie mostly focuses on the central relationship, and that's where the horror really unravels.

Overall, it's a solid horror movie with a simple idea, strong acting, and a creepy vibe that works.

summary: Best horror I've seen in a long time
text: This movie had so much range, you'd be scared shitless and then laugh the next second. Also I had my biggest jump scare ever which I never really fall for, but I literally flew back in my seat and rocked the whole chair lmao. Major respect to the girl playing Nikki she was phenomenal, and props to the crew and actors for making such a quality movie with a low budget. This really is the best movie I've seen in the past 3 years and I'm usually reluctant to ever say something like that but I'm so impressed, this is a must see!

Simple but interesting premise. What if you could get your secret crush to love you back? The girl who played Nikki (Inde Navarrette) really gets to sink her teeth into it. The movie depends on her being good in her role and she is.

I know it's a horror movie requiring substantial suspension of belief, but a lot of the guy's behavior stretched the bounds of plausibility for me. It's one thing to stick around when she's just acting a little weird, but some of the things she starts doing while he just overlooks it makes you go, no, no one in their right mind would hang around with her at that point, even if she was his longtime crush.

Still it worked a lot better than the vast majority of horror movies out there, including more comic moments than you typically see, and it managed to create the overall effect of uneasiness for more less the whole movie. So it has to be considered a success (and a good time for fans of the genre).

First of all, I honestly thought Obsession was going to be overhyped. In this day and age, almost everything is heavily marketed toward audiences just to make money, so I went into it with some doubts.

But since I'm a big lover of psychological thrillers, this one fell right into my lap.

I personally wouldn't really put this movie completely into the horror genre, even though it does lean toward it at times. For me, it feels much more like a psychological drama/thriller.

The movie carries so much anxiety, tension, and stress throughout, but I actually enjoyed that. It gave me a different kind of feeling - something fresh - with a pace and atmosphere that a lot of movies fail to capture.

The directing, lighting, acting, production quality, and sound design were all beautifully done. You can really feel the effort that went into creating the mood of this film.

There isn't much more to say other than: watch it. Either you're going to connect with it or you won't. It really depends on what kind of viewer you are and what you look for in a movie.

I'm just grateful that once in a while a psychological thriller gets good ratings and is actually understood and appreciated by many.

At first, the film sets up Baron "Bear" Bailey with all the classic tropes of a sympathetic loser. He is grieving his dead cat, he is hopelessly awkward, and he harbors a massive crush on his coworker, Nikki. But the script subtly lays the groundwork for his cowardice right away. When Nikki directly gives him the floor and asks if he likes her, Bear freezes. He is too terrified of rejection to risk his pride, so instead of taking an honest emotional leap like an adult, he resorts to a magical shortcut. He breaks the One Wish Willow because he wants the end result without any of the vulnerability. As Nikki's mind gets systematically hollowed out and replaced by an erratic, violent obsession, Bear's entitlement takes center stage. A decent person would be horrified by her immediate loss of agency. Bear, however, goes along with it. He sleeps with a woman whose consent has been erased by magic, exposing his fundamental flaw: he never cared about who Nikki actually was as a person, he only cared about what her devotion could do for his self-esteem. The phone call with customer service isn't just a world-building beat; it's a character reveal. Bear doesn't call support out of guilt for violating Nikki's soul. He calls because her obsession has gotten inconvenient and scary for him. When he tries to haggle with the representative to alter the spell rather than cancel it outright, the film makes its thesis clear: Bear doesn't want to free Nikki; he just wants a milder, tailored version of mind control that lets him play the romantic lead without getting his hands dirty.

This film started off great, and was rolling hot until the last act of the film. Inde Navarrette is an incredible actress, her performance is a definite highlight, as well as the uncomfortable tension.

But the longer the film goes on, it seems to be spinning in a circle, like a dog chasing its tail with an occasional non-sensical jumpscare or some gore. The main character, Baron, nails the part of being a main character in a horror movie who is the dumbest person you've ever seen.

With no payoff, this film leaves nothing but a bland, bad taste in your mouth like you need to take a shower afterwards to get rid of the stain of gross, disturbing horror that ends up going nowhere, and is just there for cheap thrill and insanely loud sound effects.

It's so nice when a movie has this many ideas. Dark as hell. Bear is in love with his friend Nicki, but he's so incapable of confessing his feelings that he ends up turning to a willow branch that works like a kind of "monkey's paw": it grants a wish, but there are consequences. Bear only wants Nicki to love him "more than anything in the world." And, of course, the movie takes that literally.

Bear isn't an innocent victim of the curse. At first, he seems like nothing more than a shy, lovesick loser, but little by little it becomes clear that he is the real source of everything that goes wrong. His emotional cowardice, his need for approval, and his inability to accept rejection lead him to try to control someone else's feelings. He doesn't really love Nicki. He loves the idealized version of her that exists in his head.

Bear ignores every red flag just to keep his fantasy alive. Even when Nicki starts behaving in deeply disturbing ways, he'd rather enjoy this artificial love than question what's happening. The creature inhabiting Nicki's body isn't necessarily evil either. It's basically an automaton following its only directive literally: to love Bear more than anything in the world. That makes some of the scenes even more uncomfortable. The real Nicki is trapped inside her own body, fully aware of everything happening but unable to stop it. When she manages to regain control for a few seconds and begs Bear to kill her so she can be free, he still only thinks about himself, asking what's so wrong with being with him.

The filmmaking is really impressive considering the low budget. The abrupt cuts, the use of music, the makeup, and especially the lighting, which often leaves Nicki's face in shadow against brightly lit backgrounds, create a deeply oppressive and uncomfortable atmosphere. But a huge part of the movie works thanks to Indi Navarrete. She has to make some massive tonal shifts, going from genuinely funny moments to scenes that feel like they belong in a possession movie. She's great at playing someone who still looks like Nicki but, little by little, clearly stops being her.

At its core, the movie works as a twisted allegory for teenage love taken to its darkest extreme: when loving someone stops meaning caring about them and starts meaning possessing them. Bear thinks his problem is that he isn't loved back, when the real problem is that he can't accept that another person has the right not to love him.

A very pleasant surprise.

This is easily one of my favourite movies of my festival run of 2025. A simple premise that could have easily been generic and played out.

Quite the opposite, a gripping thrill ride that kept me on the edge of my seat the entire time. A really well crafted movie that will absolutely be gaining a lot of praise from horror and movie fans alike.

The directing here by Curry Barker makes you feel the tension throughout and immediately makes me excited for what he brings us next.

summary: The Only Obsession Was the Hype
text:
I watched Obsessions because social media had me expecting the next great indie horror. What I got instead was almost two hours of whispering interrupted by random ear-destroying screaming. Apparently, the real horror was what it did to my volume controls. Absolutely criminal sound design.

Calling this a horror movie is also borderline false advertising. It's more like a twisted, toxic rom-com sprinkled with some blood and a collective refusal by the characters to book a therapist. Strip away the occasional violent scene, the "One Wish Willow", and you're left with a Gen Z relationship drama that desperately wants to be disturbing and profound.

The bigger issue, though, is how slow and predictable the plot is. About halfway through I wasn't wondering what was going to happen - I was wondering how much longer the movie was going to pretend it was building toward something shocking. Spoiler: it wasn't. A slow burn only works when the payoff justifies the wait. Here, it never does.

And the main male character? One of the most unrealistic, badly written, and unbelievably annoying protagonists I've seen in a long time.

The only character who seemed to have any common sense was Ian, who somehow managed to make the one reasonable wish in this entire movie.

I genuinely don't understand the online hype. Did we all watch the same movie?

If social media hadn't convinced half the internet this was a masterpiece, I doubt anyone would still be talking about it a week after release.

Obsession was a strong festival opener for me. The hype was already there beforehand and this time it was justified. "Be careful who you wish for" gets to the heart of the film, because this is not just about a wish, but about the ugly side of it. What happens when something you desperately want suddenly becomes real and turns wrong because of that.

That is exactly what worked so well for me. The film does not build horror in the usual way, where everything depends on jump scares or loud moments. It does something more uncomfortable. It creates this inner unease because you can feel the whole time that something is slipping. Not right away. Not with brute force. More in a way where everything just keeps feeling more wrong. "I wish Nikki loved me more than anyone in the world" is not just a line there. It is already the whole mistake.

Inde Navarrette was the strongest part for me. The way she plays Nikki is really good. That look, that stillness, that way something inside her suddenly no longer feels right. It does not need to be loud. That is exactly why it becomes unsettling. "I'll be anything you want me to be" sounds almost harmless at first. In this film, it is the opposite.

What I liked about Obsession is that the horror does not simply come from the outside. It grows out of something many people would first read as romantic. Closeness. Desire. Longing. Possession. That is where the film turns nasty. That obsessive need, that refusal to let go, that feeling of wanting someone exactly the way you imagine them. That makes it more unsettling than a lot of horror films that work in a much more direct way.

There are also good shock moments and enough scenes that stay with you. Please, no more weird s... almost fits perfectly because the film keeps pushing that line further and further.

For me, this was a strong film and above all one that did not feel like standard horror. It felt more like a wish turning more poisonous with every minute.

summary: Inde Navarrette Absolutely KILLED Her Role, I Can't Wait To See More to see more From Her
text:
I just got out of Obsession.

I hadn't even seen a trailer. So I went into this totally cold.

Some of it is generic horror formula 101, but it went a different way than I thought it would and it's a new take and when things go down, it seriously goes down.

The cast is great. Inde Navarrette is amazing, she is seriously unsettling, she is a real talent. Michael Johnston is good as the protagonist, who should have been careful about what he wished for.

It has something's for you to think on, too. I did think it was going in a certain direction, but it didn't, which was a bit disappointing, I wanted it to expand on an idea, but it was just left. That said what writer/director Curry Baker does is amazing, no silly jump scares. Just genuine tension and horror.

Overall, I really enjoyed it. My favourite horror movie of the year, so far.

I watched Obsession expecting something far more compelling considering the amount of attention and hype around it. It was not terrible and it had moments that kept me interested, but overall I felt it fell short of the expectations built around it.

Overall, I think it was an okay watch and I do not regret seeing it, but personally I do not think it justified the level of hype surrounding it. Decent enough, just not particularly memorable.

summary: A covert narcissist's version of love
text:
Now it is rare these days for a horror movie to be actually good without falling into yet another wasteland of cliches. I'd just opt out the sound effects and the brutality because I think those elements are cheap. Like, why do you need a sound effect when the guy simply walks into the store? If you can deliver great horror without those two things, then 10x kudos to you. Still, this movie was pretty good and it offers so much to unpack.

For me, the movie points at a rhetorical question about love. Some may think the title Obsession is about Nikki's obsession, but it is actually Bear's obsession over Nikki. He loves the idea of Nikki and is obsessed over it to the extend of taking away her free-will.

Do we love people, or do we love OUR idea of them? So there you have Bear. He is a coward who is scared shitless about the idea of being rejected and refuses to take the healthy way of pursuing Nikki.

Abstract concepts like love is tied to our own nature. In his world, Bear loves Nikki because of how she makes HIM feel (remember what he said when rehearsing at the start of the movie). He is a self-centered loser who shows strong symptoms of covert narcissism. She gives him the chance to open up but Bear fails at it and instead of having a conversation with her like an adult, he reaches for a quick fix. He wishes so badly this easier path would work, although he doesn't actually think it will, and ofc there's no way he would've known the outcome.

When he wishes Nikki would love him more than anyone, it takes Bear's idea and version of love. That is, obsession.

The wish does't transform Nikki's feelings for Bear or something. It just creates an instance of Nikki, some kind of entity alongside her that surpasses the real Nikki.

The dinner date scene is a tonal shift. Just after getting off the phone with Ian and realizing that the wish worked, he digs her lie about her dad. And then he pushes her about the authenticity of her feelings. "Don't do that," she says, because what's the point of these questions when they both know that he has created this situation, and none of it is real.

And then there is the moment when he talks to the real Nikki in the bedroom, when she begs him to kill her. The first thing he says then is, "what's so bad about being with me?" . Any healthy person would be devastated if someone they loved were suffering in agony like that, right? But nope. He gets pissed because her suffering means the real Nikki doesn't want to be with him, and she in fact said she's never been with him.

In that brutal scene after killing Sarah, Nikki makes Bear face the truth again: "you wanted this, you wished for this and this is all your fault". This is when the wish forces the antagonist, Bear, to face what his idea of love looks like when it is taken to its logical extreme.

Obsession has made it onto the list of horror movie classics, and fairly so.

Obsession is a pretty forgettable and, in my opinion, overrated movie. This is definitely not an 8/10. Honestly, it feels more like an episode of some random TV series than a full-length film.

Yeah, it's low-budget, but not terrible. The low budget really shows in the lack of spectacle, and the movie drags a bit at times.

One thing I have to give credit for is Inde Navarrette as Nikki. She easily gives the best performance in the movie. Everyone else is pretty average.

I also have to mention the dead cat prop. Seriously, in 2026 this was the best they could come up with? It looks like it's made out of paper. It's so fake that it completely takes you out of the movie every time it's on screen.

Overall, it's a decent low-budget horror movie. It's not scary at all, and personally, it didn't connect with me. You'd think it would, since I'm going through some similar relationship-related stuff in my own life, but it just didn't. In the end, it feels like a random episode of a random TV show.

6/10. Overrated.

Obsession is an excellently executed horror movie, using the "One-Wish Willow" as an allegory of stripping a person of their autonomy. The film uses complex storytelling and Bear's realisation of the reality of what his wish has done to convey this theme. In the film Bear realises that real Nikki is trapped within her wish-altered self he has been seeing. Although Bear realises the real Nikki is suffering, he shows little to no empathy for her. Knowing the horrifying truth of Nikki's entrapment, Bear selfishly continues to strip Nikki of her free will. Bear's cruel choice highlights the horror and proves the Willow represents losing all personal freedom.

It's a solid horror movie. The actors are good and there's a lot of tension. But is this one of the best horror movies ever made? Which if you look at the current ratings, it's certainly the conclusion you'd come up with. And the answer is no. The story is weak, and some of the ideas are kinda reused, like the director didn't know what more to add, thus it would've worked better if it was 20 minutes shorter. The main character is super stressed in one scene, only to act like anything out of the ordinary ever happened in the very next. The ending is also nothing special, so I'm not sure why some people want to point it out, like it's actually outstanding.

summary: Big numbers on socials, zero substance in theaters
text:
The film itself would deserve a fair 6, but I am lowering my rating to 4 to counter an obvious marketing maneuver driven by the fanbase for a movie that absolutely does not deserve this level of hype. The current inflated average on IMDb is an artificial bubble fueled by the millions of followers that director Curry Barker and co-star Cooper Tomlinson mobilized from their YouTube channel *"that's a bad idea"*; blind support that clashes violently with the reality of a structurally weak indie horror.

After an effective first twenty minutes, the plot stalls and does nothing but reiterate the exact same pattern without any evolution. The characters are poorly written, and their choices completely demolish any suspension of disbelief: watching the protagonist endure massive absurdities without reacting, even defending the indefensible to his friends, is simply irritating and devoid of logic.

The final blow is the total lack of substance. There are no real twists or plot turns; the initial premise drags itself wearily to the end credits, piling up old genre clichés instead of developing real tension. A derivative, flat, and severely overrated operation, turned into a masterpiece only by social media camaraderie.

Ngl this movie had me scared so many times. I kept trying to tell myself, "it's just a 5 foot nothing girl who's acting crazy why am I scared?" but it didn't work.

The actress who played the girl is 10/10 bro. She played her role so well in making her character seem so creepy.

Cherry on top with the scaryness is that someone in my theater kept making walking noises with his feet and it was my first time watching UltraAVX so I wasn't sure if it was the movie or outside noise. Then I got suddenly paranoid like he was gonna try and kill me or something which made this scary experience even more scary great.

I've watched so many horror movies, from art house to the classics to new ones, and this might be the one that stuck with me the most. I wouldn't say it was the best by any stretch, but it just makes me feel a certain way. It is the most horrifying, devastating, and sad movie I've seen in a long time. I still get nauseous thinking about it. I think this will definitely be the best movie of the last year. High rating but do not recommend to anyone because it made me feel so awful. Also kudos to Inde Navarette! Wow!

I have never wanted a horror protagonist to die more than Bear. A character that starts out with a sympathetic and relatable plight, and who spends the movie proving just what an evil, sick, monster he truly is. An amazing example of a monster that is as pathetic as he is dangerous. The ending gave me so much catharsis, Bear gets his choice robbed from him just like he robbed Nikki of her choice and it costs him his life. Just what that coward deserves. The performances are all genuinely masterful, the way the characters are written varies between horrific and comedic in a way that's deeply compelling. I kept picking out little sketch motifs in the first half. Curry's directing is top notch, his command of the camera had me on the edge of my seat. The scenes are so tense and horrific, leaving me breathless and flinching. The sound design also takes this film to another level. This is an incredibly special film, one of the best I have ever seen. I hope Curry has a long prosperous career in horror. I hope Nikki is able to heal from this all.

When I decided to watch Obsession, I expected to see something more bland, more surface-level, and more 'typical' of the horror genre.

However, I was SO pleasantly surprised.

I think this movie is a beautiful exploration of this generation's perception of love, amongst other things.

Bear's obsession with Nikki.

He does not love her, potentially the most obvious takeaway from the movie. He has this all-encompassing crush on her and views her through a Bear-centric lens. Bear sees Nikki as two things, neither being her authentic self. Bear sees Nikki as the version she has curated for the world to see, and as the solution to his internal issues. The former is expressed through how Bear doesn't KNOW Nikki; her relationship with his father, 'Just BE Nikki', and her creativity. The latter, expressed through how his consideration for her, his perception of her is motivated by how she serves him, not who she is. His perception of her is motivated by how she was there for him.. how having her makes him look.. what she can do for him.. how she makes him feel.. the gaps in his life he has decided she fills. Bear strips Nikki of her autonomy simply by how he views her; the One Wish Willow was only a means of making that tangible.

Can't be bothered getting into much more. Beautifully unexpectedly rich movie.

My opinion might be tainted by a bad theater experience. I will rant on that later.

I was planning on waiting for streaming to avoid inconsiderate idiots, but they scrapped the planned June 2nd streaming date since it was making tons of money. So I finally went to make sure it doesn't get spoiled.

This is a generally well made movie. There are lots of creepy parts, great performances (omg Inde), and one really great jaw-dropping moment. At times, it reaches the levels needed to satisfy the hype. At times.

It also has a ton of gross out horror which does zero for me. Puke, piss and dead animals are not scary to me. It's stuff I'd rather not see. And the vast majority of this movie is slow build up and in between calmer moments.

I think it's a solid movie but the hype has been blown way out of proportion. I may give it a second chance and see if I like it better, but I doubt it goes higher than 7 stars.

"Be careful what you wish for, because you just might get it" is an aphorism as old as time itself, that storytellers have spent decades exploring. In Penny Marshall's 'Big,' a kid makes a wish to be taller and wakes up as a thirty-year-old Tom Hanks (whether that's a dream or a nightmare is up to you), while in something like W. W. Jacob's 'The Monkey's Paw,' a granted wish is basically a guarantee of suffering to come.

'Obsession' is the latest film to explore the idea of wish-fulfilment gone wrong. Directed by Curry Barker, it follows Bear, a sheepish young man who is hopelessly in love with one of his best friends, Nikki. Never having the courage to admit his feelings, he purchases a magical toy that claims to grant a wish once broken. In desperation, wishing for her to love him above all else, he breaks it. Incredibly, Nikki does fall for Bear- but in a way that's truly, madly creepy.

Barker's second feature, it is a darkly funny horror that doesn't break any new ground, but remains enjoyable nevertheless. Reminiscent at times of a Parker Finn or Osgood Perkins flick, it has some deeply disturbing moments that linger in the mind like the musk of decay. Nikki's behaviour is consistently frightening- her macabrely forced expressions, how her attention to Bear becomes increasingly fixed, unblinking and inhuman. However, some may find the narrative a tad predictable, it following a trajectory that feels inevitable almost from the beginning.

Conversely, what sets the film apart from others of its ilk is its handling of questions of control and agency. Bear may initially come across as timid and sympathetic, but the film never lets him entirely off the hook for the situation he creates. Even after realising that Nikki may or may not be herself anymore, he continues to exploit the fantasy of her love for his own gratification.

That moral ambiguity gives the characterisation surprising depth. Barker resists turning Bear into either a straightforward victim or villain, instead presenting him as someone whose loneliness and insecurity morph into selfish lasciviousness. That said, the thematic undercurrent isn't always as understated as Barker seems to intend. Certain moments in the third act underline the metaphor of control so directly that they risk flattening the otherwise nuanced character work.

The film's technical execution plays a crucial role in sustaining its unease. Barker and his team adopt a largely restrained visual style, allowing performance and framing do much of the heavy lifting when it comes to tension. There's a quiet confidence to Taylor Clemons' cinematography, the camera lingering on characters just a moment longer than feels comfortable, letting small details in expression and movement become increasingly loaded.

This is complemented by Vivian Gray's immersive production design, which shifts from ordinary to oppressive, turning familiar spaces into off-kilter nightmare realms. Further, the sound design and Barker's editing work in tandem, stretching out moments of silence before puncturing them with carefully measured bursts of unease, whilst Rock Burwell's original score maintains a constant undercurrent of dread.

Michael Johnston delivers a fine, nuanced performance as Bear, capturing the complexity of the character with aplomb, while Megan Lawless and Cooper Tomlinson both impress as two of his friends. However, it is Inde Navarrette who leaves the strongest impression. As Nikki, she is magnetically malevolent, dominating every scene and imbuing the film with a constant sense of volatile unease. Much like Alyssa Sutherland did in 'Evil Dead Rise,' Navarrette brings a sinister character to life with wicked glee; announcing herself as a major new presence in horror.

Ultimately, Curry Barker's 'Obsession' is a slick, unsettling take on wish-fulfilment gone wrong, boasting a thick atmosphere of unease and featuring strong performances- particularly from Inde Navarrette. It doesn't reinvent the genre, but it executes its ideas with confidence and control, particularly in its restrained visual style and sound design. In short, be careful what you wish for- unless that wish is to see 'Obsession'. It won't let you down.

Obsession is one of the most unsettling and entertaining horror films I've caught in a while. Curry Barker's direction in his debut film is confident. Low-budget roots show in the best way tight, creative, and focused on characters and atmosphere over CGI. The practical effects and some shocking scenes land hard.

Inde Navarrette's performance is absolutely magnetic and terrifying. She nails the shift from cool, confident crush to something far more intense and psychotic. I believe she deserves an Oscar nomination atleast.

Overall, Obsession is wildly entertaining horror that respects the audience's intelligence while delivering genuine creep and thrill.

summary: The obsession with Obsession is scary, not the film itself
text:
Obsession was supremely overrated. I enjoyed Backrooms more but I also thought Backrooms was somewhat overrated. Both films were ok, neither superb.

Obsession prob had potential but what we were given was definitely not special. Too predictable, didn't really do anything new or particularly well. Even given the silly storyline, a lot of it was nonsensical.

The last 10-15 mins or so of Obsession especially seemed rushed and odd. Just a few examples: Ian wishes for a billion dollars and it immediately came tumbling out of the ceiling. They couldn't even directly film it coming out of the ceiling because it would look stupid. Then after Bear goes back to his home, Ian comes over and says it worked, he got a billion dollars. Uh, did Ian forget Bear was there when it happened? Also, Bear's decision to kill himself seemed very shortsighted when there were obviously other options.

It also relied too much on jump scares. I don't react to jump scares but I could tell that's what they were going for with the loud sudden bits where a few people around me in the theater reacted.

There were numerous more interesting horror or horror-adjacent films released in just the last year or two that if I'm not mistaken so far haven't fared as well as Obsession in terms of ratings and box office (Together, Bring Her Back, Weapons, Presence, Final Destination: Bloodlines, Heretic, Terrifier 3, to name several off the top of my head) that I wonder if there's something unusual skewing its success. Maybe marketing drew in people who don't watch many horror films. No idea.

summary: A 109-Minute TikTok You Paid to Watch
text:
I feel like I'm being gaslit by the entire film criticism establishment. 94% on Rotten Tomatoes? "The best horror of 2026"? Did we watch the same movie? Let's be perfectly honest: this barely even qualifies as cinema. It's absolutely regurgitated garbage.

For those unaware, director Curry Barker comes from YouTube sketch comedy, and boy, does it show. They gave this guy a million dollars (and another "triumph" for Blumhouse), but apparently, nobody bothered to write an actual screenplay. The setup is a tired Monkey's Paw knockoff: Bear, a passive music store employee and certified "Nice Guy," gets a magic toy to make his co-worker Nikki fall for him. Wish granted. Bad things happen. That's it. I just saved you an hour and forty-nine minutes.

Here is where the movie fundamentally fails: the creators couldn't care less about basic screenwriting laws. Normally, a character needs a journey, obstacles, and an arc. Barker decided all of that was optional. Bear is an insufferable man-child who experiences zero growth. He starts out as a mopey sad-sack, gets his one desire at the very beginning, and never once stops to rethink his choices or actually try to do anything differently. Just problems, no solutions. He exists exactly the same way from minute 1 to minute 109.

Instead of a narrative, you get a compilation of cheap sketches where the exact same joke is played on a loop. Bear is awkward, Nikki is creepy, something gross happens. Rinse and repeat. Sure, there's some horror elements thrown, but shock without substance is just a carnival trick. You could rearrange half the scenes, or chop this down to a 15-minute short, and lose absolutely nothing. It honestly feels like taking a 60-second TikTok bit and painfully stretching it to feature length.

The fact that this is breaking box office records is what genuinely terrifies me. If audiences are willing to pay premium ticket prices for a stretched-out content dump, the industry is going to learn exactly the wrong lesson. I fully expect theaters to start charging admission for literal TikTok compilations soon, while audiences sit there happily eating trash right off a shovel. Or maybe we actually deserve all of this?

Rating - 9.1:
Overall, 'Obsession' is a great horror movie elevated by its meticulous writing, well-executed direction and horror sequences, and a tour de force performance from Inde Navarrette, all of which make this movie feel like a fresh take on the possession subgenre and a modern horror classic, sticking the landing in a way that very few modern horror movies do.

Direction - Great:
The direction on a macro scale is great, as it creates a very tense and suspenseful atmosphere that feels unique and fresh for the 'possession' subgenre, creating a world that makes the viewer want to have one eye closed and the other peeking to see what happens next; The direction on a micro scale is good for the most part, as you learn a lot about these characters since their relationships are what make this movie so terrifying, though it does suffer from generic horror acting sequences at times; The storytelling is very good, as it slowly unravels the theme of 'being careful what you wish for' because by the end of the movie, it becomes total chaos, planting roots throughout to make the ending feel well-deserved; The filmmakers build tension masterfully, as the whole movie is a tense and suspenseful environment that makes you want to crawl into your seat; I really respect that this movie did not rely on jump scares and instead focused on psychological horror, which prevented it from feeling like a cheap horror movie because it works for its scares, having a high follow-through rate

Story - Great:
The concept is very good and unique, a fresh take on the 'possession' subgenre as it explores the lengths Bear will go to have his crush fall in love with him, forcing him to be 'careful what he wished for'; The plot structure is linear and standard; Character writing is very good, as the movie is a character study of Bear, a young adult who resembles the current generation by facing social anxiety and fearing the expression of feelings, showing the lengths he must go to hide how he feels and avoid doing the right thing; The character writing for Nikki is also good, as the dichotomy between her character before and after the 'obsession' takes over is very well done, illustrating what is real and what is forced; On a second watch, the movie really does play like a character study of the four main characters: the tortured one, the immoral one, the jealous one, and the righteous one

Screenplay - Great:
The dialogue is very sharp for a low-budget horror movie, as it feels realistic for these young adult characters and adds a sense of unease during the horror sequences; The dialogue is also very intentional, as even the smallest of phrases has the biggest meaning in terms of what is reality and what Bear wants to be reality; The humor is surprisingly good and helps alleviate the tension to make the horror sequences enjoyable to an extent, showcasing the comedic background of the director; The symbolism is pretty surface-level, as the movie's messaging is mostly about being 'careful what you wish for' and presenting a character study of a young adult who is afraid of sharing how he feels and doing the right thing; The foreshadowing is very good in this movie, as it sets up the ending very well and makes the movie feel bookended; On a second watch, you really do see how masterful the foreshadowing is, as they plant roots and subtle hints throughout the movie that help you see through the fog of this wishful world and help make the ending justified

Acting - Good:
Michael Johnston - Good (Plays his role well as he embodies the socially anxious/lonely generation of young male adults who are afraid to express their feelings and do the right thing, as he knows what he is doing is wrong but is too afraid to change it; he really embodies the male loneliness epidemic well as your perception of him throughout the movie turns from being relatable to being despised the way he handles the situation he's got himself in), Inde Navarrette - Very Good (A true star in the making as she plays both the original Nikki and the 'obsessed' version of Nikki very well as you can feel the dichotomy between the two characters; the original Nikki really does feel like a friend, while the 'obsessed' version is terrifying to watch on screen because of the lengths she will go to show Bear she loves him more than 'anyone in the entire world'; the switches between the personas also feel very fluid and helps show what is real and what is fake; has very good chemistry with Michael Johnston as their interactions are both heartwarming and terrifying, creating a sense of unease that slowly builds throughout the movie; she really is a scene stealer as her presence fills the entire room, making her so captivating to watch), Cooper Tomlinson - Pretty Good (Plays the comedic relief side character well), Megan Lawless - Pretty Good to Good (Acts as the voice of reason for the group as it feels like she is the only character with ambition and common sense, wanting what's best for Bear; because of this, she has a good dynamic with Bear as their chemistry is second best to Nikki and Bear), Andy Richter - Decent to Pretty Good (Funny he's in this movie, but he is basically you typical 'bigger' actor to help get this movie funding since he doesn't really have that much of a role), Rest of the cast - Pretty Good (There isn't too much of a supporting cast, but the cast feels close-knit to show the friend group dynamic well, especially for young adults who work together)

Score - Good to Very Good:
The score does a good job of building the tone and atmosphere of the movie, as it makes the horror sequences feel like they are crescendoing into something that is very hard to watch while you visibly feel unease with what is occurring on-screen

Soundtrack - Pretty Good:
The soundtrack helps build the world for this young adult friend group, as it uses a lot of indie and alternative music

Cinematography - Very Good:
The cinematography is well-executed for a low-budget horror film and makes this movie look unique; The cinematography is integral to building the suspense and tension of the horror sequences, as the constant slow zoom-ins and quick pans are vital in creating a sense of unease; The use of lighting between Bear and Nikki also really amplifies the characters, as having Nikki always show up in a dark setting makes her feel like a 'sleep paralysis demon' who makes Bear constantly question if this is real; I really enjoyed the 1.50:1 aspect ratio, as it created a sense of claustrophobia and made the movie look unique

Editing - Very Good:
The editing is instrumental in building the suspense and tension, as it uses a lot of slow zooms and quick cuts to create an uneasy feeling; Also, for a low-budget horror movie, the editing feels very innovative and unique, as it makes this movie look like it is in a league of its own

Sound - Good to Very Good:
The sound is crisp and does an amazing job of building tension and suspense throughout the movie, making you want to crawl into your seat

Visual Effects - Good:
The use of practical effects really built the gore of the horror sequences, as it adds another level of suspense that makes this movie hard to watch in a good way; The money-falling sequence looked quite fake, though

Pacing - The pacing is good, as it constantly shifts from slow to fast to create a rush of suspense that builds up the horror sequences; The runtime is a bit long, but cutting five to ten minutes really would not change much

Climax - The climax is executed very well, as it helps the movie stick the landing and feel like a complete story, which is something modern horror movies struggle with

Tone - The tone is very much that of a psychological horror movie, though the way it mixes in comedy makes the movie feel like a fresh take on the genre.

This movie is a strong 9/10. It has all the elements I personally look for in a horror movie. The entire film feels like a fever dream, constantly messing with your head and making you question what's real. I also love that the story is built around something that could realistically spiral out of control if an object like the One Wish Willow actually existed.

My least favorite part of the movie is Bear. He's honestly the true villain of the story. When he wishes for Nikki to love him, the real Nikki is replaced and trapped somewhere else. The version of Nikki we see for most of the movie is a fake, creepy, almost demonic version created by the wish. The real Nikki briefly breaks through several times, like when she's kissing Bear and suddenly freaks out before snapping back, or at the party when she tries to take her own life. Those moments show that she's still trapped inside. At the very end, we finally see the real Nikki return, only to find herself surrounded by her dead friends. To me, that's the most disturbing part of the movie. Bear's selfish wish single-handedly ruined everyone's lives and left Nikki to live with the regret of everything that happened.

Overall, the cast was refreshing, and everyone did an amazing job in their respective roles. I'd love to see more spin-off movies centered around different people discovering the One Wish Willow and exploring how their wishes create entirely new chains of horrifying events.

summary: Autonomy as a vehicle for horror
text: An instant classic and my favourite movie of the year so far. It has just the right amount of laughs paired with the right amount of WTF moments. The movies exploration of autonomy or rather, the lack of it does a great job showcasing just how terrifying it is to lose control of one's own body, essentially turning the body into a prison all while highlighting how truly dangerous the "nice guy" facade can really be.

In the forty-eight hours since watching Obsession, my opinion of it has slipped from a 7 to a 6. It hasn't dropped any lower, but the more I think or talk about it, the more flaws I notice and the more I find myself laughing at some of the script's choices and setups. The film has a very basic plot and a small cast, which means any weaknesses stand out sharply. At its core, it's a story about a wish coming true-and anyone familiar with wish-themed movies knows they rarely turn out well.

That said, Obsession has several standout qualities that make it worth a look, even with the caveat that certain issues may frustrate some viewers. The 1.50:1 aspect ratio gives it a very filmic look, the lighting is atmospheric and helps tell the story, the acting is effective overall, and the jump scares land well. The movie does rely a bit too heavily on the loud-sound-after-quiet-moment trick, but it's a slow burn that's rarely boring and features very strong practical and visual effects.

The main problems revolve around the lead character, Bear, whose decisions will have many viewers yelling at the screen in frustration. The film also makes some odd choices during its setup: it fails to clearly establish the rules of its premise and introduces potential B-plot threads that are promptly dropped and never revisited. This leaves behind a trail of unanswered questions. Any attempt to piece everything together feels strained and almost certainly misses whatever the filmmakers actually intended.

It's clear that most people hold the movie in much higher regard. If you're the type of viewer who can overlook narrative shortcomings in favor of a strong visual and audio experience, there's a good chance you'll love it. I kept hoping for a more developed B-plot and found myself waiting for a twist or some payoff to the visual clues that seemed to be planted early on-most of which ultimately led nowhere.

I enjoyed the film despite the confusion it left me with, but by the time the credits rolled, its issues had firmly grounded my rating at just above average.

This movie is genuinely bad. It is painfully surface-level, extremely repetitive, and I struggle to understand how it has earned such high ratings from so many viewers.

More than anything, the film is incoherent in a way that feels lazy rather than intentional. Its central idea, someone loving you more than anyone else in the world, does not meaningfully connect to much of what actually happens. Instead, many scenes come across as filler designed primarily for shock value.

For example, there is a restaurant scene in which one character is asked a question and suddenly begins screaming. How does that moment grow out of the film's central premise? Rather than fully exploring its main theme and pushing it to its limits, the movie repeatedly drifts into loosely related material simply to pad the runtime. At its core, the entire story could be explained in about three minutes. There is also a scene about one of the characters doing something with a dead cat, but once again, it has nothing to do with the film's central concepts and clearly is made for shock value only.

The movie also introduces fragments of dialogue that seem intended to create psychological depth, yet it never develops them. At one point, a character abruptly asks something along the lines of, "What would be so bad about being with me?" The film leaves it there. There is no meaningful exploration of the character's trauma, motivations, insecurities, or emotional history. It gestures toward complexity without doing the work required to earn it.

To make matters worse, the movie is incredibly repetitive, with much of its runtime revolving around a woman screaming. The performances do not help. Bear's character feels noticeably amateurish. Nikki, played by Inde Navarrette, is much better, but also overrated, her performance is something that supporting cast in the Smile movies achieve easily.

I genuinely wanted to like this film. It is an independent production featuring newer actors, and I am always interested in supporting projects like that. Unfortunately, it is so poorly executed, shallow, and lazily constructed that it is one of the worst movies I have watched recently.

2/10.

summary: A brilliant addition to the horror love story genre with elite horror storytelling and execution
text:
I watched Obsessions (2025) in theaters tonight. The storyline follows a guy who has a crush on a coworker but doesn't have the courage to ask her out. He breaks a "One Wish Willow" he buys at a crystal and charm shop and wishes for his crush to love him more than anything on Earth - which sounds like a good idea until she actually does.

This picture is written and directed by Curry Barker (Milk & Serial) and stars Michael Johnston (Drama Drama), Inde Navarrette (Wander Darkly), Cooper Tomlinson (Milk & Serial), and Megan Lawless (Killer Rental).

This has such good writing and execution and is essentially a horror love story, and I liked this one more than most within this horror subgenre. The acting is really good, and the expressions, mannerisms, and character delivery are elite. The guy was so frustrating, but the piña colada scene completely sank the ship. There's a nice blend of simple horror concepts, practical effects, and modern CGI, though some of the CGI scenes felt like more than they needed to be in my opinion.

The writing is so smart, and the movie is shot so well to bring those moments home. The simple concepts that really sold this for me are the screams, banging, door, and shadow-walking scenes. Just simple ideas executed extremely well. The Jenga game is an elite horror scene, and this movie has an elite use of a brick. There are some great corpses in this too - both human and animal. There's a lot to like here.

In conclusion, Obsessions is a brilliant addition to the horror love story genre with elite horror storytelling and execution. I'd score this a 7.5-8/10.

I'd call it more of a thriller than a horror, but there's definitely a couple of good jump scares involved. You really end up feeling for Nikki but as time goes on and her wish-self does more and more horrific things, you realize nobody involved can ever come back from the wish Bear made. He trapped her and turned her into a monster and victim simultaneously, and the ending leaves you wondering where and how her story might continue. You end up hating Bear and realizing how selfish and cowardly he is. I'll definitely be rewatching this one, haven't seen a thriller this good in a long time.

summary: A brilliant juggling act of genres
text:
When this showed at Fantastic Fest 2025 it was the talk of the town. It was many people's favourite film of the fest, and if it wasn't someone's favourite, it wasn't far off. So needless to say I have been excited for this one ever since. And I'm so pleased to say that it surpassed my expectations. This film was incredible.

I can't ever remember a film that was capable of being this creepy and this funny at the same time. The horror/comedy sub-genre has been juggled a lot over the years but often it involves massively toning down both in order to make it work. 'Obsession' is incredibly funny when it is trying to be, and incredibly unsettling when the time comes.

The film also features what I consider to be the best jump-scare I've ever seen. Recency bias could be at play here, but I haven't jumped like that before in my life, I'm almost certain. And the crazy thing is, a part of me knew it was coming. I knew what that scene was setting up. And I still leapt out of my skin.

But don't go thinking this is a jump-scare ridden film. In fact I can't even think of any others. The film works with atmosphere and creepy visuals. It puts situations into your mind that theoretically could happen to anyone with their significant other at any given time.

I'm so incredibly excited for Curry Barker's future. This guy just gets it. A brilliant film. 10/10.

Note: In a just and fair world Inde Navarrette would be a certainty for an Oscar nomination.

summary: Unhinged and thrilling in every way!
text: This movie is, without a doubt, one of the best films I have seen this year. The narrative is easy to follow without being overly complicated, while the atmosphere and tone keep you on the edge of your seat. But beyond these impressive qualities, it is Inde Navarrete's performance that carries the entire film. Through Bear's perspective, you never know what she will do next, while Navarrete completely surrenders herself to the role of Nikki Freeman, creating a character who will be remembered as one of the most compelling in horror. I wouldn't be surprised if Oscar nominations follow, but all I can say is that this is just the beginning for the immensely talented Curry Barker.

I honestly couldn't find much that justified Obsession's reputation. Aside from the terrifying car scene and a few strong moments scattered throughout the film, there wasn't enough to keep me fully invested. For me, it's a 6/10 at best.

The only reason I can understand the hype is that some viewers-not the majority-might see it as an exploration of how far obsession can go in a relationship. Even then, the film presents a highly exaggerated and extreme version of that idea. While I can appreciate what it was trying to convey, the execution didn't do enough to make it resonate with me.

summary: Gen Z's Masterpiece? I Don't See It
text:
Honestly, the Gen Z hype around this movie is baffling. What happened to this generation's standards? Have you watched Fight Club, Se7en, Interstellar, The Prestige, or The Silence of the Lambs and there is a lot more those are films that truly earn their reputation.

Obsession isn't even in the same conversation. I went into Obsession with high expectations. The reviews and audience response had built it up as one of the greatest horror films of the 21st century. While I can appreciate some aspects of the film, I ultimately found it disappointing.

The atmosphere is effective, and there are moments that genuinely feel unsettling. The film does a decent job of portraying emotional discomfort and toxic relationships. The performances are generally strong.

However, the pacing is a major issue. It takes far too long for the film to become engaging, and many scenes feel unnecessarily stretched out. Instead of building tension, the slow pace often becomes tedious.

Another problem is the tone. During my screening, people laughed during scenes that seemed intended to be disturbing. I found myself laughing at times as well. The film struggles to decide whether it wants to be horror, psychological drama, or dark comedy, and that inconsistency weakens its impact.

The reveals are also poorly timed, reducing their emotional effectiveness. Additionally, the world of the film feels strangely limited and underdeveloped.

Ultimately, I do not think this works particularly well as a horror film. It feels more like a psychological drama with horror elements than a genuinely frightening experience.

The lead actress, however, was phenomenal and easily the best part of the movie. Her performance was a 10/10 and carried the film from start to finish.

10/10 acting. Terrible script. Massively overrated.

summary: This year's "Weapons" - an overrated and average horror
text:
It has a few fairly interesting ideas to start but like 99% of modern horrors, the setup is better than the resolution and this movie collapsed into predictable nonsense by the end.

These days just being weird is enough....use a few jarring visuals that you've seen a hundred times since The Ring / The Grudge etc with barely any attempt at internal logic. For instance, any particular reason why certain characters start moving weirdly for a bit and then stop again? No, it just looks weird and that's enough.

I predicted both of the major "jump scares" about a minute before they happened so they had no effect.

It's a kinda lazy combination of Fatal Attraction (yeah there's a dead pet) and Weapons (breaking wish sticks). It's pretty clear to me that this film wouldn't exist if it wasn't for Weapons.

The biggest problem for me was none of the characters were remotely likeable (the main guy is a totally feeble dumbass who of course does the most stupid things possible at all times, inviting every piece of misfortune to make plot happen) so none of the climaxes that were meant to have an emotional affect landed at all.

There is some social commentary here regarding destructive / obsessive relationships, that I guess people who have never seen the afore-mentioned and far superior Fatal Attraction may find diverting, but the best thing I can say about them is that they were kindergarden level writing compared to that older film, and lead to some comedy that I don't think was usually intended. By the end I was just hoping they would all die so the film could end.

Add it to the list of overrated horror films that people who haven't seen the things it's ripping-off keep saying is the best thing ever for about two weeks then never mention again.

summary: Curry Barker's "Obsession" Just Might Be a Masterpiece...
text: Oh, what a ride this movie is. It's the best film of 2026 so far and it's not even close. I don't even want to go into detail regarding the specifics of why this film is so good. It's best to go into Curry Barker's film, "Obsession", without knowing much. They don't make them like this anymore. This is a very impressive film and a modern day masterpiece.

This story is about Bear a young man who has a mysterious crush on his work colleague friend Nikki ,a hopeless romantic that finds himself getting exactly what he asked for but soon discovers that some desires come true at a sinister price. Micheal Johnson as bear and Inde Navarrette as Nikki take the leads in this chilling romantic horror story that masterfully blends its love, temptation, and its supernatural power into one unforgettable story. What begins as a heartfelt tale of a hopeless romantic quickly spirals into something far darker and more sinister, keeping viewers emotionally invested from beginning to end.

Micheal Johnson delivers a standout performance as Bear, capturing both the innocence of a man desperate for love with the girl of his dreams and the terrifying consequences of obsession. His chemistry with Inde Navarrette, who shines as Nikki, feels authentic and emotionally clever making the film's dark twists hit even harder. Navarrette brings depth, charm, vulnerability ,persuasive character to her role, making Nikki far more than just a love interest. Obsession has a tale to tell and revolves around the concept of a mysterious possession which is believed to be overtaken or controlled by an possessive physical curse. The story in a bizarrely different way adds a haunting, almost folklore-like atmosphere that gives the movie its unique approach. The story explores on how far people are willing to go for love and whether getting everything you desire is truly worth the cost. Visually, Obsession is stunning. The cinematography balances romance and its horror beautifully, shifting from warm emotional moments to loud,dark, bloody and unsettling imagery .The soundtrack also deserves praise for enhancing the film's suspenseful and emotional tone. Which what makes Obsession stand out and its ability to combine psychological horror with its unique emotionally Petulant storytelling. It's not just about scares it's about loneliness, desire, and the dangerous nature of wanting something so so badly. Fans of dark romance and horror will find plenty to love here. Overall, Obsession is an intense, emotionally haunting and Its experience leaves a long lasting impression long after the credits roll. With strong performances, a gripping premise, and an unsettling atmosphere, this film proves that sometimes the greatest danger comes from getting exactly what you wished for.

Bear struggles to tell his crush Nikki that he is in love with her. When his initial confession goes awry, he accidentally breaks a "wish willow" figurine-a sentimental gift he had intended to give her. Desperate to fix the situation, he wishes for her to want him just as intensely as he wants her, but the magic works all too well, and the sudden manifestation of his desire quickly turns deeply problematic and dangerous.

It is no wonder this film is absolutely nailing it at the box office. One of the best films of 2026 so far, this proves that cinema isn't just about money in a year when big-budget movies keep flopping. The storytelling feels almost old-fashioned in the way it draws the audience in and forces total concentration, a quality modern cinema often lacks. It is a simple formula where every single element is on point; the writing, tone, and atmosphere combine to create something incredibly creepy and sinister, punctuated by jump scares that come completely out of nowhere and work perfectly.

This film is an absolute class act that benefits immensely from a total lack of Hollywood influence. It just goes to show that you don't need an astronomical budget, big names, heavy special effects, or a leading actor with strong political opinions to deliver straight-up, riveting entertainment without a single lecture in sight. One can only hope that the talented creative team behind this success avoids the temptation to move to Hollywood and continues to make films with this level of independence and grit.

Michael Johnston absolutely nails the role of Bear, capturing the character's desperation, particularly during the incredibly tense scene where he tries phoning the emergency help number. Inde Navarrette is equally excellent as Nikki, delivering some outstanding moments throughout; her phenomenal speech at the bar is a real standout performance. Both actors are superb, anchoring the sinister simplicity of the plot and ensuring the film deserves every bit of the plaudits it is receiving.

9/10.

summary: A well-acted but narratively anorexic experience that fails to expand on its own trailer
text:
While *Obsession* manages to be an acceptable watch, it ultimately feels like a skeletal frame of what could have been a truly compelling supernatural horror. As a viewer who looks for narrative depth and world-building, I found the experience incredibly thin. The film relies entirely on its singular main storyline, completely neglecting the richness that supporting plotlines or intricate character backstories could have provided.

The most glaring issue is the meager cast size and the lack of development for the few characters we do get. In a genre that thrives on psychological stakes, the absence of interesting pasts or complex motivations makes it difficult to feel any lasting impact. Furthermore, the film suffers from a complete lack of surprise; everything the movie offers was clearly envisioned and revealed in the trailer long ago. It never attempts to go beyond that surface-level premise.

Technically, the acting is top-notch, with the lead performances doing a lot of the heavy lifting. However, stellar acting cannot compensate for a lack of abundance in the script. Supernatural horror should feel dense and atmospheric, yet here, the production design is remarkably unlikable and lacking in character. With a bit more creative luxury-better atmosphere, more diverse characters, and layered plotlines-this could have been a standout. As it stands, it's a functional but ultimately hollow effort.

**Verdict: A well-acted but narratively anorexic experience that fails to expand on its own trailer.**

summary: Be careful what you wish for
text:
I mean this presented itself quite obviously and easily to be honest - so still no pun intended. Consequences be damned - while you may be able to connect with one or more of the characters ... hopefully you understand way before consequences appear to be clear (and bad) ... that this is not the way to go.

In other words, I would never ever even think about wishing for something like that. Of course our main character does not think it is something that will happen or become reality. He still is quite passive - overall that is who he is. So all decisions (or lack thereof - passiveness) are clear and easy to explain ... or make sense.

The acting is incredible and there are quite a few eerie scenes ... and jump scares ... you may love to love ... but sometimes that can be overwhelming ... very well done and good ideas throughout. A clear festival favorite as others have claimed and stated ... this is "fun" to watch.

I chose to watch this movie after many creators recommended it, but I found myself utterly disappointed in it. I do not consider myself an horror critic or anything of the sort, but this movie isn't my first of the genre and I found many parts where I was left more frustrated than scared, which ultimately made me lower the vote from a 7 to a 6. I would consider this movie a good choice for starting the horror genre, since the pace of the movie is slow and the gore elements aren't that many but carefully placed. I liked the lighting and the atmosphere, as well as the acting of the female protagonist, but other than that I can't find many other positive points. In the end, the actors weren't bad, the shots make you tense in the right way and the plot is an interesting one, but it's definetly not a masterpiece like many said, in my opinion at least.

I genuinely don't understand the critical praise this film is getting.

Obsession starts with an interesting enough premise, but it takes far too long to get anywhere. The opening act drags endlessly, spending what feels like an eternity following a lead character who is not only painfully passive but also incredibly unlikeable. Almost every major problem in the film exists because he refuses to act like a normal human being with even the slightest bit of backbone.

Bear is supposed to be awkward and sympathetic, but instead he comes across as frustratingly weak. The entire plot hinges on his inability to communicate, make decisions, or take responsibility for the mess he creates. Rather than feeling sorry for him, I spent most of the film wondering why anyone would root for him at all.

The horror elements are decent enough. There are a few creepy moments, some effective body horror, and Nikki's performance is easily the strongest part of the film. When the film actually leans into horror, it works. Unfortunately, those moments are buried inside a story that feels repetitive and far longer than its premise can support.

I suspect critics have responded to the film's themes about obsession, fantasy, and unhealthy relationships, which are certainly there. Many reviews specifically praise the film as a commentary on male insecurity and romantic fantasy. But having a theme doesn't automatically make a film enjoyable to watch, and for me the execution simply wasn't there.

By the end I was left more irritated than scared. A handful of decent horror scenes can't save a film built around a protagonist I actively disliked and a story that takes forever to get moving.

A frustrating, overhyped horror film that mistakes an unlikeable lead for a compelling one.

It is tense in all ways and is terrifyingly unpredictable in a sympathetic way. The screams raise your hair with scenes of primal violence. I gave this horror movie ten stars because it shook me to my core and that only happens rarely. Also very attractive actors who are great actors.

Will probably be one, if not, the best horror film watched in 2026. The movie begins light and friendly but also very ambiguous. Simple friends talking and the main character contemplating taking his friendly relationship to the next level with his other friend - Nikki. The movie slowly goes down a slow and disturbing pace as the main character realizes what he did (or wants) is not quite what he signed up for. Great use of the slow-dread pace and visuals. Movie is pretty dark for most scenes. The buildup to the dark horror turn is excellent. By the end of the movie, you are pretty shocked and so is the other main character. I highly recommend this movie for those who like this genre and build up pace.

Yeah, yeah, be careful for what you wish for. Heard it before and now we have an Obsession...with this movie.

This is one of those movies that's gonna grow on me. While I really liked it tonight, my first viewing, I think, the longer I ponder it...it's gonna spread like a disease. In a good way. (If there is such a thing.)

I was told the basic premise of this movie by my favorite YouTube Creators about a month ago. With their enthusiasm, I was stoked. Later, it gained momentum in the community. And yet, I kept my expectations low-enough to not get disappointed.

On the surface, it IS *just* a "Be Careful for What You Wish For" tale. Deep down, these people are real. It's so refreshing seeing real-life coworkers and friends interact and complete a real story. I thought at first...oh, we're just getting the background of these characters. Later, I realized, I'm enthralled into their world.

Boy meets girl...well, LONG before this story begins. Boy LIKES girl. Does she like him? We don't know yet. By chance, Boy wishes Girl loves him more than life itself. Annnnd, what could possibly go wrong?

I love movies like these, especially horror movies. So richly simple and when explored or dove into or thought about for days on end, it all becomes something you cannot shake. Stop thinking about. And love movies again because of it.

That's this movie. Simple and so real, it's almost unbearable. Well done, both-Writer and Director Curry Barker. Home run here. So sad, so real and did it all when it could've easily been an easy streaming cheap flick.

summary: A Masterclass in low budget filmmaking
text:
After a very long time, I can finally say I have watched a perfect horror movie. *Obsession* completely turns the traditional horror formula upside down and adds a completely new sense of dread to the genre.

What makes this movie an absolute masterpiece is the sheer filmmaking genius of Curry Barker. As an indie filmmaker myself who writes, directs, and edits my own short films, I am in absolute awe of what this bro achieved. To pull off a global phenomenon with this level of insane cinematography in just a 20-day shoot is mind-blowing. He lives the exact dream so many of us are chasing.

The script is tight, but the real magic is in the camerawork and the pacing. The sudden shift of the frames and the deliberate, unsettling camera angles create a claustrophobic, psychological nightmare that stays with you. Because Barker directed, wrote, and *edited* the film himself, there is zero translation loss. You can feel that he reviewed his movie frame by frame in the editing room, refusing to stand up or compromise until he got exactly what he needed to show on screen.

If you love cinema, sound design, and pure visual storytelling, watch this. It is a massive inspiration for anyone who believes you don't need a massive budget to create an absolute masterpiece. 10/10.

With all the glazing reviews leading up to its release, I knew this movie would end up being just okay for me because I've been through the "BEST HORROR MOVIE OF THE YEAR" discourse every single year since 2022. I kept my expectations in check and still left disappointed, but at least I got a One Wish Willow popcorn bucket... now what should my wish be?

Obsession is Blumhouse's latest release that's well made and incredibly well acted by Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, with some good use of practical effects and genuinely unsettling creepy moments, but that's honestly all that worked for me. There were way too many frustrating moments that asked a lot from my suspension of disbelief, some really questionable humor especially near the end, and an ending that just made me question what the actual message of the movie was because personally, I didn't like it at all.

This is a brilliant film. Inde Navarrette's performance is insane and absolutely carried this movie. She definitely deserves the oscar.

The film sets up a basic premise and executes it to near perfection.

The origins and workings of the one wish willow is probably the only plot hole in this movie I could find.

The movie uses creepy and slow burn horror rather than jumpscares which is very effective. The lighting and the cinematography is brilliant.

Overall an excellent film and one of the if not the best horror films in recent years.

This movie isn't bad, I love horror and saw this in theaters asap. It's a decent movie but to call this one of the greatest horror movies in recent time is insane. People saying that this movie left them jaw dropped and that it's soooo good is a crazy take. This movie has a great Jumpscare, a decent plot, okay acting with the main character having great acting, the ending was decent, overall just a decent movie I'd rate it no higher than a 6.5 if you think this is a 10 then idk.
