Obsession is one of the best and most unnerving horror movies that I have seen in a while! Inde Navarrette gives a truly terrifying performance as Nikki, and she definitely deserves some awards recognition for it. Even though that definitely won't happen, knowing how the academy is. The rest of the cast also gives some fantastic performances, especially Michael Johnston as the main character, Bear. This movie's script is very well written and clever all throughout the runtime. It also strikes a great balance of horrific moments and darkly comedic ones. All without undercutting the tension, which there is a lot of in this. Curry Barker's direction is awesome, and there is a scene in a car that is just executed perfectly. He also crafted multiple sequences that had my heart racing. I honestly have no negative or mixed notes on the film, besides me having 2 cats. If you know you know.

Overall, Obsession is the movie to check out this weekend! Especially if you love horror movies like I do. It also plays very well with a packed crowd.

SCORE CARD: 4.75/5, 9.5/10, "Add It To The Collection", (This movie is so close to being a 5/5, but I need to watch it again before deciding on that)

From the very first minute until the final scene, this movie keeps you glued to your seat. You simply can't take your eyes off the screen. The suspense starts almost immediately, never lets up, and only grows more intense. After the halfway point, it reaches another level and never comes back down. Not for a single second do you feel comfortable while watching it.

This is psychological horror at its finest, and for me it's easily one of the best films the genre has ever produced. As someone who absolutely loves psychological horror, this was exactly what I had been looking for. I watched the entire film with my heart racing.

It constantly surprises you, shocks you, and leaves you deeply unsettled. It's an outstanding film, and Inde Navarrette delivers an incredible performance. At a certain point, she completely takes over the movie and elevates it to another level. It's the kind of performance that deserves serious awards consideration.

The ending is just as impressive, delivering a powerful and satisfying conclusion to an unforgettable experience.

Congratulations to everyone involved. What a film!

No need to describe the story - enough people already have. Suffice to say, if infatuation and blind love are a young man's sincere wishes (that he articulates through a novelty toy), the sincerely effed-up logical conclusion is, at first, faintly hilarious, but rapidly devolves into something deeply disturbing, and eventually cruises past pathological and into the diabolical.

The performances of Michael Johnston and the Inde Navarrette, the two leads, grounds this material and helps the film transcend genre and become stern, over-the-top lessons in boundaries and male and female relational expectations.

The character of Nikki (Navarette), is pitch-perfect, starting completely measured and normal, then quickly breezing past caricature to become as deeply unhinged as anything seen in Evil Dead Rises. Highly recommended!!

750k budget horror movie? 26 year old former YouTuber making his Hollywood debut as a director? No mainstream actors? Blumhouse Productions?? CGI replaced with "COOL LIGHTING"??? Is this some kind of joke? Who's seriously watching this?? Why am I even waisting time out of my day to give this any of my attention. My name is Bob I work for Disney and I wish to never have bad taste in movies *snap*

10/10 all hail Inde Navarrette.

Obsession had a genuinely disturbing and interesting concept: getting exactly the kind of love you wished for, but in the most unhealthy and terrifying way possible. Unfortunately, the movie never fully develops that idea.

The biggest problem is pacing. Nikki's transformation feels way too sudden, so instead of being psychologically unsettling, it becomes exaggerated and unrealistic. The film also struggles with tone sometimes it wants to be a serious psychological horror, other times it feels like an overdramatic teen thriller.

There was a lot of potential here, especially with themes of obsession and control, but the movie relies more on shock value than real psychological depth.

Not awful, but definitely overrated. Strong idea, weak execution.

Behind its disgusting Hereditary-esque shocks, behind the magnificent performance by the lead actress, behind those lights and silhouettes, behind all of what makes Obsession a solid horror film, there is a deep, disturbing dynamic of a tortured relationship. Those who experienced it will have some uncomfortable memories rushing in, they will be forced to recall and compare their own lived experience with what is being shown.

Another thing that made this unique was that we see Barron (Bear) as the one who is obsessed at first, we see somehow him becoming the one who is now facing obsession, and the turmoil that ensues. He sees what obsession is about, how it feels to face it, to tolerate it, to deal with it. He gets to see what is the difference between obsession and love, the difference between what he perceived about his feelings, and what was the nature of those feelings. In a sense, this works like an analysis of obsession, nicely embedded in an enjoyable horror feature.

I will say however, that I have had problems with the film's pacing. It starts very slow, and once it gets going, it will adopt a pace that is widely different from the first act. I do feel it could have benefitted from some adjustment with the pace and rhythm, but that is probably due to the director's inexperience.

I also found the ending too much. Not that it's not fun, it surely is, but I would have liked more reflection, more realization, more spacing, possibly some flashbacks, instead of what was offered. It's probably an artistic choice of the writer-director, but it's a choice I found humbly disagreeing with. Regardless, Obsession is definitely a very good piece of art. One that will ask uneasy questions. It's also a birth of two very interesting careers to follow: Curry Barker as a new creative filmmaker, and Inde Navarrette, as a talented actress.

summary: Confused on the extremely high praise.
text: This is not a movie you're going to get upset about buying tickets for, but not one you should either. The hype and high praise on socials seems a little marketed now upon watching. New-ish concept, make a wish but only get one, and of course leads to regrettable wishes. Most of the twists were easy to predict, including the ending. I'd say it's enjoyable if you want to enjoy it, but not something to pick apart. To reiterate, this is a good movie and enjoyable to watch, but the critic scores are just much too high. For people not sure about their stomach for horror, there's some gore but it's mild and not something that leaves the theater with you. I'd also like to say, the female lead did a wonderful job. Some of her movements you could tell took heavy choreography and she made it look very natural. She was wonderful throughout and likely will enjoy better roles in the future. Hesitated posting a review so negative, but the reviews are just too high.

Obsession follows Bear, an anxious hopeless romantic who doesn't seem to understand how to act on love. He reaches a point where what he wants feels impossible, so he makes a wish. That wish ultimately causes Nikki to fall in love with him almost immediately. As things spiral out of control, Bear must find a way to stop what is happening to him.

I was lucky enough to watch Obsession two days earlier than most people, and I'm glad I chose to go. The film explores the stigma surrounding toxic obsessive relationships in a way that almost serves as a warning, showing viewers what those relationships can become.

The cinematography was amazing; it captured emotion effortlessly. The use of shadows to portray Wish Nikki was especially fascinating. The sound design was also incredibly strong. Bass was utilized in a way that made the audience physically feel what the characters were experiencing. One of the clearest examples of this comes when Bear attempts to make a second wish. As he tries to break the willow branch, the deep bass intensifies the feeling of struggle and desperation. At times, I genuinely wondered if stop-motion had been used because Wish Nikki's movements felt so unnatural. It was eerie, almost like a spider crawling across my body.

The film maintains tension throughout and creates a constant sense of secondhand anxiety. There were multiple moments where I felt paresthesia flow through my body, and it has been a long time since a horror movie made me feel that way. The choreography was deeply unsettling at times; the way Inde Navarrette's movements were directed reminded me of Javier Botet's performance in Mama. Even thinking about it gives me chills.

At times, the film evoked genuine empathy for its characters, making them feel emotionally engaging and relatable. One jump scare in particular was incredibly effective. Even though I anticipated it, I still jolted in my seat, and the aftermath left me deeply unsettled. There were funny moments, but while everyone around me was laughing, I found myself not quite sharing the same reaction. I think it may have come down to my own misunderstanding.

One final detail I appreciated was the way the wish weakened at times, allowing the real Nikki to slip through. The cliché of a person being trapped inside themselves was handled surprisingly well.

I left the theater in awe. I genuinely think this is one of the better horror films released in such a horror-filled year. If you get the chance, watch it in theaters so you can fully experience the atmosphere and emotion. Given that this is his first feature film, I'm excited to see what Curry Barker does next.

summary: This is what good marketing can do
text:
I've been seeing raving reviews for this film for the last few months, but since it wasn't playing in a theater near me (I was on a five-month work trip in Eastern Europe), I finally watched it tonight on Amazon and honestly... except for the lead actress who played Nikki who gave an incredible performance, this is the most boring film I've seen in years!

And yet, news articles and social media posts would make you believe that this is horror gold. If this is the highest grossing original movie of the 2020s so far, we're doomed.

I gave it two stars because of the superb performance by the main actress, but other than that save your money and wait until it's streaming somewhere you subscribe, because it is not worth it. At all.

The only thing that this movie proved is how clever marketing can hype up crap like this, and how (social) media still can affect public opinion very effectively. The fact that this film has such high ratings just proves that no one thinks with their own brain anymore. And that we're doomed as civilization.

Inde and Michael Johnston were incredible in this film. Their performances felt so real that every scene between them kept me uncomfortable in the best way possible. Inde especially was terrifying without trying too hard. She completely owned every scene she was in.

The first 40 minutes are definitely slow and at times it feels like the story is not really going anywhere. But once their date is over, the film completely changes. From that point onwards it becomes an intense psychological horror that never lets go.

The sound design is one of the best parts of the movie. It does not need cheap jump scares to frighten you. The atmosphere and sound alone were enough to keep me anxious and completely hooked from start to finish.

The pre climax and climax are absolutely insane. The tension keeps building until it reaches a point where you are just sitting there hoping someone survives. Even after the credits rolled, I was still trying to process everything that had happened.

It is not a perfect film, but when it gets going, it is genuinely one of the most intense psychological horror films I have watched.

summary: A new type of horror that I ever experienced in a cinema
text:
Initially I thought it's a psychological horror and shi, but when I watched it, mind blown away, it was so good, I love it.

Beneath the supernatural mechanics, Obsession serves as a sharp commentary on male entitlement, "nice guy" tropes, and toxic relationship dynamics. It forces characters to confront the heavy burden and consequences of forcing intimacy.

I just saw Obsession at the Thursday night premiere, and honestly, it's one of the best movies I've seen in years.

A complete 10.

The filmmaking, acting, cinematography, pacing, tension... everything about it was outstanding. Every scene felt intentional. The audience was completely locked in from beginning to end.

By the time the movie ended after 1 a.m., people were clapping in the theater.

That almost never happens anymore.

Obsession wasn't just entertaining. It pulled you in completely. The kind of film that stays with you after you leave the theater and makes you think about it the rest of the night.

Incredible production. Incredible performances. One of the best theatrical experiences I've had in a long time.

Go see it.

summary: One of the Best Horror Thrillers of 2026
text:
For a directorial debut, Obsession is remarkably confident in both its cinematography and storytelling. The young cast delivers outstanding performances, but Nikki's performance deserves special recognition. It easily ranks among the best acting performances I've seen in a psychological thriller.

The pacing is one of the film's greatest strengths. It never feels rushed or overstretched, and I honestly don't think a shorter or longer runtime would have made it any better. The tension builds gradually, with each turning point increasing the suspense naturally instead of relying on constant shocks. At a time when horror films have a harder time standing out in theaters, Obsession separates itself from its peers and becomes an even more rewarding experience on the big screen.

I expected a few jump scares, but one of them genuinely caught me off guard-I can't remember the last time a horror film made me jump like that. I watched the movie with my girlfriend, and during the first act we kept joking about the woman's behavior because it seemed almost relatable. As the story unfolded, though, those jokes slowly turned into an amusing but very real sense of tension that stayed with us all the way home. That's exactly what good horror should do. For me, Obsession deserves to be remembered as one of the standout horror films of 2026.

The acting and practical effects were solid, but the story has zero twists, and is too predictable. How is it possible that the B horror movies like the Wishmaster series were able to do the "careful what you wish for" plot device better than this film? The wish that kicks off the main story isn't even formulated poorly or intentionally misinterpreted. It just goes bad with no apparent reason. The main character (Bear) figures out fairly early what is going on, but then, throughout the film, he's doing absolutely nothing to try and fix the issue until the last 5 minutes. In fact, he acts so incredibly dumb that it hurts the suspension of disbelief.

I'm not sure why the movie was overhyped. Most probably it was a combination of popular themes (relationships, partnership violence and consent) and the general fatigue with Hollywood slop, especially with the flop of recent blockbuster movies such as Supergirl and others. It really looks like people wanted to stick it to the Man and overhyped this.

Still, it's not too bad, just nowhere near the rating and hype it has.

I never review movies and I don't typically watch horror movies but this was so original and fun! The acting was incredible and I found myself sweating from anxiety but also laughing a bunch.

I love that this will become a cult classic and that it cost basically nothing to make. Congrats to everyone who worked on this.

summary: A Stylish Horror Film That Never Fully Delivers
text:
Obsession is an entertaining watch with a solid central idea and a few clever directorial choices. While it falls under the horror genre, it rarely reaches the level of tension or dread that great horror films are known for. The concept feels more like an expanded version of the creative horror shorts often found on YouTube-interesting and engaging, but not particularly groundbreaking.

The standout element is undoubtedly Nikki's performance. Her acting carries much of the film's emotional weight and elevates scenes that might otherwise feel ordinary. The film also deserves credit for its visual presentation and the message it tries to convey, both of which add some depth to the experience.

My main issue is that the film feels somewhat overrated. It's a decent horror movie, but not an exceptional one. When compared to recent genre standouts such as Talk to Me or especially Bring Her Back, it falls short. Those films create genuine unease during the viewing experience and linger in your mind long after the credits roll. Obsession, on the other hand, is enjoyable in the moment but lacks the lasting psychological impact that separates good horror from great horror.

Rating: 6.5/10.

summary: Would Bear be willing to suffer the sacrifice of his identity for Nikki?
text:
At the end of Bear's phone call to the One Wish Willow helpline, after hearing the agonized screams of what sounds like Nikki imprisoned in the background, what if the operator told Bear that there was just one, single possible alteration that Bear could choose to make to his wish:

Instead of wishing Nikki loved him more than any other person, Bear could wish to become a person that Nikki could love more than anyone.

Would Bear even consider risking switching places, potentially sacrificing his own identity and autonomy for his supposed "love", in order to save and restore Nikki's identity and autonomy, while also preserving his chance to still be with her?

The only great thing about Obsession is its marketing. I don't think I have seen such a masterful display of marketing for a movie in my life, people just couldn't shut up about this move. I finally decided to go see the movie with a friend last week and we were not impressed at all. My watching experience was horrendous due to the fact that my theater would not keep quiet, but even if I did have a better viewing experience I don't think it would have changed much for me. First off this movie is REALLY slow. The story moved at a snail's pace for about 85% of the film before finally picking up a little bit toward the end. This move could have been cut to a one hour runtime if it had good pacing. The slow pacing really wouldn't have been much of an issue if it weren't for how terrible these characters are. Everyone in this movie has rocks in their skull. The main character could have easily gotten himself out of/fixed the situation he was in if he wasn't such an insolent chud. His friend is even dumber with him making a ridiculously dumb decision at the end of the movie for the sake of the plot. The acting isn't as lousy as the writing but it is still just plain bad. I visibly cringed in my seat when bear started crying, I don't think I have ever seen an actor so bad at crying. When a horror movie that tries to take itself seriously has bad acting it really takes away from the effect that the director is going for and this is on full display in Obsession. I feel like this movie actually could have been scary if there was more than one good actor (Inde Navarrette) in the movie. Almost all of the scares in this movies are obnoxiously loud noises. I jumped in my seat a couple times not because the movie was scary but because every time there was a loud noise it sounded like a 21 gun salute. The premise of the movie was basic but had potential to be a decent film however a decent film we did not get. I'm not sure that this film would have been any better with a higher budget just because of how bad the writing was. Overall this movie is a waste of a movie ticket wait for this to start streaming online if you want to waste 1 hour and 45 minutes.

summary: Way deeper than you may think.
text:
Marketed as another crazy-ex horror flick, but it's deeper than that. Bear wishes his friend Nikki will love him more than anyone else after a magic toy grants him one wish. It works instantly. Nikki gets obsessively attached, but it's clearly not really her: she's fighting it from the inside.

The key beat people miss: the "real Nikki" doesn't know Bear caused it until he asks her "is Nikki happy." That's the moment she realizes he knew all along, which is why she suddenly turns on him afterward. The "possessed" Nikki would never want to hurt him; only the real one, once she connects the dots and gets angry.

From there it spirals: she kills their friend Sarah by smashing her head against a brick after Sarah warns Bear and hints at her own feelings for him. Bear tries and fails to reverse the wish; their friend Ian gets shot dead by Nikki when he walks in on the aftermath. Cornered, Bear swallows pills to kill himself but changes his mind, right as Nikki breaks the last wish-toy, pulling"wish-Bear" out to kiss her before he dies. As she's about to shoot herself too, the real Nikki regains control and screams out all the pain she suffered while being "controlled".

It's not really a "crazy woman" horror story, it's about a guy who knows exactly what consent means and chooses to ignore it because it benefits him. Bleak, uncomfortable, well made.

Genuinely a disturbing movie, but that was the point, and man was it done so well. The underlying message of this story is so clear, and so heartbreaking. I think what makes it so much more disturbing is how you put it into context of what would happen in real life. Someone who may have unrequited feelings for someone, and that person, instead of living with it, takes what they want anyways. So many women deal with the real life version of this story. Of course, without the theatrics, possession, and gore.

Inde did such an amazing job playing Nikki, this movie wouldn't be as disturbing as it is without her amazing performance. And Bear's character- absolutely disgusting. There are so many instances where he chose himself over Nikki.

1. When he called the company about the wish, and instead of saying yes that he wanted to cancel it, his initial response was to want to alter it.

2. Making the wish in the first place.

3. Constantly realizing it was the wish that messed up Nikki and STILL doing things with her and staying with her against her will.

4. The fact that he went into the store initially to buy a crystal necklace for Nikki, and ended up buying the wish. He knew deep down he wanted it for himself, but he tried to pass it off as if it was for her.

Even his friends realized that he was taking advantage of her, despite them not knowing the full extent of what was happening, and he kept denying it, because deep down he's a selfish person. And he only tried to off himself after the fake Nikki killed Sarah. And even then, he couldn't even shoot himself, he took the pills to overdose.

The last scene where Nikki comes back to herself and realizes everything that happened and starts sobbing... it sent chills down my spine.

Props to the actors in this movie. Especially Inde. And Curry Barker did an amazing job with this movie and so tragically and accurately portraying what it's like to experience being violated like that.

I've been a fan of Curry Barker & Cooper Tomlinson for a while now; from their "That's a Bad Idea" skits to their short horror films, I've always thought their work showed real talent and creativity.

Obsession was no exception. A fantastic theater debut that was written and directed incredibly well. It had me genuinely unsettled, creeped out, laughing at times, and fully invested the entire way through. The mix of psychological horror, gore, tension, and dark humor worked perfectly together without feeling overdone.

Some of the imagery and scenes were seriously disturbing in the best way possible, and the atmosphere kept building until the end.

Definitely gonna have a sleep paralysis demon standing in the corner of my room watching me tonight.

Broooooo! This was refreshing.

I kept on thinking this guy is the weirdo not Nikki 🤣 But the jumpscares were legit and I've not had jumpscares in a long time! I really liked this one.

The movie also goes to show how what you wish for is not always what it seems.

And in our culture they always tell us a relationship born out of spells never has a good ending 🤣

This is a pretty solid psychological horror film. Now I am about to get hated on for saying this but its not as good as EVERYONE is saying it is. Its Good, but its not as good as everyone is band wagoning here. I dont know if Jason Blum is behind all this by paying tons of money for all the positivity here or not but the fact is its a basic simple story that gets repetitive and really is more of a dark comedy then anything. Theres nothing scary here (other than the movie is relatable in multiple ways of relationships), its eerie and weird, which isnt a bad thing.

This is basically a monkey paw story as young newcomer writer and director Curry Barker stated he took 'Monkey Paw Simpsons Episode' and turned it into this lol.

Now the interesting part is the fact it was shot for about $750k and has grossed over $30 million as of May 21st 2026 and its only been in theaters for about a week. Which is really impressive as that number will continue to climb, then streaming will come, etc. Whats even more impressive is the fact this A24 style feature film was sold for over $15 million to Focus Features to distribute it beating out many others. Which is crazy...but then you also have to go back and look at this as a business which Jason Blum is alot about the money. Focus Features has to have a good theatrical run to make a profit after they shelled out over $15 million for it. So I get it...and this movie is going to continue to make waves for a while and it will turn into some sort of classic

The film is shot pretty cleverly as the cinematography is basically long takes and we dont get your generic shots. Theres art behind it! Thank you God! Finally!

Barker now has nothing to worry about for the rest of his life as hes already in talks with a sequel, another Texas Chainsaw film, and another film that has Bryce Dallas Howard and Aaron Paul in it...same goes for lead actors Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette (who is about to be the next Jenna Ortega mega star from this film

My biggest complaint here and I didnt even watch a trailer or read anything about it. But ended up watching the trailer afterwards and its a good trailer. Its just not the movie you get. Theres no plot twists or anything clever in the writing unfortunately

The movie is simple. A really weird dude has a crush on a close friend but doesnt have the guts to tell her his true feelings. After breaking something of hers, he goes to the store to buy her a new one but decides to buy a 'One Wish Willow' that looks like something you would find at Cracker Barrel and wishes that this girl will be in love with him. Well she does and it gets wayyyyyy out of hand

SPOILERS
The movie centers around a really weird dude named Bear (Michael Johnston) who in reality would not be hanging with the characters hes friends with. They all work at a small music shop run by Andy Richter (who has like 2 lines and 5 seconds of screen time, I guess hes probably friends with someone that help make the film just to have a name attached). The friends are Ian (Cooper Tomlinson, Barkers good friend), Sarah (Megan Lawless), and the films focal point Nikki (Inde Navarrette) who actually does not seem like a good friend/person.

Heres the dynamics...Bear has one male friend in Ian. Bear has a crush on Nikki. Sarah has a crush on Bear (for some reason)

Somehow all 4 of these friends have their own houses working a low paying job. But anyways...

The first part of the movie consists of Bear trying to get the courage to tell Nikki his true feelings but he just cant. His friend Ian tries to help him but Bear is just that weird and cant

After repetive scenes we finally get to the main story when Bear goes into a small store to get a new necklace for Nikki that he broke. He sees a little box called 'One Wish Willow' that apparently grants you one wish. Bear ends up taking Nikki home and she tells him shes into a guy MORE ON THIS BELOW. And Bear thinks this might be the time to finally tell Nikki his feelings about her. Instead he doesnt and she gets out of the car and Bear is upset with himself and makes the wish. Immediately it becomes true

So for the majority of the movie here we get more repetitive scenes of Nikki becoming OBSESSED with Bear. Its immediately overwhelming even for Bear. The movie does introduce this possession type thing with Nikki as the real Nikki has no control over her body and doesnt know whats going on as the 'entity' seems to be trying to take over...well

The movie then proceeds to ditch that for most of the movie and Nikki gets weirder and weirder and crazier and crazier. The friends just blow it off like its nothing but they do realize Nikki is wacko and dont want her around.

Bear knows its wrong and doesnt know how to get Nikki back normal. He tries calling the number on the back of the box and the only way out of it is if he dies or someone else makes a wish to break 'the curse'

Bear goes back and forth from not wanting Nikki and scared to wanting her to himself even though she is so wacko. Theres some memorable scenes of Nikki that are creepy

As the movie goes on Nikki's behavior gets worse and becomes violent as Bear is basically hiding her in his house

Skimming through things really bad when Bear seems to be hitting it off with Sarah but Nikki ends up violently killing her...this is a good memorable scene

Bear then decides to help cover up the murder for Nikki. Though Bear is losing it more and more

Eventually Bear convinces Ian about the One Wish Willow and wishes for a billion dollars and gets it, only for Nikki to kill him quickly. Now Bear has to worry about 2 dead people

The movie finally goes back to when Nikki was first 'possessed' and they show that the real Nikki can speak to Bear as 'fake' Nikki sleeps. Which I dont know why they didnt do more of this. Basically the real Nikki sees whats going on and wants help....and I agree with her

Bear because he loves Nikki so much and its gotten so out of hand decides to take a bunch of pills to off himself to save Nikki because he does love her. He dies and right before fake Nikki is about to off herself because she is so upset that Bear is dead, the real Nikki then gets to take over her body again. Just like the 'customer service' person from One Wish Willow said. The end!

The only little plot twist and its pretty obvious and doesnt go anywhere is that Bear learns that Nikki and Ian have been hooking up. But again it doesnt go anywhere nor does it affect Bear in anyway as he continues to be friends with Ian

So back to the possesion thing with the real Nikki is actually present and is aware of whats going on shouldve been shown more and given Bear more reasons to still have HIS OBSESSION and other reasons as well

The one thing the movie shouldve done but it decides not to do, but Director Barker states he was going to have it in the movie was when Nikki tells Bear earlier in the film shes into this one guy, AND IT SHOULDVE BEEN REVEALED AT THE END THAT THE GUY WAS ACTUALLY BEAR...meaning not only is this a crazy love/obsession story and tries to do the A24 tragedy horror but really make this story hit with the real tragedy that Bear made the wish for no reason whatsoever!!! Thats the ultimate gut punch! Unfortunately we dont get that...I thought it was coming but after the reveal of the secret relationship of Nikki and Ian, I knew it was off the table

I do feel bad for Sarah as she is super cool, nice, and attractive so not sure why Bear didnt want her as the real Nikki just doesnt seem like a nice person

Anyways...the movie is good. I am not sure if Barker is a one hit wonder here but hes going to get the opportunity to showcase more filmmaking abilities. Hes still super young born in 1999 I believe. He seemed like a seasoned very talented film director here with this film. He made alot of good filmmaking choices and uniqueness. Which is great! His writing though I am not sure as this films creativity overshadowed the writing weaknesses

Everyone is going crazy over Inde Navarrette with her performance as Nikki and its definitely good. But I am going to give a TON of credit to Michael Johnston who I believe delivers the best performance, though the character can get annoying but Johnston here has the harder acting job and he pulls it off. Navarrette gets to ham act, Johnston doesnt. So again major props to Johnston!

Very solid 'Psychological Horror/Dark Comedy'...everything is well done but the writing is shaky and the lack of locations. The film also shouldve been shorter as the movie does drag regardless of people saying it doesnt.

Again its pretty good and enjoyable. Theres laughs, creepy moments, and some gore.

6.7/10.

summary: Obsession: When Human Frailty Becomes Horror
text:
I rarely like horror movies because usually we get zero character development, scary masks or absurd-looking monsters, and, in some cases, disgusting scenes of torture.

This one is a great example of how none of that is necessary. Something-or someone-doesn't actually have to look scary to be terrifying. A very good-looking, slim girl can be much creepier than any grotesque monster if the acting and psychological tension are strong enough - and Inde absolutely nailed her role.

Horror has proved again and again that it isn't grotesque appearances, graphic violence, or cheap jump scares that make antagonists frightening, but what the films make us understand and fear about them. Psycho, The Shining, The Omen - very different movies, but they all understand something similar. Yet, strangely, so many horror filmmakers still seem to ignore this.

That's also what I liked so much about Obsession. I'm glad its creators chose to rely on solid acting, atmosphere, and an exploration of damaged human psychology. What I found most disturbing, though, wasn't even the obsession itself, but Baron's response to it. His weakness, passivity, and refusal to put a stop to something he can clearly see spiraling out of control are what make the whole situation genuinely frightening to me. The horror isn't just in what happens, but in the very human flaws that allow it to happen.

Loved it! Maybe not for everyone, but for someone like me, who hates pointless violence and unbelievable monsters, this is a solid horror movie.

A decent film but overall nothing special. No idea why it's being glazed so hard. Inde is solid, if a bit over the top. The plot is weak and forced, not to mention rehashed. Most of the characters are unrelatable and unlikable. I genuinely get the feeling that most of the hype is coming from younger folks who just haven't seen many movies yet. It's like Longlegs all over again.

I'll start by saying that, for me, this movie is closer to an 8 than a 9. However, considering the current state of the horror genre, I think it easily deserves that rating. I honestly struggle to understand how so many mediocre horror films end up being so highly talked about.

As for the movie itself, it's incredibly well made, especially considering its budget. It has absolutely nothing to be ashamed of. The performances are excellent, the pacing is consistently engaging, so the film never feels boring, the soundtrack works really well, and the story is both original and compelling.

I honestly don't have many criticisms. In fact, I was quite hesitant to watch it at first. These days, whenever a movie or TV series is surrounded by massive hype, it's usually a red flag for me. But this time, the hype was deserved. I can definitely recommend it-I had a great time watching it.

This was a very well done jump scare horror movie with some great acting that could have had a much more profound meaning. While it was obvious that Nikki's free will was only being masked by the wish, the idea that no external forces other than human interaction can affect free will was not delivered.

I am genuinely stunned by the overwhelmingly positive ratings for this movie. What exactly are people seeing in it that I completely missed?

The biggest problem is that there is virtually no meaningful story or plot. The movie keeps stretching a thin premise for nearly two hours, mistaking slowness for depth and awkwardness for suspense. Scenes drag on endlessly, yet very little of substance happens. There is no compelling mystery, no engaging character arc, and no narrative momentum to keep the audience invested. Instead, the film feels relentlessly cringe and creepy in an uncomfortable way. Not because it is genuinely unsettling or psychologically profound, but because so much of it comes across as bizarre, awkward, and self-indulgent.

What surprised me most is that even classic anthology shows like The Twilight Zone managed to tell complete, engaging stories within 20-30 minutes. Their plots could be dark, dystopian, or strange, but there was always an idea, a purpose, and a payoff. This movie somehow struggles to justify an entire feature-length runtime with far less substance.

Perhaps some viewers appreciate the symbolism or metaphorical aspects, but a movie must first work as a movie. It needs a narrative that progresses, characters worth caring about, and a reason to remain invested. I found none of those here.

The high ratings are honestly baffling. If this is the direction in which modern cinema is heading, it is a little worrying. A film cannot survive on atmosphere, awkwardness, and vague symbolism alone. At some point, it needs substance.

Unfortunately, this one didn't have any.

The horror genre rarely surprises me anymore, but Obsession managed to do just that. Rather than chasing cheap scares, it builds dread around a haunting idea: sometimes the greatest horror isn't failing to achieve your lifelong dream, but finally attaining it only to watch it transform into your worst nightmare before your eyes.

Obsession was such a fun watch. It honestly had me laughing way more than I expected, but at the same time the dark horror vibe never really disappears. That balance made the whole movie feel unpredictable - one moment you're laughing, the next you're wondering what insane thing is about to happen next.

What I liked most was how it kept me guessing the entire time, especially with where the story was heading and how it would all end. The tension stayed there from start to finish without feeling boring or dragged out. Overall, it was a great watch and definitely one I'd recommend if you like horror with a twisted, entertaining edge.

summary: Solid Wish granting story with psychological thriller/drama undertones
text:
Bear (Michael Johnston), Nikki (Inde Navarrette), Ian (Cooper Tomlinson), and Sarah (Megan Lawless) all work at a musical equipment shop as a closeknit group of friends, but when Bear finds a curio shop and buys a One Wish Willow novelty item, he makes the only logical wish: to have Nikki love him more than anyone else in the world. What goes from a simple request turns into a nightmare as the personality of Nikki changes drastically in 'Obsession'.

The cinematography and the acting are all very well done! Inde Navarrette does a great job with her psychological manipulation role; she makes the film work. The script is a little predictable, but there are some neat points that may surprise the viewers. A couple of plot holes and some not clearly defined characters give a little bit to be desired, but the film does make a logical and twisty ending!

Definitely worth a watch!

Great movie! I enjoyed the storyline and the acting. It wasn't the regular horror movie that you see. There was lots to think about, and I think it was really a well thought out and well acted movie.

Makes you think about life and sometimes how the things we wish for the most are actually what we do not need. The irony of life! It was a quite interesting ending as well.

A fun darkly comedic horror that surprised me a bit.

I haven't watched much from Curry Barker but it's pretty clear Barker satirical take on the romantic horror male gaze genre is both creative and horrifying comical. The way how Barker explores the topic about love and obsession does lead into some interesting direction choices, atmospheres, and developments throughout. Particularly, how Barker presents the setting, camerawork, and style does add a lot to the writing. For a low-budget horror, Barker does take advantage of it's budget and still adds a lot of creative outlooks with how things are presented and all.

Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette are both violently insane, in the both ways possible as Johnston pathetically-like yet darkly comical performance sells, and Navarrette turning into monkey insanity mode was just awesome! The chemistry between their dynamics and dialogue are just wonderful, which does help a lot to make the characters interesting and funny to explore.

I'll be honest, not everything did sell the movie for me. Particularly some of the structure does feel a bit overlong and some aspects of the writing, to my surprise, did come off a bit predictable which I really wished I didn't have that mindset.

But overall, a good horror movie.

Finally, a horror movie that is actually interesting. There were scenes where I was truly pressed back into my seat... The music and cinematography also deserve praise, as does the atmosphere of unease. Although the plot is predictable at times, the film is compelling overall. It prompts reflection on how obsession can disrupt lives and lead to tragedy. It's a must-watch for fans of thrillers; it delivers genuine chills and keeps you guessing about what will happen next. It's a horror-thriller that manages to scare you and stays with you long after it ends. With its dark atmosphere and surprising plot twists, the film is exciting, sometimes truly terrifying, and genuinely engaging. I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys intense emotions and unexpected twists. (P. S. I almost shat myself.)

There are films that get richer days or even weeks after you watch them. You replay scenes in your head, discover new meanings, notice filmmaking choices you missed the first time. Obsession had the exact opposite effect on me.

The more I thought about it, the flatter it became. So much of the discussion around it revolves around agency, consent, "incel culture", toxic relationships... but the film itself barely engages with any of it beyond broad, painfully obvious gestures. Naming your protagonist Bear because, you know... bear vs. Man. Get it? That's about the level of subtlety we're dealing with.

I also hate criticizing the visuals of low-budget films simply for looking, well, low-budget. Great filmmakers often turn limitations into style. There's one genuinely brilliant shot here - Nikky barely visible in the darkness of a doorway - that hints at what this director is possibly capable of, visually at least. Unfortunately, the rest feels like the increasingly standardized "elevated indie horror" starter pack with centered compositions, a boxier aspect ratio to scream isolation, endless shallow depth of field to scream isolation even louder, and a color grade I'd rather not even get into.

The saving grace here is Inde Navarrette. She single-handedly gives the film the emotional layers everyone seems convinced are already there. Her presence, instincts, physicality, vulnerability - she elevates every scene almost effortlessly. If anyone deserves credit for this film's impact, it's her. The director should buy her a house.

I'm genuinely excited to see what both of them do next. But if I had to bet on who benefits most from this box-office phenomenon, the answer is easy.

For full transparency, I've been a fan of the "That's a Bad Idea" YT channel for years, and have always rooted for Cooper and Curry.

Setting that aside, this an awesome movie. This belongs in the pantheon right alongside Get Out, It Follows, Smile, and Weapons. An interesting and relatable plot, great suspense and tension building, gruesome moments, and a concise ending.

I think that Curry is going to be a huge force in cinema and I'm excited for his future projects.

I saw this one advertised & wasn't too sure if it would be any good. I'd seen trailers but wasn't convinced as it was one of those weird Horror flicks. Nonetheless, I went to see this one & went in with an open mind.

After breaking the mysterious "One Wish Willow" to win his crush's heart, a hopeless romantic finds himself getting exactly what he asked for but soon discovers that some desires come at a dark & sinister price.

I found the film to be not bad. It's got a unique concept, though I have seen similiar to this, so not entirely unique. The pacing is off as with the overly long runtime of 1 hour & 46 minutes (106 minutes). The cast do a good job with their roles & the characters they play.

The story could've used some work & the plot kind of went nowhere to an ending which felt like a copout instead of one which could've been better & conclusive. The film has some annoying overuse of naging sounds & screaming to the point where it becomes an assault to the ears.

There's some gory moments here, really gory if you ask me & some ace eye candy with the women. I did feel more backstory or history on the One Wish Willow could've been better as well as a conclusive ending instead of the copout one we got. The film has its moments, but it's decent.

Overall, it's overrated for what it is & not as good as made out. But, it's a decent watch & one you'll get some mild enjoyment out of if you're looking for something weird or something to kill off time with. It's not one I'd highly recommend or jump up & down about, but it's one I'd say you should watch at least once.

6/10.

After reading reviews and noting the high rating we were expecting a more slow burn psychological drama. Very disappointing, unbelievable and juvenile. May be popular with under 25 year olds but not for adults! I suppose the concept should have been a clue. Very disappointing. There are far better films and mini series based on obsession of a disturbing nature.

summary: Maybe in top two of the worst films I have ever seen
text:
An obsessed guy wishes a girl will fall in love with him. The wish comes true.

Obviously such a wish is bound to turn astray. So, removing a person's total autonomy to stroke the ego of oneself - what could possible go wrong?

A guy refuses to take responsible for his actions or his life, and receives a moral, metaphorical (and literal) punishment for it. Are you seriously (re-)using that trope?

I feel the need to quote Edward Norton in "Fight Club": "[...] Everything is a copy of a copy of a copy....".

So, Obsession, control and removal of autonomy in love leads to catastrophic results? Oh, really? Are you kidding me? Is this supposed to be new information? Does this go for intellectual and emotional knowledge? Is this really necessary to teach viewers of this generation?

If so, we as a species are in serious trouble.

Maybe the first great gen-z horror movie, and it feels like a bit of a middle finger to the elevated horror that those who got their breaks directing 2010s horror often seemed to make. There's no ambiguity about the supernatural element, right from when the supernatural stuff takes effect, and no "oooh is it in their heads and what if that's scarier?" thing. Don't get me wrong, I do sometimes love that kind of horror movie. I love a good horror movie that does that kind of thing well, and I hate a bad horror movie that doesn't do that kind of thing well (like the Smile movies, which make me Frown).

But in this horror movie, a guy half-heartedly makes a wish for his crush to love him, with a cursed object that works. And she does. It made me think of that one episode of Buffy the Vampire Slayer where Xander makes all the women in Sunnydale fall in love with him, just with only one person, and it was a stock plot when Buffy did it.

I'm beyond surprised they made it work here and made it scary. I'm pleasantly surprised the director's so young. I'm surprised they made the main actress (Inde Navarrette) actually progressively frightening when she looks like a model, and that's also commendable acting, of course. Same for the lead actor (Michael Johnston), who sells it all somehow.

I don't know, I felt nauseous watching this. I liked how visceral it was when it just sounded so dumb on paper, and I was skeptical of this story working with that cast and with a filmmaker so young. But they made it work. There are admittedly these little moments where I questioned things, and I think the film just doesn't include characters who would be inconvenient for the plot with a bit of a screenwriting shrug (maybe it would've been more believable to address, even just a little more, where all the older adults in these young adult's lives were, because the film does seem to take place over at least a few weeks), but then I come back to that barebones premise. It's just a wish gone wrong movie.

Maybe nothing else really matters all that much, with such a sincere approach to a dark fairy tale-like narrative. If it makes you squirm in your seat, laugh nervously every scene or two (this is a really funny movie in parts, honestly), and has you on the verge of a panic attack throughout much of its second half, then I think that's more than enough.

In my opinion, this was the best horror movie of the last couple of years. Perfectly timed comedy and jump scares.

The cast was perfect, especially Inde Navarrette. She played her character perfectly. Again, this is all in my opinion, but I really loved it.

I had the luck to see this before it was released and I would advise everyone that has the opportunity to go see it. 10/10
Will watch again. :)

summary: An Unexpected Masterpiece - The Hype is Absolutely Real (9.7/10)
text:
I kept seeing everyone talk about this movie everywhere, and honestly, I thought it was just massive exaggeration-until I finally watched it myself. I was completely blown away.

First off, the entire cast deserves a massive standing ovation. Every single performance felt raw, authentic, and deeply real. You don't just watch these characters; you feel everything they are going through.

What sets this film apart is its sheer originality. It breaks away from typical Hollywood tropes and brings something genuinely fresh to the table. On an emotional level, it's an absolute roller coaster-it hits you with moments of pure joy, deep dread, and genuine surprise. And the horror elements? Perfection. There are about six jump scares, and not a single one felt cheap or forced. They land exactly when and how they are supposed to, amplifying the tension naturally.

Then there's Sarah. Even though she didn't get the most screen time, her character arc completely stole the show. Her development, the way she was written, and the brilliant performance behind her made her conclusion incredibly impactful. She easily became my favorite character.

As for the ending, it was flawless. I wouldn't change a single frame; it wraps up the story perfectly.

This isn't just a good movie; it's a phenomenal one. A massive 9.7/10 from me.

summary: The best horror movie in recent years?
text:
Obsession might actually be one of the best horror movies out there, and it's crazy that its budget was roughly $750k. It wasn't exaggerated with some cgi monster jump scares and stuff like that, but it had me going, "What the hell?" Trust me, it has been a while since a horror movie made me feel like that.

The story is pretty basic: a shy guy makes a wish for his crush to love him. What makes it hit so hard, though, is that the characters feel completely real. Even the wishes are highly relatable like I said before, wishing for your crush or making that billion-dollar wish makes a perfect sense. It's exactly what real people would actually do. At first, you think, "What's the worst that can happen?" but then everything gets completely out of hand. The truly terrifying part is the slow tension throughout the movie and the music really works too.

Lastly, I just want to praise Inde, bro. The acting is pretty good in general, but Inde's acting skills are crazy, she has the potential to be the horror icon. I know her from Superman & Lois, and let me tell you, I could never imagine she could pull off something like "freaky Nikki" this well.

To sum everything up: "absolute cinema."

While Obsession deserves some credit for its concept and its impressive box office run as a micro-budget indie, it severely struggles under the weight of its own hype. It has been paraded around as some sort of groundbreaking Gen Z cinematic revolution, but the actual execution feels deeply flawed and structurally uneven.

The film's biggest issue is that it fundamentally doesn't know what it wants to be. It flirts with dark relationship anxiety and body horror, yet routinely undercuts its own tension by acting downright goofy on far too many occasions. Because it constantly shifts gears between disturbing psychological thriller and off-kilter, sketch-comedy-style awkwardness, the logic of the world collapses. Instead of grounding the high-stakes premise with tight character logic, the script relies on frustrating character choices and tonal whiplash.

It's an okay, mildly entertaining midnight movie if you go in with zero expectations, but it is far from a masterpiece. Strip away the internet hype, and you're left with a disjointed genre mashup that lacks a cohesive vision.

Inde deserves an award for this performance. She made this movie. What a creepy off beat movie. Inde needs to be in more movies like this. She killed this role, literally. The story was simple yet really really good. I was amazed by Indes performance. This will skyrocket her into way more leading roles.

Hear me out. A parody of the typical love story of two 20 something coworkers in a menial job having an obsessive short and toxic relationship that plays heavily into the young adult zeitgeist, with a nice guy protagonist that isn't really all that nice.

Except while 500 days was very hipster self affacing while still smelling its own farts film that fit the millennial era, Obsession is a way more nihilistic and bleak but still made to be easier to clip for tik tok and memes that fits the gen z era.

Thats part of the reason why this has gotten such hype online. Because outside its very Gen Z framing, the themes explore feelings every generation in the cultural prime struggles with: Shifty friend groups of wayward young adults hiding their feelings, esp unrequited ones. You've been there, your parents have been there, and your kids will one day be there.

As well as the idea of content creators out of the industry basically putting together a popular film with duct tape and determination with mostly online marketting is something that Gen Z likes to get behind. It is a bit of hometown heroes syndrome as well.

And to be clear, I did enjoy this movie. This is not a take down, just like I enjoyed 500 days of summer when it spoke to me at that age. And I will admit that there was one moment that made me levitate out of my seat.

But overall it's only the best horror movie of the year specifically for afformentioned reasons and because it is better than anything horror released this year. As a standalone horror movie and on its own merits, it's pretty good, but wouldn't stand up against the best from other years with better competition.

The main issue is the story and characters. If you're too old to really relate to 20 somethings doing everything but acting like adults, then you will never develop any sympathy or liking for any character prior to the horror events. I personally found them all to just be really crappy people and am way past an age where unrequited feelings and dealing with toxic friend groups is a relatable life stress.

Imo good horror needs to still have characters you actually like who are dealing with the horror and bad as that makes you feel it directly, but outside of all the events obviously being objectively unfair and horrible to most of the characters, I didn't actually care it was happening to these people specifically. I really just couldn't agree with any action anyone took any time.

Its budgetary constraints also were hard to ignore. A lot of the movie is color corrected to be really dark, which sometimes adds to the horror but often just made me think they're hiding bad effects or it was cheaper than doing effects or other ways to hide Inde's stunt double (they hired a dancer for certain scenes). It kind of got overused a lot.

As impressive as the film was relative to its constraints, it also doesn't completely compensate for them. It felt less professional and polished than a film made by a more experienced team. Kind of had extended YouTube original film energy a lot of the time. I think Curry Barker's best is to be seen, this is just his foothold into the industry.

Overall it is shocking to me this is being lauded as the best horror film made by YouTubers when the Philippou brothers are making more polished productions while on higher but still restrictive budgetary constraints, and with stories and themes that deal with much deeper and more powerful topics.

But probably why I love those films (esp Bring Her Back) is the polar opposite of why people love this film and they can make the reverse arguments to me.

A real nightmare. It feels like a creepypasta pasted straight from your mind onto the screen. Awesome balanced horror, perfect amount of jump scares, insane tension building, great pacing, gore used exactly where it's needed. I'm a big fan of the audio jumpscares they used a bunch, especially paired with the smash cut (e.g. Bear going into the bathroom to kill himself with Nikki banging on the door). Great performance by Michael Johnston, and Inde Navarrette blew me away even more with her expressions and overall acting. How can such a tiny woman be so terrifying? 2 guys from the group sitting next to me LEFT THE CINEMA after the first real scary scene (her watching him sleep from the corner). The cinematography is just amazing, the soundtrack is amazing, the sound design is AMAZING. The way mundane things are made horrifying, like Nikki pulling Sarah back in the chair during the drink game, is just exquisite. As a seasoned horror vet I haven't been properly jumpscared in years, but the way they set up Sarahs death with the acceptance letter, where I was almost rolling my eyes like "she's gonna get into Luther and instantly die" and she just got bashed before I was even ready, my god, the whole cinema JUMPED including me!

The only things holding me back from giving this a 10/10 are: lack of explanation for the mechanisms of evil. Why is she reversing back into the shadows like that? Why is she making cat sandwiches? It feels silly at times, I don't think it adds to the movie. The store as well, I don't want the clerks to be as aware as they were of the one wish willow. Lastly, the main characters decision making could be more consistent. He seemed like a smart decent capable individual at first, but then they started to build him as a worse person so killing him in the finale wouldn't feel as mean-spirited.

So disappointing. I desperately wanted to love this and the blurb is exactly the kind to woo me, but it is so unbearable boring and stale and the main actor is annoying as hell (or maybe the character). Didn't even want to continue it. Even the most popular scene was underwhelming and weird. Oh my god.

summary: Familiar (in a good way), but unpredictable and disturbing (also in a good way)
text:
I missed screening this at Fantastic Fest last year, so my anticipation has been building for months after so much good word of mouth in Austin and then at Sundance.

Happy to report 'Obsession' is terrific. Excellent performances from the two leads, especially Inde Navarrette as Nikki, the unwitting victim of a "wish" that makes her fall madly in love with Bear (Daniel Johnston).

Writer-director Curry Barker puts his own spin on a classic "monkey's paw" story and the story hits that sweet spot of feeling familiar and fun, but also frequently disturbing and unpredictable. Most surprising to me was Barker allowing the film to push beyond the surface-level horror ("this woman is so obsessed she's DANGEROUS") into more existential terror, as we start to understand what the "wish" feels like from Nikki's point of view. It's only touched on briefly here and there (I think that was the right choice to keep it a bit mysterious), but those moments really stuck with me.

Among the best horror movies I've ever seen. Didn't need any monsters or demons to scare people, just a very good actress. The plot is very original and the ending reminds me of greek tragedies. You can immediately catch the message behind the movie: the fear of rejection and the view of the woman just as an "item of love" which isn't able to decide who to love, but forced by a curse. Perfect.

summary: A Diabolical Psychological Thriller That Leaves You Completely Chilled
text:
Obsession is real, psychological horror. You know the genre is hitting exactly where it needs to when you can actively feel a scare coming, yet the execution still completely floors you.

At first, the premise sets up what feels like a standard, creepy thriller rooted in a scriptwriter's specific romantic fixation. But the moment the plot actually starts moving, it brilliantly morphs from a simple, desperate bid for affection into something entirely unhinged.

A massive highlight of the film is Inde Navarrette's performance. Her acting completely sells the nightmare; the way she utilizes voice modulation and shifts the pitch of her voice as she speaks is genuinely crazy and leaves you with absolute chills.

Character-wise, there is a lot of room for frustration, which only heightens the tension. The character of Bear is deeply flawed. While you can understand that he is deprived of love and blinded by a massive crush, his complete delusion over someone who clearly doesn't love him back pushes him into diabolical territory. The fact that he experiences things that are clearly not normal and fails to speak up to anyone about it is maddening.

There is a ton of narrative substance here-the director weaves in several intense side plots that could honestly spin off into their own standalone features. Ultimately, the ending lands perfectly. Unlike so many horror entries that fizzle out in the final act, Obsession sticks the landing by acting as a psychological thriller that terrifies you simply by showing you exactly how trapped the characters are.

If you have the stomach for genuine horror and still want to be able to sleep at night, go watch this immediately. It absolutely delivers on expectations.

First, Curry Barker - you're sensational. Especially your editing is genuinely flabbergasting.

His work really shows what happens when someone doesn't even have the bare minimum understanding of the self, society, values, and norms - especially regarding autonomy.

This film somehow took my own trauma and turned it into something that's genuinely class. Curry Barker is a brilliant filmmaker, and the way he sends the message about how awful these really important issues are...I honestly found myself wanting to clap.

The details are incredible, too - and I don't even know how to describe it properly, but the sheer, immense task of having to form your own emotions yourself is absolutely next level. In my opinion, you shouldn't be afraid of Nikki; you should feel for her.

Again, about the details: the things that are going on - you don't even think about the first time watching. Nikki just stands there the whole time - like, I think it's around nine hours?! - it's intense. Not only are ogres like onions - this film is too, and I do love these kinds of films.

Another detail many missed: this messed-up moment where she (cursed Nikki) tells him she'll take care of something really disturbing but important...and then flips it around and shows that exact circumstance right in his face. I'm not saying she's anything but the victim, because she clearly is - but it really captures what could happen when you don't care about someone's basic human rights or autonomy, and you start treating them like they're nothing. I personally see it as Bear getting his karma for not making things better for the real Nikki. "Verdict on Cat?" and the poem about Hansel and Gretel are, to me, messages from the real Nikki, who is trapped and seeking revenge.

Bear also wants everything to be convenient for him without having to face any real confrontation or consequences. No wonder many people, especially women, can relate to this film.

Hands down, my favourite film of the year. From the editing and acting to the cinematography, everything is excellent - especially the soundtrack by Rock Burwell!

It's an emotional rollercoaster. Neurodivergent people, be aware. And in my opinion, it should come with a trigger warning right at the beginning - just like in "Blink Twice".

P. S. I can also recommend Barker's "Milk & Serial" on YouTube, and while you're at it, watch his and Cooper's parody of "Talk to Me" as well ;)

summary: Made me smile and feel weird at the same time
text: Obsession was honestly a top movie. Very refreshing and different from what I expected. The storyline kept me interested the whole time and the movie had a really unique atmosphere. Obsession follows Bear, a hopeless and socially awkward young man who has the hots for his friend Nikki. Being unable to reveal to her how he feels, he acquires a 'one wish willow' from a crystal shop, intending to give it to her as a present. However, he ends up breaking it himself, wishing that she loved him more than anyone in the world. What follows is a terrifying journey that really does make you think - be careful what you wish for...

The whole horror community went kinda bonkers for this movie, with many youtubers who got to see early screenings at various festivals last year championing it as one to look out for... and oh boy, does it deliver.

The plot is nothing new really, being basically a modern retelling of The Monkey's Paw, but the way this film is shot and put together is utterly suffocating with its creepy and unnerving tone and visuals. The characters feel believable, and the performances were excellent, particularly Inde Naverrette who was absolutely incredible as the demented Nikki. The film utterly depended on her character being believably tragic yet terrifying, and she absolutely nailed it. 100% an actor to look out for in the future.

Beyond it's surface level horror, the film has a lot to say about controlling relationships and toxic behaviour... and even though Nikki provides all the scares and dread throughout the runtime, it is actually Bear who is the true monster here. Oh, and the ending is great, which makes a change for a modern horror.

I think it's fair to say that Obsession is essential viewing. It's easily the best new release I've seen in quite some time, and I look forward to seeing what Curry Barker does next.

summary: Obsession - Be Careful What You Wish For
text:
Contains spoilers

Obsession left me disgusted, shocked, upset, annoyed and, somehow, sorry for the people caught up in it.

The premise sounds simple enough. Bear is in love with his friend Nikki, gets the opportunity to make a wish at the One Wish Willow and wishes for her to love him back.

Honestly, I can understand the temptation.

Bear is young, insecure and unsure of himself. He actually seems to have the courage to tell Nikki how he feels at first, but then listens to his pretty obnoxious friend's player advice instead. He's frightened of uncertainty and rejection and suddenly gets offered the ultimate shortcut: what if you could simply know that the person you love feels the same way?

Who would genuinely believe the Willow was going to work anyway?

It's only after Nikki becomes possessed by obsession that everyone suddenly becomes interested in the rules. 😅 Realistically, I don't think that part could have happened much differently. Nobody is going to ask for the supernatural terms and conditions before making a wish they don't believe is real.

The problem is what Bear does after discovering that it is real.

At first, I could sympathise with him. Then I became increasingly frustrated.

Even when he calls the helpline, his first question is essentially whether he can adjust or edit the wish. He doesn't immediately want to free Nikki-he wants to turn the obsession down to a more manageable level.

Only later does he seriously want to cancel it.

And that's where I think the title Obsession really belongs to Bear.

Nikki becomes the supernatural embodiment of obsession, but Bear was already obsessed with her. The movie repeatedly shows beautiful women showing genuine interest in him and he barely notices because none of them are Nikki.

Even the waitress in the opening scene, who doesn't know him, swoons over his poetry. Sarah is gorgeous and interested in him too. Bear isn't some completely undesirable loner who needs magic to experience affection.

He doesn't just want love.

He wants Nikki's love.

And the frustrating part is that I think he might have had a chance anyway.

The real Nikki is charming, bubbly, gorgeous and has these cute little mannerisms that make her seem like a genuinely cool person to hang out with. She gives Bear plenty of windows where he could have simply taken the risk and told her how he felt.

Maybe she would have said yes.

Maybe she wouldn't have.

But it would have been her answer.

Instead, Bear removes the uncertainty-and therefore removes Nikki's choice.

That's what makes what happens to her so upsetting. I felt genuinely sorry for Nikki because I never saw possessed Nikki as completely replacing her. There are moments where it feels like the real Nikki briefly gets her hands back on the steering wheel, realises what is happening and completely freaks out.

Inde Navarrette absolutely nailed those moments.

Her performance was probably one of my favourite things about the movie. Possessed Nikki doesn't immediately become a generic horror villain. At first she's just wrong.

That first prolonged conversation after the wish is incredibly uncomfortable. She's desperately searching for an "in" with Bear, her smile is exaggerated and stays there far too long, and even her body starts behaving strangely. Then there's the bizarre cat memorial.

And eventually she becomes genuinely terrifying.

The scene that scared me most was Nikki standing in the corner of Bear's bedroom watching him sleep, wearing his jacket, before slowly creeping towards the bed.

That one got me.

It looked almost exactly like imagery from recurring nightmares I had as a kid: someone lurking in the darkness and slowly approaching. With Bear's oversized jacket around her, Nikki almost reminded me of Grizabella in her tattered coat-except here it looked disturbingly like Nikki was wearing Bear's skin.

That image can stay with me, thanks. 😬

There's another shot I loved when Nikki arrives at Bear's front door in the red dress. In the exact same image, I thought she looked absolutely beautiful and terrifying. Her eyes almost looked as beautiful as stars while simultaneously appearing dark and empty, like a void.

She reminded me somewhat of Hannah Fierman's character from V/H/S and Siren: someone incredibly beautiful who can simultaneously look menacing, threatening and deeply unsafe.

That's an effective kind of horror for me. Nikki doesn't have to stop being beautiful to become frightening. The attraction and threat exist at the same time.

The intimacy between Bear and possessed Nikki was unsettling for the same reason. It looked forced and fake rather than genuinely passionate.

Nikki is technically throwing herself at Bear, but we know why.

She can't freely choose not to want him.

Even her poetry starts feeling like imitation. Bear's poetry in the opening was sweet and seemed genuinely expressive of who he was. Later, Nikki begins using similar romantic language herself, including the disturbing monologue when Bear says he's going to his friend's house and she threatens to end her life.

It feels less like Nikki expressing herself and more like the obsession reshaping her into whatever will keep Bear close.

Michael Johnston did a great job as Bear too. His face constantly sells anxiety, insecurity and uncertainty. At times he almost has this exhausted, hollow look, as though the entire situation is physically draining him.

That's important because Bear is incredibly frustrating.

He sticks with increasingly crazy, freaky Nikki for far too long before seriously trying to fix what he's done. Part of that probably is fear. Part of it is guilt. And I do believe he genuinely loves Nikki.

But I also wonder whether some part of him still doesn't want to surrender the thing he wished for.

He finally has Nikki.

Just not like this.

The supporting characters worked too. Bear's friend could be obnoxious, but he was funny and had genuinely good chemistry with everyone. Something about him also made me suspect he'd previously had something with Nikki. He seemed suspiciously confident about what she liked, and at times almost jealous.

The humour generally worked because the movie knew when to let it disappear. Most of the comedy is toward the beginning and gradually fizzles out as the tension increases.

Then there's Sarah.

Good lord. 😱

I knew something was eventually going to happen to her. As soon as Nikki smashed the window, my mind immediately started running through all the brutal possibilities. With the broken glass right there, I thought that was obviously going to be involved.

Then came the brick.

It was gory, over-the-top and slightly comical in its excess, but mostly grotesque, gruesome and disturbing.

What made it worse was the pacing. The attack happens incredibly quickly, yet somehow feels agonisingly long because Nikki toys with the brutality while Bear just freezes and does absolutely nothing.

And Sarah was another gorgeous woman who was actually interested in Bear.

No happy ending for you.

Skull mash!

The cat didn't deserve any of this either.

By the end, I was desperately imagining ways the movie could get Nikki back. I wondered whether Bear could drug possessed Nikki long enough for the real Nikki to regain control and make a wish herself. I even considered whether there might somehow be a way of travelling back to before Bear made the original wish.

But that probably would've been the DreamWorks ending.

Everything resets, Bear learns an important lesson about love, Nikki smiles at him and everyone goes home.

Obsession doesn't give him that.

And I think the ending works because Bear pays the price without magically repairing the damage he caused.

Even Bear's final sacrifice isn't completely clean. He takes the pills knowing his death can free Nikki, but then survival instinct kicks in and he tries to bring them back up. Before he can undo it, possessed Nikki gets her own wish.

Now Bear loves her the way she loves him.

For a brief moment, they've achieved the "perfect" relationship Bear originally wanted.

And it's completely meaningless.

Neither of them is free.

Bear originally removed Nikki's ability to choose whether she loved him, and Nikki's obsession ultimately does the same thing back to Bear.

Then Bear dies anyway.

The original Nikki is finally freed, but that isn't a happy ending for her. She's left alive with the consequences of something she never chose. People are dead. She's been transformed into something horrifying, and she's left traumatised and scarred by the actions of the man who claimed to love her.

Bear pays for what he did.

Nikki still has to live with it.

That's probably why this movie got under my skin more than I expected.

I can romanticise the fantasy behind Bear's wish. Being completely wanted by somebody you desperately want yourself sounds wonderful. No uncertainty, no rejection, no analysing whether they actually feel the same.

I can even understand why Bear made the wish.

But Obsession takes that fantasy to its logical extreme.

If someone cannot choose not to love you, then being loved by them doesn't really mean anything.

At the end of the day, I'd rather somebody wanted me on their own terms.

And maybe that's the cruelest part of Bear's story.

The real Nikki may already have been giving him a chance.

He was just too afraid of uncertainty to find out.
