summary: Unflinching, uncompromising & unsettling... Horror dialed up to 11!
text:
Eric's Grade: A-
Along with Kane Parsons another Youtuber has released a well regarded surprise horror hit to kick off Summer 2026. Curry Barker is co-creator of the YouTube sketch comedy "that's a bad idea" with Cooper Tomlinson who co-stars in the movie. Barker uploaded a horror short which got him noticed by a producer, but instead of taking the offer to develop that project into a feature Barker pitched the idea for 'Obsession'. Barker directed a film in 2024, but 'Obsession', his sophomore film, is the first to see a theatrical release. The movie stars relative unknowns Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette with the most recognizable cast member being a smaller role for Andy Richter. The movie debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival in September 2025 where Focus Features acquired the distribution rights. The movie was released in theaters in May 2026 becoming a commercial and critical hit with a lot of attention garnered for Navarrette's performance as well as keeping this Neo-Renaissance for horror going full steam ahead.

Johnston stars as Bear Bailey who lives alone in the house his grandmother left him. He has a small friend group comprised of people he works with at a local music store made up of himself, Ian, Sarah and Nikki. Bear has been infatuated with Nikki for quite a long time, but struggles fearfully with the concept of actually confronting her with his feelings. While looking for a crystal to give Nikki as a gift Bear stumbles across a novelty item called a "One Wish Willow" and decides to buy that for Nikki instead. After his latest attempt to confess his feelings to Nikki fails Bear uses the novelty item to wish for her to love him of course thinking nothing of it. It is really more a lament than a serious wish. Almost immediately Nikki shows up at his car door almost forcing him to take her home with him. At first Bear is freaked out, and doesn't connect her sudden attention with the wish he made. Things get very strange very fast however. There are flashes, as this guise of puppy love fails, and something sharply fearful or confused in Nikki bursts forth, but almost immediately this mask of adoration reasserts itself. Both Ian and Sarah are freaked out as this seems so out of character for Nikki. To add to it Sarah has something of a crush on Bear herself. After an early and brief good period things start getting weirder and darker, and at some point Bear starts to realize that this has all happened because of his wish, and something that was supposed to be good is turning into a nightmare. Things break bad in a hurry getting super dark and super violent as thing rush to an unsettling, mind numbing conclusion.

I was not super eager to see 'Obsession' when I first saw the trailer mainly because it felt like one of those movies that seems pretty obvious as to how it is all going play out. Add to it that I am not a fan of awkward/cringe situations in any genre really, and I knew before heading in there are some very cringe scenes in this movie. After extremely positive word of mouth and even some awards discussion it certainly seems like 'Obsession' is on track to be this year's 'Weapons'. It even has a truly gruesome scene that is very reminiscent of one in 'Weapons'. Curry is smart to steer clear of getting into too much backstory with the characters or lore surrounding the supernatural elements. Instead this movie is sleek, no nonsense and gets right to the point. Performances are good all around, but Navarrette's incredible balance of crazy, scary and scared is especially noteworthy. Johnston's performance is more subtle, but no less effective as the guy who finally lands the girl of his dreams only for the situation to quickly devolve into a nightmare. I have a couple of issues with the plot progression, but for the most part the story feels genuine. I think the friend group, as presented, has a very odd dynamic. They seem more like co-workers than real friends, but the script is trying to sell them as friends who spend time together playing bar trivia. I can completely empathize with Bear trying and failing to tell this girl that he has feelings for her, but in real life I believe these failings would stem from lack of opportunity as well as feel of rejection. At one point Nikki actually point blank asks him if he likes her, and it seems like there might be a glimmer of hope for his romantic intentions at which point he still balks? That seems like a fail too far to me. The last slight plot quibble is Bear bringing Nikki to this party that Ian is having. I think given her exponentially devolving behavior there is no way anyone would bring Nikki to a party like that to prevent a scene like the very one that plays out. On the positive side it is in that scene where the horror really kicks in and the movie starts down an increasingly violent path. The violence comes like a staccato thunderclap. It is sudden, brutal and unmerciful and frankly hard to watch. The last 20-30 minutes are like running a frenetic 100 yard dash through razor blades for your eyeballs. As I was watching the credits I just felt profoundly unsettled by the whole thing for a handful of reasons, and I think a movie that can grab you like that and chew you up and spit you out (metaphorically) is a horror film that is accomplishing its mission.

Never again.

Would recommend. It has a very gritty atmosphere especially twords the end. The end kind of felt like the ending to a saw movie. This movie still be good without the gore even though there isn't much gore. I still kind of thought backrooms was better though. This movie gives you that feeling where you're happy that you're not in the main characters situation. I'm not watching it again but I would recommend it.

This movie is-in conjunction with the back rooms-the start of something great in horror. This is a movie born from the grassroots of internet horror culture, finally having broken into the mainstream. The story and themes are unbelievable. Very man out there has at some point had the same fantasy of having the girl you like just instantly love you back. This movie shows all that is wrong with that in the most disturbing way, and I feel all us men should be forced to see. The acting for Nikki is Oscar worthy and the facial expressions are terrifying are like something I've rarely seen. Please watch this movie. It is the first horror classic in years and a new cornerstone of what will be seen as Gen Z culture in the future.

Obsession has made its mark on social media lately, despite being released last year. After watching the film for the first time last night, it is easy to see why.

Inde Navarrette executed one of the most convincing performances I have ever seen on the big screen. It was captivating, powerful, and left me with a lingering feeling of dread, long after the movie had ended. The way that her character constantly fought a battle between the darkness and the light was unbelievably unsettling.

The lighting and camera work was nearly perfect. Director Curry Barker was able to create a world that was ugly and deeply suspenseful. The way in which he portrayed Inde's character (post-wish) really added to the dark themes of the film.

As someone who thoroughly enjoys horror films, I can confidently say that this was the best I have seen in a long time. I can't recall another time when I watched something that made me want to look away, but left me so captivated that I was unable to.

Obsession was dark, visceral, and relentless. The acting and directing were both phenomenal across the board. This was a profoundly disturbing story about desire, lust, and unimaginable consequences.

summary: Be Careful What You Wish For
text:
A disturbing story about just how far we're willing to go to get our deepest desires... even if the price is selling our soul.

Barker doesn't hold back, although for much of the film he uses body horror with a certain degree of restraint. But when he decides to go straight for the jugular, he does it without anesthesia. There are several particularly brutal scenes that hit hard precisely because of how suddenly they appear.

Raw, uncomfortable, and seriously twisted, because Barker shows very little mercy to any of his characters.

And to top it all off, an absolutely unhinged finale.

Be careful what you wish for... because you just might get it.

summary: Not as effective or scary as the hype
text:
Obsession is a curious one. It's a well made, well acted horror/thriller and it has some interesting aspects to its central idea but it lacks the shocks and set-pieces I prefer to see in the genre.

That's not to say this is a bad movie because it's actually a good one, but i don't think it lives up to the hype unfortunately and that meant i left disappointed.

There's a great central performance by the lead actress and the other cast members do well here but there's a definitive lack of likability in the cast (aside from the aforementioned actress).

There is one brilliant jump scare but the other than that I grew tired of the constant yelling and hollering for the two leads. I understand creating a new 'lore' so to speak allows for creative freedom but it also means (in this movie) to suspend disbelief. I just couldn't buy into some of the over the top actions (gaffer taking the front door rather than locking it and hiding the key) for example. But maybe that's just me.

There's still much to enjoy and lots to celebrate given it's made so much money on its minuscule budget.

Go see it if you haven't and make your own mind up.

I don't really know how to describe this movie. It's great in all aspects: acting, plot and cinematography is great.

Obviously, Inde Navarrette stole the show with her ability to literally mold her face into the most unnatural expressions. She was absolutely amazing to watch, creepy beyond all belief and there are scenes where I genuinely felt the pain Nikki was feeling (not gonna go into specifics to keep it spoiler free).

Secondly, Michael Johnston was great as Bear, never have I wanted a character dead as much as this guy. This movie doesn't let Bear be just another "nice guy", it makes him painfully real. He is pathetic, self-pitying, boo-hoo woe is me type of guy and the actions he takes in this movie geniunely are more grotesque than any body horror can achieve.

TL;DR
The idea of taking away a person's autonomy turned into a brilliant horror movie. Must-watch! Geniunely creepy with great performances and some good storytelling tying it all together into a new favourite.

It is what it is.

It was entertaining, but you have to dumb yourself down in order to accept what you see on the screen. It shared a few profound messages at times but for the most part the dialog felt like a 14 year old wrote the story.

This is a lot better than a typical horror movie where a masked killer brutally murders women simply for shock value. There is a story (granted a shallow one) and it did not end the usual "cat and mouse high tension ending most of these films end with."

I felt much of the film was great creepy idea, with a lost opportunity of what could have been a much better film.

The lead Male actor's choices were so Dumb and unrealistic at one point I almost wanted to walk out of the theater, because of how bad the writing became at the third act.

He's scared of the crazy girl who just committed a double homicide, yet rather than run to police for help, he helps her cover up the crime.... That took me out of the film entirely; no one would do this.

It's just bad writing.

Despite that huge stupidity driven flaw, the rest of the film was successful and some of the direction and use of lighting was HIGHLY EFFECTIVE. More of a movie to catch at home than in a theater. There are no epic shots worth seeing on a big screen. Looks more like a project made with a camera from Walmart on a youtube channel than a film.

Still was entertaining.

Not looking forward to the franchise that will come in a year or so.

The Monkey's Paw (or variations thereof) never has the owner's best interest at heart. It's obsessively literal-minded! A stickler for semantics! Needs you to be very, very, very specific or it'll mess you over but good! If you simply wish to be famous, you might find yourself on a Most Wanted poster! There's always a catch; there are always dire consequences. No matter what genre an adaptation tackles (comedy, like Bedazzled; horror, like Wishmaster), it's almost always a form of social satire displaying the folly of fools.

The Monkey's Paw variation in Obsession is "One-Wish Willow," a 1950s novelty toy that's become a sought-after collectible. (Never mind that new age shops still have plenty in stock and sell them for the low, low price of $6.99 plus tax!) Few take the willow seriously or even use it. One such customer is Baron "Bear" Bailey, who harbors a crush on his co-worker Nikki Freeman. They'd make an odd couple. Whereas Bear is insecure and socially awkward, Nikki is extroverted. (Yes, opposites attract sometimes, but these young people have no chemistry and come off as siblings.) Nevertheless, when Nikki puts in her two weeks at work to focus on her writing, Bear uses his Willow to wish Nikki would love him more than anything. It's a way to vent his frustration, yes; he doesn't expect it to work, no ... but it does!

It goes without saying that Nikki's affection isn't genuine. When her behavior becomes erratic and even downright psychotic (filet de chat on rye, anyone?), we understand that a malevolent (and mischievous) entity has taken control of her. Let's call it False-Nikki. Real-Nikki sometimes comes through in seat-grabbing moments.

As said, tales like these are social satires, showing how greedy and egotistical people can be. Case in point: What does Bear do when he can no longer deny that his wish has stripped Real-Nikki of her autonomy? He immediately has sex with her! She stares off into oblivion during the uncomfortable scene, tears welling in her eyes. It isn't until False-Nikki becomes too much to handle that Bear contacts customer service. To ask if the wish can be cancelled? No, to ask if it can be tailored to his preferences! (False-Nikki without the crazy and inconveniences, please.) The agent on the other end of the line drops a bombshell: The wish cannot be undone until Bear dies.

Things escalate further: Whenever Real-Nikki gets the upper hand for a minute, she begs for death and resorts to self-harm; False-Nikki one-ups her by killing a mutual friend. And Bear, you bet he's stopped being intimate with her. (How interesting it would have been to include a scene of False-Nikki instigating sex. Bear, too afraid to say no, would have undergone the ordeal in stunned silence with tears welling in his eyes.)

Obsession is a damn fine movie-an instant classic that'll be watched and discussed for decades to come. It's well-acted (I predict Inde Navarrette will get an Oscar nod for her turn as Nikki), well-directed, well-written, well-everythinged.

Now for the bad news: Every fanbase contains a subdivision, of what I call hoolifans (a portmanteau of "fans" and "hooligans"), gatekeepers claiming ownership of the cultural text they've embraced. They reject, even condemn, other readings (including the filmmaker's authorial intent). And like all fanatics, they'll never let facts get in the way of their narrative and preconceived notions.

Why do I bring this up? Well, despite the movie's poignant themes, editor/writer/director Curry Barker and company didn't necessarily set out to tell a story that's all doom and gloom. Barker, who originated as a YouTube comedian, stuffs Obsession with dark humor. Halloween Horror Nights, Universal Studios' annual event featuring Haunted Houses and Scare Zones, recognized the movie's playful side and announced, much to the delight of cast and crew, that Nikki would join the 2026 line-up as a Roaming Character. Hoolifans have objected to this, calling it inappropriate, offensive, vile, nasty and (excuse me for a second while I find my other list of adjectives) insulting, disrespectful, and disgusting.

I'm tempted to point out these hoolifans' hypocrisy. After all, many tragic (female) horror characters have become haunted house staples, scare zone mainstays, and subjects of parody. Take The Exorcist's Regan, a young girl possessed by a demon that commits murder and forces her to perform lewd acts. Or Fatal Attraction's Alex, an unstable woman dumped by the married man she's slept with. She's not gonna be ignored! Audiences cheer when she eventually takes two in the chest. Actress Glenn Close even reprised the role for a Saturday Night Live skit. Don't hoolifans care about them?

I know it's a bit unfair to point that out because most Obsession hoolifans were born after 2000 and are not necessarily horror fans, much less familiar with 20th-century genre classics. Still, this doesn't take away from their tendency to respond to issues in a knee-jerk fashion. No matter what generation they belong to, these people don't want a conversation or debate; they make demands and call for boycotts. If we give in to this crowd-if Halloween Horror Nights removes Nikki from the line-up and issues an apology (fear of losing revenue will bring every company to its knees)-we're several steps closer to an Orwellian society. I'm half-kidding. Well, maybe quarter-kidding.

Nikki is the victim, not the villain. Agreed. This doesn't mean she isn't or can't be a horror icon. Moreover, it's crucial to keep in mind that Real-Nikki and False-Nikki are not the same character.

Don't miss out on Obsession. It's a good one.

I had to split the film into two parts. The beginning was tedious: the protagonist droned on endlessly about his sexual issues, acting as if he were twelve. I felt like smacking him on the back of the head and saying, "Spit it out and just take action." Once I grew tired of his incoherent mumbling, I took a break... Then came the second part, which reminded me of Tarkovsky's *Solaris*. That film also features mad, obsessive love, but there is growth on both sides. Here, however, everything is steeped in hopelessness from the very start-a mutual plunge into the abyss. Which is exactly how it ends. The film has achieved cult status; it serves as a collective diagnosis for Generation Z... And the diagnosis is this: you've become too obsessed with psychology and trauma. Maybe it's time to snap out of it and just live your lives?

summary: A Predictable Story Wrapped in Social Media Hype
text:
Despite the overwhelming hype on social media, I found this film to be quite underwhelming.

The storyline is highly predictable and offers very little that feels fresh or original. While the concept had the potential to become a compelling psychological thriller, the execution falls short. The film relies heavily on familiar tropes that horror fans have seen many times before, without bringing anything new to the genre.

Rather than creating genuine suspense or fear, the narrative unfolds in a way that is easy to anticipate, making it difficult to stay fully engaged. It doesn't come close to the atmosphere, storytelling, or impact of many classic horror films that continue to stand the test of time.

I watched this movie largely because of the strong online buzz and positive ratings, but unfortunately, it did not live up to the expectations. For me, the hype far exceeded the actual viewing experience.

summary: Be Careful Who You Wish For
text: I don't think I can add much more to this film that other people haven't said already, but I think it's safe to call Obsession a horrifying cautionary tale on what happens when one doesn't think through their selfish wish. Arguably meant to comment on how insecure misogynistic men treat women more like their fantasies than actual people, seeing a shy loser like Bear wish for his friend Nikki to love him back get the worst possible outcome is executed with patient disturbance and bone chilling tension all throughout. The unstable blend of supernatural horror and dark comedy adds into how unsettling the bizarre obsessed state Nikki is in freaking Bear out to near death. Much like how the fears of being trapped in an inescapable relationship haunt today's generation, writer / director Curry Barker managed to convey a lot of mature truths about how entitled desperation can wreck someone's life in more ways than one. Obsession is truly a study to behold for those who might fear for what could happen if their deepest wishes stare at them right in the face.

Nice movie, You should also watch this movie because it's the most disturbing and clever horror film of this year. Unlike normal horror, it's not about ghosts, it's about the real terror of controlling someone you love and what it costs. It's low-budget but super effective, with breakout performances by Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, dark comedy like a twisted love story, and it became a massive box-office surprise for a reason. If you like horror that stays with you after the movie ends, watch this.

summary: Uncompromising, deeply disturbing, and not for the faint of heart.
text:
If you're looking for comfortable, mainstream horror, look elsewhere. Obsession is a grueling, masterfully crafted descent into extreme territory that pulls zero punches.

What makes this film stand out isn't just its staggering graphic violence-though genre veterans will find plenty of practical visual horror to digest-it's the deeply unsettling subject matter underneath it all. The narrative dives into psychological and thematic spaces that most directors wouldn't dare touch, building a pervasive sense of dread that clings to you long after the credits roll.

It's raw, oppressive, and executed with absolute conviction. A near-masterpiece for true extreme horror aficionados who appreciate a film that actually dares to cross the line.

I should not have watched this in the morning. This is such an unnerving film that gives me so much to think about

The most obvious strength is the performances. Inde Navarrette is PHENOMENAL in this. The way she morphhs in this role and has some of the most skin crawling moments, the way she emotes and her deliveries. Easily the best of the movie. But I will say Michael johnston is amazing in this too. He plays a snivelling cowardly insecure "Nice" guy so perfectly and you can feel it the SECOND he's on screen.

And I love all this movies themes like people blurring love with lust, how people will take your autonomy and make YOU out to be the problem, how people on the outside will look at who's a victim and a perpetrator, how men feel like they can pick and choose what part of you they get to enjoy and what they can discard. I need to rewatch this because every scene is POTENT with something much more.

And as expected, the horror is sublime. There's a really amazing and constant tension surrounding nikki as soon as she's overtaken by the wish. So many moments where I was gripping my seat for help.

Main reason i give it a 9 instead of a 10 is just because I reserve 10s for the truly greatest ever. Movies where every single aspect feels like it's firing at the highest it possibly could. I don't think obsession fits that moniker quite well, but that doesn't detract from how seriously spectacular it is.

summary: A Good Film But Could Have Been Better
text:
If there is any problem with this film that lowers it's enjoyment is that everything is from the male characters POV. In fact, it is so grounded in how he is affected by his own actions that we get little insight into what he puts the woman he supposedly loves through. In fact, I would not be surprised if film goers walked away seeing him as the victim.

In many ways, the film's premise could be played for straight comedy where a poor schlub who just wants love falls for a psycho. Honestly, take out the violence and up the jokes and you've got an Adam Sandler movie from the 90s. And that's a shame. I think seeing a lot more of what happens to Nikki, the woman who is wished into her obsession, and having her fight back would have made this a stronger film.

As it is, it's good but not great. I think strong acting by all around and excellent direction helps lift what is actually a rather weak script.

Obsession deserves a warning label: 'May cause suspicious side-eyes toward everyone for the next 24 hours. It's fantastic to see an indie horror film using just practical effects, lighting, and great storytelling. I'm looking forward as a Gen X'er to see what Curry will come up next in his sophomore career!

summary: The ending is the scariest part
text:
An initial gripe I had with Obsession revolved around the options Bear had to undo the wish. As far as the audience, and Bear, know, the wish would remain intact as long as Bear was alive. That left Bear with one option to save Nikki - suicide. But considering what I initially thought was a plot hole led me to a revelation: Bear felt entitled to Nikki's "love." He doesn't try to get her help. He brushes off his friends' concerns about her. He lies and covers up her unusual behavior. Essentially, he enables her obsession because, deep down, he feels like he deserves it.

In a moment when the real Nikki is pleading for Bear to kill her while the "other" Nikki is asleep, Bear asks, "What's so bad about being with me?" to which she admits that he was never really with the real version of her. Here, the movie makes it clear that Bear's relationship with the "other" Nikki has existed entirely without her consent. Instead of facing this fact, Bear looks disappointed - and I realized then that he was obsessed with an idealized version of Nikki, not the real her. Not just now, but not ever. He never liked her. He liked the idea of being with her.

I've seen some negative reviews of Obsession that correctly point out that Nikki's character isn't given any room to develop. While the actor did a phenomenal job, the audience primarily sees her through Bear's point of view. While this is true, it also makes the film's final scene all the more shocking. The real Nikki is left alone to face the trauma and aftermath of an abusive relationship. Whether we know more about her character or not, this is her reality - and it forces the audience to wonder how she will move forward, which to me is the scariest part of the movie.

summary: I wish we got more horror films this good.
text:
In Obsession, Bear (Michael Johnston) uses a mysterious One Wish Willow novelty to win the affection of his crush Nikki (Inde Navarrette). Bear is clearly not a horror fan: if he was, he would know - from stories like The Monkey's Paw and films such as The Wishmaster - to be extremely wary about such things, for they usually come with terrible consequences.

Initially, Bear gets exactly what he wants, Nikki suddenly finding him irresistible, but she slowly becomes overbearing and possessive, her uncontrollable desire turning into rage and violence. Bear can do nothing but watch helplessly as his world spirals out of control. Director Curry Barker does a great job, expertly handling the mounting sense of dread and unease, before suddenly unleashing a barrage of shock and gore, wrapping things up in a manner designed to leave the viewer reeling.

It also has to be said that much of the film's effectiveness is down to the excellent cast: Johnston is perfect as the wimpy Bear; Megan Lawless is very likeable as Sarah, the girl who really loves Bear; and Inde Navarrette - despite being just being 5 foot tall and slight of build - is absolutely terrifying. Her unhinged performance is outstanding, and I hope we'll be seeing more of her soon.

summary: First of all, it's NOT "The Monkey's Paw," it's John Collier's "The Chaser"
text:
I don't know whether filmmaker Curry Barker has acknowledged it -- I gather he himself claims the movie was inspired by a Simpsons take on "The Monkey's Paw" -- but that's awfully misleading. In W. W. Jacobs' famous little horror tale, two of a couple's three wishes go horribly, gruesomely wrong in totally unexpected ways. Rather, the premise of "Obsession" is that of John Collier's brilliant thousand-word humorous short-short "The Chaser," first published in The New Yorker and later adapted on The Twilight Zone: If you give a girl a magic love potion to make her fall madly in love with you, you'll live to regret it, because no one can enjoy being the object of such a mad infatuation.

That's one of the problems with the movie: You can see where it's going, right from the start, and you just have to hang around watching the simple plot play out. And the playing-out process -- as many commenters here have noted -- can really try one's patience. The movie is cleverly done but too damn long.

Another problem, also mentioned a lot here, is how frustratingly passive and inert the hero is. He's basically a doofus, and exceedingly hard to like. Michael Johnston keeps widening his eyes, looking stricken and miserable... and his baffled helplessness gets annoying pretty fast.

Finally, not to take anything away from Inde Navarrette, but I think the raves for her acting are misplaced. It's relatively EASY to play a mercurial madwoman who screams at unexpected moments and screws up her face into weird expressions; it's the sort of role in which you can't really do anything wrong, since anything goes.

Actually, I think the supporting cast, including the guests at the party, deserve some acting honors. My main feeling toward Navarrette's character is pity; she's basically a victim, a poor drugged creature robbed of her will.

So overrated. The girl was so annoying with er screams, and you couldn't feel bad for the guy because of his actions. He told no one about the behaviour of his "girlfriend". First 40 minutes very lame. Not a very bad movie but it was not worth the hype. The punchline and that what they wanted to tell the audience was good. Be aware of what you wish yourself.

"Be careful what you wish for" is a classic premise. What makes Obsession stand out is a tight script. The mechanism of how the "wish" works makes sense, and left this viewer wanting to know more about it by the end.

The cast of characters is the other high point. They were all well-rounded enough that if it weren't for the actions of Bear, this could have played out like a Gen-Z version of of the Gen-X classic "Singles". All the performances were solid, the two leads in particular.

The VFX team deserves a callout as well, doing some outstanding subtle work on the character of Nikki. There were some shots that hit that right note of not being sure when the actor's performance ends and the enhancements begin. As someone who had done plenty of commercial/film VFX work, I really appreciated the choices made to ride the ridge of the uncanny valley, and I'll be re-watching in the future just for that.

I've also become a fan of the recent trend of horror films using what appears to be open-gate framing (1.66:1 or 1.5:1 aspect ratios). Since Obsession is a more character-driven story, and often visually dark, the tighter framing allows the viewer to focus more on the characters.

summary: Give Inde Navarette all of the awards please!
text: Heard about this movie yesterday, saw all of the praise ot was getting from critics after googling and thought, hey I'm free this afternoon I'll go to the cinema and see if it's worth the hype. It was, in my opinion. I enjoy horror films that explore interpersonal human relationships, I love horrors that don't rely on a lot of gore or jumpscares to thrill and audience. This film does a great job of balancing out the comedy with the disturbing elements of the film. It's a fantastic blend of drama, psychological horror and a bit of comedy mixed in for good measure. Lead actress Inde Navarette CARRIES this film.

If there are psychological lines that horror directors collectively decided to never cross, they definitely did with this. Pure uncomfortable chills throughout the whole movie.

I haven't felt this way watching a horror movie in a long time. The acting is insanely good and will keep you glued to your screen.

summary: THIS MOVIE HAS CHANGED MY PERSPECTIVE OF LIFE
text:
Wow, this movie is amazing. I have never felt so distraught leaving a theater. I drove home in complete silence.

This may be the BEST scary movie I've seen since I was kid. Messes with your head and had me and everyone in the theater jumping out of our seats. I definitely recommend giving this movie a watch.

summary: Better Than Most Modern Horror, Not Much More. And, Not the Masterpiece It's Claimed to Be
text:
Creepy, bloody, funny, and deeply uncomfortable, it takes the '80s idea of "getting the girl" and turns it into a nightmare. It tries to be a clever mix of horror, dark comedy, and psychological thriller, but apart from a few jump scares, it never fully commits to any of them. While it has some unsettling moments and an interesting premise, the story feels repetitive, and the shock value wears thin pretty quickly. It's not terrible-just one of those films that thinks it's deeper and smarter than it actually is. But, an unforgettable performance from Inde Navarrette.

And honestly, I didn't fully get the hype. I don't see what's so cult about it. To me, it's simply a better-made horror film than most modern ones, but not the masterpiece many people make it out to be.

This is easily my favourite horror film I've ever seen. I love psychological horror, and this movie absolutely nails it. The eerie, unsettling atmosphere is unlike anything I've experienced, and it stayed with me long after it ended. Considering it was filmed in just one month on such a small budget, director Curry Baker did an incredible job. I'm definitely looking forward to seeing more of his work. If you're after a horror film that leaves you feeling genuinely unsettled and disturbed, I highly recommend giving this one a watch.

summary: Proof That Great Cinema Still Exists
text: I'm not into horror films, and lately cinema has been disappointing to say the least. With that being said, this film is an absolute masterpiece and a must-watch. It is a roller coaster of a film. It isn't predictable or recycled and its story is completely captivating and original. Unlike the majority of horror films, it does not push the envelope too far with violence or sex that make it feel excessive. The characters are realistic and memorable, and Inde Navarrette delivers a spectacular, career defining performance. This film will stick with you long after you watch it, and it it the type of movie where every viewing reveals or makes you experience something new.

summary: Nikki is the Star, Bear is the Villain 7/10*
text:
When a movie's whole social media campaign is "This is the best (genre) movie ever! 10/10, 5/5 stars", thats not usually a good sign. Artificial hype always leads to let downs. Obsession is no different. It's actually a really good movie, but it has issues and plot holes that hold it back.

Positives!

+Inde Navarrette is a star, give her the awards now.

+Genuine tension and scares. Shadows and movements make you squirm.

+Taps into social and political issues so well.

Negatives!

-Lack of lore or explanation for the wish aspect of the film.

text: One of the many movies warning us to be careful what we wish for, Curry Barker's "Obsession" manages to be intense and disturbing in every way. Shot mostly in confined spaces to create a feeling of claustrophobia, this story of a man who wishes for a woman to love him only to experience disastrous consequences goes all out with the shocks. I'd say that the horror genre has created interesting output in the last few years. No comparison to "The Shining", but quite creative. Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrete put on excellent performances.

Normally, I stay away from demon infused nightmare fuel, but I knew I needed to see this. What a hard watch, I almost shat my pants several times. The performance of the lead actress is absolutely phenomenal, this alone makes this movie a standout - but the premise of the plot is something I will discuss on many occasions in the future.

Bear, the male protagonist, lacks awareness of the morality of his own actions, going so far as erasing the woman he claims to love just to fulfill his need of being with her. The true horror of this movie lies in his egotistical motives, not only ignoring the agony Nikkie is in, but being too much of a coward to stop any of it. The plot of this movie might seem simple but I think it goes way deeper than just the idea of "be careful what you wish for". It portrays not only Nikkies loss of bodily autonomy but also Bears entitlement to her, his cowardice and unaccountability. He not only wishes for her to love him, but to love him more than anyone else in the world. If you ask me, this movie is more about his obsession with himself and an idealised version of a woman he actually knows nothing about. It's fitting how Nikkie worded it: "This is all your fault."

All in all, I really enjoyed this movie. I think its message hits deep and I quite like that horror as a genre tries to challenge deeper topics now. Should be a good watch for everyone who liked Companion and Heretic!

summary: When deep insecurity transforms into a pathological need for control.
text:
I took quite a while, maybe too long, to see what's being hailed as the best horror film of the year. I don't know if it's the best, but it's certainly the most profitable. To date, with a budget of between $750,000 and $1 million, it has grossed $479 million, making it a huge success. Is this justified? While many are jumping on the hype bandwagon and others on the hate bandwagon, I think "Obsession" is a very interesting film.

It's a minimalist film, with few locations and few actors, but with a profound and powerful, albeit painful, concept: interpersonal relationships, toxicity, and the limits one is willing to cross.

I think Curry Barker explores psychological horror through a granted wish that forces a coworker's love to a very uncomfortable extreme. It prioritizes psychological tension and anxiety over cheap scares, initially making us "empathize" with Bear in a certain way, and little by little we realize he's a monster and that Nikki is his only victim. Driven by a selfish and dark desire, he's capable of subduing and abusing his "friend" time and again, even though he knows long before everything falls apart that something is wrong, that what he's interacting with isn't really her.

Inde Navarrette's performance is phenomenal; she has an incredible range of expressions and manages to create a truly unsettling and negative atmosphere throughout the film. Throughout the movie, we see Bear reveal a complex profile where deep insecurity transforms into a pathological need for control. Although he's initially presented as a shy and harmless young man, the plot exposes a profoundly dysfunctional personality structure. He objectifies Nikki constantly, and from his position of omnipotence and control, he emerges as a selfish being whose suffering throughout the film is poetically justified, as he gradually descends into a spiral of delusion that culminates in his death. He is the most cowardly of all, initially refusing to confess his feelings to Nikki, and later failing to acknowledge to his friends that nothing he has done is normal. He is even more cowardly when it comes to taking his own life; were it not for the other Nikki's desire, he simply wouldn't have gone so far.

I believe it's a very powerful film in its message and needs nothing more to leave a lasting impression.

Lots of great things for what is essentially a Monkeys Paw story. Great example of dark humour in that things get so grim u laugh in horror. It's a delicate line but it's done really well here. As a minus the cinematography is awful, clearly a choice to keep everything as low lit as possible but just too much and it lessens the power of the shadows (ul know when u watch it). But most of all an amazing, fearless performance from Inde Navarrette. Horror films rarely get acting plaudits but she deserves every conceivable award. Unforgettable acting, everyone is good but her performance elevates everything exponentially.

summary: Be careful what you wish for!
text:
Loved it!

A Skin-Crawling Masterpiece-Inde Navarrette Gives the Performance of the year. Easily one of the best psychological horror films in years!

I walked into Obsession expecting a standard horror-thriller, but I came out completely blown away. Director Curry Barker has crafted a deeply uncomfortable, terrifyingly plausible nightmare about male entitlement and control that stays with you long after the credits roll.

The premise starts off deceptively simple, but the slow-burn atmospheric dread Barker builds in the second half is pure genius. The lighting, the lingering camera shots, and the suffocating tension in the domestic spaces make every single room feel unsafe.

Inde Navarrette Delivers an Absolute Tour de Force
While the direction and script are phenomenal, Inde Navarrette steals the entire movie. Her portrayal of Nikki is terrifying, tragic, and utterly captivating all at once. The sheer physical control she exhibits-switching in a microsecond from warm and affectionate to a unnerving, robotic, uncanny-valley stillness-is horrifying. The way she uses her voice, her eyes in the shadow, and her raw emotional outbursts will give you chills. She isn't just playing a villain or a horror trope; she conveys the horrifying tragedy of a woman trapped inside her own mind. If there is any justice, her performance will be remembered during awards season.

Michael Johnston also deserves praise for making Bear painfully believable, grounds the horror in real, skin-crawling human weakness.

The Verdict
I absolutely loved this movie. It is dark, unsettling, hilarious in the most twisted way possible, and utterly unforgettable. If you love smart, actor-driven horror that respects its audience, do not skip this. An instant classic for the genre!

As I suspected, when a "horror" movie gets so much mainstream attention it can't possibly be that good.

Don't get me wrong, the cinematography, the acting, the audio, all of that is perfection. That's why I am giving it a 7/10.

But the story is generic and the movie outstays its welcome by at least 30 minutes.

This is a YouTube short movie idea, which is what Barker was known for prior to this, extended to almost two hours for no real reason.

I felt like I was watching the movie for 6 hours straight, it just simply never ended and it goes on and on and on.

I am glad that I saw it of course, Barker can only go up from here and that's a great thing.

Also, why is all the media attention on Inde? I haven't seen anyone talk about Michael Johnston. His acting in this movie is, to me, better than what Inde delivered. Her role was to just crank it up to 11 for every emotion with no subtlety. Michael had so much range in this movie, so many subtle emotions and delivery. He also deserves the spotlight that Inde is getting.

Obsession" is a movie that promises suspense and emotional intensity but delivers very little of either. The plot feels predictable, relying on clichés rather than genuine tension, and the pacing drags for long stretches with few memorable moments. The characters are difficult to connect with because their motivations are either underdeveloped or inconsistent, making it hard to care about what happens to them.

The acting ranges from mediocre to unconvincing, with several scenes feeling overly dramatic instead of emotionally impactful. Even the twists fail to leave much of an impression because they are either obvious or poorly executed. Overall, "Obsession" is a forgettable thriller that lacks the excitement, originality, and emotional depth needed to stand out. Unfortunately, it's the kind of movie that's easier to forget than to recommend.

summary: The cursed love story of the century
text:
The greatest horror films don't always introduce something new. They sometimes just remind you how terrifyingly effective the familiar can be when every piece falls perfectly into place. Obsession doesn't reinvent the romantic horror film-it perfects it. Curry Barker finds a masterful balance within one of horror's most saturated subgenres, accomplishing what larger productions often fail to do by crafting a story where the supernatural element strengthens the human drama rather than overshadows it. Despite its extremely modest budget, the film never feels constrained. And creativity permeates nearly every frame, from subtle visual cues that destabilize the boundaries of reality to a score that serves as the film's emotional heartbeat. Rock Burwell's unnerving feature composing debut provides a haunting pulse, while the inclusion of the Little Dippers' "Forever" during the credits reframes a nostalgic love song into something tenderly sinister. The ending lingers because it perfectly symbolizes the film's central tragedy: what happens when love stops being selfless and starts demanding ownership.

Inde Navarrette delivers what I believe is the defining horror performance of the decade as Nikki. She balances innocence and seduction so naturally that every smile feels genuine while something far more dangerous lurks beneath the surface. Michael Johnston is equally remarkable as Bear, providing the perfect foil to Nikki's intensity. He captures the kind of flawed decision-making that is frustrating only because it is so believable. He isn't a victim of the supernatural but rather a man unraveling under the consequences of his own desperate choices. I related to him not because I thought he was right, but because I understood how love could lead someone to such a dark place. This kind of acting grounds every twist in recognizable human behavior, making the horror all the more inescapable. Together, Johnston and Navarrette create one of the most compelling dynamics I've seen in recent memory, but none of it would work without 26-year-old Curry Barker's confidence behind the camera. He took one of the genre's most familiar formulas and executed it with extraordinary precision on a shoestring budget, creating what is quite possibly the best horror film of the 21st century and certainly my favorite regardless.

summary: Not as good as they say
text: This movie is okay, but it is overrated, I wouldn't describe it as a horror movie either, because it's not scary. Obsession is held up by only one person - Inde - she is an absolute gem, what a performance, there is no doubt in my mind that she has a great career ahead of her. Is it possible to win an Oscar for such a good performance in such a bad movie?

I think most of us experience unreciprocated feelings at one point or another, so suddenly having the power to make that person return those feelings is quite a fun premise to play with. The idea of "forcing" someone to be with you against their true will or how this could backfire is an interesting idea to explore, but unfortunately, the film never meaningfully does anything with this theme other than using it to shock the audience.

Inde Navarrette is undeniably a brilliant actress so my issue isn't necessarily with her abilities, but more so with how her abilities were applied. While she is certainly committed to this performance, sometimes the director seems to lean on her ability to intensely scream more than what is actually needed, leading to the performance bordering on obnoxious. IMO a little bit of subtlety here and there would've worked better than her screaming like a banshee throughout the entire runtime which began feeling both repetitive and even worse, totally annoying.

Ever since Toni Collette's performance in Hereditary, it seems like a lot of horror movies have been chasing that same dramatic performance that Toni delivered with the animalistic crying and all, leading to a trend of "over-acting" in modern horror. It's not that I don't appreciate strong acting, but it often comes off as very "try-hard" or forced when such an emotional performance is inserted when the plot itself isn't heavy enough to warrant it.

Without spoiling anything, I felt it was pretty on the nose they were borrowing heavily from Betty Gabriel in Get Out, also borrowing tropes from The Exorcist, and even from more recent horror like Talk to Me. While being influenced by other movies isn't automatically a problem, the references felt a little too visible at times where this was constantly reminding me of other films I liked more.

The moral of the story is to be careful what you wish for but technically speaking, the protagonist's wish was for this woman to love him, not for her to turn into some kind of demon, so I don't think he exactly got what he wished for even if that is the overall takeaway of the story.

Overall, I had a fun time with Obsession and I don't regret seeing it, although I was admittedly laughing more than I felt any tension. With that said, my opinion is in the minority as you can tell from all of the hype, so I'd still recommend giving it a watch despite my complaining. For me, it's a 5 out of 10.

summary: Loved it, but only as a friend.....
text:
Bear is a shy music store employee, secretly obsessed with his longtime childhood friend and co-worker, Nikki.

Too cowardly to express his feelings, Bear purchases a "One Wish Willow," a supernatural trinket, from a novelty shop. While in his car, he breaks the willow, wishing that Nikki would love him "more than anything in the effing world".

The wish comes true, but in a twisted, nightmarish fashion. Nikki becomes instantly and unnervingly obsessed with Bear.

She begins exhibiting bizarre behaviours-such as sitting in one spot for hours to wait for him or watching him sleep in the corner of his room......

Imagine Shakespeare on some illicit stuff whilst writing Romeo + Juliet, or wishing for Fatal Attraction to really really happen to you, and you have Obsession...

Yes, by name, it's a horror film, but it's not your typical horror film, especially coming from Blumhouse. The film is devoid of jump scares, and those silly really quiet moments before a big scare, and it's all the better for it.

The aspect ratio is very small to begin with 4:3, and becomes bigger and bigger the more the nightmare for bear unfolds. But even though it's not scary, it's very very unsettling, and it has a unique sinister dread in the core of the story.

It's a very dark and cold film, nothing ever seems comfortable, even the scenes that are supposed to be funny have an air of fear to them, and this is to the films credit.

Single people, you'll be glad you are when you see this, and regret the day when you've said 'I wish they liked me in that way', we've all done it.

And you'll be sitting in your seat after the credits have finished, because there's no reprieve in this film, it's a dark film, and it doesn't pull its punches.

summary: An intriguing idea, but went over-the-top towards the end!
text:
I enjoyed Obsession for the first 45 minutes or so and was genuinely intrigued by where it was going. It starts off quite eerie and actually pretty scary at times, with a solid atmosphere that had me invested.

The acting is decent for what the film is trying to be, but I think it eventually takes things way too far. The further it went, the more extreme it became, and by the final scenes I found myself laughing because of how goofy it felt rather than being scared.

I did really like the message behind it, though. On the surface, Nicki is obviously the one who seems obsessed, but you could definitely make the argument that Bear is too, and that he really messed up. I thought that was an interesting aspect of the story.

Overall, Obsession had a lot of potential and I enjoyed parts of it, especially the first half. It's eerie, has a good message and is scary at times, but it becomes too over-the-top for its own good.

Overall Obsession is a well crafted film with strong technical execution. One of its most notable strengths is its effective use of sound design and lighting which work together to create a lingering sense of psychological tension and unease. Rather than relying on obvious scares the film builds a subtle, unsettling atmosphere that gradually draws the viewer in. Combined with its engaging themes and thought provoking content this makes for a compelling viewing experience.

summary: A Sharp, Scrappy Horror That Punches Above Its Budget
text:
Obsession is one of those horror films that genuinely benefits from a cinema viewing. Not because it's huge or flashy, but because you can feel how much craft went into stretching a sub $1M budget. The behind the scenes story is almost as entertaining as the film itself. Shot post Covid, made for peanuts, then suddenly triggering a studio bidding war and pulling strong box office numbers. It's a great reminder that meticulous planning can outshine money.

Inde Navarrette is the film's backbone. She delivers the kind of performance that keeps the whole thing grounded, and I'm not convinced a more seasoned actress would've hit the same emotional beats. Michael Johnston as Bear, though, didn't quite land for me. His portrayal leans more irritating than unsettling, and the script doesn't give Nikki enough "switch" moments to deepen their dynamic or show the full extent of her entrapment.

The story itself has a few bumps. Some early character relationships deserved more setup, Sarah's death scene accidentally veers into comedy thanks to an obvious dummy, and the One Wish Willow store workers feel like they belong in a different movie entirely, they truly reminded me of the store workers from Cabin Fever. Nevertheless, the jump scares are sharp, the creepy walk sequences look cool even if they don't fully make sense, and the ending sticks the landing with a few surprisingly effective touches, especially the single take of Bear trying to vomit up the overdose.

There are flashes of brilliance, especially in the subtle moments where you can see Nikki isn't Nikki anymore. Those tiny details do more heavy lifting than some of the bigger horror beats.

Overall, Obsession is a solid, scrappy horror flick with standout acting and a fascinating production story. It's not perfect, but it's absolutely rewatchable.

summary: Debut director Curry Barker doesn't reinvent the premise, but his spicy, feisty execution is fresh and tense...

summary: A beautifully shot nightmare, with an award-worthy lead role
text:
Obsession is a brilliant horror film, mostly because it isn't afraid to mix different styles. It moves smoothly between psychological mind games, gross-out body horror, and sharp scares. Plot: Absurd Fantasy and Predictable Trajectories

Overall, the story is bizarre and immature. The writer built an entire tragedy around a "wish wand," a cheap gimmick that doesn't fit the psychological horror genre. Worse still, the plot was incredibly predictable; pivotal moments like the lunch trap and the car attack were so predictable they left no room for surprise.

Characters: Lack of Motivation and Emotional Connection

The film's biggest failure lies in its superficial and underdeveloped characters, making it almost impossible for the viewer to empathize with any of them.

The film's biggest failure lies in its hollow and underdeveloped characters, making it almost impossible for the viewer to empathize with any of them.

Bear (Michael Johnston): Michael Johnston delivers a stunning performance, conveying the raw shock to the audience. He portrays a completely passive and submissive character, a victim of Nikki's (Andy Navarrete) screaming and manipulation. It was incredibly frustrating as a viewer to witness the madness Nikki inflicts upon him as she destroys his life. Bear ultimately regrets his wish and tries to undo it, but the price is his life.

The Friends (Ian and Sara): Treated like two numbers in a firing squad, they are killed quickly and callously, without any dramatic depth to evoke pity.

The End: A Frustrating and Too Late Regret
The film's climax delivers a deeply disturbing ending. After all the madness and carnage, the protagonist commits suicide to restore order-a moment I longed for throughout the film, hoping he could finally escape this insanity. Only then does Nikki snap out of her manic stupor, bursting into tears and asking, "What have I done?"

Final Verdict

Frankly, the film offers nothing more than an overdose of absurdity, twisted logic, and shock value for shock's sake. It's an experience that leaves you stunned by the story's strangeness and darkness, yet you come away empty-handed, with no emotional connection to the characters or the work itself.

I give it a 6/10, solely for the outstanding performances of Michael Johnston and Andy Navarrete.

The characters are emotionless, lifeless, and painfully dull. Terrible things happen to them, yet you feel absolutely nothing because there is no real character development at all.

And then there's the lighting... I have genuinely never seen lighting this bad in a movie before. Halfway through the film, I started wondering if the projector in the cinema was broken. Everything is ridiculously dark, you can't tell who is talking, and you can barely see anyone's face. It feels like they tried so hard to create "atmosphere" that they forgot the audience actually needs to see the movie. The cinematographer must have made this film with one hand. I seriously don't understand how this visual disaster got approved.

Some scenes feel like cheap copies of better horror movies. The film clearly tries to be psychological horror, but instead it just creates stress and annoyance. Rather than a horror movie, it felt like watching a two-hour dark TikTok edit with random screaming.

The thing I keep asking myself is this: after finishing the movie, did nobody sit down and watch it back and say "this is terrible"? The producers, director, actors... not one person realized how bad this movie was?

I walked out of the cinema feeling like I wasted both my time and money.

A large part of what makes Director Curry Barker's film OBSESSION so effective is the way it takes the basic romantic comedy premise, and turns it inside out. From the beginning, we are shown Bear's (Michael Johnston) inability to tell Nikki (Inde Navarrette) how he really feels about her. When he happens upon a supposedly "magic" trinket in a shop, he becomes just desperate enough to try it. This is the perfect setup for any rom-com plot.

Thankfully, Mr. Barker decided to use this veneer in order to take things in a different, far darker direction. This movie has a lot more in common with stories like The Monkey's Paw, or even Pet Semetary (as in: "be careful what you wish for"), than it does with any love story.

Of course, this movie's biggest asset is Ms. Navarrette, and her incredible portrayal of Bear's dream woman. Nikki goes from normal / sweet, to hyper-bipolar / deranged, but not in any sudden way. She transforms over time, in fits and starts, before blooming into one of modern horror's most memorable characters. From her meltdown in the restaurant, to her final rampage, Nikki is a marvel!

She's right up there with the great Kathy Bates in MISERY. Be prepared for a mesmerizing, shocking film, with one hell of an ending!

Note: One of the most amazing facts is how low the budget was for OBSESSION. It seems impossible that it could even exist for that amount of money! Hopefully, Hollywood gets a clue, and realizes that quality films can be successful without spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

summary: Fascinating, Disturbing, and Enchanting Cautionary Tale About Romantic Entitlement
text: Easily one of my favorite original horror movies of the year. It's a dark twist on the sitcom Pygmalion/Monkey's Paw love potion trope of casting a spell to make your crush fall in love with you. The insane rapid acting fluidity from the main lead actress Inde Navarette is extremely impressive and the best part of the movie. But thankfully all the other parts work really well too. The main character Bear is such a coward incel that knowingly keeps things going despite the lack of content from Nikki trying to break free from her control. I laughed hard during the causal willow branch customer service phone call scene. The movie is incredibly tense the whole way through, but fascinating to watch unfold and you can never keep your eyes off of it as you desperately want to know where it goes next. Bear is a great antihero that starts off somewhat normal, but gradually reveals his scumminess as he continues to make selfish and heartless decisions at the cost of the real Nikki's well being. Bear took the cowards way out 4 times (asking "Can I alter the wish?" instead of "Can I cancel the wish?", still seeing Wish Nikki even when he finds out that the real her is trapped inside after the phone call, having sex with Wish Nikki while the real version can't consent, replying to real Nikki's begging for a mercy kill with "What's wrong with loving me?", and choosing the easy way out by ending himself and leaving all the emotional and legal consequences with the real Nikki as she ends up traumatized). Sometimes Bear feels too stupid or useless to live, like never going to the police or explaining the situation to his friends until the very end. But this is also the point of his character. Like Bear refusing to answer Nikki directly about his feelings and not appreciating Sarah's feeling for him until it costs her life at the hands of Wish Nikki. The brick car scene was terrifying and a legitimately good jump scare. Ian wishing for a billion dollars was a hilarious brief break of tension. You really feel bad for Sarah and the real Nikki trapped inside. It was nice seeing Andy Richter as the grounded store manager & Sarah's father. Throughout the movie you really feel for the real Nikki trying to fight the possession Nikki and it's incredible how well Inde Navarette pulls that off with just her expressions and inflections. The ending is so tragic and leaves you riveted long after it's over. It's a fantastic deconstruction about romantic entitlement and easily one of the most creative original horror movies in years.

Obsession is one of the most unsettling horror films I've seen in years, not because of jump scares or elaborate mythology, but because it builds its terror around a deeply flawed human being. The film's real power comes from how it blends psychological collapse with visceral discomfort, creating a kind of dread that feels both intimate and suffocating.

What sets it apart is its focus on pathological avoidance and self entitled victimhood. The supernatural threat is frightening, but the film quietly suggests that the more dangerous force is the protagonist's mindset. His inability to confront reality, his reflexive self pity, and his habit of reframing every situation around his own emotional comfort become the true source of horror.

It's rare to see a film where cowardice is treated not as a weakness, but as something corrosive, a force that erodes the humanity of everyone around him. The tension is relentless. With no traditional monster to "fight," the audience is left watching a psychological implosion that feels inevitable.

The film's use of gore and filth isn't gratuitous; it's symbolic. Moments of humiliation and degradation carry emotional weight because they reflect the consequences of his inaction. The imagery is repulsive, but the deeper discomfort comes from recognising that the characters' suffering is shaped by his failures. It's horror as moral indictment.

Obsession is intense, claustrophobic, and often distressing, but it's also unusually thoughtful. It's a story about how a destructive mindset can be just as monstrous as any supernatural entity and how horror can emerge not from what a person does, but from what they refuse to do.

A unique, psychologically rich film that lingers long after the credits roll.

Stand-out film of the year Obsession follows typical 'nice guy' Bear (Michael Johnston) discovering a paranormal willow branch that allows the breaker to make one wish and the aftermath of using his to receive all-consuming love from one of his closest female friends, Nikki (Inde Navarette). Almost immediately, his endearing facade slips as his One Wish Willow causes Nikki's life to spiral out of control and his subsequent decisions reveal a much more sinister character underneath.

Perfectly contextualized by the real-world swell in redpill and manosphere content, Curry Barker's direction delivers well-timed commentary on the true horrors of male entitlement and loss of female autonomy. Even as Bear watches Nikki's whole personality change and she stops being able to care for herself, he spends more energy convincing himself he's innocent than he does helping her. Michael Johnston nails the awkward, insecure, self-involved nature of his character, keeping him as giggly and deceptively soft for as long as possible until diving headfirst into his darkness. His visceral reactions and constant nervous energy give the film an eerie feeling of paranoia.

This film wouldn't be complete without Inde Navarette, a breakout star we'll be seeing for years to come. Her soulfulness to Nikki and her gentle spirit in the in-between moments humanize her even in the depths of Bear's control, making the animalistic effects of Bear's wish all the more desperate and foreign to her. In the short time we know pre-wish Nikki, she is cool, kind, funny, and lowkey, and Inde does a masterful job at separating the two, especially in scenes where she switches between them.

I am so impressed by the collaboration made by this small production team and am so grateful for every change made to the script. All of the drafts are strong, but this particular ending sequence and final shot are the best of all. Thought-provoking and rewatchable, it makes complete sense to me why this film was so successful.

summary: Utilises its relatively simple premise in a way that feels as refreshingly entertaining as it is frightening
text:
"Obsession" is a supernatural romantic horror film written and directed by Curry Barker ("Milk & Serial"). Starring Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, it utilises its relatively simple premise in a way that feels as refreshingly entertaining as it is frightening.

For the longest time, music store clerk Baron "Bear" Bailey (Michael Johnston) has harboured romantic feelings for his co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette), but lacks the courage to ever properly ask her out on a date. One day, Bear instinctively decides to buy Nikki something from a new age shop where he settles upon purchasing a "One Wish Willow", a novelty item that promises to grant its owner one wish after being broken in two. Later that night, Nikki suddenly asks Bear if he likes her, prompting him to awkwardly deny that he actually does so right away. Annoyed that he's missed out on the perfect opportunity, an embittered Bear breaks the One Wish Willow and impulsively wishes that Nikki loved him more than any other person in the world. Almost immediately, Nikki begins to act loving and affectionate towards Bear at all times, essentially becoming exactly what he had desired from her all along. Eventually, Bear starts to realise that his seemingly harmless wish comes with deadly consequences, as Nikki's behaviour towards him becomes creepier and more erratic than he had ever anticipated.

I suppose it's human nature to feel a little obsessive towards someone or something at least once in our lives, whether it's a famous celebrity or a popular TV show. While for most of us this fixation will likely wear off soon enough, many end up taking this parasocialism too far, letting their delusions get the better of them in the worst ways possible. Such overwhelming enthusiasm often leads to dangerous ramifications, with it usually resulting in someone dying or getting seriously injured in the process. People with these kinds of demented emotional states have been depicted in the media numerous times, so much so that the Japanese have even coined the term "yandere" to describe a character with a psychotically murderous fascination with somebody. The 2026 film "Obsession" runs with that particular notion of someone's desire to be loved in a story that takes a familiar formula and twists it in a manner that will almost certainly hold your gaze until the very last frame.

Fittingly enough, the film begins in a diner with a young man named Bear innocently confessing his true feelings to his longtime crush Nikki. As Bear sappily stumbles through his words, it is soon revealed to us that this whole scenario is actually a rehearsal set up by his friend Ian (Cooper Tomlinson), and the girl he is talking to isn't Nikki at all but a waitress volunteering as a stand in. Like a true wingman, Ian steps in to give Bear the blunt truth, informing him that his entire approach is "cringey" and that Nikki isn't a girl who likes guys that pour their hearts out to her on a first date. With no other options left, Bear laments that he may never be able to conjure up the bravery to ask Nikki out, but Ian reminds him to simply wait for the right time and things could possibly work out for him. As the scene ends, Ian's impressionable words "All you have is time" echo through Bear's subconscious.

Shortly after, Bear returns home to find that his cat Sandy has died after consuming the prescription pills that fell out of his bathroom cabinet. Devastated, Bear sobs by his bedside when he suddenly receives a call from none other than Nikki herself. As the two talk on the phone, Bear overhears that Nikki has dropped her crystal necklace down the drain and secretly decides that he will buy her another one as a present for the next time he sees her. The following day at the crystal store, Bear's attention is drawn towards a strange item on the shelf called a "One Wish Willow", and upon reading of its ability to grant any single wish, purchases it for Nikki completely on a whim. That night, after Bear messes up his ideal chance with Nikki, he impetuously uses the One Wish Willow on himself to have Nikki love him more than anyone else.

Though it's pretty clear where the basic plot is going to head from this point forward, most of the fun lies in the anticipation of watching how exactly things are going to play out. Anybody who has seen similar stories like these before will recognise immediately that nothing good ever comes from wishing for something based solely on one's selfish desires. However, what makes this film distinct from others like it is the element of the supernatural that is incorporated into the story, in that it is clear that something unseen is the driving force behind Nikki's twisted reciprocation of Bear's love. In other words, this movie isn't simply a "Be careful what you wish for" parable but rather "Be careful WHO you wish for" (according to its official tagline), and as the story progresses, this becomes even more disturbingly true.

In spite of the film's relatively low production values, director Curry Barker nonetheless finds plenty of ways to make efficient use of his film's modest budget of US$750,000. For instance, simple shots of Nikki staring at Bear from the dark with the only light being what is reflected in her pupils makes for a pretty menacing image. Whether she's lying in bed next to him or hiding in the corner of a room, Nikki's unsettling fixation on Bear is something you'll be glad isn't happening to you. As well as this, Barker sometimes chooses to hold the camera solely on Nikki's face to show off her unnaturally wide smile that she has transfixed on Bear at any given time. The sheer unpredictability of what Nikki might do if Bear denies any of her "loving" requests here always kept me on my toes whenever she was on screen. I have always admired filmmakers who are able to entertain audiences on a low budget, and Barker has proven himself one worthy of such a high distinction.

As the lead character, Michael Johnston plays into Bear's socially awkward nature in a manner that is likely to feel relatable to anyone who has ever struggled to ask out their crush. Though it's easy to dismiss Bear as entirely selfish for not acknowledging the wider scope of Nikki's feelings, the film allows us to understand the aspects of his clearly introverted personality. Each time Bear tries to better himself, something always seems to go wrong for him, usually with him saying the wrong words at the wrong time or not being able to read the room. This explains why he decides to go with the simple method of wishing to have her using a supernatural item instead of working up the courage to earn her love on his own terms. Though we are in no way meant to condone Bear's actions since they were still done out of self-centredness, we can at least sympathise enough with him to hope that he won't be at the receiving end of Nikki's newfound "affections".

Of course, the real star of the movie is Inde Navarrette as Nikki, otherwise known as "Freaky Nikki". For her first horror role, Navarrette absolutely nails every important facet of Nikki's character, and watching how she can effortlessly switch between a normal, friendly girl and a deranged, lovesick monster is truly something to behold. Every moment Nikki was on screen, I was always kept in suspense over what she will do next, and without giving away spoilers, the film's climax shows the brutal extent of how far she will go to profess her love to Bear. I suppose Navarrette's performance can be seen as a more extreme version of Glenn Close's Alex from the 1987 movie "Fatal Attraction", and considering how intense a portrayal that was, this is saying quite a lot. It's a safe assumption that Navarrette has a bright future as an actress, because thanks to her, Nikki will likely go down as one of the most memorable horror characters in recent years.

Taking into account its fairly pedestrian plot, "Obsession" nevertheless succeeds at delivering as much enjoyment as possible in this disturbing, engaging, yet solidly made horror movie that definitely knows how to leave an impression. Its first rate acting from the two leads and the assured direction on a small budget help it stand out from other high profile stories that tend to lean heavily on tired cliches. While it may be a bit too early to tell, I am confident to say that Curry Barker could very well end up being an iconic face of western horror if he is able to keep up this momentum for his future projects. With that said, regardless of how things will turn out for Barker, he will always have this film to look back on fondly.

The film's plot is actually quite simple. Bear, who has been in love with his childhood best friend Nikki for a long time, becomes desperate because his feelings are never returned. In his desperation, he uses the One Wish Willow to make Nikki fall in love with him. His wish does come true, but that hope gradually turns into a nightmare with horrifying consequences.

Despite its relatively simple premise, the film manages to keep viewers engaged until the very end. The uncertainty surrounding when the conflict will finally erupt and how far the consequences of Bear's wish will escalate successfully maintains tension throughout the story. As a result, the audience is compelled to keep watching to find out whether Bear will survive the consequences of his actions or ultimately be destroyed by them.

In addition, Bear has a clear motivation, which makes his actions understandable from his character's perspective. His deep love for Nikki and the despair of having his feelings unrequited make his extreme decision to purchase and snap off a magical branch from the One Wish Willow in order to make Nikki love him feel believable within the context of the story.

Nikki's performance is one of the film's greatest strengths. Before Bear uses the One Wish Willow, Nikki is portrayed as having fairly neutral and ordinary feelings toward him. However, once the magic begins to take effect, her personality transforms into someone cruel, aggressive, and willing to take extreme actions. This dramatic character shift is portrayed very convincingly, making the transformation feel natural.

Bear's performance also deserves praise. At the beginning of the story, he is portrayed as a timid person who is too afraid to take the risk of confessing his feelings to Nikki. As the story progresses, he is forced to confront frustration and regret when he realizes that the magic he used is endangering the lives of the people around him. The actor portrays this emotional journey effectively and convincingly.

The supporting cast also delivers natural performances. The interactions between the characters feel believable, helping to make the relationships and conflicts within the story feel more authentic and engaging.

The film's synth-driven score complements the on-screen events exceptionally well and does an excellent job of enhancing the tension throughout the film. The music strengthens the atmosphere without ever feeling excessive or intrusive.

The transitions between scenes are smooth and easy to follow, allowing the story to flow naturally from beginning to end. From a production standpoint, the costumes, props, and settings all feel convincing and fit the world the film is trying to create.

Although the supernatural mechanism behind how the One Wish Willow grants wishes is never explicitly explained, this does not feel like a problem. The film is far more interested in exploring psychological horror and the consequences of a wish coming true than in providing a detailed explanation of how the magic works. Because of this, the mystery surrounding the One Wish Willow feels like a natural part of the story rather than a flaw.

summary: A thriller that understands how desire can become a prison
text: What impressed me most about Obsession is that it never treats obsession as something glamorous. So many thrillers flirt with the idea, presenting fixation as passion turned up a few notches. This movie understands that obsession is something far more corrosive. It narrows your world. It distorts your priorities. It convinces you that every bad decision is justified. The film pulls the audience into that mindset so effectively that I found myself feeling trapped alongside the characters, watching them make choices that were obviously destructive while completely understanding why they couldn't stop. The tension comes less from wondering what will happen and more from knowing that nothing good can come from the path they're on. The performances are exceptional, the atmosphere is suffocating in the best possible way, and the film trusts silence and restraint far more than most modern thrillers. By the final act, I realized I hadn't checked the time once, hadn't looked away, and hadn't been able to predict where things were headed. That's rare. This is the kind of movie that grabs hold of you early and refuses to let go.
