summary: The Monkey's Paw gets a modern twist
text:
Obsession (2026) ****

I saw this movie when it first came out, but am now finally getting around to writing my review, and I think this is going to be the sleeper hit of the summer. I am loving that this scrappy little film, made for under a million dollars, is raking in more money at the box office than the likes of THE MANDALORIAN AND GROGU and other big summer tentpole films. Taking the classic Monkey's Paw horror chestnut of wishes gone wrong, Michael Johnston's pathetic, socially awkward Bear is deeply infatuated with co-worker Inde Navarrette's likable character Nikki. When Bear uses a novelty toy, One Wish Willow, and wishes "Nikki Freeman loved me more than anyone in the f---ing world," the toy works, and he gets his wish, but it's far from what he expected. Nikki's newfound love for Bear is more than just uncomfortable smothering, but goes to frightening and darkly hilarious results. Writer/director Curry Barker does an excellent job of creating well-rounded characters you care about, including Megan Lawless, who plays another girl in their friend group with a genuine crush on Bear, which he is oblivious to. You can imagine that doesn't go over well with his newly obsessed girlfriend! While this film could have been an enjoyable one-note horror flick, the depth of characters and excellent performances by Johnston, Lawless, and, in particular, Navarrette's obsessed Nikki elevate OBSESSION a cut above most horror films. If Inde Navarrette doesn't become a star after her go-for-broke performance in this film, there's no justice in this world. She really is amazing in this film, and I hope she gets a Best Actress nod when Oscar season comes around, though horror films rarely get love from The Academy. Writer/director Barker also gets props for making a film that's not just about be-careful-what-you-wish-for, but has a timely subtext around consent and desire. Is it really love when it's not of someone's own free accord? SPOILER ALERT! The best moment of the film highlights this when Nikki is sleeping and begins talking in her sleep to Bear:

Nikki: Bear?

Bear: I'm just getting water.

Nikki: Kill me, please.

Bear: What?

Nikki: She's sleeping. It's me.

Bear: You are you, Nikki.

Nikki: Ssh. Please, don't wake her up. Just... kill me.

Bear: (Upset) What would be so bad? What's so bad about being with me?

Nikki: I've never been with you, Bear... Just kill me, please.

(Bear walks away)
Nikki: Please, please, please, please!

It's a chilling scene that spells out in stark terms that Bear has forced Nikki into this "relationship" against her will. I won't spoil the ending, but OMG, it is a wild one! There's already talk of a sequel, though I read a funny interview with Baker, who pointed out the film's glaring plot hole, saying that, "If the One Wish Willow actually works, which it does in this lore, and people are just making wishes left and right, there would be some crazy-like, dragons would exist. And none of that. The world is pretty normal from what we see in this movie. So, it doesn't really make sense." I found it funny the writer/director would come right out and name this glaring plot hole, but I respect him for that. I cannot wait to see Barker's upcoming remake of THE TEXAS CHAINSAW MASSACRE for A24! He's a filmmaker to watch for sure! Overall, the cast and writer/director have made a well-crafted horror film that's scary, darkly funny, and is also actually about something. For a film made for under a million dollars, it certainly does not look it and stands alongside the best Blumhouse and other big-studio productions.

CAPSULE REVIEW:
Obsession puts a clever modern spin on The Monkey's Paw wishes-gone-bad horror trope, using its supernatural premise to explore consent, desire, and the terrifying consequences of getting exactly what you wish for. Curry Barker balances dark humor with genuine horror, while Inde Navarrette delivers a fearless, star-making performance. Smart, unsettling, and remarkably polished for such a low-budget production, it's one of the year's standout horror films.

The story is about a young romantic man that is in love with his friend and the only thing he wants is to be with her but soon he will regret wishing that. The acting was phenomenal especially from Inde, so many emotions in one movie. It's not just a stalker movie or whatever is a story that teaches you a very valuable lesson in the end. Be careful of what you wish.

Obsession is a very strange horror movie. At the outset, it doesn't feel special. It feels and moves like a lot of other horror pictures, and it's a little slow to get rolling, but when you come out of it, you know you've seen something different. There's a uniqueness to it, and there's a distinctly offbeat wit. Curry Barker, who wrote and directed it, takes his gimmicky little idea and plays it to the hilt for maximum impact. Bear, a young music store clerk, is in love with Nikki, but can't quite tell her. He goes to a gift shop and buys (for her) a One Wish Willow, a novelty item that grants you one wish for a lifetime. But he ends up using it himself. Bear's wish: that Nikki will love him more than anyone. And that's where the trouble starts.

Michael Johnston, who plays Bear, gives what I would charitably call a one-note performance. But to be fair, he's not helped a lot by the screenplay. His awkwardness around Nikki is a little confusing. They're not in high school, and Nikki is not some unapproachable super-hot chick. She's cute, but not extraordinary. They're friends, they work together, they hang together (we see them chatting amiably in a bar), so his stuttering and fumbling when they're alone doesn't make much sense. An early sequence where Bear drives Nikki home and can't tell her how he feels is so unconscionably prolonged, there's no way to take it seriously or believe in it. Barker must have needed Bear to be a complete basket case to write the role the way he did. Later, when Bear helps Nikki cover up a murder, it's completely in line with his character; he still wants to believe in his dippy dreams that he can make the relationship work. But it's pathetic, and you lose all respect for the character and don't much care how bad things get for him or what happens to him afterward.

On the other hand, Inde Navarrette, who plays Nikki, is something else entirely. Her performance defines and dominates the movie like nothing I've seen in a long time. You have to go back to Gena Rowlands in A Woman Under the Influence for a breakdown of this magnitude, but Ms. Navarrette goes so much farther with the character than even that. In the early scenes, before she becomes Bear's zombie love-slave, she has an easy relaxed charm that's endearing and it's not hard to understand Bear's attraction to her. When she is in full demon-girl mode, going from hysteria to self-mutilation to quiet compliance (even staying frozen in place for a whole half-a-day while Bear's away at work), you can't take your eyes off her when she's on-screen and can't forget her when she's off. She's a master of controlled insanity, moving from one behavior to another seamlessly, with a psychotic ease. It's too early to tell whether Ms. Navarrette will become a star off of this performance. It's certainly original, and it's impressive, but then so is a nine-car pile-up on the interstate.

The movie also has some remarkable set pieces: Nikki's calamitous breakdown at Ian's "boys-only" party, and Bear, sitting in his car, telephoning the One Wish Willow help line and getting a late-night stoner who gives him some actionable advice. But just because Curry Barker and Inde Navarrette are maestros at ramping up the shock factor, doesn't necessarily mean Obsession is a great movie. But even considering its flaws, it can't be ignored, either. It's interesting, and in the steaming dung-heap world of horror movies, to find one with this much daring and imagination is a treat.

summary: One of the better (and potentially most game-changing) films of the year
text:
'Tis a sign of the times that one of the most exciting releases of the year -- which has also broken numerous box-office records, all thanks largely to word-of-mouth (a phenomenon comparable only to the genesis of Paranormal Activity) -- comes from Curry Barker. Known for his comedy videos on TikTok and YouTube Shorts, he got his real-movie start with 2018's less-than-stellarly reviewed Milk & Serial. And now, on his second try, he brings us one of the most expertly skin-crawling films of 2026.

Obsession is an original tale about a familiar mantra re: carefulness with wishes, supposing there even is a good way of formulating the wish at the center of this tale. (In Disney's Aladdin, it's one of the genie's no-no's.) It treats us to a recognizably, sometimes hilariously pathetic and desperate character, Bear, as he uses what purports to be a wish-granting product (which even refers him to a customer service number) to get the love of his life, Nikki, to love him "more than anyone else in the world".

The two leads, Michael Johnston and especially Inde Navaratte, are pretty fantastic, with more than a few deliveries and expressions that will no doubt stay stuck in your memory. Navaratte's body language and voice work during several key scenes is admirably unnerving, and as others have pointed out, she captures to a scary degree the loss of glimmer and joy of a woman who loses herself -- her agency, her own aspirations -- for someone she loves, or claims she does. The way she transitions between hilarity and gut-wrenching horror is, one hopes, star-making.

All the while, the blocking, editing, and use of music suggest more experience than Curry Barker actually has. Then again, I haven't actually seen his content prior to this; maybe it's kino as hell. (As far as I'm concerned, anyone who works in references to Kiyoshi Kurosawa's Pulse must "know ball", as the tots say.) The lighting makes certain shots indecipherable, but more often than not, this is the point. One particularly nifty shot uses dimmed lighting and fairly simple face makeup to create a phenomenally uncanny image. No school like old school.

There are, as mentioned, laughs in it (the biggest involve the aforementioned customer service people and, again, Navarette's wickedly unpredictable performance); some are plainly hilarious, others sort of morbid (as if daring us to laugh), and then a few that (at my screening, anyway) were of pure discomfort. But some, I gather, will laugh during the wrong moments altogether -- most probably including men who see no issue with Bear's actions. (EDIT: This, in turn, includes Gen-Z men who apparently take the film to be a tale about WOMEN, and what a "horror" it is to date them in the modern landscape, which is a whole other can of worms.)

No doubt we're made to understand his desperation, confusion, and eventual horror -- and Johnston has said in interviews that he approached the role with little judgment of the character -- but the choices Bear makes when presented with opportunities to put things right reveal something sinister; something that was already present, albeit subdued. Speaking of times and places for levity: No, I will not be making any "man vs. Bear" jokes in this review because everyone else already has.

As usual, there's been ample discourse around the idea of YouTubers graduating to movie-making. It seems there will always be some people who reject the idea, refusing to watch -- or, at worst, pretending to hate -- anything that an ex-YouTuber made purely because that is who made it. I don't see the point in fighting such a losing battle. (Yes, I rolled my eyes when Toby Turner was in a horror movie that one time -- and when somebody, probably Satan, decided that Fred was feature-film material -- but we've come a long way since all that.) 2026 contains Obsession, Iron Lung, and the upcoming Backrooms film, and it hasn't been too long since we had Bring Her Back and the admittedly unfortunate Shelby Oaks.

This wave makes it clear: the age of once-very-online filmmakers is here. We've got Newgrounds animators on Adult Swim and Markiplier on the silver screen. And when Marky's film dropped, I wrote that it was probably in the upper ranks of YouTuber movies. With Obsession, repetitive as it gets in some parts, that bar has been put quite a bit higher. (I shall also rest the case I've repeatedly made about the new golden age of horror, how originality and newness thrive in this genre like nowhere else, and how plenty movie-goers will, in fact, go see original stuff if given the choice, especially, indeed, when scares are promised.)

If pictures like this, along with Backrooms, indeed wind up beating the snot out of the Mandalorian movie, I'd say it's time to get comfy -- whether we get more YouTubers-turned-filmmakers in the spotlight or Hollywood attempting to emulate their films without understanding them, all while the Baby Greedo plushies get plucked asunder by seagulls at some landfill as God intended.

summary: My Review for Obsession (2026) by Curry Barker - A Brutal Portrait of Madness:
text:
I just watched the film Obsession (2026), and it's one of the most effectively disturbing films I've seen in a while. At its core, this isn't really a story about a villainous person; it's almost as though it is about madness itself as the true antagonist. The supernatural "wish-stick" (What I like to call the WIllow Object, that Monkey's Paw premise) amplifies it, but the horror comes from watching autonomy and identity get completely shattered.

Many viewers paint Bear (Michael Johnston) as the clear villain, but I don't see it that way. He makes one genuinely cruel comment born out of denial and fear ("being with me is so terrible"), but it stems from the unbearable weight of what his naive wish has done to Nikki. Bear isn't malicious;he's operating from fearful naivety for most of the film, clinging to the hope that the wish didn't actually work. He only confronts the horrifying reality and his extremely limited options in the final stretches, once he finally lets go of that denial. By then, it's tragically late.

The real tragedy unfolds through Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette), whose transformation into something obsessively deranged is terrifying to watch. Navarrette delivers an incredible performance: those creepy, unwavering smiles mix genuine-looking love with hidden sorrow and an overwhelming "LOVEME!!!" undertone. It's some of the best off-putting facial acting I've ever seen in this kind of horror.

The gore is mostly self-inflicted, which makes it even harder to stomach. This movie is blatantly shocking, horrific, and merciless. If anyone found it "darkly funny," I'm not sure we watched the same film; the premise has a twisted irony, sure, but the execution offers almost zero mercy. There's nothing comedic about the emotional and physical destruction on display. Though, I will say the Wish for a Billion Dollars was a bit comedic, but personally I was too immersed in the story to find it other than angering at the time I was watching.

Obsession left me emotionally disturbed. I hated how it made me feel, yet I respect what it accomplishes. It's a stark reminder to be careful who you let into your life (and maybe wary of sudden fame, given how many obsessive stories we hear). The final shot is exactly what I expected and feels like the only realistic outcome: Nikki is clearly not going to be functional anytime soon.

Would the movie be stronger without the supernatural element? Probably not. Removing the wish-stick would turn it into a much longer, slower-burning tragedy, losing the sharp escalation and thematic punch. I can't think of many other horror films that hit me with this exact mix of emotional revulsion and fascination.

Bear and Nikki are both victims of the "change": the wish and the shattering it causes. The online discourse treating this as a simple 2D "crazy girlfriend vs incel" story is missing the point.

I emotionally hated Obsession, but it's very good at what it sets out to do. I'd consider rewatching it... but I probably won't. Highly recommended if you can handle unrelenting psychological and body horror.

"Obsession" is a low budgeted film that has managed to do what only a small number of inexpensively made films has done....it's managed to make a HUGE profit at the box office...currently about 50 times what it took to make the film!

Before I talk specifics, I should point out that this is a very difficult movie to watch. The gore level is VERY high and I found myself not wanting to watch several scenes. I would never let young kids watch it...or my mother! But, despite this, it is worth seeing.

Bear is secretly in love with his co-worker, Nikki. The problem is that Bear is not only scare to tell her, but he's a complete imbecile. This is because he buys a magic wishing charm which entitles him to one and only one wish ever...and he's not the least bit careful of HOW he phrases this wish. Instead of saying something like "I wish Nikki would like me", he instead wants her to be more in love with him than is normally humanly possible. Sure, she DOES almost instantly fall for him BUT with an intensity even the most ardent serial killer would be amazed at! Nikki is insanely jealous...very possessive...and her entire existence is now Bear and nothing else. It makes for a most dangerous situation....and one you just need to see to believe.

This is a fabulous film and it deserves to be seen. It's marvelously acted and directed by relative newcomers (aside from, oddly, Andy Richter in a small role). Just be careful. The film is TOO GOOD when it comes to Nikki's obsession...to the point of blood....gallons and gallons and gallons of blood!

summary: Decent watch stay away from hype keep your expectations low
text:
I've noticed a trend over the last few years where every decent movie gets hyped to an extreme level online, especially on TikTok and YouTube. Part of that may be because Hollywood has spent so long relying on safe formulas that audiences are hungry for something different. As a result, when a lower-budget or independent film tries something new, people often rush to label it a masterpiece. We've seen it happen with films like Weapons, Bring Her Back, and several others. They're good movies, but in my opinion, the praise often goes far beyond what they actually achieve.

Obsession falls into the same category for me. It's a solid film with strong performances and competent direction, but I don't see it as the masterpiece many people are calling it. The story follows familiar themes of obsession, manipulation, psychological unraveling, and blurred boundaries between desire and reality-ideas that have been explored countless times before in thrillers and dramas. While the film executes these elements well, it rarely takes them in a direction that feels truly fresh or groundbreaking.

What disappoints me more is the way online discussion around movies has become increasingly driven by hype rather than critical thinking. Too many people seem to adopt opinions from a viral TikTok clip or YouTube video without really examining why a film works-or doesn't work-for themselves. Genuine discussion gets replaced by echo chambers, and anyone with a different opinion is often dismissed or attacked rather than engaged with.

That doesn't mean Obsession is bad. It's an enjoyable, well-acted movie that deserves recognition for what it does well. I just think there's a big difference between a good film and a masterpiece, and for me, Obsession never crosses that line.

The acting in this movie is terrible. The dialog is juvenile. The plot insists upon itself. People like this movie because it is a fad and they want to be a part of it to appear cool. This movie won't age well because there is nothing about it that is memorable. It reminded me of the bad made-for-tv movies I used to watch on TV as a kid.

The horror/thriller genre isn't usually my first choice, so I rarely go to the theater for films like this. But after hearing all the hype-and seeing a new wave of Gen Z filmmakers and actors in their mid-20s making a splash-I couldn't pass up the chance to catch it while it was still in theaters.

It was refreshing to watch something original instead of another sequel or franchise installment. While there were a few jump scares and some gore, it leaned much more into psychological thriller than outright horror, which made it an enjoyable watch.

Here's to the next generation of filmmakers-I'm excited to see what they create next.

summary: When Love Turns into a Nightmare!
text:
Obsession is a chilling blend of romance and horror that explores how love, when pushed beyond its natural limits, can turn dangerously toxic. The film follows Bear, a quiet and emotionally vulnerable young man who harbors deep feelings for his childhood friend Nikki. When he uses a mysterious supernatural object to make her love him, what begins as a dream quickly spirals into a nightmare.

The movie stands out for the way it transforms a simple "what if" scenario into something deeply unsettling. Nikki's affection doesn't just grow-it mutates into an intense, suffocating obsession that strips away her individuality and sanity. As her behavior becomes increasingly erratic and terrifying, the film forces the audience to confront an uncomfortable question: is forced love ever truly love at all?

Visually, the film maintains a grounded yet eerie atmosphere, gradually shifting from warmth to unease. The performances, especially Nikki's, add depth to the psychological horror, making her transformation both heartbreaking and frightening. Despite its modest scale, Obsession delivers a powerful emotional punch, relying more on tension and character dynamics than cheap scares.

At its core, Obsession is not just a horror story-it's a cautionary tale about control, desire, and the consequences of trying to manipulate emotions. It reminds us that love cannot be manufactured, and when it is, the results can be devastating.

Made for a remarkably modest budget of around $750,000, 'Obsession' still managed to be one of the most popular horror films of 2025 and 2026. It is genuinely impressive to see how much writer and director Curry Barker managed to achieve with so little. Beneath its deliberately simple premise (some might find it too simple, in fact) lies an ambitious exploration of obsession, desire, control, and the disturbing consequences of trying to manufacture love. It certainly is not intended to be realistic in the conventional sense, and judging it by that standard, as a lot of reviewers have done, feels somewhat beside the point. Make no mistake about it, this is a film designed to shock, entertain, and provoke discussion, and on all three counts, it succeeded for us.

What made the experience even more rewarding was the ending, which gave my partner and me plenty to debate afterwards, particularly regarding exactly what happened to Nikki and Bear and what the final wish ultimately means. That sort of ambiguity is a wonderful quality in a film because it paves the way for conversation. There are certainly moments where 'Obsession' embraces absurdity over plausibility, but I found that part of its charm rather than a fatal flaw. It is thematically bold, entertaining, and unapologetically strange, a low-budget horror film that punches considerably above its weight.

Watching the low-budget horror film Obsession, directed by the young and promising filmmaker Cury Banker, it's easy to see that sometimes, less truly is more.

Set in the small town of Miller's Point, the film follows Bear, a recent high school graduate working at a local record store, who struggles to confess his feelings for his coworker, Nikki. After countless failed attempts, even when she directly asks if he has feelings for her, Bear makes a wish through a mysterious game, wishing that Nikki would love him more than anything else in the world. From that moment on, the film makes its intentions clear, choosing to focus entirely on the consequences of Bear's wish as Nikki becomes increasingly obsessed with him instead of spending time developing every supporting character.

The film is backed by a solid soundtrack, confident cinematography, well-executed editing, and a surprisingly varied visual style despite its very limited budget. Everything works together remarkably well, reinforcing the idea that less is often more. If I had one criticism, it would simply be that I wanted to learn more about how the wishes actually work. I found myself wondering where the real Nikki was during the trance-like state caused by the wish and what exactly happened to her consciousness. Still, this is ultimately a personal curiosity rather than a flaw. The film never intends to explore the mythology behind the wishes, choosing instead to focus on the consequences of Bear's decision and on Nikki's gradual transformation into someone increasingly dangerous, chaotic, and disturbingly obsessive.

A special mention has to go to Inde Navarrette as Nikki. She is, without question, the film's biggest surprise and completely steals every scene she is in. While the rest of the cast delivers fairly standard performances, Navarrette brings an unsettling intensity that elevates the entire film and gives its central concept the emotional weight it needs.

Cury Banker's horror thriller Obsession delivers far more than you expect. Made on an extremely limited budget, it is an impressive example of how creativity and strong ideas can outweigh financial limitations. If this is what Banker can accomplish with so little, it's exciting to imagine what he might achieve with the resources to take his vision even further.

summary: A Wish You Shouldn't be Allowed to Make
text:
I can't remember the last time a film gave me a full-body reaction the way that Obsession did. I've seen plenty of scary movies with jumpscares, war movies with scenes that put you on the edge of your seat, gory ones that make you watch through your fingers, etc.

Nothing comes to mind when I try to compare with what Obsession was able to do. My body was sore and I was shaking through the credits, speechless. I felt breathless as I began to reprocess everything I had seen throughout the film, with every detail I remembered being more sinister than the last.

The more you sit with the concept of the film and parse through the details, the darker it gets.

There's a reason why most non-horror films with magic wishes include some rules like "No wishing death, no wishing for love, immortality, etc." Some things just shouldn't be able to be wished for, if only because they land you in a dark place very quickly. Obsession takes one of those dark ideas and makes it much, much darker.

Before I get into a little bit of spoilers, some things need to be said:

Inde Navarrette deserves an Oscar nomination for her performance. There's more than one scene where her facial expressions do more work than an entire page of dialogue could.

Curry Barker deserves all of the applause he's getting. The writing is believable, and his direction made the film unique to say the least. I can't wait to see his future works.

Taylor Clemons did a fantastic job on the cinematography. You rarely had space to breathe in frame, and when you did, it was never enough to make you feel comfortable. The lighting used in so many scenes made the film what it was - a nightmare.

*** SPOILERS AHEAD ***

There was a very quiet scene that I had to look up the script for immediately after the film because I I didn't want to believe what I had heard. This is the scene where Bear attempts to leave to meet with Sarah, but hears Nikki whisper to him through her sleep.

BEAR
(normal volume) You are you, Nikki?

NIKKI
(whisper) Shh! Please, don't wake her.

Bear looks at her, then looks to the ground.

NIKKI (CONT'D)
(whisper) Kill me, Bear.

Too ashamed to look at her. His voice quivers as he talks.

BEAR
What would be so bad... What's so bad about being with me?

A long beat.

NIKKI
I've never been with you, Bear.

After reading this, I realized my worst fears of what was happening were indeed true. Nikki wasn't just being controlled, it wasn't her at all. It was something else, something that didn't act like her, think like her, love like her. Something that replaced Nikki's true self, that reflected what it thought Bear had wished for, while the real Nikki was in some sort of torment since the wish was granted.

While no one should have the reasonable expectation that a $7 wish-granting toy would actually make your wish come true, Bear goes far beyond the acceptable. He knew from the beginning that something was wrong, and this scene proved that he was willing to continue the harm he was causing in order to preserve the wish he was granted. His actions made his character irredeemable, but not inhuman.

*** SPOILERS END ***

So, like I said earlier, further consideration of the concept just makes Obsession darker. I couldn't just walk away from it without the details unfolding in my mind. I can't shake it, but at the same time, I'm not sure I want to.

Maybe I'm just obsessed.

All I can say is don't go to this movie if you have a hangover, pms, or some other affliction. The nonstop screaming and crying felt like actual torture and I was racing to get out of the theater by the time it ended. None of the characters were really the least bit likeable. I really don't know how this movie is so highly rated. It's not really scary, just super annoying.

How do I take this guy seriously?! It's hard for me watching all his hilarious comedy skits that him and Cooper Tomlinson did!

It's honestly like watching Key and Peele and then seeing Get Out and being like how is this possible?!

Curry Barker absolutely cements himself as a genuine horror director that's better than anyone else out there right now!

The first 80% of the movie was brilliant. It was extremely unsettling, with almost no blood or gore. You could really feel the sense of dread as the main character fell deeper and deeper in love. Nikki's character was acted perfectly. In fact, the cast was pretty much perfectly cast.

Unfortunately, the film loses its way about 80% in. There are a couple of scenes which are extremely graphic - as in, over the top graphic.

Another big flaw is that Bear (the main male character), doesn't do everything in his power to stop this. I won't spoil it, but what would a normal person do in this situation? He made excuses for Nikki's behavior far after a normal person would have left her.

Still, this was an excellent movie, despite its flaws.

summary: How you should watch this movie: Look beneath the surface.
text:
If you analyze this film through the standard Hollywood horror lens, you might miss its actual mechanism. This is not a movie about jump scares or mindless carnage; it is a clinical exploration of the absolute destruction of human autonomy.

If you want to fully experience the tension, pay close attention to these three subtle patterns:
1. The Prison Inside the Body: This is not a "crazy girlfriend" trope. Watch the micro-expressions and the brief seconds where the real Nikki momentarily breaks through the trance-during the daytime party, the bedroom dialogue while sleeping, or the terrifying audio on the phone call. She is fully conscious, trapped inside her own flesh while her free will is forced.

2. The Architecture of Guilt: Look closely at Bear's psychological evolution. It operates exactly like real-world dynamics of toxic control: boundary violation, immediate guilt, temporary normalization, and a tragic attempt to fix an irreversible mistake too late.

3. Discomfort in Broad Daylight: Pay attention to how the director generates overwhelming anxiety in completely illuminated, ordinary settings. Creating horror without relying on darkness or shadows is a massive achievement in screenwriting.

If you actively engage with the psychological layers of both characters instead of just waiting for the next plot point, this movie will leave you deeply tensioned long after the credits roll.

There are a lot of horror movies that follow similar formulas, but this one does a lot of things differently-and does them really well! It keeps you on the edge of your seat almost the entire movie, really draws you in, and the actress playing Niki is absolutely fantastic! It's not too intense in terms of the scare factor, which I like.

summary: 8/10 - A Creepy, Thought-Provoking Wish-Fulfillment Horror That Could've Been a Classic
text:
Obsession (2025) takes the classic "be careful what you wish for" trope and gives it a fresh, darkly funny, and genuinely unsettling spin. Directed and written by Curry Barker, this low-budget indie (shot for under a million and picked up in a bidding war) punches well above its weight thanks to strong performances, smart thematic depth, and an atmosphere of creeping dread that lingers long after the credits roll.

Michael Johnston is excellent as Bear, the awkward, lovelorn music store employee whose insecurity drives the whole nightmare. His journey from sympathetic nice-guy to someone who starts exploiting the situation is nuanced and uncomfortable in the best way-it forces you to confront how desire can twist into something selfish and ugly. Inde Navarrette, however, is the absolute standout as Nikki. She delivers a magnetic, volatile performance that shifts from charming to deeply disturbing. Her unblinking intensity and increasingly inhuman devotion make for some of the most memorable horror moments of the year. The supporting cast (including Cooper Tomlinson and Megan Lawless) rounds things out nicely, grounding the story in believable friend-group dynamics.

The film excels at blending horror with dark comedy and moral ambiguity. It doesn't just scare you with jump moments (though there's a killer one that had people flying out of seats); it builds unease through prolonged stares, off-kilter silences, and the slow realization of what Bear has actually unleashed. The production design turns everyday spaces into something oppressive, and the sound design/score keeps you on edge throughout.

Why only 8/10 instead of higher? While the premise is executed with confidence and the acting elevates it tremendously, the story occasionally leans into predictability in the third act, and some character decisions stretch plausibility even for a supernatural horror. A slightly tighter script or bolder escalation could have pushed it into all-time great territory. It has the bones of a genre classic but doesn't quite reinvent the wheel as much as its biggest fans claim.

Still, this is one of the most entertaining and thought-provoking horrors I've seen recently-smartly exploring consent, control, agency, and the dangers of getting exactly what you think you want. If you're into atmospheric thrillers with real emotional stakes (think a twisted mix of The Monkey's Paw vibes with modern psychological edge), Obsession is a must-watch. Barker is a filmmaker to keep an eye on.

Highly recommended.

I am still shocked few hours after the movie ended

This was the most terrifying movie I ever watched, the horror was perfectly executed in my opinion. I was on edge for most of its runtime, my pulse was rushing, the plot wasn't necessarily unpredictable but the execution of the jumpscares and pivot points was immaculate. I've never been so disturbed and unsettled about a movie.

Getting into the meat of it, the subject of the movie is heavy and very well depicted. Each scene, each dialogue line is intentional and builds the direction of the story. Bear is consistently built as the villain in the story, and simultaneously the cursed protagonist who keeps trying to run away from the consequences of his actions, but ultimately runs out of places to hide. He is the portrait of a selfish coward: instead of being open about his feelings and letting things unfold naturally in his life, he hopes for a way to force things, to sway the narrative his own way. He miraculously achieves this, but everything is off instantly and obviously. He consistently avoids admitting to himself that Nikki isn't herself, that her love isn't real, and he is greedy trying to keep her love and attention while also trying to lead a normal life. I liked the pace of the movie and how it exponentially escalated the disturbing factor. Nikki becoming more and more twisted by the entity possessing her, Bear running out of excuses to give others or himself for fueling this charade any further, it all eventually builds up and he has to start looking for a solution. I loved how the first possibility he finds out about is his death, and yet he doesn't want to consider that he might have to sacrifice himself to make things right. He keeps being cruel to Nikki, his immorality culminating with the scene where Nikki snaps back and begs him to kill her. He refuses, still fixated on his frustration for not being liked back. The movie is very intentional with all these scenes and highlights Bear's messed up character. I loved the attention to the script in this matter, especially in this genre, where a lot of decisions are taken to play into the shock factor, to push the horrors even further.

But Obsession holds its spine straight. The conclusion of the movie is extremely well executed. I liked how each character had their own layers and flaws, and how all of them end up punished and/or doomed with the exception of Nikki. She is depicted as the victim through and through, and this is what lies at the center of this story: the horror and suffering of a woman stripped of her autonomy, forced to give her body to this spirit summoned by a man who wanted her just for himself, forced to let this man use her body for his own pleasure. He doesn't respect her right at her own life, he constantly wishes he could keep her love and just alter the circumstances so that she stops being violent and weird. He doesn't love Nikki the person, he loves the concept of her, and especially of her as his girlfriend. He is the first one to become obsessed with the idea of her and the obsession spins around against him.

And enter the finale - I loved the decision they made for the final wish. Her wishing for Bear to love her back just as he was attempting to undo the drastic decision of killing himself, and both of them staring at each other with infatuation, only for him to collapse - i loved all the details in these scenes. The spirit attempts to kill herself (or her vessel) in the despair caused by losing her "loved" one, and at the last moment, Nikki snaps back and bursts in a violent cry. This final scene perfectly encapsulates the essence I mentioned earlier. She survives, but she has to live with the unraveling Bear left behind, with the trauma, she returns to a completely changed life. So this is another interesting note the movie leaves us with: even if the inflictor of abuse gets punished, the victim isn't stripped of the trauma. Once the abuse happens, the wrong can't be undone.

I can't possibly mention all the scenes that drove me crazy in this movie, but they were consistently sustained by great acting and impressive shots. The main cast puts up a fantastic performance, especially Inde Navarrette, who convincingly fleshed out a very difficult role. Michael Johnston also counterparts quite well. The cinematography was very clever, there were many amazing shots, the use of blurry backgrounds, foggy windows and shadows accentuated the tension and horror factors, while also fueling the symbolism of the movie.

All in all, Obsession is a "be careful what you wish for" taken to the extreme, using this storytelling trope to highlight the vile nature of abusers, and the horrors of being trapped and stripped of control over your body. It's also a story about how no matter how far you try to run away from your faults and guilt, your actions will catch up with you and consequences will just turn bigger the more you avoid confronting reality.

Ever since this movie was released, people all over the internet have been hyping it up like it is the absolute best film of the year. Unfortunately, after finally sitting down to watch it, I found it to be incredibly overhyped and just not that good at all. The pacing felt off, and it completely failed to live up to the massive expectations built up by social media.

Went in expecting another low-budget supernatural gimmick movie and walked out feeling like I'd been put through a psychological blender. Curry Barker takes the dumbest possible premise (guy uses a cheap charm to make his coworker fall in love with him) and somehow turns it into one of the most relentless, mean, and genuinely unsettling films of the year.

Michael Johnston is perfect as the kind of lonely dude who thinks he's the victim of his own wish, and Inde Navarrette is just... terrifying. She doesn't play "crazy girlfriend." She plays someone whose mind is being rewritten in real time, and the way that obsession curdles into something violent and possessive is way more disturbing than most possession movies.

It's gory when it needs to be, quiet when it needs to be, and somehow funny in the most uncomfortable way possible (you'll catch yourself laughing at something that should not be funny).

The movie doesn't depend heavily on jump scares; instead, it creates horror through uncomfortable situations, psychological tension, disturbing imagery and brutal violence. Obsession is a sensational example of how to make a horror movie. However, before diving into the film's complexities, I must highlight that it wouldn't be spectacular without Inde Navarrette's outstanding performance; the way she maintains crucial facial expressions is remarkable. As for the film itself, it has a basic yet effective premise; it doesn't rely on jump scares to instill fear, which works perfectly because the horror builds progressively toward a climax. Many horror movies make one of two mistakes: they focus too much on drama, ceasing to be horror films, or they ignore drama entirely, becoming nothing but jump scares and gore. This film, however, begins with drama-allowing the audience to connect with the characters-and surprisingly culminates in horror. I struggle to name a movie or TV series quite as good as this one, as there is a distinction between iconic horror characters and genuinely good films. The psychological drama is handled skillfully, especially when compared to other failed attempts in the genre. A brilliant narrative twist is that the horror stems not from the monster, but from the victim; you fear the victim due to their inhumane actions, yet you feel revulsion toward the "good" monster. The film also offers a powerful social commentary on abusive relationships-a persistent, contemporary issue fueled by flawed mindsets. For a low-budget feature film, it is spectacular. While the drama could have been further developed, the director's intent was to provoke audience reflection, making the existing level of drama entirely acceptable. Ultimately, I cannot give it a score lower than 9; I rate this film a 10, a masterpiece of horror.

summary: A solid horror movie with pacing issues

summary: Built-In Audience More Than Breakout Horror
text:

For me, this movie felt slow and heavily dialogue-driven. It was marketed as horror, but in my theater, the audience laughed far more than they jumped or screamed. summary: Good Decent Horror, But Not the Masterpiece I Expected
text:
In the rise of YouTubers turn filmmakers, i can confidently say that Curry Barker has had one of the most successful runs so far, and personally, i think he's the most impressive director to come from that space since Danny and Michael Philippou.

That said, Obsession has been getting a lot of praise, which made me curious to see how good it actually was, after watching it, and without letting the hype influence my opinion, i still think Obsession is a bit overrated.

Curry Barker can definitely direct, but i don't think it's quite as great as a lot of people say, it's not bad either, in fact, i'd say it's somewhere between ok and good overall, there are some genuinely great moments in it, but there are also several noticeable flaws that i just can't get out of my head.

The concept is interesting, it's actually pretty silly when you think about it, but Barker does a good job making it work, and some of the horror scenes are handled really well, one of the flaws for me is that the beginning feels a little too long, i get that it's trying to set everything up, but i found myself wanting it to get to the horror stuff sooner.

Once the chaos starts, though, Obsession becomes a fun ride, it's still filled with flaws, from the way certain characters handle situations to certain moments that don't always work, but it also has some genuinely disturbing and effective horror scenes, the whole One Wish Willow concept was interesting enough, but i wasn't as invested in it as i expected to be.

The performances are great, and the filmmaking is impressive, still, a little bit of pacing issue and some character flaws kept me from seeing Obsession as the masterpiece that many people call it, it might be one for them, but it wasn't for me.

That said, there's still a lot to like here, most of the horror scenes are done really well, and the final act is actually quite strong, overall, i had a decent time with it, it's a fun and disturbing experience, even if i don't think it fully lives up to all the praise.

summary: A horrifying, unexpected, and endlessly fascinating work of art.
text:
The brainchild of Curry Barker, a YouTube sketch comedy creator. Starring Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, is a masterfully written, genuinely off-putting, and tastefully comedic film.

This emotional roller coaster is filled to the brim with creative elements that make it unique, such as a modernized version of the "mysterious pawn shop selling cursed items" trope, which was perfectly executed. It features unexpected icebreakers in the middle of tense and uncomfortable scenes, and seizes every opportunity to hide the "monster" in plain sight, making viewers want to go back and check if she was there all along.

The overall plot and dialogue are written so neatly and beautifully that, in some scenes, it feels like poetry. The two main stars perform exceptionally, especially Inde Navarrette, whom I hope to see more of in the future. She carries most of the movie on her back with her unbelievable facial expressions, dialogue delivery, and meticulous movements. Lastly, it has an immersive atmosphere and camera work, especially in the scenes where Nikki performs a Shakespearean jump scare.

In conclusion, it is probably the best "be careful what you wish for" movie to date and one of the best horror films, particularly because most recent movies where horror is the main genre have not done a great job of horrifying.

summary: An Intriguing Set Up But Falls Back on Standard Horror Tropes
text:
You always have that movie once in a while that you just do not seem to get as much out of as everyone else seems to and that very much described how I felt about Obsession. I'm hardly going to say that I don't understand where the acclaim is coming from but for me the film had a promising set up that I just don't think was capitalised on to its full potential.

The first thirty minutes or so might lay things on a bit thick but they undeniably do a good job at getting you in this characters head space whilst not directly condoning the action that he ultimately takes. But the film does have pacing issues though and that really rears its head early on when the film just montages through the early stages of this relationship where I really felt like there was a lot more worth exploring. It just feels like things go from 1 to 100 far too often in the situations it's presenting and there are times when it just comes across as shock value. I think this premise is rife with potential to explore interesting themes like misogyny and toxic masculinity and instead just seems to fall back on classic horror tropes. But while it does fall into more standard horror fare than I would have liked it's undeniably executed in a very effective way. It's consistently eerie but even more so just a very uncomfortable watch but in a very purposeful way.

It's got its jump scares but is not overly reliant on them and I really liked the way in which Curry Baker harnessed darkness to a really creepy effect and managing to make the things you don't see on screen just as effective. But the glue that really holds this entire movie together is Inde Navarrette because she is a genuine force of nature. For the issues I did have with the film overall I'm still acutely aware that none of it works without her. It's the kind of performance that in lesser hands could've been awful but every new scene is a new opportunity for her to present her stunning range. She is genuinely terrifying at points whilst still somehow managing to be the heart of the movie and I'll be just as annoyed as everyone else when she becomes the latest horror performance ignored by the academy. She does steal to movie to such a degree that things were negatively impacted for me when she wasn't on screen. Michael Johnston's performance unfortunately did not always hit the notes I wanted it to and I don't know if it's more of a writing or directing issue but I just found myself not liking the way he was playing certain scenes.

I feel very similarly about Obsession as I did with Weapons. I think it starts out very intriguing, it clearly comes from a unique voice and absolutely is effective as a horror vehicle but for me it just did not feel like it lived up to its full potential. I just felt like it had the chance to do something more compelling with its premise rather than falling back on more standard horror fare so a lot of this just felt like wasted potential. It's got one absolutely incredible performance but one that was very hit miss and I think that really sums up how I feel about the movie overall. I really wanted to join in on the overwhelming love this movie has been getting but I'd be lying to myself if I didn't say that it just did not live up to the hype for me.

summary: Brutal morality tale beneath the creepy stuff
text:
It's got a solid visual style; deep shadows, rich colours, and manicured but reserved lighting to illuminate only what is necessary to tell the tale.

The settings and costumes are spot on for very young adults in modest jobs in a creative industry but with uniform shirts. Impending career choices are set to shape their adult lives. Hormones and pent-up emotions are on the loose and untested moral compasses are having a very, very tough time reigning them in.

In the cinema, it was great to hear the younger folk fused to the screen - gasping, groaning, and muffling their scared laughter.

It's the unravelling of our lead characters in this fable that is handled so well in both direction, performance, and visual art design.

Having watched my fair share of horror movies over the decades, my following criticism should seem harsh because the movie is that solid. Nevertheless, the direction is most assured with two or three characters on screen. Conducting a larger group of people with as much aplomb is, I guess, something that comes with time, experience, and production budget.

A quality horror for Gen Z, much like Millennials had It Follows, and my crew had A Nightmare On Elm Street.

The premise to this horror film is pretty simple, and we've certainly seen it before. It's the old "be careful what you wish for," though here it's updated to remind us how important space is in a relationship. You want the other person to love you, of course, but they should also be an independent person and have their own wants and needs. Here the desperation that comes with obsession is turned up to 11 (and then some), and while it's exaggerated to a comical degree, we feel the intense claustrophobia that comes from this kind of a relationship. When you add in a delightfully over-the-top performance from Inde Navarrette, creepy moments that range from just being stared at to brutal violence, and sound design that practically growls as it reverberates, you have a pretty entertaining film.

It was also interesting to think about the film as having at its center a mirror. It's the man's obsession for his friend, despite having no evidence of her being interested romantically in him, which boomerangs into her much larger, all-possessing obsession once his wish is granted. And while her insane love for him turns her into a monster, isn't he, after all, also quite a monster? Even though he knows she is not really herself, that she has no agency over her own body and certainly hasn't consented, he has sex with her and goes through the motions of being in a relationship with her. He keeps trying to live out his fantasy even when it turns disturbing and he knows the real woman is aware and is in agony over it. I think the film could have gone to an even darker place and achieved greatness if it had given us her perspective. It's still a fun film though.

Not a big fan of thrillers movie. I decided to give it a shot simply because it didn't rely a single ghost to drive the plot. It turned out to be better than I expected.

I appreciate that this thriller doesn't just aim to scare the audience but also hides subtle clues about the backstory, leaving room for interpretation. For instance, it's easy to piece together that the real Nikki wakes up occasionally but I didn't realise is a pattern until someone told me about it. Whenever Nikki faces a mirror, her true self is brought back. And the intriguing cat walk in the middle of the scene prompted audiences to ponder whether Nikki has taken the spirit of the dead cat, an animal supposed to love its owner more than anything else in the world.

Obsession is a fitting title, perfectly reflecting Bear's fixation on Nikki. He wanted Nikki to love him more than anything in the world, but he didn't even dare to confess his feelings to her. Cowardice is what caused the tragedy. While Bear was a victim of "one wish willow", he was also the one who started everything with his unrealistic desire. Nikki was the most tragic victim of all, completely out of control and manipulated by the wish of a man.

While watching it in a crowded cinema certainly helped, the movie wasn't overwhelmingly scary for me. I could usually anticipate the jump scares before they happened. Moreover, realizing that Nikki wouldn't physically harm Bear eased my tension. For me, the most unsettling scene was when Nikki brutally beat Sara to death with a brick. It's a very bloody way of dying and Sara must felt incredibly painful before she died. The ending was also predictable. It could have been even more chilling if Nikki had made a wish that keeps Bear from dying in the ending.

The film's pacing is intense, though the director's deliberate choice to slow down certain scenes made the beginning feel a bit slow. However, a few absurd moments actually made me laugh, offering a brief moment of levity before the tension ratcheted back up.

In conclusion, the intricate details and overall theme really resonated with me. The cast, especially the actress playing Nikki, delivered stellar performances. While it might not be the absolute scariest movie out there, it is certainly a well-crafted psychological thriller.

This is a good movie. It's very well shot and acted. However I just hate horror movies, and this movie only made my stance firmer. It is probably the best horror movie I've seen (which is not saying a lot), it left me genuinely horrified and uncomfortable leaving the cinema. I hated it and it was dreadful and uncomfortable.

summary: Be Careful What You Wish For
text: Curry Barker's Obsession is a chilling psychological horror that excels through its unsettling atmosphere and compelling performances, especially from Inde Navarrette. Everything that could go right in a film, has gone right in this film. The film is 110 minutes of disorienting daze, it makes you feel the dread crippling underneath your skin with every shot, its evasive eeriness is going to stay on your left as you watch the credits roll.

It is THE definitive horror movie of the year.

The Good:
-Very solid execution of a simple troupe how wishes can turn against us in a paranormal (and horribly bad) way.

-While there are obviously more than 2 characters it's mainly a two person show so it doesn't waste more time than it's actually needed on other characters. This is a plus since many movies and tv series open way too many fronts.

The Mixed:
-While this isn't a permanent problem of the movie, like 2-3 times horror basically turned into a comedy.

The Bad:
-The film executed its premise in a good way but didn't really bother with anything apart from using the gimmick for the whole movie. There is no paranormal world building, we also don't really get to feel Nikki's internal suffering, apart from one short scene. There is no detailed logic (or well any) how this wish making thing operates. The whole thing is based on a very solid execution of a very old troupe implemented in a very basic way. Of course any potential problems like drug abuse that could be used even within a horror story were treated as just something to say once and use once. Of course there isn't really a serious character background even though the story is mostly focused on two characters.

-Honestly, I'm a person that was diagnosed as a teen with social phobia (now much better, thank you very much) I quite literally rejected a cute girl asking me for a number during those years. Yet even for me "Bear" and his attempts to say the thing towards Nikki looked hardly believable.

Overall: Despite all its faults it's a nice horror story but it simply can't get a better note with this level of (zero) ambition.

If the message of the film weren't so important, I would probably rate it somewhere between 7 and 8 stars. But let's put aside the confusing and, at times, completely unexplained parts of the film and focus on what I believe it ultimately wants to say.

At its core, Obsession is a reminder of how essential agency and autonomy are. A person's free will should be untouchable. Your life, your choices, your body, your mind, and your sense of self should always belong to you. No relationship should ever require you to surrender those things.

And I think this message is particularly important for women. There is still so much social conditioning around women being expected to accommodate, submit, sacrifice, or define themselves through their relationships with others. We are often taught that love means compromise, that being a good partner means putting someone else first, or that financial or emotional dependence somehow gives another person a claim over our lives. It doesn't.

It is never worth giving up your agency for someone else. Never worth surrendering your autonomy for financial security, emotional dependence, love, marriage, family, or friendship. Being loved should never come at the cost of being able to make your own choices.

Always remain a complete person in your own right. Keep your own mind. Keep your own boundaries. Keep your independence. The lines between yourself and another person should never become so blurred that you no longer know where they end and you begin.

A marriage is not worth losing yourself for. A friendship is not worth losing yourself for. Family is not worth losing yourself for. And certainly not romantic love. Even when someone expects your submission, demands it, or slowly tries to convince you that giving up parts of yourself is simply the price of being loved.

Never surrender your autonomy just to keep someone else.

That, for me, is the most powerful thing the film has to offer: the reminder that we should never voluntarily hand over ownership of our own lives. Love should exist between two autonomous people, not between one person who possesses and another who submits.

Whatever flaws the film may have, that message alone makes it worth watching.

And to never wish for a door to open forcefully because there is a reason why it remains shut. Don't force destiny when there are other plans that are made for you, far better plans. If something is for you, it gonna make itself known as that. If it isn't then you need patience and acceptance that the right thing gonna come into your life.

summary: An important and timely topic, but a mediocre execution
text:
Obsession is heavily overrated compared to the enthusiastic response from critics and audiences. The film has a strong, easily marketable concept: a young man uses a magical object to make his female friend fall in love with him, but the fulfilled wish turns love into a painful obsession. The subject feels fresh and relevant enough for contemporary cinema, especially in the context of young relationships, codependency, fear of loneliness, and violations of personal boundaries. But the construction itself is not particularly innovative: at its core, this is a classic story about a granted wish that turns into a curse.

The execution remains mediocre. The film depicts jealousy, dependence, the inability to be alone, and Nikki's gradual dissolution into Bear, but it barely explores the internal mechanics of her madness. Her behavior quickly becomes excessive, theatrical, and grotesque. This works effectively as a horror performance, but it is weaker as psychological observation. Instead of a subtle escalation of dependence, we mostly get increasingly loud and bloody manifestations of the same condition.

The reaction of the social circle is also underdeveloped. The friends are surprised, frightened, and drawn into the conflict, but no strong social tension emerges. The film does not show how the people close to them gradually recognize an abusive relationship, who denies what is happening, who tries to intervene, or why the help fails. The supporting characters primarily exist as functions of the plot, so even a large-scale psychological catastrophe remains rather contained and superficial.

The mythology of the One Wish Willow is barely developed either. This can be accepted on its own terms: the object can simply function as a fairy-tale mechanism that materializes Bear's wish. But when the film offers neither deep psychology, powerful dramatic construction, nor particularly strong suspense, the underdeveloped mythology becomes another missed advantage. The film introduces a hook and hints at something larger, but never transforms it into a fully realized world or system.

The strongest idea in the film is not Nikki's obsession, but Bear's moral responsibility. What he wants is not mutual love, but a guarantee that he will never be rejected. His fear of loss, cowardice, and self-pity turn into violence because he places his own desire above another person's freedom. For Nikki to love only him, she has to stop being an independent human being. The film exposes male self-deception: Bear sees himself as a romantic and a victim of loneliness, even though he effectively strips another person of her identity.

But even this commentary is strong mainly on the level of its central idea. That exploiting another person's vulnerability, controlling them, and depriving them of freedom for the sake of personal comfort is wrong is obvious even without the film. The film barely deconstructs this mechanism and does not arrive at a more complex conclusion. It shows the consequences but does not deepen the causes: where Bear's sense of entitlement to Nikki comes from, why he perceives rejection as an injustice, and how romantic self-pity turns into moral permission to coerce another person.

The direction reflects the filmmaker's experience in short-form internet content. Barker knows how to devise individual striking scenes, strange movements, sharp reactions, bloody moments, and sequences that can easily be edited into TikTok clips. But the feature-length progression is weaker: the relationship develops rather mechanically, the suspense never reaches a particularly high level, and psychological nuance gives way to spectacular theatricality. The film knows how to provoke an immediate reaction, but it is less successful at sustaining deeper analysis afterward.

Its genuinely outstanding advantage belongs primarily to the production. Obsession was made for approximately $750,000 over twenty days, yet it looks more professional than many films with budgets in the tens of millions. This is an important industry case study against the backdrop of inflated studio spending, weak management, and producers' complaints about low profit margins. The film proves that genre cinema can be made significantly more cheaply without a catastrophic decline in visual quality. But production efficiency is not the same as artistic greatness: this is a victory of management, concept, and marketing, not proof of the screenplay's depth.

The main success of Obsession is how much discussion it generates. The subject is relevant, relatable, and especially close to younger audiences; individual scenes work well in short-form videos, while the plot itself is easily connected to real stories of toxic relationships, jealousy, and dependence. The film creates a substantial foundation for discussion, but the discussion-worthiness of its subject does not make its treatment profound. Ultimately, this is not an outstanding horror film, but a competently made, superficial, and exceptionally well-packaged work whose cultural and commercial impact is considerably stronger than its artistic quality.

Audience preferences move in crests and troughs. There was a time when indie cinema was the flavour of the season before being pushed into the shadows by larger-than-life spectacles. Going by the buzz surrounding Obsession, it appears the tide is turning once again. Made on a modest budget but brimming with conviction, Obsession proves that imagination is still the biggest special effect money cannot buy.

At first, I wondered what the hullabaloo was all about. The opening twenty minutes move at a leisurely pace and test the patience of the audience. Just when you begin to question the rave reviews, the film grabs you by the collar and drags you onto a roller-coaster ride that seldom slows down thereafter.

The biggest strength of Obsession is its novel premise. In an industry where familiarity is often mistaken for creativity, here is a film that dares to venture into uncharted territory. The writing deserves special praise. Not only are the situations relatable, but the characters feel like people one may actually encounter in everyday life. Their decisions, flaws and emotions ring true, making it easy to invest in their journey.

Kudos to the entire team who have poured their sweat, blood and energy into the proceedings. The performances stand out because the characters are identifiable. No one appears to be merely going through the motions. Rather, there is a collective sense of belief in the material that elevates the film.

Horror and thrillers often mistake loud background scores for suspense. Thankfully, Obsession understands the value of anticipation. Yes, there are enough jump scares to satisfy genre enthusiasts, but the moments leading up to them are often even more effective. The tension quietly builds and keeps the audience guessing what lies around the corner.

Interestingly, the fulcrum of the plot reminded me of the adolescent boy's wish fulfilment in Tom Hanks' Big. While the comparison ends there, it speaks volumes about the film's willingness to explore ideas that go beyond conventional genre boundaries.

Technically, the film punches far above its weight. The makers maximise every resource at their disposal and ensure the narrative remains the hero. Most importantly, the climax is an absolute show-stopper. "Oh NO!" was the first thought that crossed my mind in the climax.

The writing on the wall is clear. Films like Obsession deserve support. If creativity is to flourish, audiences must encourage passionate storytellers who dare to dream differently. Otherwise, genuine talent risks being overshadowed by the marketing muscle of larger studio houses.

Overall, Obsession is proof that heart, ingenuity and perseverance can achieve what budgets often cannot. Imperfect in places, but refreshingly original and immensely rewarding.

summary: Familiar concept, but it has NEVER been done this well.
text:
We've all probably seen this concept done before or similar in movies, and even some TV shows, but this is by far the best I ever seen it executed, and to me, execution is WAY MORE important than the story told itself. Though the story itself still has some crazy twists.

Reason the execution is perfect is the acting, how unsettling it is, pacing, lighting, atmosphere and soundtrack. All the main actors do perfect in the their role. The obvious best performance is Nikki as she is required the most to do and executes basically everything perfect, one of the most obvious Oscar performances I seen. But even Bear's actor does a phenomenal job as playing the super insecure guy, who kinda seems like a good guy, but might not be not so nice deep down, and that's hard to pull off as well, but he pulls it off perfectly.

There is two other main characters that don't require as much hardcore acting, but they still do perfect in their smaller roles and essential and perfect for the story.

The entire movie is perfectly paced and just gets better and better and more engaging as it goes on. It's been a long time I seen a movie execute the unsettling feeling this perfect. I've seen many possession movies of people not being control of their bodies, but never seen it done this unsettling and disturbing before.

It's been so LONG I seen a horror movie actually do jumpscares properly! And there wasn't too much jumpscares or not enough, it was just the perfect amount for the story. And there was better scary moments that weren't jumpscares but just very unsettling things, mainly from Nicki's phenomenal performance. There's even some gore which I wasn't expecting as much, but it's all still perfectly balanced.

The movie is perfect in terms of just pure entertainment factor, but it's also very deep in it's themes and a movie you really want to talk about and think about long after. I kinda saw it as an allegory for drugging and taking advantage of drugged women, but you can go much deeper than that, and interpret it in many other ways. It's been very long since I seen a movie balance it's entertainment value and it's deep themes and messaging(that aren't too much shoved in your face) so perfectly. I see a lot of movies get caught up in their preachy messaging that the entertainment value tanks, vice versa. But Obsession is the rare exception, perfect balance of flawless entertainment and flawless deep themes messaging.

Now let me say, I'm not the type of guy who always buys into new movie hype. I don't care if a movie is super hyped or not, if it's a good movie, I will praise it regardless. Lots of new Horror movies I wanted to like, but I just couldn't, like Jordan Peele movies do nothing for me, same for Zack Kreggor movies, despite their extreme hype. But I'm happy to say with Obsession, I finally absolutely LOVE a horror movie that a lot of other people love, and can understand where so many people are coming from. Super excited to see what Curry Barker does next. With how perfect he made the movie unsettling plus that dreamy score soundtrack, he would literally be the best candidate for a proper good Silent Hill movie.

Seriously that is a WTF movie. Very well done and I have never rated a movie 10/10 but here it is. Best horror I have seen. Just watch it!!!!

From start to finish it has you thinking what the hell is going to happen next in this crazy movie. Well written, well executed and its no wonder everyone is talking about it. Well done.

text:
This movie was just a bunch of stress and noise for no reason. Who are you supposed to be rooting for? Bear is cowardly and morally rephrensible. Like the writers said "Oh, let's just throw in a dead cat, that'll really shock them! Oh and then make him eat it, that'll be really gross!" It's like a bunch of teenagers wrote this movie.

summary: An idea that's scarier than the monster
text: The thing I liked most about Obsession is that it takes a concept that could have been played for cheap thrills and turns it into something surprisingly uncomfortable. The story follows Bear, a lonely young man who uses a supernatural "One Wish Willow" to make his longtime crush, Nikki, love him, only to discover that getting exactly what he wanted is far more horrifying than rejection ever could have been. Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette are both excellent, especially as the film gradually transforms from an awkward romance into something genuinely disturbing. I also appreciated that Curry Barker never lets the movie become preachy, even though it's clearly saying something about entitlement and the fantasy of controlling another person's feelings. A few of the middle stretches dragged for me, and I think the ending loses a little momentum after such a strong buildup, but the central idea is so unsettling that it kept me thinking long after the credits rolled. It's creepy, original, and refreshingly different from most studio horror.

This is the first horror movie in a long time that was genuinely terrifying.

Simple in terms of premise but the execution, direction and of course the actors of this film made it unique.

A highly recommended film for horror fans looking for properly unsettling sequences.

I've also heard the director was a kid who made YouTube videos which really puts the cherry on the top considering how great this move was.

A story about how magical young love can really be when you really wish you for it.. without deserving it.

The chatter hasn't stopped, and I finally get to watch it. Immediately, I understand why it has captured the audience in the way that it has, as it is clearly very well executed and somewhat fresh! It has a very "It Follows" feel, so it is no wonder it is doing numbers. The Horror genre, being a relatively low barrier to entry for filmmakers while consistently finding its audience, seems to make quality product stand out more than usual.

It is visually very interesting and appealing, has the right amount of unsettling moments and little creative touch-ups. The rules are properly setup from the start (though the magic element is utterly tacked on), gives enough clues and keeps things mysterious. The girls stand out with their performances (the leading lady steals the show with a very fun role), while the rest of the cast is okay.

I personally don't really "seek out" these kind of films for myself, but I enjoyed it and thought it was quite memorable. I did find it, quite sadly, rather predictable in its developments.. with the somewhat-unlikeable main character reaching a conclusion I arrived at almost immediately (I am, of course, someone watching a movie), with everything else playing out exactly as I expected in the end.

In retrospect, the premise is obviously simple and straightforward, but it doesn't really need to be anything else. This is execution over foundation, and still a fun watch.

This movie felt quite overhyped compared to the expectations surrounding it. The pacing is very slow, making it difficult to stay fully engaged for most of the runtime. summary: Psycho Girlfriend Who Doesn't Let Go
text:
"Make sure the wish lands right."

That is the bloodline running through Curry Barker's *Obsession*, a film built on the oldest warning there is: want something hard enough, and watch it come back wrong.

At the center of it all is the One Wish Willow, a force that doesn't just grant desire. It listens to it, opens it up, and lets the rot bloom from the inside. What starts as Bear reaching for something he aches for turns vicious fast, then tighter, then inescapable, until longing stops looking like hope and starts breathing like a nightmare.

From the first moments, the film lays everyone in its path out in front of you like a promise already headed for ruin. You know something is coming for them. You can feel it in the air before it fully takes shape. Inde Navarrette is especially devastating here, the kind of presence that gets under your skin without asking permission. Even when the structure feels like it might turn where you expect, the film still finds a way to hit with a sharper blade than you were ready for.

*Obsession* doesn't rely on chaos to break you. It doesn't need gore flooding the frame or violence screaming every second. It moves quieter than that. Meaner than that. It pulls you in slow, gets its hand around your throat, and keeps tightening. What begins like a low engine in the dark turns into a full wreck by the end, precise, ugly, and impossible to shake off.

Nikki becomes the purest shape of the film's warning: desire without understanding, closeness without control, love warped into possession. What should have been a wish becomes a lock. A grip. A suffocating thing with no mercy in it.

And Michael Johnston's Bear carries that collapse well, because his mistake never feels distant from him. It stalks him. Breathes on him. Closes around him until there is almost nowhere left to stand inside his own life.

By the final stretch, *Obsession* leaves its mark clean: be careful what you wish for. Because obsession has never been love; it's hunger without end. It is control wearing the mask of devotion. And this film makes that truth feel terrifying.

This is a dark romance wrapped inside a psychological horror. The premise is simple but effective. A hopeless romantic gets exactly what he wishes for, only to realise that desire can turn into something disturbing. What makes it stand out is how confidently it shifts between funny, romantic, creepy and gory without feeling messy.

Inde Navarrette is the highlight as Nikki. She gives the character enough range to make the obsession believable and unsettling. The film is dark and most time literally, which adds to the sinister mood. The ending was well written, properly executed, and gives the story a satisfying payoff.

Overall, this is a solid and original horror film with more range than it first appears to have.
