summary: Loving Is Not Possessing: The Lesson Obsession Teaches with Blood.
text:
My highest praise for Obsession, directed by a 26-year-old kid who just two or three years ago was uploading sketches and horror shorts to YouTube. That already marks a standard right from the start, because what is on screen has nothing amateur about it: it is a work that, in terms of production quality, rubs shoulders without issue with prestige Hollywood cinema-and the box office numbers are there to prove it.

The film was made with a budget of barely $750,000 and has already grossed over $430 million worldwide, becoming one of the biggest financial successes modern horror has produced. Filming lasted just 26 days in California, with a relatively small crew and leaning heavily on practical work rather than digital effects. Curry Barker took on practically everything: direction, screenwriting, and editing supervision (something that is almost a signature of filmmakers coming from YouTube, accustomed to doing everything with minimal resources).

Obsession is an outstanding project because of its premise. It takes the classic "careful what you wish for" trope and builds psychological horror out of something as everyday as unrequited love until it twists it into something grotesque. Bear believes he loves Nikki, but what he desires is to control her, and the entire story revolves around his self-deception. That is why the horror would work even if the magical aspect were stripped away; Bear portrays extreme emotional dependency, incapable of accepting rejection, and Nikki is a projection of that impossible desire. In this, the film's core theme is unveiled: the difference between loving and possessing.

Barker chooses to avoid conventional dark horror. This aspect only appears in specific moments when Nikki is at her most psychedelic. Otherwise, there is an abundance of natural light. In other words, the horror happens right out in the open, without hiding in overwhelming shadows.

In terms of structure, the film begins like an indie romantic comedy that gradually mutates into a grotesque puzzle box. Bear neither learns nor corrects his mistakes; instead, he reveals himself as an unreliable narrator-even to himself-convinced he is doing the right thing while committing increasingly questionable acts. If anything weighs the film down slightly, it is that the third act falls into repetitions that rob the pacing of some of its force, though the visual impact of its most violent moments largely compensates for it.

In the subtext of his character, Bear is a predator disguised as a "nice guy." His passivity in the face of Nikki's deterioration is a deliberate script choice. He stays with her when he should be afraid, in part because he enjoys the attention he never had before. Ian, his best friend, is the mirror of that same hypocrisy: at times validating Bear's worst decisions and at others donning the mask of a moral compass, while being no better a person than him.

There are those who see it as a portrait of "incel horror," where the monster is the entitlement to a woman's body and affection; others prefer to speak of emotional cowardice rather than toxic masculinity; and some argue that, since magical desires do not exist in real life, the metaphor loses some ground when trying to tell us something about the real world from such a fantastic premise.

Finally, we must talk about Inde Navarrette, because her performance is the technical backbone of the project: physically demanding, it has ultimately earned her a spot among the great actresses of cinema, and very soon we will see her in major commercial franchise films. Without having been paid a massive fortune and with a somewhat subtle resume, the actress joins a constellation of elements that, when brought together, make Obsession a masterclass in how a well-executed idea outweighs any budget.

I really enjoyed Obsession for most of its runtime.

This micro-budget horror punches well above its weight - it looks sharp and professional, never cheap. The two leads, Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, are excellent, bringing real heart and intensity to their roles, while the supporting cast holds their own too. The film keeps a constant creepy vibe going, even when the actual horror scenes are spaced out. That lingering unease works well.

Where it loses me is the predictability. You can feel the story heading down familiar paths, and I kept hoping for a clever twist or something fresh in the final stretch. Instead, it plays things pretty safe and lands on an ending that feels like a cop-out.

Still, the strong performances and steady dread make it worth watching if you like slow-burn psychological horror with a supernatural edge.

summary: Thick atmosphere and dread create a captivating viewing experience.
text:
So, I finally watched Obsession. I've heard nothing but rave reviews. Personally, I love the resurgence of horror as a popular genre. It has been fantastic seeing horror regain its place as a serious genre. I had very high hopes for Obsession. That being said, the film absolutely lived up to my expectations and then some. This was one of the most enjoyable horror films I have seen in quite some time. It is proof that bigger budgets do not necessarily equate to better films. Sometimes, you just need an interesting story and some good storytellers to keep the audience engaged.

The story follows a young man who has a crush. He appears to be stuck in the friend zone but doesn't have the courage to communicate his feelings. At a novelty shop, he purchases an item that sets the entire film in motion. The film quickly unravels into an anxiety-inducing mix of tension and occasional dark humor that eventually explodes into a crescendo of violence. Without spoiling anything, this film absolutely leans into the classic monkey's paw premise, enhanced by tight filmmaking and impressive direction from a rookie director.

Admittedly, I'm very familiar with the director's work. Curry Barker makes absolutely hysterical YouTube videos. I've been watching them for years and never once considered that there was a genius filmmaker underneath the goofy skits. However, this film absolutely shows that he is going to be a force to be reckoned with. For a lower-budget film, this is expertly shot. It is classic filmmaking at its finest. The camera angles really brought you into the thick of the story, and you almost felt as if you were in the room watching as everything progressed. On top of that, Curry Barker created a tight script filled with atmosphere and tension. I absolutely love horror films that constantly give you a feeling of unease, and this film truly captured a constant sense of impending doom.

I also felt that the script as a whole was smart and well-written. The script itself was tight and self-contained but blended horror and comedy perfectly. I feel that when you're able to combine horror and comedy seamlessly, it creates a very engaging viewing experience. Nothing felt forced or out of place. The dark humor felt perfectly natural and really showed the director's range. I also felt the underlying themes regarding desire versus love were handled very well. The overall commentary regarding unhealthy expectations and relationships building toward codependency and eventually despair created a smart script. A simple monkey's paw film could have been shallow, but I found that this had surprising depth, which enhanced the viewing experience.

Of course, if we're talking about horror, we need to talk about the actual thrills. Again, the film created a constant feeling of dread that steadily built tension. I find jump scares to be cheap. Tension, however, is what creates terror. I felt the film did an incredible job creating tension that made the extreme violence all the more shocking. The film had elements of The Exorcist-style body horror, along with a couple of truly shocking and memorable acts of violence. The body count in the film isn't insanely high, but it does have one of the most shocking and brutal deaths I've seen recently. The story was a slow-moving train of tension that continuously accelerated until it hit a brick wall. It felt like an old-school horror film that they just don't make anymore. It's great seeing actual horror come back into popularity from a filmmaking standpoint.

As I mentioned, I really enjoyed the script, and I felt the directing was well done. That all being said, the performance from Inde Navarrette was an absolute standout. I think this is going to be one of those performances that is talked about for years. Her range was impressive all around. Her ability to go from charming and likable to absolutely terrifying, and then return to loving in the blink of an eye, was incredibly impressive. Her performance felt genuine and very real. The emotional outbursts, the rapid mood changes, and the toxic, codependent love bonding all felt very real, which made her eventual break all the more engaging. It was a slow-moving train that very quickly escalated, and her performance remained genuine and grounded despite the narrative. I very much look forward to seeing where her career goes.

Is this a perfect film? No, of course not. The script is left intentionally vague and ambiguous regarding some overarching questions. There's talk of a potential TV series that could add some backstory. For now, the film asks a lot of questions but doesn't really elaborate, which I'm actually okay with. Still, I think those expecting the narrative to be spoon-fed will be frustrated by the lack of explanation. While I enjoyed the film greatly, I can also see it being off-putting to a number of individuals. That is not just because of the violence, but also because of the underlying themes of exploitation and objectification of the female form. I believe it was Curry Barker's intent to make an uncomfortable film about an uncomfortable topic. Still, those looking for conventional supernatural horror will likely be disappointed.

I've grown to despise jump scares over the years. I find that kind of horror talks down to viewers and tells them when to be afraid. The best horror brings you on a journey, and Obsession certainly did that. The tension and dread of the film kept me on the edge of my seat, the filmmaking was excellently done, the acting was sharp, and the shocking deaths were engaging all around. I really enjoyed Obsession and am certainly looking forward to seeing more from Curry Barker in the future.

8.75 out of 10.

Honestly, I didn't expect a low-budget film to create this much tension. It's creepy, terrifying, and constantly makes you feel like something is about to go horribly wrong. The atmosphere does a lot with very little, and that's what impressed me most. It doesn't need blockbuster-level visuals to keep you uncomfortable. Some parts are exaggerated, but overall it completely pulled me in and kept me tense until the end.

Masculinity here is a door that creaks. Obsession films desire as possession, and possession as a terror that ricochets between the one who looks and the one who is looked at. The monster is the certainty that the other belongs to you. And that certainty is filmed with a naturalness that sends chills down your spine.

The camera clings to bodies with a suffocating intimacy. Every close-up invades. The photography bathes faces in dense shadows, light touching only half the face. No one reveals themselves completely. You search the characters' eyes for an exit and find only an abyss. It is a beautiful and genuine capture of how power is wielded through a look.

The sound works with what is yet to come. Muffled beats that blend with a heartbeat. Footsteps on the floor above that might be your own. The score drips in the background like a faucet leaking at four in the morning, and each drop carries a silent accusation. The nuance of the nearly inaudible turns every scene into unbearable waiting.

What makes the film touching and suffocating at once is how it captures love as an acquired right. The idea that someone owes you something. That affection is a debt. Possessive masculinity spreads through the rooms like smoke, and everyone breathes it in without realizing. Until they choke. The fantastic thing here is the naturalness with which terror settles into everyday life.

Obsession ends and you find yourself staring at your own reality and similar scenarios of everyday horror amplified, yet at the same time nullified by the routine and the ultra cynical modern world. What you just watched is a topography of something you have felt on your skin or witnessed or feared in the dark. Something you recognize in someone close or in the mirror. The film laughs quietly and the echo lingers.

summary: A Small Film That Deserves the Hype
text: The enormous hype may leave you expecting a once-in-a-generation masterpiece, so the ending can feel slightly underwhelming. Still, considering the limited budget, Obsession is genuinely impressive. The two leads are convincing, the direction is confident, and the film looks far more expensive than it is. You must forgive the pun in the title - I just had to, because it's simply true. I've rewatched this film twice already in one week, and anticipate that I'll rewatch it many more times from here out. Every aspect of this film, from its unique cinematography to stellar and chilling acting to dark and provocative character writing is deserving of praise. It's not a film deserving of just one watch - it's deserving of two, three, four, and manages to grow more and more eerie each time.

First, each of the four main characters are written with foresight and nuance, no matter how much or little screentime they wind up receiving. After watching the film the first time, you become first aware of their deeper, hidden motivations that wind up popping out as you rewatch the film. The dialogue is remarkably sharp, realistic for their age group, and not a single line is wasted. Every line packs either characterization, foreshadowing, or both, meaning that subsequent rewatches leave you stunned as to how you could have missed the little hints. For instance, Ian either sabotaging Bear or downright misunderstanding Nikki due to his surface-level relationship with her. Sarah's enduring concern. Nikki's longing for change contrasted with Bear's desperation for the status quo. Every moment and interaction is key to understanding them as people and their roles in relation to the ideas of the film.

These ideas themselves are unique and underexplored in cinema. Bear as the protagonist- turned closeted villain- is phenomenally written. On one hand, his actions are understandable based on his psyche; on the other, they grow increasingly deplorable and sickening as the film goes on, leaving you wondering just how far he'll go - or refuse to go, more aptly - to keep the thing he wants most in his life, even if it's an utter lie. The most terrifying part is that Bear is a completely average person; his evil is only revealed once he is truly given his deepest desire. His cowardice and fear of risk-taking leads his accidental wish to prove disastrous for every person around him.

A quick note on this disaster and how it unfolds in the film: it is so, so chilling to watch. Inde is a fantastic actress, and you wind up feeling so sorry for Nikki while genuinely terrified of her at the same time. From the first moment she turns around, spellbound and coated in shadow, she carries an immense and sickening cloud of danger that clings to her skin and thickens every scene. This danger is a creeping sort, gradually and slowly escalating to more and more bizarre and disturbing actions, from cooking a cat to stalking Bear's bed in the shadows late at night to viciously murdering Sarah in one of the most brutal scenes I've seen yet in horror. To touch on Sarah's death as well: the gore in this scene is just simply so effective. The film's prior restraint in displaying blood and injury beyond Nikki's self-harming means that the film's one jumpscare is utterly shocking when it comes about, with the image of Sarah's mutilated face and sinking eye like a broken egg searing itself into your mind for days to come.

Yet still, through all Nikki's terrifying actions against herself and others, the most frightening character of all is the one who took the least action: Bear. And that is what makes this film so intelligent and even important. The male loneliness epidemic, isolation, and socially conditioned passivity and cowardice has slipped hidden monsters into society. But the greatest pity is the number of people who will watch this film seeing Bear as nothing but a story villain, failing to realize that they, themselves, are a Bear simply lacking a One Wish Willow to make their secret little dreams come true.

But Nikki was trapped somewhere, so his wish didn't come true - that's my nitpick. Overall, it's a solid stalker horror with strong tension.

I expected Obsession to scare me, but instead it made me angry at Bear. Once he realises his wish caused Nikki's obsession, he still expects her to "act normal," hides the truth, and barely tries to get help. Watching him avoid responsibility was more frustrating than the horror itself.

Great concept and excellent acting, especially Nikki. I just spent most of the movie thinking, "Bear, what are you doing?!"

Obsession is a psychological horror movie about Bear and Nikki, two friends with very different feelings for each other. Bear is in love with Nikki, but she does not feel the same way. One day, he finds a mysterious willow branch that can make wishes come true. He wishes for Nikki to love him more than anything in the world. At first, his wish seems perfect, but things quickly become much darker.

Bear is a shy young man who really wants Nikki to love him. Nikki is confident and friendly, and she is one of the most interesting characters in the movie. However, as the story continues, Nikki becomes more unpredictable and erratic because of the wish while Bear is trying to convince himself that Nikki really loves him.

My favorite parts are the moments when the psychological tension turns into pure horror. For instance, while they are having a romantic dinner, Bear confronts Nikki about a lie, and the atmosphere suddenly becomes very uncomfortable. At that moment, Nikki suddenly starts to scream in a very creepy way, and Bear has to calm her down before things get even worse. The cherry on top is when Bear goes outside to talk to his friend in the car, and Nikki suddenly appears from the shadows and kills her. These unsettling scenes are some of my favorites because they show how dangerous Nikki's new behavior is becoming and how quickly the situation can change.

I recommend Obsession to people who like horror and psychological thrillers. The movie is creepy, but it also makes you think about love, control and obsession. After I watched it, I wondered who was really obsessed: Bear or Nikki. Maybe the real horror was not only what happened to Nikki, but how far someone could go when they wanted to control another person's feelings. The movie leaves this question open, and that is what stayed with me after it ended.

Ian could've told him that he had been with Nikki and he would have probably inadvertently prevented Bear from making such a self-serving wish that took away Nikki's autonomy. There were so many things that were creepy about their relationship from the get go that Bear blames on Nikki and not his own actions. I need to watch again but I think I'll settle for waiting for it to stream.

Be careful what you wish for is the entire takeaway from this film. Reaching for ultra disturbing heights, the film doesn't quite reach it's aspirations. However, you can't help but to admire Curry Barker's ambition here.

There is an impressive amount of uncomfortable, awkward moments that are undercut with just the right amount of dark humor to make the film feel inviting as opposed to feeling exploititive. Barker has just enough wit to his writing understand the difference between off-putting and being put off. I also enjoyed how his script seems to enjoy in playing with the audience. Almost like he's giving the viewers a nudge and a wink through some key moments in the film. It made for a fun viewing experience. The audience at my screening was both gagging and laughing through most of the runtime.

There was a specific sequence in the film that my theater handed out sandwiches for. As the scene played out, you could hear the audience unwrapping and eating their newly arrived food. I found this to be completely random and odd until everything came into focus. About 5 minutes passes and we finally get to the point of the scene. I will not divulge what was witnessed onscreen, but I will tell you I don't think I have ever heard so many people simultaneously start gagging in my 30 years of going to the movies. It was fantastic hahahaha!

The film was not without it's flaws and I cannot go on to say that it is a perfect film. There are a few scenes where the film slows down a bit too much, and there was a few plot points that needed a bit more explaination. With that said, I'm still pretty satisfied with what we got here, and as far as a second feature film, it's a pretty great place for the creator to pick up momentum with his career.

Overall, I enjoyed it and recommend it. It's a movie that likes to have fun with the audience which, in the days where movies are pretty disconnected from the audience, was very refreshing. I want to say more and go into detail about some things, but the film has not been released yet and there are a few good sequences in the film that are best left for the viewer to discover.

4 Willow Branches Out Of 5.

The acting by the Nikki character is great to be fair. The story is decent and there are some really good scares. I recommend it but curb your expectations a bit I guess. The rating of 8 is unrealistic considering which other films have that score. Hope you enjoy it in any case. When done well, there's no wrong way to make horror. Horror stories may be creepy, disturbing, anxiety-inducing, unnerving, deliciously sinister, or maybe just outright fun, to say nothing of instances that are gross and repulsive (as they're intended to be), and still more. Among all the great horror films in the world, though, there are relatively few that I would describe as "genuinely horrifying." To my pleasure, this is one of them. The low-key trailer stoked some interest, but the premise seemed very common, following the "be careful what you wish for" plot arc, so I wasn't specifically intending to see it. Very strong word of mouth and personal recommendations drove me to see 'Obsession' during its theatrical run, however, and I'm very glad they did, because this is outstanding, and makes a big, lasting impression.

It's easy to get criticism out of the way because ultimately I don't think there is much to lay at this picture's proverbial feet. The one thing I will say that doesn't sit quite right with me is the particular vision of filmmaker Curry Barker, or more precisely, what to me feels like a unity of vision that just hasn't fully crystallized. The wish is very clear, and in the film's lore, so are the possible resolutions, and the extra layer of insidiousness underlying the results of the wish. The wish manifests in ways that seem to be kind of all over the place, though, and if there is rhyme and reason to them, I'm just not on the same wavelength as Barker to see it. Then again, maybe I'm nitpicking; maybe this is reflection of that critique I've seen in recent years, that audiences are too hung up on plot and can't enjoy something in and of itself. After all, the plot device is purely magical, so who am I to say how magic might manifest?

Meanwhile, it's true that the plot is based on that common idea in fiction of a fervent wish that comes true, but with terrible, consequential ramifications that far outweigh any benefit gained. Yet any concerns of this feature being a tired new iteration of that trope are laid to rest quite quickly, above all as Barker takes that idea to an intense, grotesque new extreme. Deeply unsettling themes and notions lay the foundations for the plot, drawn from the daily horrors of real life, namely the suppression of a person's agency or identity by someone or something else. Even these are somewhat pushed to the side, however, by scene work and a developing narrative that are very uncomfortable and difficult as a baseline, and often visceral, or starkly impactful on an intimate level. Owing to the characterizations, the dynamics between them, the hellish progression of events, and among still more, not least the violence, this is not an easy movie to watch, and one hesitates to give a blanket recommendation because it's so raw and ghastly; this is not for everyone. But that's exactly why we watch horror films in the first place, isn't it?

These 100 minutes buzz with a fiercely dark, nefarious energy, keeping us in a constant state of unease even when nothing discrete is happening. With that, each concrete step along the way in the story is a jarring spike of nastiness, and there's more here to speak of than can be easily elucidated. The grim spiral of the plot itself is horrid enough, but the scene writing is potent and striking at every turn; there are precious few turns away from the core macabre tableau, and still the writing is so vibrant as to keep us fervently entranced. Even the dialogue is unexpectedly rich and vivid at points, and the characterizations offer fertile ground in which the stars can inhabit their roles and bring them to life. Rest assured that they do. Michael Johnston is playing the customary horror protagonist in Baron, a young man desperately struggling with the nightmare he unwittingly willed into existence, but his portrayal is so fraught and shaken that he catches our attention more than some leads might in other instances. Yet if Barker's fevered imagination is one of the key highlights of this title, and it is, then Inde Navarratte is the other. Nikki is a demanding role, but Navarrate nails it: small in frame, but giant and looming in stature; sweet and beautiful, and utterly chilling; switching emotions on a dime; testing the limits of her voice, if not also her body. Nikki is a character of terrifying presence, and Navarratte embodies her so well that the performance alone is one of the most unnerving elements on hand.

This is to say nothing of horrific, ugly, jolting violence, unnatural behavior or movement that immediately raises one's hackles, and sound design that makes psychological bursts of loud audio all the more effective. Outstanding lighting and cinematography, and even shot composition, are essential to building the haunted atmosphere that pervades this flick, nevermind the superb score of Rock Burwell, commonly sticking to the background but feeding into the ambience at any given turn. The stunts and practical effects are excellent, and even the computer-generated imagery that I tend to disfavor is blended seamlessly into the presentation. The production design, costume design, hair and makeup, and all other facets of the production are impeccable, and catch our eyes again and again. In every regard this is just as well made as we would suppose of modern fare, if not more so. But it bears repeating that the result of it all well outpaces countless other works in the genre, and surely stands rather confidently alongside genre exemplars: from the tale Barker spun on paper, to his expert direction that faithfully brings the gnarly course of events to bear, to the acting that makes these characters so stunning and palpably real, 'Obsession' is something that hits hard and won't let us forget it any time soon. Once again, it is genuinely horrifying, that sort of piece that makes us flinch, shrink back in our seats, and wonder if a given scene isn't too much at the same time that evokes the precise feelings we seek out of horror to begin with.

It won't appeal to all comers, nor meet with equal favor; I repeat myself but I cannot emphasize strongly enough that this is a difficult, uncomfortable film. It is also plainly terrific. I had mixed expectations when I first learned of it, and those expectations were heightened as word of mouth and recommendations grew. The high praise is no jest, and I am astounded by just how good this is. One needs to be prepared to fully sit with whatever a horror movie might offer, but for those who appreciate this genre and all it can do and be, I can only give 'Obsession' my very high, hearty, and enthusiastic recommendation!

Um...

Not sure how to put this. But this movie isn't particularly... horrific... as it is... a black comedy of hyperbolic silliness taken to an extreme that leans so hard that it's just not scary. Not Horror

I went into Obsession with extremely high expectations. The reviews, audience reaction, and "best horror of the 21st century" discourse set the bar very high. Unfortunately, I came away more frustrated than impressed.

To give the film credit, there is atmosphere here, and a handful of genuinely unsettling moments. It captures emotional discomfort reasonably well, particularly the suffocating feeling of being trapped inside a manipulative or emotionally unhealthy relationship. The performances are generally solid, and there are flashes of something more compelling.

The biggest issue for me was pacing. For a film positioned as horror, it takes far too long to properly build tension, with close to forty five or fifty minutes passing before the film becomes genuinely unsettling. Rather than building dread, many sequences simply felt overextended.

What struck me most, however, was the audience reaction. In my screening there was frequent laughter, often during moments that appeared intended to be disturbing. I found myself laughing at points too, sometimes with the room, sometimes independently of it. The emotional response felt oddly fragmented, as though the film never quite settled on the tone it wanted to create. That inconsistency weakened the tension considerably.

The reveals also felt awkwardly timed, with key information arriving late in ways that reduced rather than heightened emotional stakes.

I also found the world of the film surprisingly narrow. The social environment felt oddly insular, with very little meaningful diversity in who occupies the story world, which made parts of it feel less lived in and more limited than intended.

Ultimately, I am not convinced this works particularly well as horror. It plays more like an intimate psychological drama with unsettling elements, occasionally drifting toward dark comedy, rather than something genuinely frightening or suspenseful.

I can understand why some viewers connected with it more than I did, but for me the film never came close to living up to the extraordinary level of praise surrounding it.

I loved watching Obsession in a packed theater. The collective gasps, jumps, and nervous laughter created the kind of tension-filled atmosphere that reminds you why horror plays best in a theater. It's rare for a film to hold an audience in that kind of shared tension from start to finish. Overall, Obsession turns a seemingly simple premise into a nerve-rattling exploration of love, control, and unintended consequences. It's unsettling, unpredictable, and proof that sometimes the most terrifying thing isn't the supernatural force behind a wish, but the human desire that made the wish in the first place.

text:
"You are the most beautiful girl in the entire world" and "Oh, we are going to be together forever and ever and ever" define the movie for me. The first line, quoted from Obsession, and the second, one of the most iconic lines from Kubrick's The Shining-which I believe Curry Baker pays homage to through this reference. From Bear's perspective, the first line was genuine: he truly felt she was the most beautiful girl in the world. The second, spoken by Nikki, expressed exactly what Bear wanted, though it unfolded in a way he never intended.

The film's horror relies less on sound design or jump-scares, staples of the genre, and more on lighting, acting, cinematography, and writing. Curry crafts atmosphere that is more terrifying than most conventional horror films. Inde Navarette elevates the movie-her performance strikes the perfect balance; a notch higher would feel like overacting, a notch lower not scary at all. Shout out to John Marston as well for playing Bear brilliantly.

summary: A Dark Look at Love, Desire, and Control
text:
Obsession follows Bear, a man who has a crush on a woman named Niki. The film opens with him imagining how he would confess his feelings to her, revealing his desire for a connection that may exist more in his mind than in reality.

Later, Bear discovers a mysterious shop and purchases a wishing stick. He makes a simple wish: that Niki would love him more than anything else in the world. His wish is granted, but the result is far from the love story he imagined.

An unnatural force takes hold of Niki, transforming her feelings into something obsessive and disturbing. Her behavior becomes increasingly unpredictable and self-destructive, while Bear struggles to accept what is happening. At first, he ignores the warning signs, caught between the fantasy of finally being loved and the reality of the consequences caused by his own wish.

The movie explores the darker side of desire and the danger of wanting something that cannot happen naturally. It questions whether love still has meaning when it is forced rather than freely given. Bear's inability to take responsibility for what he created adds another layer to the story, as he begins blaming Niki for something he set in motion himself.

While the "wish gone wrong" concept is familiar, Obsession uses its supernatural elements to explore toxic relationships, emotional dependence, and the consequences of trying to control another person's feelings.

The acting and visuals are strong, and the strange atmosphere fits the unsettling nature of the story. It may not reinvent the supernatural thriller genre, but it offers an interesting perspective on unhealthy attachment and the difference between being loved and being possessed.

Fans of psychological horror, dark fantasy, and stories about dysfunctional relationships may find something worth watching here.

summary: A Masterclass in Low-Budget, High-Tension Psychological Horror
text:
Obsession is a perfect reminder that you don't need massive budgets or heavy CGI to create a genuinely terrifying psychological horror. By stripping away the special effects and focusing entirely on story and atmosphere, the film crafts an experience that grabs you from the first frame and never lets go.

The execution of the "One Wish Willow" concept is brilliant. Instead of relying on cheap jump scares, the movie thrives on unpredictability and escalating dread. Every scene carries enough tension to keep you completely locked in, and it manages to earn some genuine scares something that is incredibly hard to pull off in modern horror. You truly never know what is coming next.

The film isn't without its frustrations, however. While the narrative momentum is strong, the protagonist's logic frequently falters. Bear's choices often border on the irrational specifically his reluctance to seek help when things spiral out of control. It is left a bit too ambiguous whether he is paralyzed by fear or simply oblivious to the danger. Additionally, the sequence surrounding the hospital is murky; it is entirely unclear why he couldn't get treatment, whether he was turned away, or if he just decided to leave with Nikki. These narrative gaps can momentarily pull you out of an otherwise gripping story.

Despite those logical hiccups with the characters, the core story is so effective and the pacing is so tight that it easily overshadows the flaws. It is a highly effective, anxiety-inducing thriller that leaves a lasting impression, and it is absolutely a film worth revisiting to see how the tension holds up on a second watch.

It's impressive how a young director of only 27 years old like Curry Barker managed to do this with just $750,000. Obsession is a horror film released in 2026, written, directed, and edited by Barker. The film tells the story of Bear, who works in a music store and is in love with his co-worker Nikki Freeman. summary: Take note. This is how to do horror.
text:
Curry Barker's comedic sensibility shines through a prevalence of dark shadows in his studio debut, Obsession. In no way does that mean the tale of one man's foundational Make-A-Wish moment gone terribly wrong is a comedy. Obsession doesn't even deserve the dreaded Horror Comedy moniker. This is straight horror with wince inducing whiplash splattered all over the screen. You'll be laughing because you don't want to cry or scream.

We are immediately introduced to Michael Johnston's Bear fixating on his super crush Nikki, played by Inde Navarrette. Movies of this nature often lead the audience to understand the object of the preoccupation is undeserving. Not our Darling Nikki. She is equal parts beautiful and cute, with the tomboy attitude to seem obtainable and sufficient come hither glances to be desirable.

One night Nikki lowers her guard and offers our sad sack protagonist the opening he so desperately longs for. It isn't a split second. There's a sizeable pause. One may even call it pregnant. He fumbles the opportunity entirely in an inexorable display of diffident indecisiveness. At that point Bear commits an even larger gaffe.

What follows is Nikki's shockingly quick descent into manic monomania. The film plays on stereotypes of the crazy girlfriend without allowing the commentary to overwhelm the good times. Obsession has a number of standout scenes but nothing that quite compares to Navarrette doing her best impersonation of someone who is determined to make a scene of her own at a house party. It is an unforgettable snippet of acting bravado that is bizarre yet grounded.

Obsession intentionally telegraphs its ending but adds several small twists and turns to keep the audience engaged. Barker's screenplay is delightfully demented. It is littered with scary quiet moments (Nikki watching Bear sleep) and scary loud moments (Nikki disfiguring herself). At its heart, Obsession is the story of a young man and a young woman that want to find connection with each other but don't know how.

Sounds familiar.

This movie is an anomaly. It has all the ingredients of something truly great, and you cannot help it but admire it, but there is still some level of refinement left to achieve greatness. And do not get me wrong: that is something you cannot say about 99% of the movies released each year, despite all the overhyping and empty praise, so that is already a good sign. But I don't know, something inside me yearns for directors to have some level of experience and discipline that can channel all his talent, like this guy Curry Barker. I think he is what ultimately holds the movie back from being really, really great. Because man, there are things in this project that are exceedingly well.

Inde Navarrette. Where did this woman come from? She has been in a couple of productions before, but let's face it, she was a relatively unknown actress until now. So now she is cast in this very low budget horror movie nobody was betting on, and wow! She gives a performance that is among the best horror performances of the two last decades, and I am not prone to exaggerate virtues. The way she contorts her physical presence (something I have not seen since Jim Carrey), and the way she can shift between morbidity, cuteness, goofiness, humor, and rage, is perfectly balanced. (Almost) everything comes together and works beautifully within the context of the film. On top of that, her character is wonderfully written. There is an inner struggle there, a sadness that comes through in the constant switching back and forth and hurts in a way that feels deeply human. You feel the anxiety, the unease, the explosive physicality, the almost childish and obsessive impulsiveness. All of that is what gives the film its power, and it is easily the best thing about it.

Another strong element is the score and the directing. Again, you can tell the director is still inexperienced in some areas, but he makes smart use of lighting and tight spaces to create a sense of dread in a relatively restrained environment, which I really appreciate. I am not entirely sure the use of darkness and shadows is always justified, but overall I cannot complain too much. The score, interestingly, shares the same highs and lows as the direction. Its atmospheric, psytrance-inflected synths reminded me of Juno Reactor and help pull you into this world of obsession and inner torment. Still, I am not convinced they are always the best fit for the scenes, and maybe the film would have benefited from a slightly more varied score in those instances. But again, that is not a major issue. I also find the premise interesting, and the way it is handled is amusing. We have seen stories like this before, but the film puts its own spin on the idea and gives it thematic freshness, touching on consent, inaction as a moral failing, puerile fantasies, and other modern concerns that emerge from discussions about unhealthy relationships.

So why is the movie not great? There are a few reasons. First, Bear (MAJOR SPOILERS AHEAD). I do not fully buy this character, especially in the ending, where he feels somewhat contradictory. I understand what the film is going for: a shy, passive, coward, weak man driven by this childish attraction to a beautiful childhood friend. I get that. But I still found him underwritten and not especially believable. Most of what the film explores about him is his reaction to Nikki's craziness. And yes, I know that is the point: he is the more morally corrupt person because he is ultimately fine with the messed-up situation. But the film does not always sell that convincingly, and at times it stretches credibility. Being honest: I don't care if you are a horrible person, but who in her/his right mind would stay with somebody who duck tapes the door so you cannot exit? Come on, that was too much to swallow. And who has all that duck tape? A footnote: All the "what?" in Bear dialogues was a bit distracting.

That problem extends to other parts of the script too, and that brings me to my second, and most important, issue: it goes a little too far sometimes. I could give several examples of this. Nikki, for example. I have praised the performance a lot, but I have to admit that some of the physical choices feel out of place, far-fetched, and exaggerated to the point that they break both immersion and horror. For example, the scene where she walks backwards in that awkward way felt absolutely ridiculous. I know some people argue that it is supposed to be the "other Nikki," as in other scenes, but in this one it came off as too goofy for its own good. And that is not an isolated case. The vase scene and the Michael Jackson bit with Nikki point to the same issue: the direction lacks control, and it feels like the work of someone who has not yet fully polished his craft.

I also found the third act somewhat disappointing. I do not think the film needed to move into slasher territory. In a way, it cheapens Nikki by turning her into a horror cliché, which weakens the character and makes the whole thing feel a bit like the worst parts of Fatal Attraction (1987). Maybe that kind of turn is something producers expect in these films, as if the audience will lose interest without a bloody third act. But that is never the case, and it is certainly not the case here, since the film is already anxiety-inducing from the first act.

The script also cheats at times, which is another mild issue. For example, after Nikki begins her antics under the influence of the hateful Bear through the One Wish Willow, we are shown footage of the couple spending time together as if everything had been fine for an unspecified period. But that does not make much sense, since Nikki's behavior was already erratic before that, so the montage feels inconsistent; her behavior should have been deteriorating there too. There are also cheap contrivances in the script, such as the character of Ian, which do the film no favors. I thought the way he makes a wish, despite the attempt of Bear to make his wish for him, was forced so that the third act can happen, and the way the billion dollars magically fall down the roof was just too goofy.

All in all, Obsession could have been incredible. Inde Navarrette already is, and I hope she chooses her projects carefully from here on, because if she does, she could have an extraordinary career. The script could have been tighter, and the direction more controlled, but even so, this is a very rewatchable film with plenty to admire and get lost in. 7/10.

summary: THIS MOVIE WON'T SCARE YOU WITH MONSTERS... IT WILL SCARE YOU WITH HUMAN OBSESSION
text:
I went into Obsession because of all the hype surrounding it. People were calling it a disturbing, unforgettable horror experience, and after watching it, I can say one thing clearly... this movie definitely leaves an impact.

But is it the revolutionary horror film everyone is claiming it to be? Not really.

Obsession takes a very simple "be careful what you wish for" concept and turns it into a disturbing psychological nightmare about obsession, insecurity, love, and the terrifying consequences of trying to control someone's emotions.

The biggest strength of this movie is undoubtedly Inde Navarrette's performance as Nikki.

What she does here is not easy. She has to balance vulnerability, fear, obsession and pure terror within the same character, and she completely commits to it. Nikki is unpredictable, uncomfortable and genuinely frightening because the performance makes you believe there is a person trapped inside this nightmare.

Michael Johnston as Bear also deserves appreciation. His character is emotionally weak, desperate and flawed, but Johnston makes his choices understandable. The horror works because the audience can connect with the emotional desperation behind the supernatural situation.

Director Curry Barker also deserves credit. Coming from the world of YouTube sketches, delivering a feature horror film with this much confidence is impressive. He successfully mixes dark humor, tragedy and horror without making the movie feel completely disconnected.

The smartest thing about Obsession is that the supernatural element is not really the main horror. The real horror is the idea of someone wanting another person's love so badly that they destroy everything around them.

The movie also proves that a big budget is not always necessary to create fear. It clearly looks like a low-budget production in many places, but Barker uses silence, uncomfortable moments and sudden bursts of violence effectively. Some of the jump scares are genuinely well executed.

And the ending deserves special mention.

The final moments, especially Nikki's reaction after everything unfolds, stay with you. The crying continues even after the movie ends, creating an uncomfortable feeling that many horror films fail to achieve.

But yes, the movie is not perfect.

The biggest issue is the concept itself.

The "wish gone wrong" storyline is something we have seen many times before. In fact, for Nepali audiences, the comparison with Kaagbeni is unavoidable because that film explored a similar idea years ago and handled the concept with a different level of emotional depth and atmosphere.

Because of that, calling Obsession something completely never-seen-before feels exaggerated.

Another problem is predictability. If you have watched enough psychological horror movies, many of the twists and consequences become easy to predict. The film is disturbing, but it is not as unpredictable as many people claim.

The cinematography is also a mixed bag. The low-budget approach itself is not a problem, but visually the movie often feels plain and flat. A stronger visual style could have elevated the atmosphere significantly.

The movie also chooses emotional violence over traditional horror. Instead of relying heavily on spooky atmosphere, it focuses on disturbing imagery, gore and uncomfortable situations. For some viewers, this will be effective. For others, it may simply leave a bad taste.

My theatrical experience was also affected by technical issues at QFX Jalma. I had to watch one important scene twice, first without audio and then with audio. Surprisingly, the second viewing showed how much the sound design added to the horror, but the interruption definitely affected the overall experience. I also noticed some scenes felt abruptly cut, possibly due to censorship.

Last Words: Obsession is not the greatest horror movie ever made, but it is a solid theatrical experience. If you enjoy disturbing psychological horror, uncomfortable emotions and intense performances, give it a watch. Just lower your expectations because the hype around it is bigger than the actual movie.

This is genuinely a disturbing story about how cruel someone can be to a person they claim to love. To me, it's clear that the real problem isn't the wish itself. It's Bear. Right from the beginning, he shows his cowardice by refusing to admit his feelings for Nikki and choosing to make the wish instead. That already reveals the darkness within him. You could argue that he was naive and didn't fully realize how inhumane it is to violate another person's free will just to make her love him "more than anything else in the world."

Why don't I think the wish is the real problem? Because Ian, Bear's friend, wishes for a billion dollars and gets it instantly, with no twisted consequences. That makes it clear to me that this isn't one of those stories where the magical object is simply cursed. The real horror comes from Bear's selfish and obsessive wish. He asked for something fundamentally inhuman, completely ignoring Nikki's autonomy and humanity. In the end, the entity is a reflection of Bear's own obsession, not the wish itself.

I really liked where the story began and where it ultimately ended.

summary: Slick Atmosphere Choked by a Pathetic Protagonist
text:
Despite the massive marketing push, Curry Barker's Obsession easily avoids the trap of being pure overhyped fluff by delivering top-tier production value. It's less of a traditional horror jump-scare fest and much more of an anxiety-inducing psychological thriller. From the gorgeous lighting and meticulous set design to the unsettling, tense sound design, the filmmaking team puts immense, palpable effort into cultivating an incredibly stressful atmosphere. When the film actually pivots into raw horror-unleashing creepy imagery and highly effective body horror-it works beautifully, heavily anchored by a powerhouse, standout performance from Inde Navarrette.

However, any genuine terror or suspense the film tries to build is completely choked out by Bear, an intensely weak protagonist. Because the entire plot relies strictly on his total inability to communicate, make an adult decision, or take an ounce of responsibility for the catastrophic mess he creates, it becomes impossible to root for or even pity him. Instead of leaving you with high-hope chills or terrifying dread, the film ultimately abandons its sharp psychological tension. A handful of decent horror sequences simply cannot rescue a movie built around a thoroughly unlikable lead who kills the stakes entirely.

I think the movie was great.

It's been a long time since I got scared while watching a horror film.

What I enjoyed most was how the movie highlighted the way Bear's insecurities, his lack of personality and his selfishness affected Nikki's character. We get to see that he never actually cared about her and even enjoying her psychotic behaviour as long as she still loved him.

Even though she clearly tells him she wants him to kill her ,in one of the moments her real self resurfaces, his main concern is why being with him is so bad.

But what I had an issue with, were a couple of scenes that looked really fake.

For example, Sandy, Bear's cat , looked more like a plushie than an actual cat.

Another scene is the one with Sarah at the end of the movie. I couldn't help but notice that during the scene where Nikki kills her, it seems like they used a really cheap mannequin. The body is way too skinny to be Sarah's or any other person's to be exact.

I'm a little disappointed by this because ,aside from those details,it's a really good horror movie.

Overall it's a good movie with a little defects here and there,but I would still recommend it!

summary: A Caustically Modern "Monkey's Paw" Defined by Somatic Dread and Acerbic Irony
text:
Curry Barker's feature debut Obsession takes a well-worn supernatural catalyst-a supernatural "be careful what you wish for" relic-and weaponizes it as a visceral examination of romantic objectification. Anchored by Michael Johnston's meek protagonist and a terrifyingly uncanny performance from Inde Navarrette, the narrative eschews conventional lore exposition in favor of psychological claustrophobia. Barker, drawing from his background in high-concept absurdist comedy, deftly recalibrates the tonal equilibrium, shifting effortlessly from darkly wry comedic beats to oppressive, silhouette-driven dread.

While the film excels at visual minimalism and spatial tension, its structural momentum encounters friction as the sinister enchantment escalates. The third-act progression relies slightly on fragmented narrative transitions, occasionally undercutting the emotional gravity established during its meticulous middle chapters. Nevertheless, Obsession succeeds as an atmospheric, sharply directed genre exercise that subverts romantic tropes through unrelenting, visceral disquiet.

Obsession as a movie shows that even the simplest concept can enamour an audience with how its executed, and the movie doesn't need a ghost or a serial killer to scare and shock you. And the discourse on if Bear is evil or not is interesting as well, since to me bear isn't pure evil but he is evil in another sense of how being a coward and not being ready to fight for others or not thinking about others well being even when you dont personally want to hurt them is still evil.

summary: Obsession: Finally, A Critically-Acclaimed Horror Movie That I Love
text:
I have my qualms whenever I hear a lot of buzz and acclaim from critics towards horror movies. If somebody calls it "one of the best of all time", I wrongfully put my hopes up and thought that was what I was going to get. In the past years, when film lovers put Weapons and Longlegs as the next best things in horror, I remembered watching them and coming out of the theater disappointed by their final acts. And now, with Obsession, I am afraid that I might fall into the same trap again. Fortunately, I am happy to say that Obsession is an amazing horror movie because of the fantastic lead performances, creative cinematography and editing, as well as a great and satisfying story in general.

The lead performances are off the charts in this horror movie. Inda Navarrette as Nikki is the obvious main highlight because of how many facial reactions she needs to make to have the audience feel unsettled. Apart from this, her performance from normal to weird and actually riveting in many scenes showcase the range of her acting capabilities. She deserves an Oscar for this one. Even the protagonist, Bear played by Michael Johnston, shows how complex he is as a character. On the one hand, you root that his romance will survive after making a wish. But on the other hand, you also feel some disgust towards him because of how far he is willing to continue the unreal love he has with Nikki. Because of their strong chemistry with each other, we see how obsession can lead to very dramatic and horrific turns for the both of them.

Technical elements were great throughout the duration of the film. I have to give props to the cinematography done by Taylor Clemons because there were scenes that made you feel like something is going to happen any time, even if nothing really does. The wide camera angles panning from one character to another, alongside the close-up shots of the character makes you feel immersed and tensed up by what might happen in the next minutes of the movie. Even the editing done by Curry Barker was solid in which there are montages of character conversations that were timed well, while also matching the tone of the scenes, whether it is just them chilling out or suddenly the horror is kicking in. Even Rock Burwell's score, when something creepy or dark is about to happen, it adds a lot to the audience's immersion to the movie.

The best part of the movie, which I saved the best for last, is how riveting and unsettling the story was from beginning to end. For the first couple of minutes, you are greeted with excellent exposition with the kind of protagonist Bear is, the types of friends he is surrounded with, and the personality that Nikki has and how it changed after the first act of the movie. Once we get to the second act, everything goes way bizarre and terrorized at that point because it all focuses on Bear trying to struggle with the wish he had made that changed Nikki as a person entirely. Without giving too many spoilers, compared to movies like Weapons and Longlegs, it all comes full circle for me. It did not feel disappointing and was very satisfying because it all makes sense in the end. This is all thanks to the great direction and writing done by Curry Barker. Just some minor gripes such as a specific horrific scene that felt misplaced, as well as another scene about the explanation of the wish, but those did not ruin my enjoyment of the movie at all.

If it is not that obvious throughout the essay, I think Obsession is great. After not seeing a movie in theaters for the past few months, I am glad that it was Curry Barker's movie that encouraged me to actually get out of the house and watch cinema again. Not only is it my number one of the year as of now, but it has also become an instant favorite of mine when it comes to horror or films in general. And seeing how it made history for being one of the rare movies that got a second-weekend increase, alongside how I watched it in a packed theater, I encourage everyone to watch it because it's definitely worth it.

summary: Great look into an obsessive man's head
text:
The movie starts as slightly boring and mundane while setting up but left be feeling disturbed and unsettled. The main character starts out with a situation that made me pity him, but that stopped quickly. Almost the entire movie feels much longer than it is, which could be a good or a bad thing. The pacing makes you think multiple times that the story is ending soon, but it doesn't and the tension rises. The whole thing made me wish the suffering would just end already.

Overall, I think the movie is a good look into the mind of an obsessive man and a great allegory for how horrible the actions of normal looking dudes can be. It made me think a lot about the implications of consent, sexual assault, and how women are viewed in society.

The acting is great, especially Nikki is fantastic. The directing is amazing especially seeing how young the director is. The breaks in Nikki are a great plot device to uphold the tension throughout the entire duration of the movie. The car scene made my jaw drop, it's the culmination of Bear's incessant ignorance to the reality of his situation throughout the movie and it was a great moment to get delivered, it symbolizes what Bear could have had built up with Sarah had he not decided to try and take an unthought through shortcut and that possibility is literally destroyed in front of him and he gets reminded this is what he wished for by Nikki (which is a shame wasn't kept more subtle). The sex scene is absolutely gut wrenching and cemented the viewer's distain for Bear and I went into the movie feeling sorry for him, even after the wish I thought he was defendable on the grounds of having mental struggles stemming from his clearly troubled earlier life, somehow defendable through all of this as just an unwise and slightly ignorant young man but that he would surely find a way to realize his misdeeds and repair the situation, and even tho it's implied - actually having to see this scene really reminds the viewer just what kind of a person the protagonist is, how undefendable he actually is and just how bad this is all going to end.

"Just kill me" scene was amazing and unexpected although not surprising.

That's all the notable things i can think of, just from the first viewing (will definitely be rewatching it).

All in all the movie is incredible and serves as a reminder to be careful what we wish for, to keep ourselves in check when in love and to keep an eye out for the Bear's in the world, it can be very tempting to empathetically turn a blind eye to someone's seemingly minor deviant behavior because of their poor circumstances but it's exactly this that can spiral out into a cocktail of neediness, ignorance and arrogance that can have catastrophic consequences for anyone involved. People like him (who are more common now than ever unfortunately) can and should be getting help so they can do better because as the movie greatly presents you can't take shortcuts in life, you need to take responsibility and accountability and the only real way to try and get what you want is to become stronger. The only way out is through.

Thrilling, refreshing & delightfully deranged, Obsession is an ingeniously crafted & consistently chilling supernatural horror from a new filmmaker in town who brings his twisted premise to life with a level of clarity, confidence & composure that's seldom expected from emerging talents. Tense, gripping and powered by a star-making showcase from its leading lady, it is one of the best surprises of the year.

Written, directed & also edited by Curry Barker, the story is rather simple & straightforward but the steady escalation of terror and the terrifying consequences it leads to makes it an edge-of-the-seat experience for the most part. Barker exhibits full control over all aspects, narrates the plot with sustained intensity, allows the long takes to create tension, and envelops the imagery with an unnerving & unsettling atmosphere.

The picture is a cautionary tale that digs into the nice guy syndrome, toxic mentality, unhealthy fixations, suppressed desires and loss of agency & control through the central relationship that unravels. Intensifying the horror elements some more is the claustrophobic camerawork, stellar sound design & sudden burst of violence. And then fab performances from the cast take things up a notch, with Inde Navarrette effortlessly stealing the show.

Overall, Obsession is a deviously wicked & surprisingly assured piece of work from a promising new voice that feels fresh despite treading familiar grounds and delivers the shocks, surprises, thrills & scares in enormously satisfying dosage. As tragic & heartbreaking as it is disturbing & spine-chilling, the film makes for one of the most impressive & diabolical new entries in the world of horror and has all the makings of an instant classic. In short, a masterpiece.

I'm NGL, I wasn't sold on the film until the wish was made. I had already watched videos that spoiled the entire film, which I often do when it comes to horror because I love horror but I don't love wasting my time. When it started, no one was likable, the acting was awkward, and the dialogue was bad/vapid/cliche', and the first and last things didn't change as it progressed, but I did feel bad for the female lead. I liked that the cast was played by unknowns (to general audiences, at least), though it seemed like the film was shot in sequential order, as the performances of the two leads weren't great (even amateur) at first but got better as the film progressed. The rest of the characters were generic AF, however.

Also, I found it hard to believe the female lead and the best friend of the male lead would bang. I mean, yeah, they seem to be in a small town with nothing going for anyone and no hot guys, but seriously? Neither guy looked like they could give anything that would be worth spinning the block on (and we know that for sure given the "love" scene with Bear), so that useless fact was actually the most unbelievable part of the film, TBH.

Anyway, I'm glad I stuck with the film, because it's as freaky and creepy as I was sold by think-pieces and "explained" videos. I think the main actress is definitely the MVP of the film.

However, I could do without the early-2000s manner of blasting music to add to intense moments. It actually would have been creepier if she'd done those things when it was silent or with ambient music. Don't add jump-scare music to scenes that aren't jump-scares. You lost a star for that.

Anyway, once it got going, it was good. I was originally putting it on as background entertainment (in case it was overrated) but ended up paying attention straight through.

Also, to people pointing out how Bear was the bad guy and giving examples, I'd point out an earlier one: the fact that he went to the shop to buy HER something, found the exact thing she would have wanted/appreciated, but decided to ONLY buy something for HIMSELF instead. He bought HIMSELF the gift of her love instead of the gift he'd gone to get her to show HER his love. That's a good, subtle touch. Kudos to the writing there.

summary: Demonic Horror Tropes Leavened by Navarette's Fierce Turn
text: Curry Barker's sensibilities as a filmmaker are downright demonic in this meticulously crafted 2025 mashup of absolute horror and dark comedy. Written by Barker with an obvious devotion to the genre, the story is tethered to the relatable premise of watching the methodical downward spiral of someone getting exactly what they wished for, only for it to completely backfire. The fairly basic plot follows Bear, a dweeby music store employee, who breaks the mysterious "One Wish Willow" in order to spark a romantic relationship with his longtime crush Nikki. Initially his wish is fulfilled, but it becomes an escalating psychological nightmare as her feelings turn into a horrific fixation. Although Michael Johnston plays Bear with appropriately desperate conviction coupled with dry humor, it's Inde Navarette's unpredictably unhinged turn as Nikki that elevates the film's shock quotient. Much like Amy Madigan's similarly shocking performance in "Weapons", Navarette's work is fearsome without compromise. The supporting cast is mostly serviceable, and I only wish Barker introduced a deeper level of complexity to the female characters to make the darker themes resonate more.

summary: One of the Best Horror Movies I've Seen in Years
text:
I had been wanting to watch Obsession for a while because of the incredible reviews and the fact that it was directed by someone who originally came from YouTube. Even weeks after release, screenings were still selling out, so I was curious to see whether it deserved the hype.

After finally seeing it, I can honestly say that it absolutely did.

What impressed me most was how unique the movie felt. Horror movies often rely on the same formulas, but this one felt fresh and genuinely unsettling. It reminded me of Smile and Smile 2 in the way it creates an atmosphere of constant discomfort and dread.

The acting was phenomenal, especially from the lead actress. There were several scenes that were genuinely creepy, and the makeup effects and overall presentation were excellent. The movie managed to be disturbing without relying solely on cheap jump scares.

I also appreciated that the story leaves room for interpretation. It's the kind of film that makes you want to watch analysis videos afterward because there are themes and meanings beneath the surface. In many ways, the tragedy could have been avoided if the characters had simply been honest about their feelings, which made everything even more heartbreaking.

The ending was particularly haunting. Although the protagonist survives, it hardly feels like a happy ending after everything that happens. Survival and victory are clearly not the same thing.

Original, creepy, beautifully acted, and memorable, Obsession is easily one of my favorite horror movies in recent years.

summary: A Dark Reminder That Love Without Boundaries Can Become a Nightmare
text:
Obsession is one of those movies that only asks you to accept a single impossible premise. Once you do, everything else falls into place surprisingly well. Instead of questioning the fantasy, you're pulled into a psychological nightmare that feels disturbingly believable.

The film immediately reminded me of the phrase, "Be careful what you wish for." In fact, that's exactly what this story explores. Sometimes getting exactly what you want turns out to be the worst possible outcome.

What I appreciated most wasn't the horror itself, but what the horror represented. At its core, this isn't just about obsession. It's about toxic love, emotional control, and the frightening idea that someone can genuinely love you while slowly destroying your freedom. Many people mistake possessiveness for love, and this film takes that unhealthy mindset to its absolute extreme. It's exaggerated, of course, but the emotional truth behind it feels very real.

The suspense works because the movie plays with your mind more than it relies on cheap scares. It creates an atmosphere where every romantic gesture slowly becomes unsettling, making you question where love ends and control begins.

The concept is strong, the pacing kept me engaged, and I found the psychological aspect far more interesting than the supernatural one. My only criticism is that I expected a few more clever psychological twists. The film had the potential to surprise the audience even more and reach a perfect ending.

Still, this is one of the more memorable psychological horror films I've seen recently. If you're willing to accept one fantasy element, you'll probably enjoy everything that follows.

I did really enjoy this moving for something a bit different in the array of mediocre movies that have become the norm. I have been a fan of Curry and his YouTube since the beginning, and still am.

I just felt like he could have done a little more with the concept once the ball got rolling. For the horror aspect, it could have been a little creepier before we hit max gore/gross. Another twist I thought might be coming was the girl that liked him, ended up getting a wish too. Karma and all.

Overall, still a great movie! I think I liked Milk better though, even if it was lower budget. Either way Curry is a talented writer, actor, and director.

summary: The comedy sketch to horror directing pipeline remains rock solid
text: This was one of the most unique films I've seen in ages- in a genre littered with cliches and cheap jump scares, Curry Barker manages to carve his name next to top tier directors with his first feature film. The understated cinematography, the soundtrack, and the script made for the most tense and gripping journey. I was on the edge until the end and left sick to my stomach in the way only good thrillers can leave you. Can't wait to see more of these guys in the future.

It starts with something almost embarrassingly simple: a guy has feelings for a girl and doesn't have the courage to tell her. Nothing unusual, nothing particularly dark. Then one stupid wish changes everything.

Bear has been in love with his childhood friend and co-worker Nikki for years. After once again failing to tell her how he feels, he uses the mysterious "One Wish Willow" and wishes for Nikki to love him more than anything else in the world. Technically, he gets exactly what he asked for. Unfortunately for him, the word "anything" turns out to be pretty important.

What follows is a surprisingly effective mixture of psychological horror, dark comedy, body horror and increasingly brutal violence. The movie doesn't immediately throw everything at you. Nikki's behaviour changes gradually, and at first there is almost something amusing about Bear finally getting the relationship he desperately wanted. But her affection quickly becomes uncomfortable. Then disturbing. And eventually completely terrifying.

Inde Navarrette absolutely carries some of the film's best moments. Nikki can switch from vulnerable and almost innocent to completely unhinged within seconds. Her strange movements, facial expressions, screaming and moments of unnatural stillness make her unpredictable, and the film wisely allows some scenes to linger long enough for that discomfort to settle in.

The gore also caught me somewhat by surprise. Obsession can be funny and awkward one moment and suddenly extremely violent the next. Barker isn't afraid to make certain scenes nasty and uncomfortable, and once things really start falling apart, the movie goes considerably further than its relatively innocent beginning would suggest.

But underneath all the blood and supernatural madness is a very simple idea: Bear wanted Nikki without ever really considering whether Nikki wanted him. His wish removes her choice entirely. The irony is that once he finally receives the unconditional love he wanted so badly, he discovers how horrifying unconditional love can become when there are literally no boundaries left.

I also liked that Bear isn't presented as some completely innocent victim. He makes a selfish decision, sees increasingly obvious evidence that something is terribly wrong and still struggles to let go of the fantasy he created. That gives the story considerably more weight than if this were simply another movie about a crazy girlfriend chasing an innocent guy.

The premise itself isn't revolutionary. "Be careful what you wish for" has been done countless times before, and there are moments where the story could have been tighter. But the execution makes the difference. Curry Barker takes a very basic concept and gradually pushes it into increasingly bizarre, grotesque and uncomfortable territory.

Obsession starts almost like an awkward romance and ends somewhere completely different. Strange, violent, darkly funny and genuinely unsettling at times. Definitely one of those horror movies where knowing less before watching it makes the experience considerably better.

Sometimes rejection really is the better option.

summary: The Dark Price of Forced Affection
text:
There's a fine line between genuine affection and possession, and horror movies usually thrive when crossing it. I went into Obsession expecting a psychological deep dive into emotional dependency, but what we actually get is an experience that violently swings between brilliance and frustration. Directed by Curry Barker, the film swings big in its attempt to show toxic masculinity and the loss of free will. The first thirty minutes are genuinely suffocating, doing a great job of making you feel trapped. But while Barker takes huge risks for his debut feature, the movie stumbles trying to keep that momentum going.

The real trouble starts when the story needs to stretch past its initial premise. The second act drags hard, trapping the viewer in a repetitive loop of jealousy and chasing that goes nowhere. They could have easily chopped at least twenty minutes in the editing room. On top of that, the indie budget really shows; scenes meant to be psychologically oppressive are ruined by amateurish lighting and set designs that break the immersion. Worse still is the jarring mix of tones. Right when the discomfort peaks, the script throws in bizarre dark humor. A badly timed joke or a goofy reaction completely kills the dramatic weight, making it clear the director hasn't quite learned how to trim the fat from his own ideas.

The whole plot with the mystical artifact hooks you at first, but it loses steam once the curse actually kicks in. Instead of building tension, the narrative just stalls. This makes the interactions suffer, too. Dedicated actors are stuck delivering stiff, unnatural dialogue, forced to spell out feelings that their body language was already showing perfectly. It makes some of the more dramatic scenes feel like a bad teen soap opera draft.

Following the protagonist, Bear (Michael Johnston), for almost two hours is a tough pill to swallow. He's a pathetic guy whose harmless neediness quickly turns into a sick, one-dimensional selfishness. While the movie doesn't shy away from exposing the ugliest sides of possessiveness disguised as romance, Bear has zero redeeming qualities, making the watch tedious since there's no one to root for. If the movie survives its structural flaws, it's almost entirely thanks to Inde Navarrette. Tasked with playing a character who gets psychologically beaten down by both the male lead and bad writing, she delivers an incredibly mature, visceral performance. Her subtle shifts in posture and gaze anchor the whole movie, making her the only real emotional core in the story.

Using folk horror to talk about toxic masculinity is the coolest idea here, but the execution completely lacks subtlety. The movie talks down to the audience, hammering its message home so hard that it feels more like a lecture than an organic psychological study. This also exposes a major flaw in how it handles its female lead. In trying to call out abuse, the narrative reduces her to a mere tool for suffering, tortured just to push the bad guy's arc forward. It leaves you wondering if it's genuinely critiquing misogyny or just exploiting women's trauma for shock value.

The film's early strength is its grounded tension, relying on everyday paranoia rather than monsters in the dark. But by the third act, the director throws all that out the window and goes full grotesque. Instead of feeling earned, this sudden bloodbath of graphic violence feels like a desperate crutch to shock an already bored audience. The sound design also fumbles; they went for an eerie lack of music, which works at first, but ends up making long scenes feel empty. When loud noises do happen, they're poorly mixed and feel like cheap jump scares.

After racing through a chaotic, blood-soaked climax, the movie just ends. An abrupt cut to black rolls the credits without explaining the artifact or the rules of the curse. It doesn't feel like a thought-provoking open ending; it just feels like the writers painted themselves into a corner and didn't know how to wrap things up, leaving you waiting for a payoff that never comes.

In the end, Obsession is a tough, uneven watch. Curry Barker has the guts to poke at the painful wounds of toxic relationships, and Inde Navarrette's amazing acting keeps things afloat. But the pacing issues, weird tonal shifts, and the rushed, gory climax really test your patience. Still, it forces you to think. Horror is supposed to push us out of our comfort zone, right? If you want to feel that oppressive atmosphere, it's worth a watch. Just go in with a strong stomach, ready for the messy pacing, and see how you handle the sudden silence when those credits finally roll.
