Unlike Jordan Peele and his ventures into horror films through a comedian's lens, Curry Barker is no Jordan Peele when it comes to putting together a great horror flick.

The plot revolves around a lonely geek named Bear, played by Michael Johnston, who has fallen hard for his coworker Nikki, portrayed by Inde Navarrette. Bear is firmly stuck in the "friend zone" and desperately wants to take the relationship to the next level, but he can never seem to find the right moment. Out of frustration, he buys a gag gift called the "One Wish Willow" and jokingly wishes for Nikki to love him more than anything else in the world. Unfortunately for Bear, she does...to horrifying results.

If you can overlook that issue, there are some genuinely effective jump scares, and the film definitely delivers enough gore to satisfy hardened horror fans. Barker does show flashes of creativity behind the camera, but the screenplay simply wasn't strong enough for me to fully buy into the madness.

Overall, I'd give "Obsession" 5 out of 10, a middle of the road movie. It's pretty "meh" in my opinion, but that's just me.

Obsession (2026) Dir. Curry Butler
Butler's wickedly entertaining horror film induces as many cringes as gasps - and it produces plenty of both. The film follows four twenty-somethings working together at a local music store, friends who have known each other long enough that they finish one another's sentences. Yes, think an updated version of Friends. And, of course, one of the friends, Bear (Michael Johnston), is obsessed with the spunky, cool girl of the foursome, Nikki (Inde Navarrette). Friends again.

But one quickly senses that there are darker undertones, which Butler surfaces slowly.

Bear is so desperate and hangdog that he makes Ross look like an extrovert. And then he makes his fatal, if understandable, mistake. Having missed his opportunity to say something to Nikki, he uses a toy "make a wish" dime-store charm that, because this is horror, works all too well.

The premise adds gender commentary to this traditional "careful what you wish for" setup. Guys fall in love with the bad girl but wish for the devoted nice girl. What happens if the guys get their wish? Obsession starts slowly, with Nikki becoming increasingly clingy, providing cringeworthy moments that would be right at home in a comedy. Navarrette does a devilishly good job of portraying the subtle difference between liking and obsessing before the full crazy arrives.

And the crazy does arrive. As Nikki becomes more obsessive, abusive, and self-abusive - and as the complexity of the foursome's relationship becomes more apparent - the film turns darker and more gruesome, with audience-pleasing amounts of bloody surprises, even when you think you see them coming. Obsession gets points for maintaining the courage of its convictions, refusing to give us an ending that neatly cleans up the mess.

But while Obsession is entertaining, I'm not sure the film always explores its complexities in meaningful ways. Perhaps it works best as a blood-soaked parody of the male fantasy of the devoted girl. But that fantasy is not really what any of the characters wanted, or even wished for. Bear wasn't asking for a different Nikki - just the same one who liked him a bit more. Would it really take voiding Nikki's free will to make that happen? Perhaps the film is suggesting that wishing for any change at all means forcing oneself onto the girl. But that feels like a stretch from the film's context. There is a message, or an examination, the film was trying to get to but couldn't quite reach. Perhaps that is still better than being too literal - say, last year's overpraised The Substance. If the film never quite lands its thesis, it still delivers enough wit, blood, and bad decisions to make Obsession a smart addition to new horror, and Butler's next work well worth watching for.

Curry Barker's "Obsession" is a startling delight. While the internal logic is clunky, I prefer it, because the film takes the single concept-- a woman forced into obsession over a man-- and gets weird with it! In a genre often oversaturated with tropes and cliche, "Obsession" is fresh because, for the most part (looking at you, Sarah car scene), you have no idea what's going to happen next. The best scares are not shorthand gimmicks, but moments of stillness and anticipation of Nikki's (Inde Navarrette) behavior. It dives headlong into the uncanny valley, something horror does not take NEARLY as much advantage of as it should as it was certainly the most thrilling part of the film, and invents a new avenue for classic 'possession' horror.

As for the theme(s) itself, "Obsession" is a clear conversation about female autonomy and emotional insecurity. At first, you might want to root for a guy stuck in such a nightmarish situation because of a wish he never imagined would come true, let alone escalate to the extent it did. There is also something to be said about abusive relationships in that the danger posed by Nikki increased incrementally so Bear's (Michael Johnston) wellbeing was too thoroughly jeopardized by the time he wanted to leave. However, you can't help but circle back to true tragedy of the situation every time he indulges in his wish: the abuse of Nikki's autonomy. These moments are especially surprising (with the help of an intense but loud score), serving as consistent reminders that Bear was, in fact, taking advantage of the situation (despite his insisting he was not). At every corner, he convinces himself of this reality and centers his own feelings over Nikki's. He only reasons to finally put an end to things when the consequences were beyond irreversible. Nikki was freed and left the final girl, but at what cost? Only a few dead bodies and permanent damage to her reputation, life, and, of course, face. But, hey, at least Bear got to cosplay romance with his friend for a little while there. Worth it!

summary: Starts off strong, then drops off
text:
Maybe this was supposed to be symbolic of how some men don't respect women's autonomy and instead view them as accessories?

It just didn't land. Probably because it's been done so many times already. I suspect the hype is from younger generations who haven't seen truly great films, or The Twilight Zone, Wishmaster, The Monkey's Paw, The Box, Needful Things, and so many other examples of "be careful what you wish for."

That said, I do want to praise Inde's performance specifically at the beginning of the movie when she's outside Bear's car and struggling with her "sense of self." The quick back-and-forth between the two versions of Nikki was really well played. I also found the acting at the end where they aren't talking and are just communicating through facial expressions to be top tier, for 15 seconds anyway. The rest of the performance was amateur. Nikki acted like a toddler throwing a fit in a grocery store, or maybe just an average 15-year-old girlfriend. Ian was poorly played, and unbelievable. They should have put a different actor in that role. I have no idea how he got the part.

Is it scary? No. There is gore and some uncomfortable moments. The most disturbing part wasn't the gore, it was when Nikki made her "food critic" his special lunch, which resulted in Bear eating something grotesque.

The pacing was also off, and I had to skip back a couple of times because I thought I must have missed something. I guess that's just not very good editing? At first it seems like a lot of time had passed since Bear made the wish, but then Ian mention how Nikki "friend-zoned" Bear a week earlier, so I guess it hadn't been that long? I don't know, maybe that was intentional.

I don't think you're supposed to like anyone in this movie, and that's fine, but it is still worth mentioning that the entire friend group was rotten, including Bear. His wish might have been innocent at first - lots of people wish their crush also wanted them - but he understood exactly what he was doing to her, ignored her pleas, didn't want to undo what was done, and was never going to make it right.

I think the ending would have been better as written... One Wish Willow: Romeo & Juliet.

During the movie I was genuinely scared by the screaming that happened and the actions of Nikki and Bear. And never in my life have I hated a character like Bear. The whole time he gets freaked out and scared and knows something isn't right with Nikki during the movie until the last part of the movie. All the while everyone is saying that what is going on between them isn't healthy - he would still say it's ok when it's not! I hate the fact that he was too selfish to ignore Nikki's request to kill her because she was being forced by the wish and trying to snap back to herself - Only for the wish to take control - it made me so angry.

I was so scared in the end, when I thought the controlled Nikki made the wish to make Bear love her back only for him to die and her to finally be free - but with a price to pay, knowing what she is done because she was aware the whole time

My headcanon for after the movie is that she either gets help or run away or just kill herself so she can be in a better place (in the movie).

summary: More of a Disturbing Tragedy Than a Horror Film
text:
I think I viewed this movie differently from many other people. For me, Obsession was less of a horror movie and more of a psychological tragedy.

The scariest part was not the supernatural elements or the violent scenes. What truly disturbed me was seeing how dangerous obsession can become and how completely it can destroy a person's life. Bear's biggest mistake was not that he had bad intentions, but that he never stopped to think about the consequences of what he was doing.

Nikki was the strongest character in the film for me. One scene in particular deeply affected me: after Bear leaves for work, Nikki remains standing in the same place, waiting for him for hours, completely neglecting even her basic needs. That scene didn't feel like horror to me. It felt like watching someone's freedom, identity, and humanity slowly disappear. I genuinely felt sorry for her.

The message of the movie was very clear: when the desire to have someone becomes more important than that person's own free will, it is no longer love-it becomes obsession.

I also felt that the ending could have been more shocking and impactful. Considering the title is Obsession and the dark direction the story was taking, the climax had the potential to leave an even stronger impression. The ending wasn't bad, but in my opinion, it could have been more powerful.

Despite that, this is one of those films that stays in your mind after it ends. If you're looking only for jump scares, this may not be the movie for you. But if you're interested in character psychology and the destructive consequences of obsession, it is definitely worth watching.

This is how its done. No need for gore, big jump scares with stupid sounds or mirror reflections or some shadow when they close the fridge.

Just a decent premise and some good old fashioned tension.

Whether you are a fan of horror or not, you will enjoy it. I personally view it as an amazing scary thriller, not a horror movie.

Curry Baker has just delivered one of the best horror/thriller films in years. A genre that usually leans too heavily on cheap jump scares finally gets a movie built on pure tension, realism, and atmosphere. Every scene feels unsettling because it feels believable, and that's what makes it hit so hard.

The entire cinema was reacting throughout the film - people jumping out of their seats, shouting, laughing nervously. That's when you know a horror movie is doing its job.

Massive credit to Curry. He achieved what so many directors in this genre fail to do.

P. S. I wonder how many (now single guys) said to their partner "you do that" after watching the movie 😂

The original screenplay really keeps you hooked from start to finish, and the lead actress delivers an absolutely phenomenal performance that is truly Oscar-worthy! However, despite these strong points, I simply cannot give this film a rating higher than a 7 out of 10. Having a great script and stellar acting is just not enough on its own; the overall direction could have been significantly better. With a more skilled directorial vision, this movie genuinely had the potential to become a true masterpiece.

What completely ruined the film for me was the scene involving the 1 million dollars . It felt entirely out of place and utterly random. That plot point could have been handled in a much more natural, realistic manner later in the story. For instance, the character could have won the lottery or found a believable way to come into that money, rather than having such a massive sum literally fall out of the blue. Moments like that break the immersion and detract from the realism of the narrative.

In conclusion, the screenplay is exceptional and deeply rooted in real-life situations, albeit pushed to an extreme degree at times. The directing, unfortunately, remains average at best, failing to elevate the material to its full potential. On the other hand, the lead actress's performance is flawless and unquestionably deserving of an Oscar. It is a solid film with incredible elements, but poor execution in key scenes holds it back from greatness.

summary: Ian and I have the Same Wish
text:
This film is written, directed, and edited by Curry Barker. This is a supernatural horror film. I tend to love these types of horror, because it's more about consequences and less about jump scares and gore. They remind of dark fairytales.

This horror focuses on Bear (Michael Johnston) and the Nikki (Inde Navarrette). Bear is not only timid and passive, but also a terrible communicator. I found it difficult to like him. My first impression was he had the IQ of a fly. He was irritating from beginning to end due to his passivity and incapacity to communicate or react appropriately in most instances.

The thing about Bear is he's not a catch. He's not a monster. He's not even particularly manipulative in the conventional sense. He's just painfully passive, emotionally closed off, and frustratingly incapable of saying the obvious.

The friends Ian (Cooper Tomlinson) and Sarah (Megan Lawless) are much more grounded, fun, and easy to listen to, but they sometimes came off as prying parents rather than friends. The few arguments or disagreements between the friends are trivial and overblown. It's as if the writer's lacked the creativity to create real conflict between them. Or maybe that's how normal non toxic people argue. You be the judge.

Nikki is frightening, and her performance makes this film. Unfortunately, the dialogue with her and Bear at times is uncomfortably awkward or abnormal. It's like the conversations three-year-olds have with each other--slow and incoherent with random facts sprinkled in. She is the straight forward one and he's just...himself.

Her progression into depravity was perfect. The ending was nice, and bittersweet. Despite the rocky start, and so-so dialogue, the story is entertaining. The colors are dark and vibrant. It isn't overly gory or grotesque. Shadows are expertly used appropriately. The pacing was good towards the end. The direction was on point.

Overall, it's a great movie that would've been fantastic with better dialogue. At the same time, I recognize the fumbling Bear is what makes us feel for Nikki. Also, the male lead being unlikable worked well for this movie, because if he was a great catch we wouldn't understand why Nikki didn't reciprocate his feelings.

In conclusion, it's a fascinating story that shows how ones obsession can spiral out of control in a horrific way. It also shows that the, "nice guy" is a subjective term.

P. S. Hats off to the writer, director, and editor.

Considering one person (Curry Barker) brought this to life, deserves serious recognition. I've seen terrible films with larger productions, budget, and staff. Kudos to proving a great script, a big imagination, and great direction can make a movie on a low budget work.

This is exactly the type of movie that I'd find one night just scrolling for something to watch, enjoy it, and then probably never think about it again.

I love that a lower-budget film with lesser-known actors/actresses is doing so well. All of the performances in this were amazing, and I look forward to seeing these people in other movies.

That said, I'm not exactly sure why it got so popular. It's a pretty run-of-the-mill physiological thriller/horror movie, and I really wish they would've leaned into the horror aspect more. The creepiness & suspense of some scenes was so good-I just feel like there weren't enough of them.

Overall, I liked it, and I'd say most people who are into the genre would as well. Just don't do into it with expectations through the roof (like I did).

summary: I can't understand so many high rated reviews...
text:
Ok, so this is a competent film, but no more than that. To see so many 8/10 and higher reviews is highly suspicious.

The plot is adequate, the acting is passable, it's nicely filmed, and edited. The premise is somewhat unique, without being mindblowingly so.

My big issue with this film is that the lad wished that she'd love him more than anyone else, not for her to turn into an utterly obsessed psycho.

His reaction to her behaviour was also unrealistic. Ok, the title of the film is 'Obsession', and as the film progresses, and her behaviour gets more and more extreme, i feel they want the viewer to forget that he was the one originally obsessed with her, and clearly still is, even though she turns total nut job, so we have the double edged sword of him being obsessed with her, and her, being 'under a spell' becoming increasingly obsessed with him. Even so, there would've come a point where he'd have walked away( or run away). That might've made a better film, where he gets so freaked out by her behaviour, that he leaves, drives across country, finds a job in some hick town, rents a place, finds another girl, and all is well, until one day, 'Nikki' shows up more obsessed than ever, having left a trail of destruction in her wake, jealous, envious, ready to take her Man back, and all Hell breaks loose.

As it stands, this was just decent. Some of the effects with her movement were quite nice, but didn't really make much sense, unless they're trying to suggest that the 'spell' is some kind of demonic possession which could only be broken by one of them dying, but there was absolutely no hint of that.

Another thing that was skipped over, was... Just how many of these Sticks had that shop sold? The worker stated that anyone who had snapped the stick had come back in to complain, or had complained to someone. Particularly in this day and age(and the film is clearly set in 2025/2026), if people had been buying this product, and things were going 'wrong', it would all over Social Media. People would've been posting about it everywhere, warning people not to buy them.

We did see him go online once, asking if they really worked, and got a series of mixed reviews, but if they were causing the kind of carnage that we saw in the film with other people, then there's absolutely no question that 'influencers' would be all over it, leading to the media covering it, and potentially the stick being removed from circulation.

So, perhaps they might've been better setting the film in the 60's or 70's, when any negative effects of these sticks wouldn't have circulated so rapidly.

I have to rate this as a decent film, certainly nowhere close to the 8, 9, or 10 ratings we see here. A 5 star rating is fair.

summary: Interesting story but seems a little forced.
text: I enjoyed the movie; however, I'm not quite sure why it has such a high rating. The story itself was interesting, but the main boy character seemed unrealistically naive. I found it hard to believe some of the decisions he made and the way he handled certain situations. At times, it felt like his actions were forced simply to drive the plot forward.

Obsession was one of my most anticipated horror films of the year because I've always enjoyed stories about obsession. They're almost a guilty pleasure for me, and this film seemed ready to fully embrace that concept through psychological horror.

The story follows a young man who buys a magical object capable of granting wishes. His wish is for Nikki, the girl he's obsessed with, to love him above everyone else. Naturally, things quickly begin to spiral out of control.

What I appreciated most is that Obsession doesn't try to be a conventional mainstream horror film. Anyone expecting a slasher full of jump scares and nonstop kills will probably be disappointed. This is a slower, stranger and much more psychological experience, and I think that works in the film's favor.

The cast is very strong, especially the actress playing Nikki. Without spoilers, she delivers a demanding and genuinely disturbing performance in several scenes. There was even one moment that made me react out loud in the theater because of how intense it became.

That said, the pacing can feel uneven. Some scenes and dialogues drag longer than necessary and the film would probably benefit from tighter editing.

My biggest issue, however, was the soundtrack. I know many people will probably enjoy it, but I personally hated the synth-heavy score because it constantly reminded me of Stranger Things. Instead of helping the darker atmosphere, it often pulled me out of the experience. I understand what Curry Barker was trying to do, but for me it didn't work at all.

Still, once the film fully grabs you, it becomes genuinely intense and uncomfortable. I also liked how the story slowly builds toward its ending, which still managed to surprise me during the final minutes.

Obsession is not a horror film for everyone, but for fans of slower psychological horror with uncomfortable situations, it's definitely worth watching.

summary: Be Careful What You Wish For
text:
Obsession has a unique supernatural concept and does a great job creating a creepy atmosphere. The cinematography, setting, and overall tone make the movie genuinely unsettling, and the horror relies more on tension and atmosphere than cheap jump scares. Inde Navarrette delivers an excellent performance as Nikki, making her character both believable and disturbing.

What impressed me most was the atmosphere. Every location and visual element fits the mood perfectly, and the movie succeeds in making you feel uncomfortable throughout. As someone who enjoys horror, I appreciated that it tried to build suspense instead of depending on constant jump scares.

My biggest disappointment was the story. Although the premise is original, I felt the movie didn't explain its supernatural rules clearly enough. I kept waiting for the concept to develop further, but instead it stayed relatively simple and left many questions unanswered. The idea had much more potential than what was actually explored, and I think more detail would have made the story much stronger.

Before watching, don't expect every question to be answered. This is a mysterious, open-ended horror film that focuses on atmosphere rather than explaining everything. If you prefer horror movies with clear rules and neatly wrapped-up endings, this one may leave you frustrated.

Overall, I think Obsession is worth watching for its unique idea, outstanding atmosphere, and strong performances. While I expected more from the story, I would still recommend it to fans of supernatural and psychological horror who enjoy mysterious, atmospheric films and don't mind leaving with a few unanswered questions.

summary: Be Careful What (and How) You Wish For
text:
"Obsession" is a lean, focused, genuinely unnerving little horror film that earns every bit of the attention it's gotten. Curry Barker has a real instinct for tone, keeping things grounded and even a little darkly funny before slowly letting the dread seep in, and the result feels much more confident and controlled than its micro budget origin story would suggest.

The script is where a lot of that control lives. The writing is sharp, particularly the lines written for Nikki, which thread a needle between charming, unsettling, and quietly devastating in ways that feel carefully considered rather than just written to shock. But none of it would land without Inde Navarrette, who is frankly extraordinary in the role. It's a physically demanding, emotionally layered performance that she commits to completely, oscillating between warmth and something deeply wrong with a precision that makes you uncomfortable in exactly the right way. The film essentially rests on her shoulders and she doesn't wobble once.

Visually, Barker is already developing a real voice. The use of shadow is deliberate and expressive, framing characters in darkness in ways that feel psychological rather than decorative, giving the film a visual texture that punches well above its weight. There's a care in how shots are composed that you don't always expect from first time theatrical directors, and it gives the whole thing a sense of intentionality that keeps you locked in.

Thematically it's doing something more interesting than the premise might imply, quietly poking at ideas about consent, projection, and the way romantic obsession can twist someone's perception of another person into something they never actually were.

If there's any gripe it's that the lead protagonist occasionally tests your patience in ways that feel slightly more like a script convenience than genuine human behavior, asking you to buy into some choices that stretch believability even within the film's own logic.

Still, this is a striking, confident piece of horror filmmaking from someone clearly worth watching. Barker arrived, and Navarrette made sure nobody in the room could look away.

summary: My Favorite Movie of the Year
text:
I would be remiss to give this movie anything lower than an 8 for the moviegoing experience alone. When I saw it in theaters, the crowd was completely locked in, laughing and gasping together in a way I honestly cannot remember experiencing in a long time.

Go into this movie completely blind if you can. A lot of what makes it work is not knowing where it is going.

This is more psychological horror than traditional horror. I was not necessarily scared, but I was constantly uncomfortable, tense, and on edge. What I really liked is how much the movie does with relatively little. The situation feels grounded enough that even the more exaggerated horror elements hit harder, and the characters feel believable even when you completely disagree with what they are doing.

It is definitely not without plot holes, and there are things you can pick apart if you think about them too much, but I think it works best when you let yourself stay immersed in the moment.

I could go on and on because this movie gives you so much to talk about afterward. It is probably my favorite movie of the year so far, and I have a hard time imagining another movie giving me a more fun viewing experience.

summary: the best horror movies of recent years.
text:
"Obsession" is one of the best horror films of recent years. The story is solid, and Inde Navarrete is perfect as Nikki-it was undoubtedly the best performance of her budding career.

The story makes you uncomfortable even in ordinary settings, like a gathering of friends; there are scenes that provoke disgust and revulsion, moments that are genuinely frightening-such as the way Nikki behaves-and cringeworthy sequences that drag on, becoming excruciatingly awkward even for us, the viewers.

The protagonist is so misguided that, even when friends question him about Nikki, he insists on lying and claiming everything is fine and normal. Even when the real Nikki begs him to end her suffering, he hesitates, questioning whether her life trapped in hell-while her possessed body dates him-is truly that bad. Ultimately, the only person we root for to get a happy ending is Nikki herself, yet the way it concludes leaves her as the one who has suffered the most trauma and lifelong scars.

The director is so skilled that even the few comedic moments work within the horror universe-a rare feat.

It has been one of the best surprises I've encountered in years; I highly recommend watching it-preferably with that female friend you dream of dating, even though she only sees you as an older brother.

First things first. I loved this movie. It took a simple overly used concept and improved on it. Guy makes a wish that a girl would fall in love with him and it goes wrong. Simple concept. But good horror takes ideas we know and either improves on them or twists them. This movie excels at both.

During the opening minutes, Bear, our love sick antagonist of the film, comes home and finds his cat dead after getting into a bottle of medication. I knew that's how Bear would die eventually right off the bat. But by the time we finally got to the end, I didn't care that I called it because this movie did something that few movies do for me anymore.

1. It valued my time. 1 hour and 49 minutes. In an age of over exposition, cheap jokes that undercut the plot, and moronic characters, Obsession didn't feel the need to explain away what was going on with Nikki. There was a scene where Bear called the number on the back of the box of the One Wish Willow and this uninterested dude on the other end of the phone doesn't explain anything except that the only way for the wish to end is for Bear to die. And then offers to let Bear talk to Nikki. We are then met with the blood curdling screams of Nikki, like her soul is being held somewhere else, while her body remains being worn by something else. And that's the only explanation we get. No scene where he finds someone else who lived through this and explains it's a demon or spell. The director let the audience draw their own conclusions. Love it.

2. It genuinely shocked me. There are so many scenes where you think it's gonna go one way only for it to flip into something completely different. The party scene is one. It's eerie and disturbing and then, she snaps out of it and starts screaming out of nowhere. Inde Navarette (Nikki) does an incredible job with this role. I had never seen her in anything but I hope to see her in more. She is creepy when she needs to be. Unhinged when the need arises, and ultimately believable. There is genuine terror on her face when she snaps out of it for a moment. There's a scene towards the end of the movie when the curtain is pulled back for a moment when they are in bed and Bear is sneaking out of the room. The real Nikki begins whispering and begging for him to kill her. It was heartbreaking because you then realize she has been observing all of what's been happening and she has been in agony. Only for the climax of the film to happen and she is released from her prison and she is left with a life in ruin from what the other Nikki did. It doesn't explain what happened to Nikki but you get the sense that she is deeply scarred by this, is likely going to prison and will need serious help for something she is ultimately a victim of. It's a bleak ending. But damn it made for a good movie.

Only a few nit picks. Some of the scares you can see coming. There's a scene where Bear and this other girl Sarah are in her car having a convo and she is about to confess that she loves him, only for Nikki to break the window in and murder her. The gore was good, but you know, just because the camera is off center on her face, that the window is about to break in. And the letter. Sarah has been talking about art school then entire movie and she was waiting on her acceptance letter and before she and Bear get a chance to open it she is murdered by Nikki. Once bear is alone again he opens the letter and she was accepted. Like okay we get it. It's supposed to be tragic.

Not much else to say. Would watch it again. Looking forward to more out of this director and cast. Solid work all around. 8/10.

summary: A Griping Thriller with Plenty of Twists
text:
I went into Obsession hoping for a tense psychological thriller, and it definitely delivered. From the beginning, the film builds a strong sense of mystery that kept me interested throughout. Every time I thought I had figured out what was happening, another twist made me rethink everything. It's the kind of movie that keeps you engaged from start to finish.

The performances are convincing, and the cast does a great job bringing the characters to life. I especially liked how the film focused on suspense and atmosphere rather than relying solely on shocking moments. The cinematography and soundtrack work really well together to create an uneasy feeling that fits the story perfectly.

The pacing is mostly excellent, although there were a couple of moments in the middle where the story slowed down slightly. Even so, those scenes helped build the characters and made the ending more satisfying. The final act ties everything together in a way that feels rewarding without giving away too much too early.

Overall, Obsession is a well-made thriller with strong performances, an engaging mystery, and plenty of suspense. While it isn't completely perfect, it offers a memorable and entertaining experience that fans of psychological thrillers should enjoy. I'd definitely recommend it, and I'd happily watch it again. **9/10**.

The dialogue is so awful, I find it hard to believe anyone vetted it. Too many extremely awkward pauses by Bear, and his character is absolutely ridiculous. None of the other characters have much to do besides passively watch. There isn't anything scary or creepy throughout the movie, which is a first for me with Blumhouse. Might have been better at about 85 minutes, but probably not, and the silences make the runtime feel terrifically longer than its near two hours. And what's the deal with all the shadows? There's nothing hidden, which makes the movie even more dull. I am completely missing what the rave reviews saw, though maybe it is a generational thing, and younger people actually talk and act like utter morons? Disappointing.

summary: A Stylish, Unsettling Throwback to 1970s Brian De Palma
text:
Obsession (2025) feels like a film that could have been discovered in a forgotten vault alongside the psychological thrillers and horror films that defined the 1970s. More than anything, it evokes the atmosphere of early Brian De Palma-those feverish tales of voyeurism, guilt, desire, and paranoia that blurred the line between reality and nightmare.

What impressed me most is the film's confidence in its visual storytelling. Rather than relying on cheap jump scares or excessive exposition, it builds tension through camera movement, composition, and carefully controlled pacing. Every corridor, reflection, and lingering glance seems loaded with meaning. The film understands that suspense often comes from what remains unseen rather than what is immediately revealed.

The cinematography deserves special praise. There are moments that feel directly inspired by the elegant, dreamlike style of De Palma's classics, with slow zooms, elaborate tracking shots, and an almost hypnotic use of color and shadow. The result is a movie that feels simultaneously modern and nostalgic.

The performances are equally strong. The cast commits fully to the heightened emotional tone, making the story's increasingly disturbing developments believable. The protagonist's descent into obsession is portrayed with enough nuance to keep the audience invested even when the narrative ventures into darker territory.

The score is another highlight. Like the best psychological horror films of the 1970s, the music doesn't simply accompany the action-it becomes part of the atmosphere, amplifying the sense of dread and tragic inevitability that hangs over the entire film.

If I have one criticism, it's that the film occasionally prioritizes style over narrative clarity. Some viewers may find its ambiguity frustrating, particularly in the final act. However, for me, that uncertainty is part of its appeal. Like many of De Palma's most memorable works, Obsession lingers in the mind long after the credits roll.

This isn't a conventional horror film. It's a slow-burning psychological nightmare, rich with visual flair and old-school suspense. Fans of 1970s Brian De Palma, particularly films like Sisters, Carrie, and Obsession, will find a lot to admire here.

A haunting, beautifully crafted thriller that proves classic psychological horror techniques still have tremendous power.

summary: Fun creative take on a simple premise
text:
I really loved the acting in this one, especially from the girl playing Nicky. The range of emotions she shows thru out this film is just insane. She does it perfectly!

This movie could have been totally generic like "Smile" or any other of those high concept horrors but the direction and acting really makes it something special.

The stage curtains open ...

I've been hearing a lot about this movie lately, so I had to go see it. Despite hearing about it, I've been able to avoid any major spoilers, so I went in pretty much blind and with my own ideas on what it would be about. I was fairly close. This is a movie that delivers on all levels. There is a lot to like about "Obsession". It is well written, well filmed, and well acted. It has easily become one of my favorite films of the year so far. It was nice to get something new and fresh like this.

Bear is a quiet, awkward young man who is an acquired taste when it comes to relationships. Especially with his co-workers - one in particular who he is majorly crushing on, a girl named Nikki. He is having the hardest time working up the courage to ask her out, even when she gives him the opportunity to do so. He comes across something called the One Wish Willow, a stick of wood that apparently has the magical properties to grant a person only one wish after the wood has been snapped in half. Out of frustration, he wishes for Nikki to fall in love with him more than anyone else in the world. That is exactly what he gets - and a whole hell of a lot more.

Back in 1992, there was a Rom-Com titled "Love Potion No. 9" which featured an unknown Sandra Bullock (at the time) where the premise was similar. In that film, all they had to do was spray a little love potion on their tongue and start talking. Whoever heard them talking would fall madly in love with them. This film takes that a big step further and in a much darker place. Knowing the title of this film and watching the behavior of Bear, it was clear that he was the one obsessed with her initially - even to the point where she was subconsciously annoyed by it. She asks him at one point if he had feelings for her and he said "No" ...to which she says, "Good." Then he makes his ill-fated wish, snaps the wood and tables are turned.

There is a lot of allegory to be taken from this film. Since my reviews are spoiler free, I won't get into it. But, I will say that this isn't a film about his obsession, or even hers. It is about the dangers of obsession period. Both mild and aggressive. The horror elements all work here. I loved the camera work, the use of music and sound, and the special effects. They all work to full effect here. There are a couple of good jump scares to be had, and some very dark humor that made me laugh. I guess that means I'm a sick individual. LOL - so be it. This was a very good movie. Worthy of a high recommend and one I will be watching again.

Horror has never been my favorite genre, so Obsession already had a disadvantage before I even pressed play. Surprisingly, it managed to keep me entertained from beginning to end.

The first thing that stood out to me was the direction. The movie is extremely well-directed, with tension that builds naturally and never feels cheap. It also knows exactly when to ease that tension with humor. There are several funny moments throughout the film, but they're placed carefully enough that they never ruin the atmosphere. Instead, they make the characters feel more natural before the story becomes unsettling again.

Inde Navarrette was easily one of the biggest highlights. She delivers a performance that carries much of the film's emotional weight, and it's hard to imagine the story working nearly as well with a weaker lead.

My biggest criticism is the mythology behind the story itself. I'm someone who enjoys supernatural movies when there's some logic behind the rules. Here, everything begins because of a magical stick that grants wishes simply because... it does. The film never really develops that idea beyond what is necessary to move the plot forward. It works well enough for entertainment, but it's difficult to become fully invested in the supernatural side of the story.

What completely surprised me, however, was Bear.

I honestly think he's one of the most interesting parts of the movie.

It's easy to watch the film and come away believing he's just another victim of the situation. I don't see him that way.

The moment Bear understands what's actually happening, his choices stop being driven by confusion and start becoming selfish decisions. That's what makes him such an uncomfortable character to watch.

One particular scene perfectly summarizes who he really is. When Nikki desperately tries to communicate what she wants, Bear's response is essentially, "Is it really that bad being with me?"

That line completely changed the way I saw him.

Instead of accepting reality, he's willing to ignore someone else's suffering because reality isn't what he wants. Even if everything had gone his way, I genuinely believe he would've continued making the same selfish choices. He's not evil in a cartoonish sense, which is exactly why he's so frustrating. His actions come from denial, obsession, and selfishness, making him far more believable than a typical horror antagonist.

The ending was another pleasant surprise. It felt satisfying without relying on unnecessary twists, and after reading about the alternate ending the filmmakers considered, I honestly think either version could have worked. It's rare for a movie to have two endings that both feel appropriate for the story.

Obsession isn't a film with particularly deep mythology, and its supernatural premise asks you to accept a lot without explanation. But thanks to confident direction, strong performances, well-balanced humor, and surprisingly layered character writing, it becomes much more than just another horror movie.

Even as someone who rarely enjoys horror, I never found myself checking the time or waiting for it to end.

And that's probably the biggest compliment I can give it.

summary: I'm embarrassed I went to see this.
text: I hope nobody I know saw me there. I think this movie is aimed at 15-25 year olds so I was way out of the age range. But even for them this movie is moronic. I do not usually watch horror films but I was curious because of the box office numbers. God save us all if this is what the movie ticket buyers want.

Obsession, directed by Curry Barker, is one of those horror films that sneaks up on you. At first, you think you know exactly where the story is headed. The trailer already gives away the setup: a lonely young man becomes obsessed with a girl named Nikki and makes a wish for her to love him more than anything else in the world. In lesser hands, that premise could have easily fallen into tired horror clichés, but this film manages to avoid most of the familiar traps and becomes something much darker and more unsettling.

The obsessive young man is played by Michael Johnston, an actor I was not familiar with before seeing this movie. His performance is what really drives the picture. Johnston slowly transforms from awkward and sympathetic into something genuinely disturbing, and the gradual descent is what makes the movie work so well. Nikki is played by Inde Navarrette, who audiences may recognize from Superman & Lois. She gives Nikki warmth and realism, which makes the escalating horror feel even more uncomfortable and believable.

What impressed me most about Obsession is its slow-burn style. Horror movies today often rely on jump scares or nonstop violence, but this film takes its time building tension. You know things are going to spiral out of control, but the way the obsession grows becomes increasingly manic and horrifying. Blumhouse really found something special here because the movie understands that psychological terror can be more frightening than cheap scares. By the final act, the story dives fully into terrifying obsession and even some disturbing body horror that may be too intense for some viewers, but horror fans will appreciate just how far the film is willing to go.

There was very little I disliked about the movie. My only issue was what I would call the "billion-dollar drop" moment near the end - viewers who see the film will probably understand exactly what I mean. Still, that small complaint does not take away from how effective the overall experience is. It takes a lot for a horror movie to genuinely creep me out, especially since so many online critics constantly recycle the same recent titles in their "Top 10 Horror Films" lists. Obsession deserves to be part of that conversation because it delivers tension, atmosphere, and genuine discomfort in a way many modern horror films fail to achieve.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Obsession and highly recommend it, especially to horror fans looking for something disturbing and memorable. It is creepy, unsettling, and emotionally intense, with strong performances and a story that keeps tightening the screws until the very end. On a scale of 1 to 10, I would easily give it a solid 9. Don't miss this film if you love horror.

The best horror movie that I watched in the last years, it's shows how u don't need high budget and a lot of cgi to make a good and horrified movie. It's a simple ideia very well maid the sound track helped a lot to build the atmosphere, I'm really hyped to see what the director will do next and the nexts movies that Inde Narrative will appear.

Obsession is uniquely disturbing. Curry Barker has crafted a truly exceptional film that is equal parts horror classic and feminist social commentary. I haven't stopped thinking about the film since I watched it, and the more I think about it, the more obviously brilliant it becomes.

Inde's standout performance as Nikki is generational. I think we'll be talking about her for decades to come. The way she's able to flip between harmless girl next door and violent psychopath is truly astonishing. It's a testament to her range and charisma that I liked "Real" Nikki so much after the first 20 minutes, that I was sympathetic as "Wish" Nikki spiralled into madness and violence.

The quality of production belies the relatively tiny budget. The editing, cinematography, special effects, and soundtrack are all phenomenal. You could tell me this film cost $20 million and I'd believe you.

Few films are able to rock me the way Obsession has. It's now firmly in my top 10 films of all time. Everyone invovled should be immensely proud of this sensational film.

Either these critics are being paid to praise it, or they've never seen a good movie in their lives. It's all marketing.

Everyone take a bow to Curry Barker! Now usually after walking out of a horror movie I feel fine and don't think much about it but now I'm genuinely feeling uneasy and my heart is still pounding. Obsession truly exceeds the hype for me. I can't remember a movie since Hereditary that really made me uneasy for so long , where I felt a genuine terror constantly throughout the second half of the film. Curry barker has crafted something truly original and fresh and it's such an amazing thing for a YouTuber in his 20's to pull off something that I haven't seen from big studios in a really really long while. The movie really hooks you with its outstanding performances from Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette. She was exceptional in this film with her expressions and her body language that can really make one nervous. The lighting work, camera angles and cinematography is absolutely stunning. Like I would say the direction and the execution of how the film is presented is truly the soul of this film. I swear there were some scenes that showcase some genius camerawork where you are watching one character in focus and you can just sense the sheer creepiness of the character who's out of focus and that is enough to keep you on your edge. The last movie that did this really well was Longlegs where my mind was just too focused on the background and what might happen which just built and built the anticipation of what's to come. You can't really keep your guard down for long enough. The story is quite unique too, the film also has some really good moments that make you appreciate the writing and the performances by the main leads. The film also has it's fair share of comedy which I'm so glad is not some cheap lame humor but crafted in such a way that it's scary but one also feels the need to laugh. Music is also something I feel was spot on where one moment you feel this ease , you are having a sweet moment and out of nowhere you get jumped by something you'll prolly not see coming. I really loved the background score. One of my favorite parts about the movie is the climax. It's the crucial point that makes or breaks the film but Obsession pulled a really beautiful, eerie almost poetic perfect ending. You can't help but feel bad about certain characters but also applaud at the ending which I thought was simply brilliant. A must watch with a packed theater at a night show. I can't wait to see what Curry Barker does next. The movie really makes you think , what sort of obsession was more dangerous.. the obsession for Nikki by bear or vice versa.

summary: Nothing Left to Wonder, Yet Still Worth Watching
text:
An unhealthy obsession with strange, irrational, and even dangerous behavior is something that could easily happen in the real world. There was actually a lot of potential to explore it as a psychological horror story-showing what was really going on inside Niki's mind and how the people around her, especially Bear as the one most affected, responded to it.

But none of that really matters anymore because the movie answers everything from the start: the spell works because of Bear's careless use of the One Wish Willow.

After that, it almost feels like there's nothing left to wait for or wonder about by the end of the film.

Even so, the movie is still worth watching because it somehow feels fresh and different.

I'm not exactly sure why.

Maybe it's the expectations surrounding it and all the hype that came with its viral popularity.

summary: No, No, No... Don't Do It!
text:
It's been a long time since a movie had me this invested. Obsession grabbed my attention from the very beginning and never let go. There were so many moments where I found myself thinking, "No, no, no... don't do it!"-which is exactly what you want from a good psychological thriller.

The performances were strong across the board, and the actors did a great job making the characters feel believable. The suspense kept building, and the tension stayed high throughout the film. While a few moments were predictable, there were enough twists to keep me engaged until the end.

If you're a fan of thrillers that keep you on the edge of your seat and make you question what's coming next, Obsession is definitely worth watching.

A small film crafted like many 70s B-movies-featuring a compelling premise and a low budget, yet brimming with ideas and total commitment. Barker steers his course with insolent mastery and manages to make us feel uneasy thanks to some rather impressive actors (the girl will certainly appear in the next blockbusters).

summary: Accidental genius, or a microcosm of any response to coercive control of one's free will
text:
"It's not me!"

The Willow is a corporation or political system that controls one's free will (take your pick), Bear is a corporate employee or worker for the enterprise, and Nikki "Free-MAN" is the worker or citizen. Nikki just wants to be loved and feel love and have free will working on her book, but the corporate/and/or political entity is obsessed with her talent or individual will and wants to use her for its own desires and abuse, to take advantage of her. As such, she loses her free will and true self, and she has to suffer and be traumatized in the system and find her way out to free herself. The entity will not let her because it is self-serving and indifferent, or inconsiderate, to her free will.

In any abusive, denigrating, self-serving system or relationship, the manipulative entity is only out to serve itself (Bear represents this). Nikki is coerced to pretend to love things she doesn't love and do things that are not true to her true self.

This is a perfect metaphorical illustration of any vicious cycle of selfish abuse wheter a relationship, a corporation, or a narcissistic family.

Inde Navarette perfectly depicts the loss of free will that every enslaved person goes through in any abusive relationship, losing her autonomy and individualization at the hands of the abuser or abusive organization. When she finally breaks free, the damage is done because the selfish organization or abuser has altered her true self against her free will. Most viewers will miss it in the horror context and superficial depiction of a contemprary abisuve relationship, but it is all there in the analogy.

What a wake up call. "It ain't me". Let's stand up to abuse victims of all coercive and subjugating systems, people, and corporations. And with AI arriving, this is even quadrupally relevant.

8/10.

As a horror fan, it takes a lot to genuinely scare me these days, but this movie absolutely delivered. The tension never lets up, and it had me on edge from beginning to end.

It was refreshing to watch a film that focused on telling a compelling story instead of feeling like it had to make a political statement or push an agenda. The characters felt like people first, not vehicles for a message, and that allowed the story to stand on its own.

Rather than trying to check boxes or lecture the audience, the filmmakers simply focused on making a great horror movie. The pacing is excellent, the atmosphere is genuinely unsettling, and the suspense keeps building until the very end. If you're looking for a horror film that trusts its audience and remembers that its primary job is to entertain and scare, this one is absolutely worth watching.

summary: A chilling horror movie on toxic relationships
text:
Probably the best horror film I have seen in a long while.

Curry Barker absolutely crushes it in his feature length theatrical debut. The cinematography is absolutely fantastic and it's mind boggling that it was actually done with digital cameras. The cast all do fantastic work especially Inde Navarrette as Nikki, who gives a genre defining performance on par with Toni Colette in Hereditary, Daniel Kaluuya in Us and Mia Goth in Pearl.

The writing especially is incredibly strong centring on the trials and tribulations of being in a relationship, the old 'be careful for what you wish for' troupe and how when someone loses their free will, they lose a lot of themself in the process. I mean if Bear had just told Nikki his true feelings for her then she wouldn't have become so dependent on him loving her and he wouldn't have become trapped in their relationship.

Overall, a truly amazing horror movie featuring both moments on levity, absolute horror and at the end shock for what you saw that I couldn't recommend enough.

summary: Obsession: Craeful what you wish for
text:
This movie was disturbing, but I think that's exactly what it was meant to be. It wasn't made to make the audience feel good or comfortable it was designed to make us sit with discomfort, unease, and moral confusion, and in that sense it succeeds.

More than scary, the film was genuinely unsettling. The scene where he comes back home and finds her still standing in the exact same position was incredibly disturbing. Another moment that stayed with me was when she quietly moves into the corner of the room just to watch him sleep. These scenes created a constant sense of dread throughout the film. Even Bear's death left me feeling strangely uneasy for reasons I can't fully explain.

I was glad Ian died because I strongly disliked his character, although I wish his death had been more impactful given how much emotional damage he caused throughout the story. Sarah's death felt predictable but still heartbreaking. She came across as the only genuinely kind and decent person in the film, and she didn't deserve what happened to her. The aftermath of her death, especially when Nikki brings her body home and continues interacting with it, was one of the most disturbing parts of the entire movie.

Ian, in particular, felt like the worst character in the film. From the beginning, he came across as a disloyal friend who did not respect Bear's feelings. He encouraged Bear to call Nikki "Freaky Nikki" even though she clearly disliked it, which made it feel like he enjoyed putting Bear in awkward situations. He also seemed to push Bear toward confessing his feelings while simultaneously pursuing Nikki himself, almost as if he was waiting for Bear to be rejected so he could make his move. Learning that Ian and Nikki had been hooking up behind Bear's back only reinforced how unfair he was to Bear. Even after Nikki and Bear got together, Ian continued questioning how Nikki could suddenly be in love with Bear, which made him feel bitter and unsupportive. Because of all this, I found it hard to sympathize with him at all.

At the same time, I also empathized deeply with Nikki. She may have suffered the most in the entire film. Imagine being conscious of everything happening around you but having no control over your own body or mind. She was essentially trapped inside herself while another version of her acted on her behalf. That idea alone was terrifying. The fact that she was forced into actions she did not choose makes her situation extremely tragic.

A lot of people have debated the intimate scene between Bear and Nikki. Personally, I found it disturbing because Nikki was not in control of her actions and likely did not genuinely consent. From her perspective, it was forced, as the version of her created by the wish was acting in her place. However, from Bear's perspective, I don't think he realized at that point that there were effectively two versions of Nikki the real Nikki trapped inside and the "wish controlled" version acting externally. That doesn't make the situation less disturbing, but it does make it more tragic rather than intentionally malicious on his part.

Bear himself is also a deeply tragic character. He never intended for any of this to happen. He genuinely believed the wish was a joke and did not understand that it would actually work. His actions come from love, loneliness, and emotional desperation rather than cruelty. However, the consequences of that wish are devastating, and the thought that Nikki might blame him forever makes his ending especially painful.

I also empathized with Nikki's fate at the end of the story. Once she regains consciousness, she has to live with the knowledge that her friends are dead and that she was responsible for those actions, even though she was not truly in control of herself. The emotional and psychological burden of that realization is horrifying, and she may even face legal consequences for something she did not willingly do. In many ways, she becomes the biggest victim of the entire situation.

The acting from both lead actors was excellent and carried much of the emotional weight of the film. My biggest criticism is that the movie leaves too many important questions unanswered. I wanted to know exactly how the wish worked, whether there was a supernatural entity behind it, who was speaking on the phone when Bear called the number on the One Wish pack, and what Nikki was seeing sometimes when she looked at Bear or freaked out with fear. These unanswered questions made it feel like a significant part of the story was missing. Maybe the filmmakers are leaving room for a sequel, but I would have preferred more clarity in this film.

Overall I would rate the movie 7.5/10. It was disturbing, emotionally engaging, and featured strong performances from the lead actors. While I appreciated how it made me sympathize with multiple characters Bear, Nikki, Ian, and even Sarah the lack of answers to its central mysteries kept it from being truly great.

summary: Believe the Hype: Obsession is a Masterclass in Unconventional Horror
text:
I created an account specifically to leave a review for this film. In a landscape often dominated by predictable Hollywood blockbusters, stumbling upon Obsession was incredibly refreshing, and it absolutely delivered.

As a seasoned horror fan, I am constantly searching for the unpredictable and the unconventional. So many modern films follow a formulaic path where the outcome is never in doubt, but Obsession breaks that mold entirely. From start to finish, the attention to detail is nothing short of astounding.

Inde's performance is terrifyingly accurate; she captures the unraveling psyche of an obsessed person with haunting precision. She absolutely deserves award recognition for this role. For a film produced on a $750K budget, the technical execution is near perfection. The cinematography is striking, and the script, while deceptively simple, makes every word count. I particularly loved the inclusion of easter eggs, such as the subtle nod to Curry Barker's voice as the One Wish Willow salesman.

The true strength of Obsession lies in its ambiguity. It's a film that demands you analyze it long after the credits roll. Is Bear the true villain, or just another victim of the supernatural wish? Was Nikki ever actually interested in him, or did we witness a warped exaggeration of Bear's own desires?

The concept; a person trapped within their own mind while their body is hijacked by an external force is pure nightmare fuel. It perfectly illustrates how Bear's obsession manifests and consumes everything in its path. While I've landed on the conclusion that Bear is the clear antagonist (though Ian is certainly no saint), the emotional weight really rests on the tragic arcs of Sarah and Nikki.

If you are tired of generic horror, you need to see this. The score is masterful, perfectly mirroring the film's suffocating tone, and the open-ended nature of the narrative is exactly what makes it so, well, obsessive.

This is a rare, polished gem that earns every bit of its 10/10. Do not miss it.

summary: Best Horror Movie of the Year!
text:
I had watched this movie after the hype had died down a bit.

My sister (a fan of horror movies) and her friends had watched it before I did, and my sister said it was a 3.5/10. She thought the movie was fine, finding it more sad than scary.

She couldn't relate to the themes and circumstances; she felt extremely bad for Nikki and hated everyone else. I can't fathom why she gave it such a low rating; I think it's because she's more of a "dramatic" horror fan than a psychological horror fan.

Dramatic horror, being the type of horror that is more openly scary? Like gore or supernatural- the type of stuff that jump-scares you, giving that adrenaline rush.

I went in with rather low expectations, thinking it was probably overhyped to an extent (plus my sister's review). BUT OH MY GOD, I LOVED THIS MOVIE!!!!

I usually give VERY low scores to horror movies since I rarely get scared or they're just straight-up shit. But THIS movie genuinely had me on edge the entire time.

I haven't seen many psychological horrors that have genuinely been able to scare/ disturb me; most of it is just slow-paced, boring, religious, or shock value. It's like the genre peaked in the 80's.

I had stayed spoiler-free as much as I could, so I went in COMPLETELY blind. I was visibly distraught, gasped, flinched, and covered my mouth in horror. That is huge coming from ME.

Sure, there were one or two parts of the movie that made me raise an eyebrow, but I can ignore the minor flaws, since it's an overall masterpiece. Especially for such a low-budget project.

I genuinely sat there--once the movie was done--with a heavy feeling in my chest and started crying for 15 minutes straight (Although, that was mostly triggered because I had a minor argument with my sister, and I'm the more emotional one of the two)

TBH, I had advice to make this movie more horrific than it already is, but I'm happy with what we got since I don't think I could've mentally recovered otherwise.

I literally watched "Red Shoes and the seven dwarves" right after to recover; I would recommend that movie too if you want to watch a light-hearted animated movie to recover as well.

I care more about the viewing experience than critiquing, but I'd recommend watching this alone in the dark, as I did. Probably don't watch this with family or friends unless you guys are chill like that. (Thank god, I was wearing headphones)

I'm so proud of Indie creators, making such a huge wave on the film scene.

summary: Hit close to home for me
text: I heard great things about Inde Navarette's performance in this and yes, she should be nominated and win everything she is amazing in this. summary: An interesting, dark horror film with minor pacing issues
text:
Obsession was carefully written and constructed, and It makes quite an impact. It is a low-budget horror film, where the budget doesn't affect the quality of the film. Kudos to the gentleman who wrote, produced, edited, and directed "Obsession".

The only criticisms I have with the film are some of the writing, particularly for the boyfriend, "Bear", character, and the pacing. His vocabularly is limited in his dialogue and, at times, waiting for him to say his lines was excruciating. We hear "WTF!" consistently and it gets old. Maybe this was intentional, I don't know, but it impacts the momentum of the film as he struggles to answer questions or explain his feelings to both "Nikki" and his friends.

Regarding pacing, there are a few scenes that I think could have been trimmed down, for example, "Nikki's" extended monologue during the Jenga game at the party, and some of her odd ramblings in the bedroom with "Bear". We know she's under a spell, and some of the crazy rambling took away from the impact of her performance. She did an excellent job!

Story still matters in horror, and this is a creative horror story with a heavy theme of suffering and emotional turmoil. It is probably better for more mature viewers due to the graphic scenes presenting possession or madness. Highly recommended.

summary: I think it's worth the hype
text: I think Obsession was worth the hype, I saw it twice in theaters. I've been a huge fan of horror movies since I was a kid and honestly have been rather disappointed in recent years with what has been put out in the horror genre with the exception of a handful of movies. Was Obsession's storyline something we've heard before? Yeah maybe, kinda. However it's the delivery and cinematography that really makes it stand out. Especially considering the low budget of the movie while still delivering quality on par with other big budget films that weren't even half as decent. I appreciate the use of gore and jump scares only when needed to emphasize a point rather than over utilizing them just for reactions. Sprinkles of comedic relief help tie things together. Inde really takes the cake with her acting, she made me so uncomfortable at times. I think it goes to show how one's innermost desires can ruin them, wanting something so bad that you don't care how it comes about or who it harms in the process as long as you're "happy." Only to realize that what you thought you wanted most ended up in your demise. I think what was also really uncomfortable for me, as a female, was knowing Nikki was cognizant of everything happening to her but a prisoner in her own body. Even the few times she was able to cry for help, Bear ignored her for his own pleasure. I wonder if that's where a lot of the "this was overly hyped up" remarks come from. Yes this movie was about toxic behavior but more so the complete lack of body autonomy at the hands of someone who claimed to be your friend and care about you, that you at one point trusted. Plenty of women know that feeling all too well. You're made to feel bad for Bear in the beginning. Poor Bear, he loves a girl who will never love him. But slowly and surely he becomes the villain in his own story. Instead of accepting things for what they were and moving on, letting Nikki live her life, he chose to destroy her for his own gain. Only deciding to try and reverse his wish once it became too much for him. I'm not saying this is the best horror movie ever made but I do think it is an instant classic. I'm interested to see what else Barker comes out with. I've enjoyed several of his shorts so was thoroughly impressed with his first full length film.

After an intriguing start, the pace began to dawdle to such a degree that I feared "Obsession" would turn out to be another in a long line of over-hyped recent horror flicks.

But the last 30 minutes are so bat s**t crazy (in a very good way!), I felt like applauding.

Definitely anxious to see what Curry Barker does next.

summary: "Obsession" emerges as a work that, although based on mystical elements, addresses very real and contemporary issues
text:
Synopsis:
A man's desire for a beautiful woman to fall in love with him has terrible consequences when she begins to exhibit increasingly disturbing and obsessive behavior.

Review:
"Obsession," directed by Curry Barker, stands out as a disturbing reflection on love and human behavior. The plot revolves around Bear, a young man who, in his desperate search for love, resorts to an object called the "willow of desire" to manipulate the feelings of his childhood friend, Nikki. This premise, although fantastical, becomes a raw representation of the realities surrounding toxic masculinity and emotional dependence. What could be just a tale about misdirected love transforms into a deep dive into human vulnerability, exposing the pitfalls of desire and possessiveness.

Inde Navarrette's performance as Nikki is, undeniably, one of the film's highlights. Her ability to move between moments of apparent fragility and explosions of uncontrolled rage is both impressive and unsettling. She manages to capture the essence of a woman whose own desires are distorted by Bear's selfish ambitions, becoming a mirror of the emotional complexities many women face. Navarrette brings depth to her expressions, elevating the film to an emotional sphere that evokes empathy and reflection.

Curry Barker's choice to avoid typical jump scares is one of the most notable aspects of his direction. Instead of relying on cheap scares, he opts for a more subtle and psychological approach, using suffocating framing and low lighting to create an atmosphere of unease. The shadows that distort Nikki's expressions at crucial moments heighten the tension and allow the audience to experience a persistent sense of anguish. This suspenseful engineering transforms the film into an immersive experience, where true terror emanates from human interactions, not supernatural elements.

Complementing this heavy atmosphere, Rock Burwell's soundtrack stands out as a central element in building the film's mood. In his feature film debut, Burwell uses music as an emotional tool, intensifying the sense of despair and instability that permeates the narrative. The compositions, which evoke a sense of unease, are absolutely essential in translating the feelings of claustrophobia and tension surrounding the characters, serving as a driving force for the film's overall experience.

"Obsession" emerges as a work that, although based on mystical elements, addresses very real and contemporary issues. By questioning the expectations that men often place on women, the narrative provokes a necessary reflection on relationships and our own vulnerability.

But I did enjoy this film. It reminded me of a past version of myself and made me feel compassion for her. I did not like the main character at all though. Brought up at lot of uncomfortable feelings and made me question things that otherwise maybe I wouldn't have. It also made me laugh a couple of times (I wasn't supposed to though). It wasn't great but it was good enough.

I finally watched Obsession after seeing so much hype all over social media, and honestly, I don't think it lives up to the expectations. Based on the online reactions, I was expecting a genuinely terrifying movie that would keep me on the edge of my seat from start to finish. Instead, I found it to be a fairly average horror film with only a handful of memorable moments.

Yes, there are about two or three scenes that are genuinely creepy and well executed. Those scenes deserve credit because they create real tension and deliver the kind of scares horror fans look for. Unfortunately, once those moments are over, the movie slows down considerably. The rest of the runtime feels predictable, with long stretches where not much happens and the suspense never reaches the same level again.

I also felt that the marketing and online reviews exaggerated how scary the film actually is. Social media made it seem like people couldn't sleep after watching it, but that definitely wasn't my experience. If you've watched a decent number of horror movies, you'll probably see many of the twists and jump scares coming.

The cinematography and atmosphere are solid, and the actors do a respectable job with the material they're given. However, strong visuals alone can't carry a horror movie if the story and pacing aren't consistently engaging. I wanted more psychological tension, better character development, and a stronger payoff in the final act.

Overall, I don't think Obsession is a bad movie-it's just nowhere near as frightening or groundbreaking as the internet makes it out to be. If you're looking for a few effective scares, you'll get them. But if you're expecting a nonstop nightmare based on the hype, you may end up feeling disappointed like I did.

My rating: 6/10. Worth watching once, but I wouldn't call it a must-watch horror film though the direction is good but to be honest that's does not make it an exceptional movie. The ending is good but the first half is not that scary. I would suggest you to first check your budget and then choose to go because it will definitely disappoint you.

summary: A Masterclass in Subtle Psychological Horror
text:
I thoroughly enjoyed this film; the storytelling is incredibly tight and it delivers exactly what it promises.

If you view the events from the protagonist's perspective, the horror becomes truly unsettling. Frankly, I would be terrified if I were in that situation. The performances are a huge highlight, especially Nikki's. She plays her role so convincingly that I found myself wondering if that was just her natural personality. Overall, this is a great movie. Those who are strictly into "jump-scare" horror might find it lacking, but for anyone who appreciates a story that delivers horror through tension and atmosphere rather than cheap thrills, this is a must-watch. It subtly, yet effectively, gets under your skin.
