Obsession marks Curry Barker's feature-length theatrical debut. Shot entirely in Los Angeles over just twenty days, the film carried a mere $750,000 production budget. Few predicted this tiny independent horror picture would spark a fierce bidding war at the Toronto International Film Festival. Focus Features sealed the deal with a $15 million acquisition offer, setting a new record for the highest distribution price ever paid for a genre title at the festival. Forty days post-release, its global box office gross surpassed $300 million, landing it among the top three highest-grossing original horror films of all time, trailing only The Sixth Sense and Signs by M. Night Shyamalan.

The film draws its core premise from an age-old folk taboo legend centered on the One Wish Willow, a classic cautionary framework that every wish comes with a devastating toll. Barker transplants this timeless folklore into the mundane daily lives of modern young adults. The entire cast consists of four close friends and co-workers at a music shop: Bear, Nikki, Ian, and Sarah. Shy, timid Bear has nursed a long-standing unspoken crush on Nikki, too nervous to confess his feelings openly. By chance, he stumbles upon a wooden twig from the One Wish Willow at a crystal boutique. The shop clerk warns him the artifact invites ruin, yet blinded by unrequited longing, Bear snaps the twig and makes his desperate wish: for Nikki to love him more than anyone else in the world.

The wish takes effect instantly, unleashing suffocating, all-consuming possessiveness from Nikki. The fleeting sweetness of their new romance curdles rapidly, giving way to paranoia, relentless surveillance, self-harm, and unbridled violence. Viewers watch helplessly as a one-sided infatuation mutates into a nightmare that destroys everyone in its orbit. The movie avoids cheap, formulaic jump scares at every turn; its terror stems from the claustrophobic toxicity of broken human connections, with every uncanny sequence mirroring warped romantic dynamics audiences recognize from real life.

The film features an unplanned, serendipitous Easter egg. During an in-car scene, lead actress Inde Navarrette forgot her blocking directions, spinning 180 degrees on the spot in flustered, self-deprecating panic. The natural, unscripted awkwardness fit perfectly with Nikki's disjointed, externally controlled demeanor. Barker chose to keep the unplanned take intact, resulting in one of the film's most haunting and memorable shots.

In interviews, Barker revealed his 2027 follow-up feature Anything But Ghosts shares a unified cinematic universe with Obsession. A news report featured in the sequel references a female suspect charged with triple homicide, heavily implying Nikki was arrested for the murders of Sarah and Ian, while Bear ultimately died by suicide.

The One Wish Willow does not conjure malice out of nowhere; it merely materializes the possessive urge simmering in Bear's subconscious. The manipulated version of Nikki is nothing more than a physical projection of his unspoken desires. The film repeatedly cuts to fleeting moments where the real Nikki breaks through the supernatural fog, trapped inside her own body. She weeps and begs Bear to end her torment, telling him he never truly knew or possessed her. Bear, however, only retorts with a self-absorbed question: what could possibly be terrible about loving me? The true villain of the story is never the deranged Nikki, but Bear, the man who made the selfish wish in the first place.

Countless young people today fall prey to the anxiety of platonic friendship zones, clinging to the delusion that total, unwavering devotion from another person equals perfect love. Manipulative dating tactics circulating across the internet operate on the exact same toxic logic as Bear snapping the Willow twig. People crave one-sided adoration free of compromise, understanding, and mutual effort, yet any relationship built by stripping another person of their free will is not love-it is control.

Obsession adopts the folk tale trope of wishful consequences as a mere narrative shell, centering its entire storytelling weight on modern romantic dysfunction. Folklore acts only as a vessel; the film's central mission is to critique toxic contemporary relationships. If this same story were produced as a domestic Chinese horror feature, it would undoubtedly face unfair backlash from viewers unable to parse its layered thematic core.

Inde Navarrette's performance stands as the beating heart of the entire picture, tasked with portraying the agonizing internal tug-of-war between two versions of Nikki. One moment she is a warm, smiling ordinary young woman; the next her eyes hollow over and her body stiffens, moving like a puppet yanked by invisible strings. Her eerie frozen stances, involuntary physical breakdowns, and unhinged, illogical outbursts are delivered entirely through raw physical acting, with zero reliance on CGI effects, generating an overwhelming sense of oppressive dread.

The authentic Nikki, seen in her rare lucid intervals, evokes profound sympathy. She harbored independent dreams and planned to quit her dead-end job to pursue writing full-time. Bear's single selfish wish stripped her of all self-determination, trapping her in a cage where she exists solely to fawn over, monitor, and cling to him. Every violent, destructive act she commits is not of her own volition, but an unyielding command forced upon her by the Willow's cursed magic. She is simultaneously the perpetrator of harm and the tragic casualty of Bear's self-centered longing.

Many people in real life mask unreciprocated romantic fixation as pure devotion, refusing to respect clear rejection while fantasizing about supernatural shortcuts to win someone's heart. There are no shortcuts to genuine love. Anyone who seeks to seize control over another person's feelings will eventually be consumed by the darkness they themselves summoned.

Rated R for graphic violence, full nudity, and brutal disturbing sequences, Obsession rarely lingers on drawn-out murder sequences. Instead, it builds dread through shadowed framing, dim muted lighting, and contorted, tormented facial expressions from its cast. That said, mainland China lacks a formal film rating system, forcing many audiences to settle for heavily censored theatrical cuts and become unwitting victims of compromised artistic vision.

The film's true terror never derives from graphic killings, but from mundane, suffocating domestic details. Nikki stands motionless outside Bear's front door for entire workdays, relieving herself on the spot rather than leaving his vicinity. She erupts into violent fits at parties if Bear so much as interacts with another person. She claims every part of Bear's life as her exclusive property, cutting him off from all friends and family. These quiet, unsettling beats instantly resonate with anyone who has witnessed toxic, controlling relationships in real life.

All four central protagonists are twenty-something young adults living in run-down inherited family homes, stuck in dead-end retail jobs with no clear path to a better future, drowning in pervasive anxiety about what lies ahead. This captures a universal mental crisis facing modern youth: crippling fear of solitude paired with a desperate hunger for closeness, yet a complete inability to communicate emotions honestly. Each character is trapped within their own isolated emotional bubble.

Introverted Bear never voices his inner struggles, escaping uncomfortable vulnerability through fantasy and reckless wishes instead of honest dialogue. His best friend Ian holds a cynical, flippant view of romance, incapable of engaging with sincere emotional connection. Soft-spoken Sarah harbors quiet romantic feelings for Bear yet always steps back without confessing. Nikki, originally sharp, self-aware, and grounded, loses all agency to speak her truth after the wish takes hold. Though the four spend every day side-by-side and appear inseparable, none dare lay bare their authentic thoughts, hiding behind performative masks around one another.

Beneath its horror genre packaging, Obsession functions as a piercing fable dissecting modern romantic disconnection. Young generations today gravitate toward superficial group socializing while avoiding deep, committed one-on-one partnerships, terrified of opening their hearts and risking hurt. Every conflict, awkward exchange, and heartache depicted on screen mirrors relatable struggles ordinary viewers face day-to-day.

The film industry requires a tolerant, diverse creative landscape. Genre films carry vital critical and reflective weight, and moderate depictions of violence and intimacy are integral tools for fully realizing thematic intent. Indiscriminate blanket censorship fractures narrative coherence and dilutes a filmmaker's intended message.

For the domestic film industry to break free from its current stagnation, two changes are essential. Filmmakers must dedicate time and care to crafting thematically rich, fully realized scripts, while regulators must implement a mature, tiered film rating framework. This balanced system would protect vulnerable audiences while granting genre creators the space to present their artistic vision without compromise.

The One Wish Willow itself may be fictional, yet every person carries a hidden twig of selfish desire within their heart. We all crave unconditional adoration, yearn to dictate the trajectory of romantic bonds, and refuse to accept heartache, compromise, and mutual compromise as inherent parts of love. Healthy, lasting romance can only flourish on three foundations: individual autonomy, mutual respect, and reciprocal devotion. No person holds the right to make a wish that strips another human being of their free will.

Wishes come easy, but repayment is agony.

A searing dissection of control within romantic obsession.

summary: Be careful what you wish for.
text:
'Obsession' continues to amaze by smashing box office records, and is fast becoming one of the most successful films ever made in terms of box office returns. At the time of writing this review, the film already made back its production budget 540-fold, earning over $400 million on a tiny $750,000 budget! This proves good movies can still be made on a small budget.

Although there are moments in 'Obsession' reminiscent to 'Paranormal Activity' and 'Smile', 'Obession' manages to make it feel original. In fact, if ever there was a fresh and original way to make a possession movie, 'Obsession' probably nailed it - to a certain extent. There are a few really freaky moments, and the small cast delivered superb performances.

Baron 'Bear' and Nikki work together, and he literally can't stop about her, but believes her to be out of his league. When they go out together with their friends Ian and Sarah, Bear buys a 'One Wish Willow'. He gives Nikki a ride home afterwards and after saying goodnight to her, he opens the 'One Wish Willow' and makes a wish: for Nikki to love him more than anyone in the world.

"Be careful what you wish for" could not have been better illustrated. Almost immediately, Nikki starts acting weird, coming on to Bear and eventually proclaiming her love for him. They become inseparable, but in his wish Bear got more than he bargained for. Nikki becomes completely obsessed with Bear, but it becomes clear she possessed, and things take a turn for the worst...

No film is perfect, though, and 'Obsession' has pacing issues. I found the middle a bit slow. Although engaging, I felt the film could have been shorter. 90 Minutes would have been perfect (instead of 108), because I started getting a sense of deja vu. Still, a small budget delivered a quality and somewhat disturbing and creepy film.

summary: Best Horror Movie I have seen all year!
text: This movie was genuinely so good, I really enjoyed every aspect of it. The setting was really good in my opinion, a small generic American town. Before watching the movie when I'd only seen the trailer, I thought I had a clear idea of what was going, and a simple solution. And I think that's what made me enjoy the movie even more, the uncertainty of it all. The acting was phenomenal, I really felt the actors emotion. I was honestly happy with the ending, I was a little surprised though because I actually was expecting something totally different considering the type of person Bear is, the kind of person I thought Bear is anyways.

I'm guessing the over the top nature of the lead performance is probably what most people are raving about? Or the shock value which made watchers not think about the senselessness of the plot?

To me, the movie just didn't make sense. I think the biggest problem with this movie could've easily been resolved in the young man's wish. He specifically wished for the girl to love him more than anyone else in the world. summary: Great first half, then derails towards tasteless stuff.
text:

Obsession has an interesting premise but really fails to engage the audience beyond a "what happens next" storyline. What could have been a fascinating tale of a fake fairytale romance slowly turning into a nightmare, instead becomes yet another "horror" film where violence is the only scary part. Nikki, played incredibly well by Inde Navarrette, goes from a relatable character to a psychotic, obsessed woman in a matter of minutes. And our suffering protagonist just, well, suffers and stutters no matter what is happening in the scene.

Other films have done a much better job of showing the transformation of an ideal relationship into a truly horrifying tale--think Fatal Attraction. It's too bad, as the Barker and his DP created some intriguing visuals and mood that could've been further enhanced by characters who had more life to them.

Nothing from the movie stuck out to me or made me get lost in deep though-as many people claim- but I instead forgot about watching it nearly as soon as the movie was over.

To begin with, I'm certain I didn't miss the main plot and how Bear was manipulating Nikki through his wish. However, I really can't see how this fact has made everyone assess the movie as a masterpiece. Even in modern society and without One-wish-willows men end up controlling the women in their life and still manage to frame themselves as the victims. So, is this Horror? No. It's painfully close to reality and even so it somehow misses the mark and -in my opinion- makes it seem even less important.

Another thing that struck me as odd is that the movie's set was basically fished out from an 80's movie, while the events where meant to be happening in modern day? The protagonists work in a music shop that, realistically, should barely employ 2 people. That and Bear's apartment were the main things that made me feel the vibe was off.

What is more, the characters seem shallow to me, probably because the main plot is less about the people and more about the titular "Obssession" of Nikki. We don't know anything about them and that made me extremely uninterested in them and reluctant in deciding whether they are worth trusting or not. They lack any depth and barely seem like real people, seemingly there only as "the side characters" that are "there for the plot to advance".

In conclusion, I don't think I would have the same strong opinion about the movie if it was less hyped and marketed as something other than horror. A psychological thriller would be a more accurate categorization in my opinion. It wasn't necessarily that the movie was bad, I just don't think it was that good. summary: Food for thought in one SCARY package
text:
The film opens with schluby twentysomething Baron ("Bear") being coached by his friend Ian on how to confess his feelings for Nikki, another member of their friend group, who all work at a music store. It doesn't go well, in Ian's opinion. More upsetting, Bear's cat dies after ingesting left-out painkillers, and he also hears from Nikki she's planning to leave her job. Wanting to give her a gift, he buys a "one wish willow" magic stick at a new-age shop. Missing a golden opportunity to share his feelings with her, he impulsively wishes on the stick that Nikki would "love him more than anyone in the world".

Nikki immediately starts gravitating toward Bear, though in a way that's initially disturbingly erratic. Once that phase passes, they briefly experience happy coupledom. From there, things get REALLY weird. Soon, minor slights or questions from Bear send Nikki into a possessive rage, or behavior even more frightening. Imagine the most unpleasant or unsettling exchange you've ever had with a significant other, scaled exponentially; these become daily occurrences for Bear. Destructive, violent, terrifying and sick events ensue. While it would be easy to see Bear as the victim and Nikki as the villain, it's completely the reverse. Bear, even though realizing he's unleashed something supernatural and horrible, won't own up to the situation or confide in his friends. Bear doesn't even really know Nikki, and his infatuation/obsession is based solely on his own imagination. His wish that Nikki should love him (regardless of who she is or what she wants) is magically projected into reality. It's a spiritual boomerang, in which every objectifying, unreasonable, deceptive, possessive feeling he held comes back at him, with the potential for deadly results. Even when he knows that the person cohabitating with/stalking him isn't really Nikki, but rather a manifestation of his own dark impulses that has usurped her body while the real Nikki suffers, he's unwilling to do what's right unless it's also easy. He thinks that being his love slave shouldn't really be all that bad. In the end, the decision-making is taken away from him, and he leaves a horrible mess in his wake.

The film had a surprisingly small budget, surprisingly since it in no way feels cheap. The settings feel genuine. The cinematography is very effective, especially in creating an eerie, disturbing, anything-can-happen mood, as well as serious scares. The cast of unfamiliar (to me at least) actors is very good, with Inde Navarette as Nikki doing a real tour-de-force embodying a crazy (literally) range of personas.

I'd not recommend watching this film alone at night, on a first date, or if you don't want to be seriously spooked. If you're not averse to horror, it's a powerful and haunting film.

summary: An Incredible Indie Debut Anchored by a Generational Lead Performance
text:
Curry Barker's feature debut is a masterclass in low-budget filmmaking. Obsession proves that you don't need a massive Hollywood budget to create a visually beautiful, deeply unsettling psychological thriller. The cinematography, crisp editing, and sharp dialogue work together flawlessly to create a deeply engaging narrative that flips the dynamic of obsession right back onto the obsessed.

The acting elevates the material to another level. Inde Navarrette is a revelation as Nikki, the true victim of the film's tragic downward spiral. Her performance is phenomenal and absolutely worthy of awards consideration. Michael Johnston is equally superb as the co-lead, portraying a self-absorbed, unthinking character whose bad choices act as the wrecking ball for everyone around him.

My only critiques are relatively minor nitpicks, but they are the only things holding me back from a perfect 10/10:

The Influences: The film heavily and proudly borrows thematic and visual cues from modern horror giants like Hereditary, Get Out, and Pearl. It's a great homage, but sometimes it wears those influences a bit too openly.

The Tone Shift: For a film that functions so brilliantly as a psychological metaphor, the scene where the friend breaks the wish stick and literal billions of dollars drop from the ceiling felt a bit too literal and pulled me out of the established atmosphere.

Still, a massive achievement in indie horror. Barker is a massive talent to watch.

summary: An overhyped psychological thriller with great acting but a disappointing ending.
text:
With all the massive internet hype surrounding Curry Barker's Obsession (2026), I went into the theater expecting the next big horror masterpiece. Unfortunately, while it is a decent psychological thriller, it doesn't quite live up to the overwhelming praise.

The strongest asset of the movie is undoubtedly the performances. Inde Navarrette is phenomenal as Nikki; her shift from a normal friend into an unhinged, intensely physical, and terrifyingly possessive presence is genuinely unsettling. The film does a great job building a claustrophobic atmosphere early on, and the moments of tension and physical confrontation hit incredibly hard.

However, the film suffers from major pacing issues in its second half. Once the initial shock of Nikki's creepy, cursed behavior wears off, the script starts running in circles, making the middle act feel highly repetitive and stretched.

My biggest issue, though, is the ending. After building up so much psychological tension, the final resolution felt incredibly flat and unsatisfying. The way the curse breaks and how the story wraps up didn't match the cleverness of the initial "One Wish Willow" setup. Instead of delivering a truly jaw-dropping conclusion, it fell back on frustrating choices that killed the momentum completely.

Ultimately, Obsession is a solid low-budget thriller with fantastic acting, but a weak third act and a repetitive middle keep it from being great. Don't believe all the hype-it's a decent 6/10 watch, but nothing revolutionary.

Some movies impress with spectacle. Others prove that a compelling story, strong performances, and confident direction are all you really need. This is firmly in the latter camp.

The standout performance belongs to Inde, who plays Nicki. She carries the emotional weight of the film with a performance that is believable, vulnerable, and unsettling as events spiral further and further out of control. The rest of the cast is equally committed, making every relationship feel authentic.

This is another reminder that a low budget doesn't have to mean a low-quality movie. Rather than trying to hide its limitations, the film embraces them, focusing on character, atmosphere, and tension instead of expensive effects. The result is a thriller that feels intimate and personal.

At its heart, it's a classic "be careful what you wish for" story. The overall plot is fairly linear, and seasoned moviegoers will probably see many of the twists coming well before they arrive. Surprisingly, that never hurts the experience. The real enjoyment comes from watching how the director unfolds the inevitable, steadily tightening the tension until every decision carries painful consequences.

The film strikes an excellent balance between psychological discomfort and bursts of bloody violence. It never overplays the gore, using it only when it has the greatest impact. The creeping sense of unease is far more effective than constant shock value.

Creepy, uncomfortable, and consistently engaging, this was an unexpected gem that proves once again that thoughtful filmmaking and outstanding acting will always matter more than a massive budget.

summary: One of the greatest horror movies in the past decade
text:
Obsession stands as one of the most genuinely terrifying horror films of the past decade. What makes it so effective is its refusal to lean on the usual crutches-there is essentially only one jump scare in the entire movie, yet it generates far more dread than films that rely on constant jolts. The real tension comes from the constant uncertainty of what Nikki will do next. That unpredictability keeps the anxiety elevated in a way few recent horrors manage.

Curry Barker's writing and direction are the film's strongest assets. The plot twists land with precision, and the deliberate use of lighting to signal that something is deeply wrong with Nikki is quietly masterful. One particularly sharp moment, Nikki sharing a page from the novel she's writing, reveals how carefully Barker constructs both character and theme. After this film, he has firmly established himself as one of the most exciting writer-directors working in the genre. I am already looking forward to whatever he does next.

The cast delivers across the board, but Inde Navarrette's performance as Nikki is exceptional. She moves from sweet and disarming to completely unhinged with startling control, and the shifts never feel forced. Her screams, the obsessive clinginess, and especially the moments where the "real" Nikki begs Bear to kill her are all delivered with remarkable precision. It is the kind of performance that deserves serious awards attention; an Oscar nomination would not surprise me in the slightest.

Bear, meanwhile, emerges as the film's true selfless villain. His obsession with Nikki leads him to rationalize and enable every disturbing choice she makes, and the movie refuses to let him off the hook emotionally even as it grants him a practical free pass at the end. Every decision and line of dialogue steadily darkens his character until the final frame.

I rarely call a movie perfect, but Obsession comes remarkably close to a 10/10. More importantly, it proves that contemporary horror can be deeply unsettling without constant jump scares or the grotesque body-count excess of traditional slashers. It trusts atmosphere, performance, and psychological pressure, and the result is one of the most confident and effective horror films in recent memory.

summary: No Unnecessary Jump Scares; Pure Psychological Dread
text:
This movie is great, primarily because it doesn't lean on the clichés of modern horror. No cheap, loud jump scares to startle you, nor shows unnecessary, mindless gore just for shock value. More importantly, there is none of the frustrating tropes where characters make inexplicably dumb decisions that get them killed or completely blunder obvious chances to end the entire plot on the spot. Instead of focusing on a monster or demon the film plants a seed of mental horror that slowly builds up.

The execution here is amazing. The direction uses visuals and sound design not to startle the audience, but to build a layer of tension. The sound effects were pretty good in my opinion, while the framing and lighting add to the feeling.

Inde Navarrette's performance as Nikki is the driver behind the movie's psychological horror weight. She shifts between a grounded, independent person and an uncanny, distorted shell of herself, and does it rather well.

Michael Johnston's performance as Bear is also completely on point. No flawless hyper-competent hero. He grounds Bear in realistic, messy insecurity. His desperation, "passivity," and panic feel simply human. Even when his choices become hard to watch, his reactions remain believable.

Edit: Not saying his choices were good, They are questionable at best. But his terrified reactions and that 'shock' is human. That's what I meant with my last statement.

summary: A good movie, but also overhyped
text:
This is undoubtedly a good movie. Better than any major Hollywood movie that I have seen in a while. But, at the same time, it is not perfect and the hype surrounding it is not fully merited.

Good things first: Inde Navarrette did an absolutely amazing job as Nikki. Really great acting. The overall atmosphere of the movie is also very good - the feeling of unease and tension that, again, is mostly due to Navarrette's great acting. I personally prefer this type of horror to the "supernatural creature that can't be killed and murders a bunch of people" borefests. The story is also fine, though it is a story that has been done so many times before.

Not all is great, though. The movie drags sometimes, especially in the first half. It feels like it was unnecessarily stretched to pad the run time. This is especially felt in the dialogue, with characters delivering 15 nothing-sentences to convey the information that a regular person would say in a single short sentence.

Then there are the characters - non of them are really likeable nor good people. Bear is the absolute worst - wimpy, weak, sneaky, conniving, but the others are not much better. Ian, his supposedly best friend, deliberately gives him bad advice about his love interest and sleeps with her behind his back. Nikki, as the cast has confirmed, knows that Bear likes her, supposedly also likes him, yet does absolutely nothing to show him that and sleeps with his best friend. She is the epitome of a girl who supposedly likes a guy, but then friendzones him, uses him for emotional support and sleeps with virtually everyone except him. Sarah is perhaps the least bad of them, but that is mostly because she has the least screen time. But she is also shown to have a generally annoying personality.

But the weakest part of the movie has to do with the one wish willow and the way it works. Director/writer Curry Barker said that the willow is neither good nor bad, but the plot clearly contradicts his words. Bear wished for Nikki to love him more than anyone in the world. That should not mean that she becomes pathologically jealous, cooks his dead cat, soils herself while standing catatonic and staring at the door waiting for him to come back, tapes the door shut so that he could not leave the house and generally acts like a complete psycho. Great love does not mean pathological behavior and psychotic outbursts. So, since there was nothing ambiguous about Bear's wish, either the willow is inherently evil and actively trying to ruin its users' lives, or Barker doesn't know what great love is.

But there is an even bigger problem, possibly related to the fact that Barker said that he didn't have a "willow lore book" that would describe how it actually works. That is the fact that, strictly speaking, Bear did not get his wish at all. He wished for Nikki to love him, yet the movie shows very clearly that the person (or rather entity) who is in love with Bear is not Nikki. It is clearly shown that Nikki is, for lack of a better word, possessed, that the real her is trapped and watching as this imposter controls her body. The scene where Nikki is in bed and the real her tells Bear that this evil entity is asleep, and begs him not to wake her up explains that clearly. So if Bear never got the real Nikki to love him (again nothing ambiguous about the wording here), than the contract in null and void and Bear should be able to back out of it and reverse it. Unless, of course, the willow is inherently evil and just wants to ruin people's lives.

Still, this is a good movie, even though it is not perfect and kind of starts to fall apart the more you try to think about its plot. I was entertained and I was not sorry for the time I spent watching it, which is more than I can say for most of the Hollywood movies these days.

The single bright spot of this showing was when the credits rolled at the end. New lows for a movie experience. It started slow and got worse. I want that hour 48 minutes of my life back. Totally don't understand the reviews and how anyone could/would like this piece of trash. People leaving the theater were like a deer in the headlights.

summary: This is gonna stick with me
text:
I had heard things about this film, but was completely unprepared for how totally bonkers and terrifying it is. I wouldn't have thought a YouTuber of all people could create such a smart, unnerving film, but there you go. The first 30 minutes or so are relatively tame, but when the craziness starts, it's cranked up to eleven and stays there until the end. The female lead's constant mood swings, and erratic/gross/disturbing behavior leads to some of the biggest "What am I watching" moments I have seen in a long time, and I mean that in the best possible way. And as the film goes on, her actions get more and more messed up. It probably says a lot that making a memorial of the main character's dead cat using its corpse is one of the least nuts things she does, isn't it? The script is solid, with some decent lines that get a few laughs at first, then get increasingly weird as the film goes on. And the directing is top notch, especially when it's nighttime and the woman is standing in the shadows. About the only complaint I have is some of the early stuff is a little too predictable. Actually, some of the later stuff is, too.

Inde Navarette single handedly makes this film; I wouldn't be surprised if she at least gets an Oscar nomination. She starts out as very charming, funny, and likeable, but once she goes under the spell, it's an excellent slow burn from her being slightly off to completely mad. And once she hits that point, all bets are off. Some of the scariest moments feature her just standing there for several moments, leaving us waiting and worrying about what she's about to do. Of course, her freakouts are just as terrifying, as they come completely out of nowhere, and she jumps back and forth between them and normal effortlessly. Michael Johnston is really good too as the love-struck protagonist, and seeing his slow descent into madness over the monster he's created leads to some excellent drama. And the two actually have decent chemistry despite everything. The rest of the very small cast does a good job, too.

Overall, Obsession is a surprisingly smart, creative, and thoroughly creepy film that takes its recognizable premise and successfully turns it on its head. It's a film I can guarantee I'll never forget even if I don't watch it again. Ah, who am I kidding? I probably will.

summary: A funny film, but not fun to watch. A love story, but not a Romance.
text:
I've been tracking Obsession for months now since it came out of Fantastic Fest with so much buzz. The idea of a monkey paw conceit where a young man makes a wish for his crush to love him more than anyone else on Earth seemed like a really fun concept for a Horror film. While this movie has some incredibly funny parts, the last thing I would call this movie is fun.

For better or worse, the protagonist of the film Bear goes through experiences that really conjured emotional memories from the past. I know the pain of being young and in love with a woman who will only ever see you as a friend. I also know what it's like to have been with someone toxic, and being completely overwhelmed and freaked out by their behavior while letting it go on for far too long. At least it wasn't the result of a wish gone wrong. Barker expertly crafts the pain of living those experiences. I'm sure women who've had male friends pine for them, or have been emotionally manipulated will also have a painful experience watching this.

Despite this movie existing in an obviously fictional world, it's amazing how authentic everything feels. The fact this is Curry Barker's first feature film is nothing short of astonishing. His confidence absolutely shines through, his vision is clear, he gets the most out of his actors, the mood is always uncomfortable and this movie has some of the best jump scares since Hereditary. I always wonder why directors choose to telegraph that a jump scare is about to happen. To me the most effective ones occur when you have no idea it's about to happen. Barker does that perfectly here, and even in a later scene when you sense something bad is about to happen, he holds the tension perfectly.

As anyone following this film knows, Inde Navarette gives a star making (and she WILL be as star after this) performance as the victim of the wish, Nikki. This is not a one note performance either. She gives absolutely everything to this role, and it is so agonizingly painful to watch. I also have to mention as a 90's kid that she looks stunningly similar to Amy Jo Johnson who was the Pink Ranger in Mighty Morphin Power Rangers. Just like Toni Collette in Hereditary, Naomi Scott in Smile 2 and Mia Goth in the X Trilogy, this performance will be discussed for years.

I also think Michael Johnston's performance should not be overlooked. His is much more subtle, but his reactions to the consequences of his actions always feel pitch perfect. One of the more interesting debates I've noticed as I've been watching videos about the film is whether Bear is a villain. While he made an unintentionally terrible decision, I was surprised at how many people viewed his character through a much more critical lens. It's given me more to think about than I anticipated.

There are a lot of horror films that I love to rewatch, but I don't think Obsession will be one of them. For me it was a too painful and uncomfortable watch. However it's far too good to be missed, and leaves a very real lasting impact.

Obsession surprised me in a very positive way. I usually don't pay much attention to heavily hyped movies because they often end up feeling overrated, but this one genuinely deserves the praise it's getting.

The movie feels completely original, even while keeping some classic horror/thriller elements. It creates a constant sense of discomfort for the viewer, building tension and awkwardness in certain moments in a way that feels deliberate and indredibly effective. The suspense build-up is honestly spectacular, slowly pulling you deeper into the atmosphere without relying on cheap jump scares.

The cast is phenomenal as well. Even though most of the actors are not huge household names (yet), everyone delivers surprisingly strong performances and plays their role perfectly. I honestly wouldn't be surprised if we start seeing them much more often after this film.

summary: A Good Horror film from a young filmmaker !!
text:
Obsession (2025) is a really solid horror film that understands exactly what kind of movie it wants to be. Director Curry Barker delivers a stylish, well-paced horror with some genuinely tense moments, and one sequence in particular features a legitimate jump scare that completely caught me off guard - the kind where the entire room reacts at once.

The biggest standout here though is easily Inde Navarrette. This feels like a full-on scream queen breakout performance. She carries the emotional weight of the movie surprisingly well, and the lighting/cinematography surrounding her character was fantastic throughout. There are several scenes where the visuals almost elevate her presence into something dreamlike or unsettling, which really helped the atmosphere. I'd genuinely like to see her in a lot more horror films after this.

Curry Barker also deserves credit because, for someone still very young as a filmmaker, there's a lot of confidence in the direction. Some of the writing can feel a little exaggerated at times, and a few character choices are undeniably silly - although, honestly, that's part of the horror genre DNA at this point. There's one side character decision in particular that was unbelievably dumb. Still, most horror movies live and die on whether they keep you entertained, and Obsession absolutely does.

The film is somewhat conventional overall and follows a lot of the story beats you'd expect, especially if you watch a lot of modern horror. The "breaking the willow" concept is interesting and feels like it could have had deeper lore behind it, but the movie never fully dives into the mythology or explains it as much as I hoped. That said, the ending was smarter than expected and avoided the kind of underwhelming finish that could have easily ruined the experience.

There's honestly room for this to become some kind of franchise if they wanted to expand the mythology further. The world feels like it has more potential than what we fully see here.

Overall, Obsession is a stylish, entertaining horror film elevated heavily by Inde Navarrette's phenomenal performance and a confident directorial effort from Curry Barker. It may not reinvent horror, but it absolutely succeeds at being creepy, tense, and fun.

7.5/10.

From a psychiatric standpoint, Nikki's (Inde Navarrette) transformation after the wish is a terrifyingly accurate portrayal of extreme Erotomania (the delusion that another person is deeply in love with you) combined with severe Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The film brilliantly visualizes a complete hijacking of the brain's limbic system and dopamine pathways. Her behavioral shifts ranging from micro-social tracking to the erasure of basic survival empathy feel less like typical horror acting and more like a real world clinical case study.

I'm glad I saw it in theaters. I love the lighting on Nikki's eyes in the beginning. I left the movie feeling disgusted, psychologically disgusted all over for at-least 45 minutes. I'm happy the movie did well. It really is refreshing. I compare it to Evil Dead 2013 two films I had low expectations for and felt really impressed by it towards the end.

The concept of the film isn't entirely unique, but it elevates the classic "be careful what you wish for" premise to a whole new level. The opening ten minutes had me wondering what all the hype was about, and some of the acting initially felt a little tacky. However, as the film progressed, the cast grew into their roles and became much more convincing.

Inde Navarrette delivers one of the single greatest performances I've ever seen in a horror film. She successfully walks the fine line between overacting and underselling the material, making Nikki's descent into this demonic wish curse feel completely believable. Her performance is so convincing that you genuinely feel the desperation, fear, and obsession consuming her as the story unfolds. For an actress I had never even heard of before, the performance is incredibly impressive. The performance is without a doubt award worthy. Michael Johnston also delivers a strong performance as the co-lead alongside Navarrette.

The film manages to hold your attention throughout, largely because you're never quite sure what to expect or how Nikki's obsession will continue to manifest as the story unfolds. It also succeeds in telling a compelling story while maintaining its horror elements, something many films in the genre struggle to balance. The film even manages to inject small moments of comedic relief in just the right amounts and at exactly the right times, providing brief breaks in tension without ever undermining the horror.

Overall, this is easily the best horror film I've seen this year. It comfortably tops Hokum for me.

When I went to see Obsession, I wasn't entirely sure what to expect. Like everyone else, I had seen the famous trailer in which Nikki-the film's co-lead and antagonist-acts completely unhinged while repeatedly screaming, "No, no, no." I hated it. It irritated me so much that I actively avoided the film for quite a long time.

Eventually, however, curiosity got the better of me. I wanted to understand what all the fuss was about-and now, finally, I get it.

Inde Navarrette is good. That is what I understood. In fact, she is an excellent actress, although she would benefit from a stronger screenplay. There are moments when the writing simply isn't solid enough, and it shows: certain scenes feel inconclusive, as though the film itself isn't entirely sure where it is going.

The male lead, on the other hand, is mediocre. He simply cannot hold his own opposite Navarrette. I understand that he is supposed to be playing a somewhat awkward and emotionally subdued character, but some of the ways he expresses emotion never feel entirely convincing.

As for the direction, I thought it was excellent. First of all, there are no jump scares-which I love, because by now I sincerely hope we have realised that horror films do not need them. That said, I wouldn't even describe Obsession as a conventional horror film. It is closer, in some respects, to a psychological thriller, and its central message is fairly clear: be careful what you wish for.

The framing is particularly effective. The film makes excellent use of classic horror language, frequently leaving part of the frame empty to create tension and using shot-reverse-shot compositions very well. There are also a few brief long takes that employ clever visual tricks to reveal certain details, and I enjoyed them a lot.

The colour palette is another strength. It is varied and atmospheric, rather than relying on the usual desaturated look of so many horror films. The colours have a distinctive quality that genuinely helps build the film's atmosphere.

The gore is also excellent precisely because it is used sparingly and executed well. There isn't much of it, but what is there looks convincing: the damage to Nikki's face, for example, or the now-famous scene in which she launches herself headfirst into the car and kills Sarah. That was a genuinely effective moment.

On a conceptual level, I also think the film has a very good premise. It isn't a traditional horror story, and its central idea is genuinely interesting.

Even so, the film is carried primarily by Inde Navarrette, who, as I have already said, is very good.

My only truly serious criticism is that the final act loses its way. There are a few twists, and they can be entertaining, but the ending feels strangely arbitrary, almost as though events are simply happening at random.

I respect the choices made by the director and screenwriters, but personally, I would have confined a film of this kind-especially one called Obsession-entirely to its two main characters. I would have added no further distractions and kept the whole story inside the house, using that isolation to explore their descent into madness in far greater depth.

All things considered, Obsession is not bad. It certainly isn't an enormous masterpiece, but it is not a bad film either. And now, at last, I understand the hype.

summary: A paper thin plot carried by Inde and sharp screenplay!
text:
If I had to sum up my thoughts, I would say that the movie has a fairly insubstantial plot, but it's brought to life by some striking performances and an incisive screenwriting.

The makers did an excellent job of using pauses and moments of silence in between scenes, which allows us to hone in on the actors and their subtle, macro expressions. And I feel this technique added a lot to the unnerving energy of the tale.

However, from a storytelling perspective it tends to stick to recognizable tropes, especially those that are popular these days, like graphic cruelty and self-injurious acts. Because of this, the plot feels a bit confined, restricted in its endeavours, more so to me, because I wanted the writing to delve deeper into the lore of the "One Wish Willow," but the writing does not really explore that!

On a positive note, I have to give credit to Inde Navarrette. Her performance is what really holds everything together for me. She, as Nikki, is genuinely terrifying and remains quite convincing throughout. Not once did her act come off as exaggerated or unpersuasive, it's truly impressive considering she's someone relatively new to the scene!

I went into Obsession expecting suspense, twists, and a payoff that would make everything click. Instead I got a movie that felt like it was trying way too hard to seem deep and mysterious while barely making any sense. The pacing dragged, scenes went on forever, and by the middle I was checking how much time was left.

The characters made decisions that felt unrealistic just to force the plot forward, and the dialogue sounded like people talking in riddles instead of actual conversations. The "twists" felt predictable or random rather than clever, and when the ending finally came, it felt more confusing than satisfying.

The biggest problem is that the movie acts like it's saying something profound, but underneath all the dramatic music and serious looks, there just isn't much there. By the end I wasn't shocked, emotional, or even angry - just relieved it was over.

Save your time and watch literally anything else. 1 star.

summary: Cloaked in the vestments of a psychological thriller, yet burdened by prolonged intervals of stagnation
text:
Here is another Popcorn reel review for your movie experience ...

"Obsession" arrives cloaked in the vestments of a psychological thriller, yet what ultimately unfolds is a curious and often bifurcated cinematic enterprise. One possessing intermittent flashes of genuine ingenuity, whilst simultaneously burdened by prolonged intervals of narrative stagnation and creative indecision.

Set across a concise 108 minute runtime, the film concerns itself with the perilous boundaries between affection, fixation, desire, and psychological deterioration. At its conceptual nucleus lies an intriguing premise. The notion that a seemingly innocuous yearning may precipitate consequences far beyond the ordinary parameters of human control. It is a thematic foundation replete with promise, and for fleeting moments, "Obsession" demonstrates precisely how compelling such material can become when handled with conviction.

One of the film's most commendable attributes is its title, which proves remarkably apt. The screenplay consistently returns to the notion of emotional fixation, exploring how devotion can become distorted and how perception itself may become increasingly unreliable. The audience is frequently invited to question motivations, intentions, and even the nature of reality itself. Those moments of uncertainty constitute the film's strongest dramatic currency.

Particular commendation must be afforded to Inde Navarrette, whose performance provides the production with much of its psychological gravitas. Her portrayal oscillates between vulnerability and unnerving volatility with admirable dexterity. Through subtle shifts in expression, posture, and demeanor, she creates a character whose behavior remains simultaneously fascinating and deeply disquieting. There are occasions where her performance evokes the unsettling aura of possession narratives, despite the film never fully venturing into conventional horror territory. Indeed, many of the production's most memorable sequences belong entirely to her.

Visually, the filmmakers make the unusual decision to present the entire feature in a restrictive box like aspect ratio. While such a choice may occasionally serve a thematic or artistic purpose, its application here feels less persuasive. Within modern cinema auditoriums designed to showcase expansive imagery, the constrained presentation often appears more limiting than enlightening. One continually searches for a compelling narrative justification that never fully materializes.

Nevertheless, the film succeeds admirably in delivering moments of acute tension. The sudden auditory shocks and carefully timed impact sequences are executed with considerable proficiency. Even seasoned viewers who seldom react physically to cinematic surprises may find themselves momentarily startled. These sequences demonstrate that the filmmakers possess a genuine understanding of the mechanics of suspense.

Unfortunately, those exhilarating peaks are too frequently followed by lengthy plateaus of inertia. The narrative repeatedly ascends towards psychological intensity only to linger in extended passages where momentum dissipates. Rather than sustaining a continuous escalation of unease, the film often appears content to pause its own progress, diminishing the cumulative impact of its strongest moments.

The supporting cast likewise struggles to justify its prominence. Numerous ancillary characters feel less like organic participants in the story and more like narrative diversions designed to temporarily delay the central conflict. Each time the focus drifts away from the principal psychological relationship, the film's energy noticeably diminishes. One cannot escape the impression that a more concentrated examination of its two central figures would have yielded a far more potent experience.

Production limitations are similarly evident throughout. The film's modest budget manifests in its restrained locations, limited visual scope, and economical presentation. Much of the action unfolds within a small collection of interiors and familiar environments, lending the production an occasionally claustrophobic quality. While financial constraints need not impede effective storytelling, they are sufficiently visible here to affect the overall cinematic texture.

What ultimately renders "Obsession" a fascinating rather than wholly successful endeavor is the abundance of unrealized potential residing beneath its surface. There are numerous moments where the audience glimpses a superior film struggling to emerge as a darker, more psychologically intricate meditation on desire, identity, and control. The foundations are undeniably present. The execution simply lacks the consistency required to transform those foundations into something truly exceptional.

Particularly effective are several scenes in which darkness and selective lighting envelop the female protagonist, creating an almost spectral visual language that suggests forces beyond ordinary comprehension. These images linger in the memory long after the credits roll and exemplify the atmospheric sophistication the film occasionally achieves.

"Obsession" is neither the terrifying phenomenon some promotional materials might suggest nor the complete misfire its detractors may claim. Rather, it exists in a curious middle ground. A film containing authentic flashes of brilliance, compelling performances, and worthwhile psychological concepts, yet one that never fully capitalizes upon its considerable promise.

It is a psychologically intriguing premise, elevated by an arresting central performance and several genuinely effective suspense sequences, yet undermined by uneven pacing, underdeveloped supporting characters, and unrealized potential. "Obsession" remains an interesting curiosity. One that occasionally captivates, frequently frustrates, and ultimately leaves the audience contemplating what might have been.

For viewers who appreciate psychological thrillers driven more by atmosphere and emotional instability than by conventional horror mechanics, there is still enough intrigue to warrant a viewing. One simply wishes the filmmakers had possessed greater confidence in their strongest ideas and fewer distractions from the compelling psychological labyrinth they had already constructed.

summary: Forget Streaming. Obsession Demands to Be Seen on the Big Screen
text:
Obsession is one of the best films I have seen in years. Curry Barker announces himself as a major filmmaking talent, and I will absolutely be checking out his YouTube shorts after this. The man is the real deal.

But let's talk about Inde Navarrette, because she is a revelation. This woman is a star. Her performance is physically and emotionally demanding in ways that are almost impossible to describe without spoiling the film, and she delivers on every single level. She deserves every award available to her this season. Remember her name, because you are going to be hearing it a lot.

The film itself is a blast - gory, tense, clever, and surprisingly moving. It takes a simple premise and wrings every last drop of dread and emotion out of it. The scares are earned, the pacing is tight, and the payoffs are deeply satisfying. There is one jump scare in particular that had me completely out of my seat. I genuinely cannot remember the last time a movie got me like that.

Do yourself a favor and see this one in a packed theater. The collective energy of the crowd makes it that much more of an experience. Obsession is the kind of film that reminds you why going to the movies matters. Don't wait for streaming. Go now.

A solid low-budget horror movie

I want to start by saying I am not a huge fan of horror movies, but I wanted to give this movie a try. There wasn't a lot of jump scares per se, but throughout the movie, I felt unsettled and tense. It was really disturbing and kinda disgusting in some parts. Nonetheless, it was still pretty scary. It reminded me of the daylight horror Midsommar.

Story-wise, it is predictable. Halfway through the movie, you can easily guess what the ending is, but it still kept me in suspense, especially the randomness and unpredictability of Nikki's behaviour. Talking about behaviour, as you watch the movie, your perception of Bear changes from a quiet, innocent, and shy person to an evil and almost psychotic man.

In the end, it was a good watch. If you have an hour and a half to spare and are in the mood for a psychological horror film, I recommend it.

I'm honestly starting to believe that the more a horror movie is praised, the worse it is.

At this point, seeing critics and audiences collectively insisting that a horror movie is "terrifying," "disturbing," or "brilliant" has become less of a recommendation and more of a warning sign.

Because apparently, in modern horror, being boring is considered terrifying, being pretentious is considered intelligent, and doing absolutely nothing for two hours is somehow praised as "slow-burn atmospheric filmmaking."

I'm sick of it.

The Boogeyman. Nosferatu. Barbarian. Weapons. These movies are constantly presented as examples of great modern horror, and I genuinely cannot understand what people see in them. They are praised to the heavens, critics compete to explain how "deep" and "unsettling" they supposedly are, and audiences hand them glowing ratings. Then you actually watch them and discover that the emperor is wearing nothing at all.

They are not terrifying.

They are not masterpieces.

They are barely entertaining.

They are the cinematic equivalent of being forced to listen to an incredibly dull story from someone who keeps promising, "Trust me, it gets really good."

It doesn't.

That is why I was extremely skeptical when Obsession (2025) started receiving praise everywhere. I kept seeing clips across social media, people describing it as frightening, and the usual flood of exaggerated enthusiasm that has made me deeply distrust the horror community's judgment.

Still, the premise looked genuinely interesting.

So I gave it a chance.

Then I discovered that it was a Blumhouse production.

Suddenly, my expectations went from cautious curiosity to the highest possible level.

Blumhouse has certainly produced some disappointments, but at least the company generally understands something that far too many "prestige" horror films seem to have forgotten: a horror movie is supposed to be entertaining.

And Obsession understands that perfectly.

From the opening minutes, the film had my full attention.

It does not spend an eternity crawling toward a supposedly profound conclusion. It does not mistake an unbearably slow pace for suspense. It does not throw a few strange images at the audience and expect everyone to call it "psychological horror." It does not spend two hours desperately demanding recognition for how clever it supposedly is.

It tells its story.

It moves forward.

It builds tension.

Most importantly, it is genuinely enjoyable to watch.

The biggest surprise was the humor. Obsession combines comedy and horror without ruining either one. The humor feels natural, the darker moments still work, and the film has an energy that keeps you invested.

I actually laughed.

Not the polite little reaction you give when a movie technically includes a joke.

I mean I genuinely laughed.

That alone felt remarkable after sitting through so many supposedly brilliant horror films that left me staring at the screen, wondering whether I was watching a movie or enduring a test of patience.

And then there is the horror.

When Obsession wants to make you uncomfortable, it succeeds.

The horror sequences are genuinely disturbing, and the sense of dread works because the film earns it. It does not rely on constant cheap jump scares and then expect applause. Instead, it creates situations that are difficult to watch and allows the performances and atmosphere to carry the tension.

Imagine that: actual horror that makes you feel something.

The absolute standout is Inde Navarrette.

Her performance is phenomenal.

The rest of the cast is good. Nobody weakens the film, and everyone does what is required. But once Navarrette appears on screen, the other performances fade into the background.

Her facial expressions, eyes, body language, and smallest changes in demeanor are all remarkably effective. She communicates fear, confusion, anxiety, vulnerability, and discomfort without having to explain every emotion through dialogue.

There are moments when you can understand exactly what her character is experiencing simply by watching her face.

She does not merely carry her scenes.

She carries the entire film.

Her performance is one of the main reasons the horror works so well.

This is also what makes Obsession so refreshing compared with the endless parade of overhyped "elevated horror" that currently dominates the genre. It does not feel like a film created by a committee desperately trying to produce something critics will label "important."

It does not confuse ambiguity with intelligence.

It does not confuse boredom with atmosphere.

It does not confuse strangeness with originality.

And it certainly does not confuse being unpleasant to watch with being frightening.

It is a horror movie.

It wants to entertain you.

It wants to unsettle you.

It wants to make you laugh.

It wants you to care about what happens.

Somehow, that now feels almost revolutionary.

After being disappointed by so many supposedly incredible horror films, I went into Obsession expecting another overhyped failure.

Instead, I got one of the most enjoyable horror experiences I have had in a long time.

For once, I completely understand the praise.

In fact, I agree with it.

Obsession deserves the attention it has received. It deserves people talking about it. Unlike so many critically adored horror films I have watched recently, it does not require a lengthy essay explaining why I am supposed to admire it.

I liked it because it is genuinely good.

It kept me engaged from beginning to end. It made me laugh. It made me uncomfortable. It made me care about the characters. And it gave me a performance from Inde Navarrette that completely impressed me.

After everything I have had to sit through lately under the label of "the future of horror," Obsession felt like a breath of fresh air.

This is the kind of horror I want more of.

Give me movies that are entertaining instead of self-important.

Give me movies that are frightening instead of merely depressing.

Give me movies that understand pacing instead of confusing sluggishness with sophistication.

Give me movies that actually make me feel something.

And please give me more performances like Inde Navarrette's.

Obsession did not merely survive the hype.

It earned it.

More of this.

Less of the pretentious, overpraised nonsense that keeps being presented as "masterpiece horror."

summary: 2026 is a great year for horror movies
text: I am amazed how they can turn such a cliche concept of "oh, careful what you wish for" into such a gripping experience. The execution is flawless. With a budget that low they relied a lot on shadows and audio for the horror and I never felt it was cheap at all. The actors did amazing. What a great year for horror movies in general, and we're only halfway through the year. I don't give a 10/10 rating so easily, but in my opinion, this is the best modern horror movie.

Obsession film follows a young man named Bear who has a crush on his co-worker Nikki. They are two good friends, but it is evident Bear wants to take their relationship to the next level.

Obsession is an incredibly well made and terrifying horror/dark romance/dark comedy. It's as funny as it's scary, and it's as well made as it's well acted. The film makes amazing use of Michael Johnston and Inde Navarette, neither of which I had heard of before watching the film. Newcomer Curry Barker has made a Great film.

Back to the plot: during a key conversation, Nikki straight up asks Bear is he likes her, to which he lies, and ends up making a wish by breaking a One Wish Willow in order to make Nikki love him.

And the wish works. Nikki however gets extreme personality changes, one moment she is obviously very deeply attracted to Bear, the next she is confused and doesn't know where she is. Since there isn't really a logical explanation for these personality changes, I think it's fair to say that they are simply there to manipulate the audience into being scared. In the first scenes, Nikki's dialogue excellently develops her character, and Inde Navarrette is superb at making her a concrete person we understand. However once the One Wish Willow is broken, Nikki ceases to be a character with an interesting personality and motivations, and simply becomes the horror component of a story that would otherwise be void of horror. Sometimes she reminds me a bit of Alicia Vikander in Ex Machina, which isn't really a compliment, although it's not the fault of Inde Navarrete. Although these might sound like criticisms, they're more like observations. The film uses a One Wish Willow in its main premise, it was never going to be logical. In fact, the film seems as if Curry Barker wanted to make a horror film but had the script of a romance gone wrong, and decided just to make one into the other. I don't think the film had to be a horror, but I'm glad that it is. It's very, very creepy, and includes very possibly one of the scariest jumpscares I've ever seen. Unlike a lot of contemporary horror films, the film does not crumble in its final act. In fact, the film finds its greatest meaning and emotion in its ending, which is stark contrast to most modern horror films, which mostly just conclude in loud dissipation of all the tension which the film spent two hours building.

Many people have also referred to it as a "careful what you wish for" fable, but I don't think it is. Ultimately, Bear wished for something that he got, but there were a lot of unintended side effects that he had no way of knowing about. He also didn't know that the One Wish Willow would even work. In reality, I think the film is an exploration of a non-consensual relationship, and that to some extent, Bear didn't really care about Nikki if not for his feelings for her, and that he would rather be with her regardless of her true feelings toward him than accept that she might not like him back. The interesting thing is that Bear isn't really someone that is portrayed as a villain, and I don't think he is one. There's nothing unwholesome about his crush on Nikki, and on the first night when Nikki sleeps at his place, I think there is a metaphor for their entire relationship. Nikki is obviously hesitant around Bear when he starts flirting with her but then he breaks the One Wish Willow. Now all of sudden she really does want him, even though on some level Bear must know that this is artificial, it's not what Nikki really wanted. If he truly loved Nikki, he would want her to do what would make her happy, not just to do what made him happy. Originally, he doesn't take advantage of the situation, but sooner or later he does end up kissing Nikki even though he must know deep down that this isn't who Nikki really is. It's a metaphor for their artificial relationship, because eventually Bear kind of tricks himself into thinking that the new Nikki is the old Nikki, who he wanted to love him, which also shows that since Nikki has had an extreme personality change, we can see Bear doesn't really care too much that the old Nikki is gone, which means he has objectified her, that she was meant to be his, and he doesn't care for who she truly is as long as she is with him, much less whether the other Nikki would actually want this.

This was easily one of the best disturbing and creepiest films I've ever seen. From the very beginning, the movie creates an atmosphere of tension and unease that never lets up. What impressed me most was how effectively it built suspense without relying on cheap scares. Instead, it used its unsettling tone, strong performances, and unpredictable storytelling to keep me completely invested from start to finish.

I also loved that the actors and actresses were mostly new faces. It made the experience feel even more authentic because I wasn't distracted by familiar celebrities. Every performance felt genuine, and the entire cast did an absolutely phenomenal job bringing their characters to life. Their commitment to the material helped make the film's darker moments even more impactful and believable.

One of the standout aspects for me was Bear's character. I loved the complexity of his role and how much depth he brought to the story. He wasn't a simple character that could be easily defined as good or bad. There were layers to his personality, motivations, and decisions that kept me thinking about him long after the movie ended. The way his character developed throughout the film added a fascinating emotional and psychological element that elevated the entire story.

There were also so many scenes that genuinely gave me chills. Several moments left me feeling uncomfortable in the best possible way, and there were times when the tension was so intense that I could feel it throughout the theater. The film did an incredible job creating memorable sequences that linger in your mind long after the credits roll. Such as the scene where Nikki is standing in the corner telling Bear she was watching him while he was sleeping. Her creepy body movements from the film were outstanding.

Overall, this was a fantastic and unforgettable experience. It's rare for a movie to affect me this much, but this one absolutely did. I enjoyed it so much that I already booked tickets to see it again, and I can't wait to experience it a second time.

summary: A movie that makes one bad decision feel truly catastrophic
text: I don't think the premise of Obsession should have worked as well as it did. A lonely guy makes a supernatural wish for his longtime crush to fall in love with him, only to discover he's created something far more terrifying than rejection. On paper, it sounds like a simple cautionary tale, but the execution is what elevates it. Curry Barker constantly walks a tightrope between dark comedy, cringe-inducing social awkwardness, and outright horror, and somehow those tones never feel like they're fighting each other. Michael Johnston makes Bear sympathetic enough that you understand why he makes such a terrible choice, while Inde Navarrette delivers a fearless performance that becomes more unsettling with every scene as Nikki's affection twists into something suffocating and inhuman. I also appreciated that the film isn't just about a cursed object or a love spell. It's really about control, entitlement, and the fantasy of being loved without earning it. There are several moments that made me laugh, only to realize a few seconds later that I was incredibly uncomfortable, and that's a difficult balance to pull off. My only minor criticism is that a handful of story beats require you to fully embrace the movie's heightened reality, but once I accepted its nightmare logic, I was completely on board. Original horror can be hard to find, and this feels like exactly the kind of bold, weird swing the genre needs more of.

I've seen conjuring 3 and 4 in movie theaters blind but I have never sat through a movie so psychologically unsettled as this one. The plot the scripts and the acting are all superior when it comes to a mix between dark romance and psychological horror. Inde truly deserves an Oscar for her acting, never seen anything like it to be honest. Although the ending is pretty messed up and sad, it is a film you need to watch a positive movie afterwards for. I can't get over the acting. It's truly incredible.
