summary: A Beautiful, Creepy and Deeply Disturbing Experience
text:
Obsession is genuinely one of the most uncomfortable, anxiety inducing and impressive movie experiences I have ever had. And what makes it even crazier to me is that I went into this movie almost completely blind. I did not know the cast, did not know Curry Barker, did not know the story, and honestly barely even knew what kind of movie it was going to be. I randomly saw the trailer and instantly felt something I almost never feel with movies anymore, urgency. I needed to see it in theaters.

And the reason for that was almost entirely Inde Navarrette.

The restaurant clip from the trailer where Bear asks Nikki if her father really has cancer genuinely sold me on the entire film. Her acting in that scene alone was so deeply uncomfortable, uncanny and believable that I instantly became obsessed with the movie before even watching it. There is something about the way she switches between vulnerable, loving, obsessive, creepy and emotionally unstable that feels way too human to comfortably watch. It never feels like classic horror acting. It feels real, and that is exactly what makes it terrifying.

That is also why I almost hesitate to even call Obsession a horror movie in the traditional sense. This is not Insidious, not The Conjuring, not a zombie movie, not a masked killer movie, not a "curse gets passed on" type of story like Smile. The horror here is not the starting point of the movie. It is the consequence of the story itself.

That is what makes it so brilliant to me.

The One Wish Willow is not really presented as some evil horror entity manipulating people for fun. The wish simply works. Ian wishes for money and gets rich instantly. Nothing horrifying happens because his wish is simple. Bear on the other hand wishes for something emotionally impossible and unhealthy. He wishes that Nikki loves him more than anyone else, and because of the way he words that wish, it completely destroys reality around both of them.

That idea alone is horrifying.

Because throughout the movie Nikki is not just "possessed" in a classic horror sense. The movie constantly shows that the real Nikki is still trapped underneath whatever the wish created. The phone call scene where Bear briefly hears the real Nikki screaming and crying underneath it all was one of the creepiest moments in the entire movie for me. Same with the bedroom scene where she quietly tells him to kill her while "she is sleeping." Those moments completely change the feeling of the film because suddenly it becomes tragic too. Nikki becomes a victim of Bear's own obsession and wording, while simultaneously still being forced to serve the wish itself.

That makes the movie so much more disturbing than a normal possession movie to me. It does not feel like some demon randomly haunting people. It feels like the horrifying emotional consequence of something that technically worked exactly as intended.

And the movie constantly plays with that tension in such an insanely effective way. Nikki can go from deeply unsettling and almost inhuman behavior straight back into acting sweet and apologetic the second Bear gets uncomfortable or scared. The moment she suddenly says things like "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to scare you" almost feels worse than the creepy moments themselves, because it creates this emotional whiplash where your brain never gets to relax. The movie traps you in this nonstop state of anxiety and paranoia without constantly relying on jumpscares.

I honestly cannot remember the last time a movie physically stressed me out this much. My heart rate was genuinely through the roof during multiple scenes. Not because something suddenly jumped into frame, but because the movie creates this overwhelming feeling that something is deeply wrong at all times. It is pure uncanny valley horror. Human behavior that feels just slightly broken in a way your brain cannot fully process.

And the craziest part is how grounded and modern everything feels. The movie never feels gothic or fantasy-like. The art direction is super clean and contemporary. Even the Obsession title design itself with the RGB split chromatic aberration effects and pulsing audio feels modern in a weirdly stylish way, almost like it could be branding for some premium fashion or tech product instead of a horror movie. Everything about the film feels rooted in reality, which only makes the horror hit harder because nothing feels exaggerated or disconnected from the real world.

Visually the movie is also incredible. The framing, the darkness around Nikki's face in certain scenes, the subtle glowing eyes, the editing, the pacing, everything feels so carefully controlled. That reverse hallway scene genuinely messed me up. Such a simple idea on paper, but executed so perfectly that it instantly became one of the creepiest scenes I have seen in years.

The editing and sound design deserve massive praise too. One thing the movie does constantly that worked insanely well on me was the way it abruptly cuts music completely dry in certain moments. No smooth transition, no dramatic build-up, just instant silence. It perfectly matches the emotional switching happening inside Nikki herself. One second the movie feels emotional or romantic, the next second it becomes deeply unsettling again. That constant emotional instability is what makes the atmosphere so stressful and immersive.

And the soundtrack itself is unbelievable. Interstellar has always been my favorite movie ever, both as a film and as an overall sound experience, and Obsession is honestly one of the only movies in years that gave me that same feeling of the soundtrack crawling completely under my skin. Rock Burwell absolutely killed it. The score is creepy, emotional, lonely, romantic and paranoid all at once. Sometimes it almost feels comforting before suddenly making you feel deeply uneasy again.

Michael Johnston is also fantastic throughout the movie. His performance feels incredibly genuine and grounded, especially in the more desperate and emotionally overwhelmed moments. That balance is really important because the movie only works if Bear feels believable as an actual person instead of just "the guy causing the horror." Both performances together completely carry the film.

What shocked me the most is that this movie technically started as an indie festival film, because it genuinely does not feel small at all. It feels extremely cinematic and confident in every aspect. Not like something trying to imitate mainstream horror trends, but more like a filmmaker with a very specific vision who accidentally made something that could genuinely become mainstream because of how good it is.

I also want to be fair and say I am not some professional film critic. I am an editor myself, just in a completely different branch and not in film. So I definitely look at movies from a production and artistic perspective, but at the end of the day I still mainly watch films as a fan of the artform itself. And this movie genuinely affected me in a way that almost no movie ever has.

Interstellar has always been the only movie I personally considered a true 10/10 experience for me. Not because I think it is objectively the greatest film ever made, but because of the emotional impact it had on me. Obsession honestly gave me that same type of feeling. Whether this is objectively one of the greatest films ever made, I do not know. But personally, based on what this movie made me feel, this is absolutely one of my favorite movie experiences of all time.

And honestly, the funniest part is that the title could not possibly be more accurate.

I think I am literally obsessed with Obsession now.

I never buy movies after seeing them in theaters. I always wait until they hit streaming services eventually. This is the first movie I have ever instantly pre-ordered just so I could "own" it later (digital so not really owning lol).

Obsession is an entertaining film that takes a familiar genre premise and develops it into a solid, artistically crafted experience. The movie lays out its central conflict, builds the tension effectively, and delivers a well-rounded conclusion. While the screenplay relies on a few narrative conveniences and tropes typical of generic thriller writing, it is remarkable how well this indie feature holds together. For a directorial debut, the execution feels impressively confident and polished.

In terms of pacing and direction, the movie keeps a great rhythm that prevents the story from ever feeling boring. The plot progression and timing are well handled throughout the runtime. A major point in its favor is that it avoids relying on excessive gore - a trap many modern horror releases fall into - choosing instead to lean into psychological suspense. While it could have used a bit more genuine scares to deliver a truly terrifying impact, the underlying commentary comes through clearly and the overall tension works well.

On a technical level, both the cinematography and production design are remarkably well crafted, proving that a modest budget can still yield a polished visual presentation. Watching this brings back a distinct nostalgia for classic indie thrillers like Saw, where familiar concepts were taken completely seriously and transformed through dedicated craft. Much like Kane Parsons' debut with The Backrooms earlier this year, this project showcases an emerging director capable of delivering a remarkably cohesive first feature.

The performances are solid across the board, with a committed cast that grounds the dramatic stakes. Ultimately, Obsession is a tight, enjoyable thriller that, while far from being a groundbreaking masterpiece, fully accomplishes what it sets out to do. It's an engaging watch that captures the spirit of classic indie horror and is definitely worth checking out.

summary: This is exactly how psychological horror should be done
text:
Obsession is precisely what psychological horror should be. I loved how beautifully uncomfortable it became. There are extremely powerful moments where we feel ourselves being stared at by Nikki - and the acting is absolutely top-tier. The editing is interesting and inventive, too.

What really impressed me is the restraint. There aren't too many jumpscares, which is exactly why they land so well - each one feels carefully placed and genuinely effective. The pacing is masterful. You catch yourself thinking you've known the solution to Bear's problem from the very start, but the film keeps pulling you right back into the situation, sucking you into the story until you're left thinking, "shit, what do we do now?" - and realizing there is no obvious fix, or at least nothing remotely easy.

It's a brilliant example of how a great film doesn't need cheap gimmicks or sensationalism. When the story is strong and well told, a single look into the actors' eyes is enough to make you afraid. Simply wonderful. Highly recommended.

Rule of Horrors n.1: mainstream usually sucks. Does that apply to Obession? Pretty much. Directed by some "YouTuber" on a small budget (according to two teens behind me in the cinema), it actually gets a few things right. The music, sound design, directing, and cast are surprisingly solid, and I found myself laughing quite a bit. The real issue? It lacks actual horror and thrill. At 109 minutes, the plot gets tiring after half an hour, and the psycho "Nikky" after about ten minutes. The rest is just the same scene on repeat. If you're looking for gore (like I was) you'll be disappointed. As the credits rolled, I was left with a sense of "what if this had been made by someone willing to push the envelope?" Great premise, but far too family-friendly for my horror taste.
